## Test Data Versioning Strategies  [community]

As your domain model evolves through migrations, factories and fixtures must evolve in
sync. Without a versioning discipline, factories become stale — they produce objects that
no longer match the current schema, and DB integration tests fail with cryptic column
errors.

### Strategy 1: Migration-Aligned Factory Versioning

Tag factory files with the migration version that introduced the schema they reflect.
When a migration adds a required field, the factory update is part of the same PR:

```typescript
// factories/user.factory.ts
// Schema version: migration 2024_03_15_add_locale_to_users
// If a new migration adds/removes fields, update this factory in the same PR.

import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';
import { User } from '../domain/user'; // keep in sync with migration 2024_03_15

export function buildUser(overrides: Partial<User> = {}): User {
  return {
    id: faker.string.uuid(),
    email: faker.internet.email(),
    name: faker.person.fullName(),
    status: 'active',
    subscriptionTier: 'free',
    locale: 'en-US',              // added in migration 2024_03_15
    createdAt: faker.date.past({ years: 2 }),
    paymentMethodId: null,
    ...overrides,
  };
}
```

**Enforce via TypeScript:** Because factories return typed objects (`Partial<User>` / `User`),
TypeScript will produce a type error the moment a required field is added to the `User` type
without updating the factory — the factory becomes a compile-time schema drift detector.

### Strategy 2: Schema Version Tagging in Factory Metadata  [community]

For teams running multiple simultaneous migration branches (e.g., a feature branch that
adds a column before the main branch merges), attach a schema version tag to the factory
and validate it at test startup:

```typescript
// factories/registry.ts
// Central registry of factories with their minimum required schema version.
// Startup validation ensures the DB schema is at least as new as the factory expects.

export const FACTORY_SCHEMA_REQUIREMENTS: Record<string, string> = {
  'user':     '2024_03_15_add_locale_to_users',
  'order':    '2024_02_01_add_currency_to_orders',
  'product':  '2024_04_10_add_category_id_to_products',
};

// vitest.globalSetup.ts — validate factory schema requirements on startup
import { db } from '../db';
import { FACTORY_SCHEMA_REQUIREMENTS } from './factories/registry';

export async function setup() {
  const appliedMigrations = await db.getAppliedMigrations();
  for (const [factory, requiredMigration] of Object.entries(FACTORY_SCHEMA_REQUIREMENTS)) {
    if (!appliedMigrations.includes(requiredMigration)) {
      throw new Error(
        `[test-data] Factory '${factory}' requires migration '${requiredMigration}' ` +
        `but it has not been applied. Run: npx prisma migrate dev`
      );
    }
  }
  console.log('[test-data] All factory schema requirements satisfied.');
}
```

### Strategy 3: Fixture Snapshots Pinned to Schema Version  [community]

For E2E tests using static JSON fixtures (not factories), pin the fixture to a schema
version and validate on load:

```typescript
// test-fixtures/baseline-users.fixture.ts
export const FIXTURE_SCHEMA_VERSION = '2024_03_15_add_locale_to_users';

export const BASELINE_USERS = [
  {
    id: 'usr-fixture-001',
    email: 'fixture-alice@example-test.invalid',
    name: 'Fixture Alice',
    status: 'active' as const,
    subscriptionTier: 'free' as const,
    locale: 'en-US',   // required since migration 2024_03_15
    createdAt: new Date('2024-01-01T00:00:00Z'),
    paymentMethodId: null,
  },
];

// playwright.globalSetup.ts — validate fixture schema compatibility
import { FIXTURE_SCHEMA_VERSION, BASELINE_USERS } from './test-fixtures/baseline-users.fixture';

export async function globalSetup() {
  const appliedMigrations = await checkAppliedMigrations();
  if (!appliedMigrations.includes(FIXTURE_SCHEMA_VERSION)) {
    throw new Error(
      `[e2e] Fixture 'baseline-users' requires schema version '${FIXTURE_SCHEMA_VERSION}'. ` +
      `Rebuild fixture after running migrations.`
    );
  }
  await seedDatabase(BASELINE_USERS);
}
```

**Checklist — test data versioning:**
- [ ] Every factory has a `// Schema version: <migration>` comment
- [ ] Factory files are co-located in the same PR as the corresponding migration
- [ ] TypeScript types enforce schema compliance at compile time (not just runtime)
- [ ] Static fixtures are pinned to a schema version and validated at test startup
- [ ] CI pipeline runs `tsc --noEmit` on factory files before executing tests

## Community Gotcha #38 — Snapshot tests with `faker` random data fail every run  [community]

**[community]** If a factory that uses `@faker-js/faker` random data is used as input to
a snapshot test, the snapshot will fail on every single run because the output changes
with each new random value. This is one of the most common misuses of snapshot testing.
**Why harmful:** The test looks like it should work (it captures a real output shape) but
it produces a new "snapshot mismatch" failure on every run, forcing developers to update
the snapshot constantly — destroying the value of the golden-master comparison. **Fix:**
Snapshot tests must use **fixed, stable factory data** — Object Mother variants (which
return hardcoded values) or factory calls with all randomised fields explicitly overridden.

```typescript
// BROKEN: faker generates a different email/name every run → snapshot mismatch every time
const user = buildUser();  // uses faker.internet.email() — different value each run
expect(serializeUser(user)).toMatchInlineSnapshot(`...`); // always fails

// CORRECT: pin all volatile fields when using factory output in snapshots
const user = buildUser({
  id:    'usr-snap-001',
  email: 'snapshot-user@example-test.invalid',
  name:  'Snapshot User',
  createdAt: new Date('2024-01-01T00:00:00Z'),
});
expect(serializeUser(user)).toMatchInlineSnapshot(`
  {
    "createdAt": "2024-01-01T00:00:00.000Z",
    "email": "snapshot-user@example-test.invalid",
    "id": "usr-snap-001",
    "name": "Snapshot User",
    "paymentMethodId": null,
    "status": "active",
    "subscriptionTier": "free",
  }
`);
```

---

## Community Gotcha #39 — `fast-check` arbitraries with `satisfies` require exact enum union types  [community]

**[community]** When writing `fc.constantFrom('active', 'suspended') satisfies fc.Arbitrary<User['status']>`,
TypeScript infers the narrowest possible type for the constants in `fc.constantFrom()` —
a union of string literals. If `User['status']` is a wider union (e.g., adds `'deleted'`
in a migration), the `satisfies` check silently passes because the existing literals are
a **subtype** of the new union. The arbitrary now generates an **incomplete** subset of
valid statuses — missing `'deleted'` entirely. **Why harmful:** Property-based tests that
should exercise all status variants never generate the new `'deleted'` state. Defects in
`'deleted'` handling pass CI invisibly. **Fix:** When a domain enum changes, explicitly
update `fc.constantFrom(...)` to include all values; add a compile-time exhaustiveness
check using a type assertion.

```typescript
// FRAGILE: satisfies only checks subtype — new enum values are silently omitted
export const statusArb = fc.constantFrom('active', 'suspended')
  satisfies fc.Arbitrary<User['status']>; // passes even if User['status'] adds 'deleted'

// ROBUST: use explicit type assertion that requires all values to be listed
const ALL_STATUSES: Array<User['status']> = ['active', 'suspended', 'pending', 'deleted'];
// TypeScript error if User['status'] adds a value not in ALL_STATUSES:
const _exhaustive: [User['status']] extends [typeof ALL_STATUSES[number]] ? true : never = true;
export const statusArb = fc.constantFrom(...ALL_STATUSES);
```

## Community Gotcha #40 — PII fields scrubbed in the factory are re-introduced by `fishery` `afterCreate` hooks calling the real ORM  [community]

**[community]** When using `fishery` with a `afterCreate` hook that persists via Prisma
or TypeORM, the ORM may populate computed or default fields from the database — including
fields that were intentionally left `null` in the factory (e.g., `ipAddress`, `lastLoginAt`
from session triggers). If the test database is pre-seeded with production data that was
incompletely scrubbed, the `afterCreate`-fetched row may contain real PII that was never
in the factory object. **Why harmful:** The factory appears to produce scrubbed data, but
the `create()` return value (fetched from DB after insert) contains unscrubbed rows from
a partially-scrubbed seed. **Fix:** Always verify scrubbing at the DB layer, not just at
the factory layer. Run a scrubbing assertion in the global test setup.

```typescript
// vitest.globalSetup.ts — verify no PII fields remain after scrubbing
export async function setup() {
  // Verify no real email domains exist in the test DB user table
  const suspiciousUsers = await db.user.findMany({
    where: {
      email: {
        not: { endsWith: '@example-test.invalid' },
      },
    },
    take: 1,
  });
  if (suspiciousUsers.length > 0) {
    throw new Error(
      `[test-data] Test database contains non-test emails. ` +
      `Re-run the scrubbing pipeline before executing tests. ` +
      `Found: ${suspiciousUsers[0]?.email?.replace(/@.*/, '@[redacted]')}`
    );
  }
}
```

### Temporal API Date Factories  [community]

The JavaScript `Temporal` API (TC39 Stage 4, shipping in Node.js 22+ and available via
`@js-temporal/polyfill` for earlier runtimes) eliminates the longstanding problem of
`Date`-based test data being timezone-dependent. When a factory uses `new Date()`, the
resulting value includes the system timezone offset — causing tests to fail in CI
environments with a different `TZ` setting than the developer's machine.

**Why it matters for test data:** `Temporal.PlainDate` and `Temporal.PlainDateTime` are
always timezone-naive. `Temporal.ZonedDateTime` carries an explicit timezone. Neither can
silently absorb a system timezone offset. Factories that use `Temporal` types produce
stable, portable test data regardless of where the test runs.

```typescript
// factories/temporal-date.factory.ts
// Requires: @js-temporal/polyfill (Node < 22) or native Temporal (Node 22+)
// Install:  npm install --save-dev @js-temporal/polyfill
import { Temporal } from '@js-temporal/polyfill';

export interface SubscriptionRecord {
  id: string;
  startDate: Temporal.PlainDate;      // timezone-free date
  endDate: Temporal.PlainDate;        // timezone-free date
  createdAt: Temporal.ZonedDateTime;  // explicit timezone
  trialEndsAt: Temporal.PlainDateTime | null;
}

// Factory helper — produces a canonical "active subscription" with stable test dates
export function buildSubscription(
  overrides: Partial<SubscriptionRecord> = {}
): SubscriptionRecord {
  const start = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2024-01-15');
  return {
    id:           'sub-test-001',
    startDate:    start,
    endDate:      start.add({ months: 12 }),   // exactly 1 year — no DST ambiguity
    createdAt:    Temporal.ZonedDateTime.from('2024-01-15T09:00:00[UTC]'),
    trialEndsAt:  Temporal.PlainDateTime.from('2024-01-29T23:59:59'),
    ...overrides,
  };
}

// Factory variant: subscription that is "about to expire" (2 days from a given anchor date)
export function buildExpiringSubscription(
  anchor: Temporal.PlainDate = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2026-01-15'),
  overrides: Partial<SubscriptionRecord> = {}
): SubscriptionRecord {
  return buildSubscription({
    endDate: anchor.add({ days: 2 }),
    ...overrides,
  });
}
```

**Verifying temporal arithmetic in tests:**
```typescript
// specs/subscription-expiry.test.ts
import { test, expect } from 'vitest';
import { Temporal } from '@js-temporal/polyfill';
import { buildExpiringSubscription } from '../factories/temporal-date.factory';
import { isSubscriptionExpiringSoon } from '../domain/subscription';

test('isSubscriptionExpiringSoon returns true when end date is within 7 days', () => {
  const anchor = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2026-01-15');
  const sub = buildExpiringSubscription(anchor);

  // Pass the same anchor — no system clock dependency whatsoever
  const result = isSubscriptionExpiringSoon(sub, anchor);

  expect(result).toBe(true);
});

test('isSubscriptionExpiringSoon returns false when more than 7 days remain', () => {
  const anchor = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2026-01-01');
  const sub = buildExpiringSubscription(
    Temporal.PlainDate.from('2026-01-15'),   // endDate = Jan 17
    { id: 'sub-test-002' }
  );

  const result = isSubscriptionExpiringSoon(sub, anchor);
  expect(result).toBe(false);
});
```

**Migration from `Date` to `Temporal` in factories:**
```typescript
// BEFORE (timezone-sensitive — may fail in UTC-0 vs UTC+9 environments)
export function buildEvent(overrides = {}) {
  return {
    id: 'evt-001',
    startAt: new Date('2026-03-01T10:00:00'),   // interpreted as local time!
    ...overrides,
  };
}

// AFTER (explicit timezone — portable across all CI environments)
export function buildEvent(overrides = {}) {
  return {
    id: 'evt-001',
    startAt: Temporal.ZonedDateTime.from('2026-03-01T10:00:00[Europe/Berlin]'),
    ...overrides,
  };
}
```

**Checklist — Temporal-aware test data factories:**
- [ ] All date fields in factories use `Temporal.PlainDate` or `Temporal.ZonedDateTime` — never `new Date()` with a bare string
- [ ] CI pipeline sets `TZ=UTC` to surface any remaining `Date`-based timezone sensitivity
- [ ] `@js-temporal/polyfill` is in `devDependencies` (not `dependencies`) — polyfill is test-only
- [ ] Factories that compute relative dates use `.add()` / `.subtract()` — never `getTime() + milliseconds` arithmetic

### `zod-fixture` + Zod v4 Auto-Factory Pattern  [community]

`zod-fixture` (by Tiim Clausen) generates test fixture objects automatically from Zod
schemas. In Zod v4 (released 2025, re-engineered API), `zod-fixture` v3 supports the new
`z.string().email()`, `z.string().uuid()`, `z.enum()`, `z.object()`, and `z.discriminatedUnion()`
refinements as generation hints — producing semantically correct data without any manual
factory authorship.

**Why it matters:** For teams with a fully Zod-validated domain model, `zod-fixture` eliminates
the gap where a new field is added to a schema but not to the hand-written factory. Every
`ZodObject` schema automatically becomes a valid factory — schema drift is structurally
impossible.

```typescript
// factories/auto-factory.ts — zod-fixture + Zod v4 integration
// Install: npm install --save-dev zod-fixture
// Requires: zod v4 ("zod": "^4.0.0")
import { createFixture } from 'zod-fixture';
import { z } from 'zod';

// Domain schema (Zod v4 syntax — same file used for runtime validation + test factories)
export const UserSchema = z.object({
  id:               z.string().uuid(),
  email:            z.string().email(),
  name:             z.string().min(2).max(100),
  status:           z.enum(['active', 'suspended', 'pending']),
  subscriptionTier: z.enum(['free', 'premium', 'enterprise']),
  createdAt:        z.date(),
  paymentMethodId:  z.string().nullable(),
});

export type User = z.infer<typeof UserSchema>;

// Auto-factory — generates a structurally valid User from the Zod schema
// Every field uses Zod refinements as generation hints:
//   z.string().email()  → generates a valid email address
//   z.string().uuid()   → generates a valid UUID
//   z.enum([...])       → randomly picks one of the provided values
export const buildUserAuto = (overrides: Partial<User> = {}): User =>
  ({ ...createFixture(UserSchema), ...overrides });

// Nested schema example — associations are resolved recursively
export const OrderSchema = z.object({
  id:         z.string().uuid(),
  userId:     z.string().uuid(),
  status:     z.enum(['pending', 'paid', 'cancelled', 'refunded']),
  totalCents: z.number().int().min(0).max(1_000_000),
  items:      z.array(z.object({
    productId: z.string().uuid(),
    quantity:  z.number().int().min(1).max(99),
    priceCents: z.number().int().min(0),
  })).min(1),
  createdAt:  z.date(),
});

export type Order = z.infer<typeof OrderSchema>;
export const buildOrderAuto = (overrides: Partial<Order> = {}): Order =>
  ({ ...createFixture(OrderSchema), ...overrides });
```

**Usage alongside existing Object Mother patterns:**
```typescript
// HYBRID: zod-fixture for baseline, Object Mother for named domain variants
import { buildUserAuto } from '../factories/auto-factory';
import { UserMother } from '../factories/user.mother';

it('validates auto-generated user passes domain validation', () => {
  // zod-fixture guarantees structural validity
  const user = buildUserAuto();
  // Confirm zod-fixture output passes the same schema used to generate it
  expect(UserSchema.safeParse(user).success).toBe(true);
});

it('checks suspended user behaviour (Object Mother for semantics)', () => {
  // Object Mother communicates INTENT — "a suspended user" is a domain concept
  const user = UserMother.suspended();
  expect(checkoutService.initiate(user, cart).status).toBe('blocked');
});
```

**When to prefer `zod-fixture` over hand-written factories:**
| Scenario | Use `zod-fixture` | Use hand-written factory |
|----------|------------------|------------------------|
| Domain is fully Zod-typed | Yes — zero maintenance | Not needed for structure |
| Needs named domain variants ("suspended user") | No — use Object Mother | Yes |
| Property-based tests needing many valid objects | Yes — pair with `fc.record` | No |
| Schema has complex cross-field invariants not expressible in Zod | No | Yes |
| Rapid scaffolding for new domain entities | Yes — instant factory | Needed later for test semantics |

**Anti-pattern:** Using `zod-fixture` for snapshot tests — `createFixture` generates
random values each run. Pin overrides for all volatile fields before snapshotting (same
rule as `faker`-based factories; see Community Gotcha #38).

### OpenTelemetry Trace-Correlated Test Data  [community]

When testing distributed systems with integration tests, factory-generated data is often
difficult to correlate across service boundaries. A test that creates an order, triggers
a payment, and expects a notification email involves three services — and when it fails,
finding the right logs is painful. Embedding a stable **trace ID** in factory data
automatically links all spans produced by a single test case.

**Why it matters:** With a factory-injected `traceId`, every log line, DB query, and HTTP
call from a test carries the same correlation ID — making post-failure diagnosis in
Grafana/Jaeger/Zipkin immediate instead of a grep-and-guess exercise.

```typescript
// factories/traced-factory.ts
// Requires: @opentelemetry/api ("@opentelemetry/api": "^1.9.0")
import { context, trace, SpanContext } from '@opentelemetry/api';

// Generate a deterministic W3C trace ID from a test-scoped seed string
function testTraceId(seed: string): string {
  // Encode seed as a lowercase 32-char hex string (truncate/pad as needed)
  const encoded = Buffer.from(seed).toString('hex').padEnd(32, '0').slice(0, 32);
  return encoded;
}

function testSpanId(seed: string): string {
  return Buffer.from(seed).toString('hex').padEnd(16, '0').slice(0, 16);
}

// Factory-level tracing context — injects a stable W3C traceparent into the test
export function withTestTrace<T>(
  testName: string,
  factory: () => T
): { data: T; traceId: string; traceparent: string } {
  const traceId = testTraceId(testName);
  const spanId  = testSpanId(testName);
  // W3C traceparent header: version-traceId-parentId-flags
  const traceparent = `00-${traceId}-${spanId}-01`;
  return { data: factory(), traceId, traceparent };
}

// Usage: inject traceparent into HTTP headers so all downstream services share the trace
export function buildOrderWithTrace(testName: string, overrides = {}) {
  const { data: order, traceparent } = withTestTrace(testName, () => ({
    id:         `ord-${testName.replace(/\s+/g, '-').slice(0, 20)}`,
    userId:     'usr-test-001',
    status:     'pending' as const,
    totalCents: 4999,
    ...overrides,
  }));
  return { order, traceparent };
}
```

**Integration test using trace-correlated factory data:**
```typescript
// specs/payment-flow.integration.test.ts
import { test, expect } from 'vitest';
import { buildOrderWithTrace } from '../factories/traced-factory';

test('payment flow: order → charge → notification', async () => {
  const testName = 'payment-flow-happy-path';
  const { order, traceparent } = buildOrderWithTrace(testName);

  // Inject traceparent header — all downstream service calls carry the same trace
  const chargeResponse = await fetch('/api/payments/charge', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', 'traceparent': traceparent },
    body: JSON.stringify({ orderId: order.id, amountCents: order.totalCents }),
  });

  expect(chargeResponse.status).toBe(200);
  const charge = await chargeResponse.json();
  expect(charge.status).toBe('succeeded');

  // If this test fails: search Grafana for traceId = testTraceId(testName)
  // All spans from the payment service, notification service, and DB are linked
  console.info(`[trace] Search for traceId: ${traceparent.split('-')[1]} in Grafana/Jaeger`);
});
```

**Checklist — trace-correlated test data:**
- [ ] Factory-generated IDs embed a deterministic trace component derived from the test name
- [ ] `traceparent` header is included in all inter-service calls from integration tests
- [ ] Test log output includes the trace ID so failures link directly to Grafana/Jaeger
- [ ] Trace IDs use the W3C format (32-char hex traceId, 16-char spanId) — compatible with all OTEL collectors
- [ ] Factory trace IDs are never reused across test runs (seed from test name + run timestamp if parallel)

### Playwright `test.step()` Named Factory Labels  [community]

Playwright test reports and traces show a timeline of `test.step()` calls with their names.
When factories are invoked inside `test.step()` blocks with descriptive names, the trace
becomes a self-documenting audit log of the test data setup — invaluable for diagnosing
E2E failures in CI where the full browser trace is the only debugging artefact.

**Why it matters:** An unnamed `await createUser(db)` call in a trace shows as a gray
"network" span. Wrapping it in `test.step('Seed: active premium user with payment method')`
produces a named, labelled span with a clear boundary — making it immediately obvious
which part of the setup failed when a flaky E2E test drops its factory data.

```typescript
// specs/checkout.e2e.ts — Playwright test with named factory steps
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { db } from '../db';
import { buildUser, buildOrder, buildProduct } from '../factories';

test('checkout: premium user completes purchase', async ({ page, request }) => {
  // Named factory steps appear as labelled spans in Playwright HTML report + trace viewer
  const user = await test.step('Seed: premium user with Stripe payment method', async () => {
    return await db.user.create({ data: buildUser({
      subscriptionTier: 'premium',
      paymentMethodId:  'pm-stripe-test-visa',
    }) });
  });

  const product = await test.step('Seed: in-stock product at $49.99', async () => {
    return await db.product.create({ data: buildProduct({
      priceCents: 4999,
      stockCount: 10,
    }) });
  });

  await test.step('Seed: empty cart for user', async () => {
    await db.cart.create({ data: { userId: user.id, items: [] } });
  });

  // The test steps above appear as: "Seed: premium user with Stripe payment method" etc.
  // in the Playwright trace viewer — clearly separated from action steps below

  await test.step('Action: add product to cart and proceed to checkout', async () => {
    await page.goto(`/products/${product.id}`);
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to Cart' }).click();
    await page.getByRole('link',   { name: 'Checkout' }).click();
  });

  await test.step('Assert: order confirmation is displayed', async () => {
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Order Confirmed' })).toBeVisible();
    await expect(page.getByText(`$49.99`)).toBeVisible();
  });

  // Cleanup step — also labelled for trace visibility
  await test.step('Teardown: remove seeded user and product', async () => {
    await db.user.delete({ where: { id: user.id } });
    await db.product.delete({ where: { id: product.id } });
  });
});
```

**Naming convention for factory steps:**
| Step type | Naming pattern | Example |
|-----------|---------------|---------|
| Create test object | `Seed: <description>` | `Seed: suspended user with expired card` |
| Bulk seed | `Seed: <N> <entities> for <purpose>` | `Seed: 50 products for search pagination test` |
| Override/mutate | `Mutate: <field> → <value>` | `Mutate: user status → suspended` |
| Teardown | `Teardown: <what>` | `Teardown: remove seeded users and orders` |
| API factory | `API Seed: <endpoint>` | `API Seed: POST /api/users (admin)` |

**Integration with `test.step.skip()` (Playwright 1.50+):** guard data-dependent steps:
```typescript
// Guard downstream steps when factory precondition fails
const userCreated = await test.step('Seed: user account', async () => {
  const result = await db.user.create({ data: buildUser() }).catch(() => null);
  return result;
});

// test.step.skip() prevents subsequent steps from running if precondition fails
await test.step.skip(!userCreated, 'Action: login with seeded user', async () => {
  await page.goto('/login');
  await page.fill('[name="email"]', userCreated!.email);
  // ...
});
```

### Factory Composition via TypeScript Intersection Types  [community]

As domain models grow, factories often need to compose multiple partial entities together —
for example, a "user with billing info" that combines a base `User` with a `BillingProfile`.
A common approach is to write separate builders and merge them at the call site, but this
creates type-unsafe spreads. TypeScript intersection types (`A & B`) make factory composition
type-safe and refactor-proof.

**Why it matters:** Without intersection-typed factories, a merge like
`{ ...buildUser(), ...buildBilling() }` creates a wide `User & BillingProfile` union but
TypeScript cannot verify that required fields from both types are present. With typed
composition helpers, the compiler enforces completeness.

```typescript
// factories/compose.ts — type-safe factory composition helpers
type Factory<T> = (overrides?: Partial<T>) => T;

// Compose two factories into one — TypeScript enforces both shapes are fully present
export function composeFactories<A, B>(
  factoryA: Factory<A>,
  factoryB: Factory<B>
): Factory<A & B> {
  return (overrides: Partial<A & B> = {}): A & B => {
    const a = factoryA(overrides as Partial<A>);
    const b = factoryB(overrides as Partial<B>);
    return { ...a, ...b, ...overrides } as A & B;
  };
}

// Domain types
interface User {
  id: string;
  email: string;
  name: string;
  status: 'active' | 'suspended';
}

interface BillingProfile {
  billingEmail: string;
  addressLine1: string;
  addressLine2: string | null;
  country: string;
  vatNumber: string | null;
}

// Base factories
const buildUser: Factory<User> = (overrides = {}) => ({
  id:     'usr-001',
  email:  'user@example-test.invalid',
  name:   'Test User',
  status: 'active',
  ...overrides,
});

const buildBilling: Factory<BillingProfile> = (overrides = {}) => ({
  billingEmail: 'billing@example-test.invalid',
  addressLine1: '123 Test Street',
  addressLine2: null,
  country:      'DE',
  vatNumber:    null,
  ...overrides,
});

// Composed factory — TypeScript infers return type as User & BillingProfile
const buildUserWithBilling = composeFactories(buildUser, buildBilling);

// Usage:
const entity = buildUserWithBilling({
  email:        'alice@example-test.invalid',   // overrides User.email
  billingEmail: 'alice-billing@example-test.invalid', // overrides BillingProfile.billingEmail
  country:      'FR',                            // overrides BillingProfile.country
});
// TypeScript error if a required field is missing from either factory's output shape

export { buildUserWithBilling };
```

**With fishery `Association` pattern (for DB-persisted compositions):**
```typescript
// factories/user-with-billing.fishery.ts
import { Factory } from 'fishery';
import type { User, BillingProfile } from '../domain/types';
import { db } from '../db';

// Fishery's transient() fields allow composition without polluting the DB shape
const userWithBillingFactory = Factory.define<User & BillingProfile>(({ sequence }) => ({
  // User fields
  id:     `usr-${sequence.toString().padStart(4, '0')}`,
  email:  `user-${sequence}@example-test.invalid`,
  name:   `Test User ${sequence}`,
  status: 'active',
  // BillingProfile fields
  billingEmail: `billing-${sequence}@example-test.invalid`,
  addressLine1: `${sequence} Test Avenue`,
  addressLine2: null,
  country:      'DE',
  vatNumber:    null,
}));

export { userWithBillingFactory };
```

## Community Gotcha #41 — Temporal `PlainDate.compare()` returns a number, not a boolean — using it as a boolean silently always passes  [community]

**[community]** `Temporal.PlainDate.compare(a, b)` returns `-1`, `0`, or `1` (a number)
following the `Comparator` interface convention — it does NOT return a `boolean`. If a
factory or test assertion writes `if (Temporal.PlainDate.compare(startDate, endDate))`,
this is always truthy for any non-zero result — including the case where `startDate < endDate`
(which returns `-1`, a truthy value). **Why harmful:** A factory invariant check like
`assert(Temporal.PlainDate.compare(startDate, endDate) < 0, 'Start must be before end')`
is correct, but `assert(Temporal.PlainDate.compare(startDate, endDate), '...')` always
passes even when dates are in the wrong order. This masks factory bugs where a builder
produces a subscription with an `endDate` before `startDate`.

```typescript
// WRONG: compare() returns a number — truthy for -1 and 1, falsy only for 0 (equal dates)
const isOrdered = Temporal.PlainDate.compare(startDate, endDate);
if (isOrdered) {
  // This runs even when startDate > endDate (returns 1, which is truthy!)
}

// CORRECT: compare against the expected sign
const isStartBeforeEnd = Temporal.PlainDate.compare(startDate, endDate) < 0;
if (!isStartBeforeEnd) {
  throw new Error(`[factory] startDate (${startDate}) must be before endDate (${endDate})`);
}

// CORRECT: in factory invariant checks
export function buildSubscription(overrides: Partial<SubscriptionRecord> = {}): SubscriptionRecord {
  const result = { ...defaultSubscription, ...overrides };
  // Validate ordering invariant — compare() < 0 means start is strictly before end
  if (Temporal.PlainDate.compare(result.startDate, result.endDate) >= 0) {
    throw new Error(
      `[buildSubscription] startDate ${result.startDate} must be before endDate ${result.endDate}`
    );
  }
  return result;
}
```

## Community Gotcha #42 — `zod-fixture` uses Zod's internal `_def` API which is not public — Zod v4 changed `_def` shape, breaking zod-fixture v2  [community]

**[community]** `zod-fixture` v2.x accessed Zod's internal `schema._def` structure to
introspect field types and generate fixtures. When Zod v4 shipped (2025), it reorganised
`_def` — removing `typeName` from `ZodString._def` and replacing it with a flat `type`
property and new `checks` array format. This silently broke `zod-fixture` v2: calling
`createFixture(UserSchemaZodV4)` returned an object with every field as `undefined`.
**Why harmful:** The breakage is silent — TypeScript does not catch it because the generated
object still passes type inference (all fields are `undefined`, which satisfies `Partial<User>`).
Tests that use `createFixture` in Zod v4 pass TypeScript checks but operate on empty objects.
**Fix:** Upgrade to `zod-fixture` v3+ which rewrote introspection to use the stable Zod v4
public API (`schema._zod.def`). Never use hand-written `_def` introspection in test helpers.

```typescript
// BROKEN with Zod v4 + zod-fixture v2
import { createFixture } from 'zod-fixture'; // v2.x
import { z } from 'zod'; // v4

const user = createFixture(z.object({ email: z.string().email() }));
console.log(user.email); // undefined — _def.checks is not where Zod v4 puts refinements

// FIXED: upgrade zod-fixture to v3+
// npm install --save-dev zod-fixture@^3.0.0
import { createFixture } from 'zod-fixture'; // v3.x
const user = createFixture(z.object({ email: z.string().email() }));
console.log(user.email); // "example@example.com" — correct
```

**Compatibility matrix:**

| Zod version | zod-fixture version | Status |
|-------------|--------------------|----|
| Zod v3.x | zod-fixture v2.x | Compatible |
| Zod v4.x | zod-fixture v2.x | Broken (silent undefined fields) |
| Zod v4.x | zod-fixture v3.x | Compatible |
| Zod v3.x | zod-fixture v3.x | Not supported (zod-fixture v3 dropped v3 support) |

## Community Gotcha #43 — `composeFactories` with overlapping field names silently uses the last-spread value, discarding the first factory's intent  [community]

**[community]** When two factory types share a field name (e.g., both `User` and
`AuditRecord` have a `createdAt: Date`), a naive spread composition —
`{ ...buildUser(), ...buildAuditRecord() }` — silently uses `buildAuditRecord().createdAt`,
discarding `buildUser().createdAt`. If the two factories produce different timestamps
(e.g., User's `createdAt` is pinned to `2024-01-01` for reproducibility, but AuditRecord's
`createdAt` is `new Date()` for realism), the test operates on a chimera object where some
fields come from one factory and some from another — making assertions brittle.
**Why harmful:** Test failures caused by overlap are extremely difficult to diagnose:
the factory call looks correct, the types pass TypeScript checks, but the resulting object
has a semantically wrong `createdAt` field. **Fix:** Make overlap explicit by listing
conflicting fields in the override:

```typescript
// FRAGILE: overlapping 'createdAt' — AuditRecord's value silently wins
const auditedUser = { ...buildUser(), ...buildAuditRecord() };

// EXPLICIT: resolve overlap at the call site
const PINNED_CREATED_AT = new Date('2024-01-01T00:00:00Z');
const auditedUser = {
  ...buildUser({ createdAt: PINNED_CREATED_AT }),
  ...buildAuditRecord({ createdAt: PINNED_CREATED_AT }),
  // Both factories receive the same value — overlap is intentional and visible
};

// OR: use the composeFactories helper which surfaces overlap as a TypeScript intersection
// that forces the caller to provide a single override for conflicting fields:
const buildAuditedUser = composeFactories(buildUser, buildAuditRecord);
const entity = buildAuditedUser({ createdAt: PINNED_CREATED_AT }); // single override applies to both
```

## Community Gotcha #44 — Playwright named factory steps with `test.step()` add to HTML report timing but NOT to CI exit code — a failing step does not fail the test without `expect` inside  [community]

**[community]** `test.step()` in Playwright is a **labelling and timing mechanism**, not
an assertion mechanism. If a factory step like `await test.step('Seed: user', async () => { await db.user.create(...) })` throws an error inside the callback, it DOES fail the
test — but if the factory step silently returns an empty result (e.g., DB create returns
`null` due to a constraint violation that was swallowed), the test continues with a
`null` user and may fail later with a confusing `Cannot read properties of null` error
rather than a clear factory failure. **Why harmful:** The Playwright trace shows the
`Seed: user` step as a green check (it didn't throw) but a downstream action step fails
with a null pointer — hiding the real root cause. **Fix:** Always assert factory
preconditions inside the step using `expect`:

```typescript
// FRAGILE: factory step does not assert the result — null propagates silently
const user = await test.step('Seed: active user', async () => {
  return await db.user.create({ data: buildUser() }).catch(() => null);
  // Returns null on constraint violation — step is "green" but user is null
});

// CORRECT: assert inside the step — step turns red immediately on factory failure
const user = await test.step('Seed: active user', async () => {
  const created = await db.user.create({ data: buildUser() });
  // This expect() turns the step red in Playwright traces and HTML report
  expect(created, 'Seed: user creation must succeed').toBeTruthy();
  expect(created.id, 'Seed: user must have an id').toBeTruthy();
  return created;
});
```

### `fishery` Transient Parameters — Non-Persisted Factory Options  [community]

`fishery` v2.4.0 introduced **transient parameters**: extra inputs to the factory that
influence what gets built but are *not* included in the produced object. This is the
TypeScript equivalent of FactoryBot's `transient` block.

**Why it matters:** Before transient params, factories that needed conditional logic
(e.g., "create a user with 3 associated orders") required caller-side post-processing.
With transient params, the factory encapsulates that logic and the call site stays clean.

```typescript
// factories/user.factory.ts (fishery v2.4.0 transient params)
import { Factory } from 'fishery';
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';
import { db } from '../db';
import { User } from '../domain/user';

// Transient: { withOrders?: number } — never written to the User table
interface UserTransient {
  withOrders?: number; // how many orders to seed alongside the user
}

export const userFactory = Factory.define<User, UserTransient>(
  ({ sequence, transientParams, afterCreate }) => {
    const { withOrders = 0 } = transientParams;

    afterCreate(async (user) => {
      if (withOrders > 0) {
        await db.order.createMany({
          data: Array.from({ length: withOrders }, () => ({
            id: faker.string.uuid(),
            userId: user.id,
            status: 'pending',
            totalCents: faker.number.int({ min: 500, max: 50000 }),
          })),
        });
      }
    });

    return {
      id: faker.string.uuid(),
      email: `user-${sequence}@${faker.internet.domainName()}`,
      name: faker.person.fullName(),
      status: 'active' as const,
      subscriptionTier: 'free' as const,
      createdAt: new Date(),
      paymentMethodId: null,
    };
  }
);

// In an integration test — creates user + 3 orders in one call:
const userWithOrders = await userFactory.create(
  { subscriptionTier: 'premium' },
  { transient: { withOrders: 3 } }
);

// In a unit test — build only, no DB, transient params are ignored:
const user = userFactory.build({ status: 'suspended' });
// transient params accepted but afterCreate hooks never fire for .build()
```

**Key rules for transient params:**
- Transient params are passed in the *second argument* to `.create()` / `.build()`: `factory.create(attrs, { transient: { ... } })`
- `afterCreate` hooks fire only on `.create()` — never on `.build()`. This means transient-driven side effects (e.g., seeding related rows) are always DB-only, never in-memory.
- TypeScript enforces that transient fields do not appear on the returned type: passing `withOrders` as a top-level attribute (not inside `transient`) is a type error.

---

### Playwright `TestStepInfo` — Step-Level Attachments for Factory Diagnostics  [community]

Playwright 1.52+ provides a `TestStepInfo` object inside `test.step()` callbacks, enabling
steps to attach diagnostic artifacts (screenshots, JSON blobs, log files) directly to
individual steps rather than to the overall test.

**Why it matters for factories:** When a database seeding step fails in CI, attaching the
raw SQL error or the failed factory payload directly to the step dramatically reduces
debug time. The step shows as red in the HTML report *and* carries the artifact.

```typescript
// e2e/fixtures/db.fixture.ts
import { test as base, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { db } from '../db';
import { buildUser } from '../factories/user.factory';

export const test = base.extend<{ seedUser: { id: string; email: string } }>({
  seedUser: async ({}, use, testInfo) => {
    let user: { id: string; email: string } | undefined;

    await testInfo.step('Seed: create test user', async (step) => {
      try {
        const data = buildUser();
        user = await db.user.create({ data });

        // Attach the created payload for debugging in CI
        await step.attach('factory-output', {
          contentType: 'application/json',
          body: Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(data, null, 2)),
        });

        expect(user, 'Seed user must be persisted').toBeTruthy();
      } catch (err) {
        // Attach error details — step turns red, artifact is visible in HTML report
        await step.attach('factory-error', {
          contentType: 'text/plain',
          body: Buffer.from(String(err)),
        });
        throw err; // Re-throw so the test fails cleanly
      }
    });

    await use(user!);

    // Teardown: remove seeded row after test
    if (user) {
      await db.user.delete({ where: { id: user.id } });
    }
  },
});

// Usage in a test:
test('premium checkout succeeds', async ({ page, seedUser }) => {
  await page.goto(`/users/${seedUser.id}/checkout`);
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading')).toContainText('Checkout');
});
```

**`step.attach()` vs `testInfo.attach()`:** Use `step.attach()` when the artifact is
logically owned by a single step (e.g., factory output, migration error). Use
`testInfo.attach()` for artifacts that span the full test (e.g., final screenshot,
full request log).

---

### `faker.helpers.multiple()` — Idiomatic Batch Factory Generation  [community]

`@faker-js/faker` v10 introduced `faker.helpers.multiple()` as an idiomatic alternative
to `Array.from({ length: n }, () => fn())`. It accepts a generator function and a count,
and returns an array. When combined with a seed, the output is fully reproducible.

**Why it matters:** `Array.from` + arrow function is the status quo for batch generation
but is syntactically noisy. `faker.helpers.multiple()` is self-documenting and integrates
cleanly with factory functions.

```typescript
// factories/user.factory.ts — batch helpers
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';
import { User } from '../domain/user';
import { buildUser } from './user.factory';

// Generate N users with optional per-item overrides
export function buildUserBatch(
  count: number,
  overrideFn?: (index: number) => Partial<User>
): User[] {
  return faker.helpers.multiple(
    (_, index) => buildUser(overrideFn ? overrideFn(index) : {}),
    { count }
  );
}

// Build 10 users with sequential emails for pagination tests
const users = buildUserBatch(10, (i) => ({
  email: `user-${i + 1}@example.com`,
  subscriptionTier: i % 3 === 0 ? 'premium' : 'free',
}));

// Build a list where only one user has a specific property (useful for search tests)
const usersWithOneAdmin = buildUserBatch(9).concat([
  buildUser({ role: 'admin', email: 'admin@example.com' }),
]);
```

**Seeded batch for reproducibility:**
```typescript
// Force reproducible batch by setting seed before the call
faker.seed(42);
const stableUserBatch = faker.helpers.multiple(() => buildUser(), { count: 5 });
// Every run with seed 42 produces the same 5 users — safe for snapshot tests
```

**`faker.helpers.multiple()` vs `buildList()` (fishery):**

| Approach | When to use |
|----------|-------------|
| `faker.helpers.multiple()` | Standalone factory functions (no library); when index matters |
| `fishery.buildList(n)` | fishery-managed factories with `afterCreate` hooks |
| `factory-ts.buildList(n)` | factory-ts with sub-factory composition |
| `Array.from({ length: n }, fn)` | Legacy code; acceptable but noisier |

### Neon DB Schema-Only Branch Strategy  [community]

Neon's copy-on-write branching enables a lightweight **schema-only branch** pattern:
branch from a migration-applied empty database (not production data) to give each test
run a clean, isolated schema without copying potentially sensitive production rows.

**Why it matters:** Production-cloned branches carry PII risk and grow stale (schema drifts
from production migrations). Schema-only branches are always in sync with the latest
migration, are safe to share across teams, and cost almost no storage.

```typescript
// scripts/setup-test-branch.ts
// Run once per CI job: neon branch create --from HEAD
import { execSync } from 'child_process';
import { randomUUID } from 'crypto';

const branchName = `ci-${process.env.CI_RUN_ID ?? randomUUID().slice(0, 8)}`;

// 1. Create a schema-only branch from the migration-baseline branch (not main/prod)
//    --no-default-db avoids copying any rows; migrations are pre-applied on the baseline
execSync(
  `neon branches create --name ${branchName} --parent migrations-baseline --no-default-db`,
  { stdio: 'inherit' }
);

// 2. Get the connection string for this branch
const connString = execSync(
  `neon connection-string ${branchName} --database-name testdb`,
  { encoding: 'utf-8' }
).trim();

// 3. Write to .env.test.local for the test run
import { writeFileSync } from 'fs';
writeFileSync('.env.test.local', `DATABASE_URL="${connString}"\n`);
console.log(`[neon-branch] Created: ${branchName}`);

// Teardown: in CI afterAll or a teardown project
// execSync(`neon branches delete ${branchName}`);
```

**Pattern rules:**
- The `migrations-baseline` branch is a long-lived Neon branch that only receives `prisma migrate deploy` (or equivalent) — never data writes.
- Each CI run creates and deletes its own branch. Neon's copy-on-write means creation is near-instant regardless of schema size.
- For local development, reuse one branch per developer (reset with `prisma migrate reset --skip-seed`) rather than creating/deleting per session.

### MSW `WebSocketHandler.test()` — Programmatic Handler Validation  [community]

MSW 2.14.x exported the `WebSocketHandler.test()` static method, enabling test code to
check whether a given URL would be handled by a specific handler — without starting a
full mock server. This is useful for validating that factory-generated WebSocket URLs
match the expected handler before committing to a full E2E setup.

**Why it matters:** When factories generate dynamic WebSocket URLs (e.g., including a
user ID or session token), a typo in the URL pattern means the handler silently passes
all messages through to the real server in tests. `WebSocketHandler.test()` lets you
assert the match explicitly in a fast unit test.

```typescript
// mocks/ws-handlers.ts
import { ws } from 'msw';

// Handler for per-user notification channels
export const notificationHandler = ws.link('wss://api.example.com/users/:userId/notifications');

export const wsHandlers = [notificationHandler];
```

```typescript
// factories/ws-url.factory.spec.ts
import { WebSocketHandler } from 'msw';
import { notificationHandler } from '../mocks/ws-handlers';
import { buildNotificationChannelUrl } from '../factories/ws-url.factory';

describe('buildNotificationChannelUrl factory', () => {
  it('generates a URL that matches the notification WS handler', () => {
    const url = buildNotificationChannelUrl({ userId: 'usr-abc123' });
    // WebSocketHandler.test() returns true if the handler's pattern matches the URL
    expect(WebSocketHandler.test(notificationHandler, url)).toBe(true);
  });

  it('does NOT match other user channels', () => {
    const url = 'wss://api.example.com/orgs/org-001/notifications';
    expect(WebSocketHandler.test(notificationHandler, url)).toBe(false);
  });
});
```

**Availability:** `WebSocketHandler.test()` is a static method on the `WebSocketHandler`
class exported from `msw`. Available from MSW 2.14.0+. Use it in unit tests alongside
your factory tests — no server setup required.

## Community Gotcha #45 — `fishery` `afterCreate` fires even when the hook throws — leaving partial DB state that poisons subsequent tests  [community]

**[community]** `fishery`'s `afterCreate` hook does not roll back when it throws. If
your `afterCreate` creates related rows (orders, addresses) and one of those creations
fails mid-loop (e.g., a unique constraint on the 3rd order), the first two orders are
committed. The factory call throws, but two orphaned rows remain in the test database.
**Why harmful:** When the next test runs, it may encounter those orphaned rows (e.g., a
uniqueness check unexpectedly returns `false`), causing a cascade of unrelated failures.
**Fix:** Wrap `afterCreate` bodies in a database transaction, or explicitly delete the
parent object (and rely on cascade deletes) in the test's teardown fixture. Never leave
cleanup to the next test's setup.

```typescript
// FRAGILE: afterCreate without transaction — partial rows on failure
export const userWithOrdersFactory = Factory.define<User, { withOrders: number }>(
  ({ transientParams, afterCreate }) => {
    afterCreate(async (user) => {
      for (let i = 0; i < (transientParams.withOrders ?? 0); i++) {
        await db.order.create({ data: { userId: user.id, ... } }); // may fail midway
      }
    });
    return buildUserAttrs();
  }
);

// SAFE: afterCreate wrapped in a transaction — all-or-nothing
export const userWithOrdersFactorySafe = Factory.define<User, { withOrders: number }>(
  ({ transientParams, afterCreate }) => {
    afterCreate(async (user) => {
      await db.$transaction(async (tx) => {
        for (let i = 0; i < (transientParams.withOrders ?? 0); i++) {
          await tx.order.create({ data: { userId: user.id, ... } });
        }
      });
    });
    return buildUserAttrs();
  }
);
```

## Community Gotcha #46 — `faker.helpers.multiple()` does NOT reset the internal sequence counter — calling it twice with the same seed produces non-sequential indices  [community]

**[community]** `faker.helpers.multiple(fn, { count: 5 })` passes `(value, index)` where
`index` is the position within that single call (0–4). But if you call it twice in the
same test (e.g., once for `users` and once for `orders`), the second call's index also
starts at 0. If your factory uses `index` to generate unique emails (`user-0@...`,
`user-1@...`, etc.), the second batch produces duplicate emails unless you add an offset.
**Why harmful:** Tests that build multiple batches in a single test function get duplicate
emails, triggering unique-constraint violations in DB integration tests — but not in
in-memory unit tests where the DB is not involved. The defect is environment-specific.
**Fix:** Use `fishery`'s `sequence` (auto-incrementing, global per factory) or derive
uniqueness from `faker.string.uuid()` rather than `index`.

```typescript
// FRAGILE: index-based emails — duplicates across multiple calls in one test
const users1 = faker.helpers.multiple((_, i) => buildUser({ email: `user-${i}@x.com` }), { count: 3 });
const users2 = faker.helpers.multiple((_, i) => buildUser({ email: `user-${i}@x.com` }), { count: 3 });
// users1[0].email === users2[0].email === 'user-0@x.com' — DB constraint violation

// SAFE: uuid-based uniqueness — always unique across calls
const users1safe = faker.helpers.multiple(() => buildUser(), { count: 3 });
const users2safe = faker.helpers.multiple(() => buildUser(), { count: 3 });
// buildUser() internally uses faker.string.uuid() — guaranteed unique
```

## Community Gotcha #47 — Playwright `TestStepInfo.attach()` attachments are not included in the JUnit XML report — they only appear in the HTML report and trace viewer  [community]

**[community]** When factory diagnostic artifacts are attached via `step.attach()`, they
are stored in the HTML report and the `.zip` trace file. The JUnit XML report
(`--reporter=junit`) does not embed attachment content — it only writes the attachment
name and path as an attribute. CI systems that parse JUnit XML (e.g., some Jenkins
integrations) and display test failures will show the factory step name but not the
attached JSON payload. **Why harmful:** Teams migrating from a Jenkins JUnit-based
dashboard to Playwright HTML reports may believe factory diagnostics are visible in CI
when they are not — leading to longer debug cycles on factory failures. **Fix:** For
factory diagnostics that must appear in JUnit output, write them as console.log() output
(which JUnit captures as `system-out`) in addition to attaching them:

```typescript
await test.step('Seed: create test user', async (step) => {
  const data = buildUser();
  const user = await db.user.create({ data });

  // JUnit-visible: written to system-out in XML
  console.log('[factory-output]', JSON.stringify(data));

  // HTML report & trace visible only:
  await step.attach('factory-output', {
    contentType: 'application/json',
    body: Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(data, null, 2)),
  });
});
```

## Cycle 22 — 2026-05-13

<!-- iter-49-cycle22: "Construct with Collaborators, Call with Work" principle applied to factory design; Playwright v1.51 IndexedDB storage state for auth fixtures; Playwright v1.59 setStorageState() for resetting auth context between tests; MSW v2.14.x NetworkApi typed handler container pattern; fishery v2.4.0 DeepPartialObject explicit type override; test data for agentic AI systems (tool call sequences, multi-turn conversation factories); community gotchas #41–#43; 3 new Key Resources (2026-05-13) -->

### "Construct with Collaborators, Call with Work" — Factory Design Principle  [community]

The **"Construct with Collaborators, Call with Work"** principle (Shahar Roth, Google Testing Blog, May 2026) draws a sharp distinction between two kinds of things you pass to an object:

- **Collaborators** — services, dependencies, and infrastructure an object uses to do its job (database clients, email senders, loggers, clocks). Pass these at construction time (constructor injection).
- **Work** — the specific data or inputs for a single operation (a user ID, an order payload, a list of IDs). Pass these at call time (method arguments).

**Why it matters for test data factories:** The principle clarifies *why* factories exist and *what* they should produce. A factory builds a **work unit** — the test-specific data that describes the scenario. The *collaborators* (the service under test, the DB connection, the fake clock) are configured once in fixtures or `beforeEach`. Blurring the boundary — a factory that also creates services, or a fixture that generates test data — produces tests that are hard to read and hard to isolate.

The practical rule: if a factory call returns something you pass to a *method*, it is work. If it returns something you pass to a *constructor*, it is a collaborator and belongs in a fixture, not a factory.

```typescript
// ANTI-PATTERN: factory that blurs work and collaborators
// The factory creates BOTH the service (collaborator) AND the data (work)
function buildCheckoutContext(overrides: Partial<User> = {}) {
  const user = buildUser(overrides);           // work — correct
  const service = new CheckoutService(db);     // collaborator — WRONG place
  const cart = buildCart();                    // work — correct
  return { user, service, cart };
}

// CORRECT: separate collaborators (fixture) from work (factory)

// fixtures/checkout-fixtures.ts — collaborator wired once, shared across tests
export const test = baseTest.extend({
  checkoutService: async ({}, use) => {
    const service = new CheckoutService(testDb);  // collaborator
    await use(service);
  },
});

// In a test — work is built inline or via factory; collaborator comes from fixture
test('suspended user is blocked at checkout', async ({ checkoutService }) => {
  const user = buildUser({ status: 'suspended' });   // work
  const cart = buildCart({ items: [buildCartItem()] }); // work

  const result = await checkoutService.initiate(user.id, cart);
  expect(result.status).toBe('blocked');
});
```

**Factory checklist:** Before adding code to a factory, ask:
1. Is this data consumed as a *method argument* in the test? → factory (work)
2. Is this an infrastructure object a service depends on? → fixture (collaborator)
3. Is this a DB row that the service reads during execution? → factory + `create()` / Vitest fixture with teardown

**Common boundary violations and their fixes:**

| Violation | Why it's a problem | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Factory that creates service instances | Tests can't swap collaborators independently | Move service creation to `test.extend()` fixture |
| Fixture that generates test-specific data | Fixtures are shared — data needs to be per-test | Move data generation to factories called inside the test |
| Factory that imports `db` directly for inline persistence | Mixes construction concern (memory) with DB concern (persistence) | Use `build()` for memory, explicit `create()` for DB |
| `beforeAll` that builds both DB connection and test users | Connection is a collaborator; users are work | Split into worker-scoped fixture (DB) + `beforeEach` factory call (users) |

### Playwright v1.51 IndexedDB in `storageState` — Auth Token Fixtures  [community]

Playwright v1.51 (late 2024) added IndexedDB support to `browserContext.storageState()`.
This is significant for test data fixtures that deal with modern auth patterns: Firebase
Authentication, Supabase Auth, and Web3 wallet connections all store tokens in IndexedDB,
not in cookies or `localStorage`. Before v1.51, capturing and restoring these auth states
required manual JavaScript injection.

**Why it matters:** E2E tests that need an authenticated state for a Firebase/Supabase app
can now save and restore the full auth fixture — including IndexedDB tokens — without any
custom auth injection code. This makes fixture-based authentication setup dramatically
simpler.

```typescript
// scripts/generate-auth-fixture.ts — one-time script to capture auth state with IndexedDB
// Run manually: npx playwright test scripts/generate-auth-fixture.ts
import { chromium } from '@playwright/test';
import { writeFileSync } from 'fs';

(async () => {
  const browser = await chromium.launch();
  const context = await browser.newContext();
  const page = await context.newPage();

  // Perform real login (Firebase, Supabase, etc.)
  await page.goto('https://your-app.example.com/login');
  await page.fill('[data-testid="email"]', process.env.TEST_USER_EMAIL!);
  await page.fill('[data-testid="password"]', process.env.TEST_USER_PASSWORD!);
  await page.click('[data-testid="submit"]');
  await page.waitForURL('/dashboard');

  // Capture storage state INCLUDING IndexedDB (new in Playwright v1.51)
  const state = await context.storageState({ indexedDB: true });  // ← v1.51+ option
  writeFileSync('./fixtures/auth-state.json', JSON.stringify(state, null, 2));

  console.log('[auth-fixture] Saved auth state with IndexedDB tokens');
  await browser.close();
})();
```

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — use the saved auth state as a global storage state fixture
import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  projects: [
    {
      name: 'authenticated',
      use: {
        ...devices['Desktop Chrome'],
        storageState: './fixtures/auth-state.json',  // includes IndexedDB tokens
      },
    },
    {
      name: 'unauthenticated',
      // no storageState — tests start logged out
    },
  ],
});
```

```typescript
// specs/dashboard.spec.ts — test inherits full auth state (cookies + localStorage + IndexedDB)
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// No login step needed — auth state (including Firebase/Supabase IndexedDB tokens) is pre-loaded
test('authenticated user sees dashboard', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="user-greeting"]')).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Limitation:** IndexedDB in `storageState` captures a point-in-time snapshot of token state.
If the token expires (e.g., Firebase ID tokens expire after 1 hour), the fixture needs
regenerating. Use Playwright's `--update-snapshots` equivalent: schedule a nightly fixture
regeneration CI job, or check token expiry and regenerate before the test run starts.

---

### Playwright v1.59 `browserContext.setStorageState()` — In-Test Auth Reset  [community]

Playwright v1.59 added `browserContext.setStorageState()`, which clears ALL existing
cookies, localStorage, and IndexedDB for all origins and then loads a new state in a
single call. Before this API, resetting auth state between tests in the same `browserContext`
required either creating a new context (expensive) or manually calling `clearCookies()`,
`clearLocalStorage()`, and an IndexedDB-clearing script separately.

**Why it matters for test data fixtures:** In tests that need to check behavior for
multiple user roles (admin, member, guest) within a single spec file, `setStorageState()`
enables atomic role-switching without spinning up a new browser context per role.

```typescript
// fixtures/auth-states.ts — pre-generated auth state fixtures for each role
// These are captured once via the generate-auth-fixture.ts script
import adminState from './auth-states/admin.json';
import memberState from './auth-states/member.json';
import guestState from './auth-states/guest.json';

export const AuthStates = { admin: adminState, member: memberState, guest: guestState };
```

```typescript
// specs/rbac.spec.ts — role-switching test using setStorageState()
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { AuthStates } from '../fixtures/auth-states';

// Start test as admin
test('admin can access user management; member cannot', async ({ page, context }) => {
  // Load admin auth state — clears any previous session and loads admin session atomically
  await context.setStorageState(AuthStates.admin);  // ← v1.59 API: single atomic reset+load
  await page.goto('/admin/users');
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="user-table"]')).toBeVisible();

  // Switch to member role in the SAME test — no new context needed
  await context.setStorageState(AuthStates.member);
  await page.goto('/admin/users');
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="access-denied"]')).toBeVisible();

  // Switch to unauthenticated state (empty storage state)
  await context.setStorageState({ cookies: [], origins: [] });
  await page.goto('/admin/users');
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="login-redirect"]')).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Integration with the Playwright `storageState` project config:**

```typescript
// When used with the indexed-DB-aware fixture from v1.51:
// setStorageState() also accepts inline state objects (not just file paths)
// This enables dynamically generating auth state in globalSetup and passing it in-memory

// playwright.config.ts globalSetup generates fresh auth tokens at the start of each run
// and stores them in process.env for use with setStorageState() in fixtures
```

**Tradeoff:** `setStorageState()` does NOT clear in-flight network requests or pending
navigation. If a test calls `setStorageState()` while a page is loading, the new auth
state may not apply to the in-flight request. Always await navigation completion before
switching states:
```typescript
await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');    // wait for current page to settle
await context.setStorageState(AuthStates.admin);  // then switch
await page.goto('/new-route');                 // navigate with new auth
```

### MSW `NetworkApi` Type Export — Typed Handler Containers  [community]

MSW v2.14.x (May 2026) added the `NetworkApi` type export from `msw`. This enables
TypeScript-first **handler container patterns** — strongly typed objects that group
related mock handlers by domain, with compile-time guarantees that the handlers are
the correct type.

**Why it matters:** Large test suites with 50+ MSW handlers often spread them across
multiple files, losing type safety at the composition point (where handlers are combined
for `setupServer()`). The `NetworkApi` type gives a named, typed container for domain-aligned
handler groups that compose cleanly without losing types.

```typescript
// mocks/handlers/user-handlers.ts — typed handler container
import { http, HttpResponse, type NetworkApi } from 'msw';
import { buildUser, buildUserList } from '../../factories/user.factory';

// NetworkApi is the type of a handler or handler group
// Using it as a return type ensures the handler file exports only valid MSW handlers
export function createUserHandlers(): NetworkApi {
  return [
    http.get('/api/users', () => {
      const users = buildUserList(5);
      return HttpResponse.json({ data: users, total: 5 });
    }),

    http.get('/api/users/:id', ({ params }) => {
      const user = buildUser({ id: params.id as string });
      return HttpResponse.json(user);
    }),

    http.post('/api/users', async ({ request }) => {
      const body = await request.json() as { email: string; name: string };
      const user = buildUser({ email: body.email, name: body.name });
      return HttpResponse.json(user, { status: 201 });
    }),
  ];
}
```

```typescript
// mocks/handlers/order-handlers.ts
import { http, HttpResponse, type NetworkApi } from 'msw';
import { buildOrder, buildOrderList } from '../../factories/order.factory';

export function createOrderHandlers(): NetworkApi {
  return [
    http.get('/api/orders', () => {
      const orders = buildOrderList(3);
      return HttpResponse.json({ data: orders });
    }),

    http.post('/api/orders/:id/cancel', ({ params }) => {
      const order = buildOrder({ id: params.id as string, status: 'cancelled' });
      return HttpResponse.json(order);
    }),
  ];
}
```

```typescript
// mocks/server.ts — compose typed handler containers
import { setupServer } from 'msw/node';
import { createUserHandlers } from './handlers/user-handlers';
import { createOrderHandlers } from './handlers/order-handlers';

// TypeScript validates that all composed handlers are valid NetworkApi entries
export const server = setupServer(
  ...createUserHandlers(),
  ...createOrderHandlers(),
);

// test/setup.ts
import { server } from '../mocks/server';
beforeAll(() => server.listen({ onUnhandledRequest: 'error' }));
afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers());
afterAll(() => server.close());
```

**Per-test handler overrides with typed containers:**
```typescript
// In a test — override a single domain's handlers without affecting others
import { server } from '../mocks/server';
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw';

test('shows error banner when user API fails', async () => {
  server.use(
    http.get('/api/users', () =>
      HttpResponse.json({ error: 'Service Unavailable' }, { status: 503 })
    )
  );
  // order handlers remain active — only user handlers are overridden
});
```

### fishery v2.4.0 `DeepPartialObject` — Explicit Type Overrides  [community]

fishery v2.3.1+ exports the `DeepPartialObject<T>` utility type, enabling factory callers
to specify override types explicitly in contexts where TypeScript's inference needs
assistance — such as generic helper functions that accept factory overrides as parameters.

**Why it matters:** Without `DeepPartialObject`, writing a typed helper that accepts
factory overrides requires duplicating the `Partial<T>` constraint inline. With
`DeepPartialObject`, the type is a named import from fishery, consistent with the
library's own internal typing — and it handles nested objects correctly (unlike a
shallow `Partial<T>`).

```typescript
// test-helpers/factory-helpers.ts — using DeepPartialObject for typed override helpers
import { type DeepPartialObject } from 'fishery';
import { userFactory } from '../factories/user.factory';
import { orderFactory } from '../factories/order.factory';
import type { User } from '../domain/user';
import type { Order } from '../domain/order';

// Generic seed helper: accepts typed overrides for multiple factories
// DeepPartialObject<T> handles nested object overrides correctly
export async function seedUserWithOrder(
  userOverrides: DeepPartialObject<User> = {},
  orderOverrides: DeepPartialObject<Order> = {}
): Promise<{ user: User; order: Order }> {
  const user = await userFactory.create(userOverrides);
  const order = await orderFactory.create({ userId: user.id, ...orderOverrides });
  return { user, order };
}

// Usage — TypeScript validates override keys and values against User and Order types
const { user, order } = await seedUserWithOrder(
  { status: 'active', subscriptionTier: 'premium' },
  { status: 'pending', totalCents: 4999 }
);
// TypeScript error if a wrong key or wrong type is passed in overrides
```

**`DeepPartialObject` vs `Partial<T>` comparison:**

```typescript
import type { DeepPartialObject } from 'fishery';

interface Address {
  street: string;
  city: string;
  country: string;
  coordinates: { lat: number; lng: number };  // nested object
}

// Partial<Address>: only top-level fields are optional — coordinates is still Address['coordinates']
// Mutating nested object in a Partial<Address> override replaces the whole object, not individual fields

// DeepPartialObject<Address>: ALL levels are optional — you can override just lat without providing lng
type DeepPartialAddress = DeepPartialObject<Address>;
// DeepPartialAddress = { street?: string; city?: string; country?: string;
//   coordinates?: { lat?: number; lng?: number } }

// In a factory — DeepPartialObject handles nested merge without replacing the whole nested object
export function buildAddress(overrides: DeepPartialObject<Address> = {}): Address {
  const defaults: Address = {
    street: faker.location.streetAddress(),
    city: faker.location.city(),
    country: 'US',
    coordinates: { lat: 40.7128, lng: -74.0060 },
  };

  return {
    ...defaults,
    ...overrides,
    coordinates: {
      ...defaults.coordinates,
      ...(overrides.coordinates ?? {}),
    },
  };
}

// Override just lat — lng retains its default value
const nyAddress = buildAddress({ coordinates: { lat: 40.7128 } });
// nyAddress.coordinates.lng === -74.0060 (default preserved)
```

### Test Data for Agentic AI Systems — Tool Call Sequences and Multi-Turn Factories  [community]

AI agents orchestrate sequences of tool calls across multiple conversation turns. Factories
for agentic systems must model not just individual messages but the *full conversation state*
— including tool call IDs, tool results, and the conversation history that brings the agent
to a specific decision point.

**Why it matters:** Agentic AI tests that use a single static response mock (`{ role: 'assistant', content: '...' }`)
miss the multi-turn structure that drives agent behaviour. The same agent prompt can produce
different decisions depending on whether a prior tool call succeeded, returned partial data,
or failed. Factories that model full conversation history expose these decision branches
in tests.

```typescript
// factories/agentic-conversation.factory.ts
// Models multi-turn AI conversations with tool call sequences for agent testing

import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

// Message types matching the Anthropic Messages API structure
type UserMessage = { role: 'user'; content: string };
type ToolUseBlock = {
  type: 'tool_use';
  id: string;               // unique tool call ID — must match ToolResultBlock.tool_use_id
  name: string;
  input: Record<string, unknown>;
};
type TextBlock = { type: 'text'; content: string };
type AssistantMessage = { role: 'assistant'; content: (TextBlock | ToolUseBlock)[] };
type ToolResultBlock = {
  type: 'tool_result';
  tool_use_id: string;      // matches the ToolUseBlock.id that triggered this result
  content: string;
  is_error?: boolean;
};
type ToolResultMessage = { role: 'user'; content: ToolResultBlock[] };

type ConversationMessage = UserMessage | AssistantMessage | ToolResultMessage;

// Factory for a complete tool call round-trip (assistant calls tool → result returned)
export function buildToolCallRoundTrip(options: {
  toolName: string;
  toolInput: Record<string, unknown>;
  toolResult: string;
  isError?: boolean;
}): [AssistantMessage, ToolResultMessage] {
  const toolCallId = `toolu_${faker.string.alphanumeric(20)}`;

  const assistantMessage: AssistantMessage = {
    role: 'assistant',
    content: [
      {
        type: 'tool_use',
        id: toolCallId,
        name: options.toolName,
        input: options.toolInput,
      },
    ],
  };

  const toolResultMessage: ToolResultMessage = {
    role: 'user',
    content: [
      {
        type: 'tool_result',
        tool_use_id: toolCallId,
        content: options.toolResult,
        is_error: options.isError ?? false,
      },
    ],
  };

  return [assistantMessage, toolResultMessage];
}

// Factory for a full multi-turn conversation that leads to a specific agent state
export function buildAgentConversation(options: {
  initialUserRequest: string;
  toolCallHistory: Array<{
    toolName: string;
    toolInput: Record<string, unknown>;
    toolResult: string;
    isError?: boolean;
  }>;
  finalUserMessage?: string;
}): ConversationMessage[] {
  const messages: ConversationMessage[] = [
    { role: 'user', content: options.initialUserRequest },
  ];

  for (const toolCall of options.toolCallHistory) {
    const [assistantMsg, resultMsg] = buildToolCallRoundTrip(toolCall);
    messages.push(assistantMsg, resultMsg);
  }

  if (options.finalUserMessage) {
    messages.push({ role: 'user', content: options.finalUserMessage });
  }

  return messages;
}
```

```typescript
// specs/agent.test.ts — testing agent behaviour with multi-turn conversation history

import { test, expect } from 'vitest';
import { buildAgentConversation } from '../factories/agentic-conversation.factory';
import { AgentOrchestrator } from '../services/agent-orchestrator';

test('agent retries on tool error before giving up', async () => {
  // Build a conversation where the tool failed twice
  const conversationHistory = buildAgentConversation({
    initialUserRequest: 'Search for all users created in the last 7 days',
    toolCallHistory: [
      {
        toolName: 'search_users',
        toolInput: { days: 7 },
        toolResult: 'Connection timeout: database unreachable',
        isError: true,   // first attempt failed
      },
      {
        toolName: 'search_users',
        toolInput: { days: 7, retry: true },
        toolResult: 'Connection timeout: database unreachable',
        isError: true,   // second attempt also failed
      },
    ],
  });

  // Give the agent the history that represents two prior failures
  const result = await AgentOrchestrator.continueConversation(conversationHistory);

  // Assert agent enters fallback behaviour after 2 consecutive tool failures
  expect(result.action).toBe('escalate_to_human');
  expect(result.reason).toContain('tool_failure_threshold_reached');
});

test('agent synthesises result after successful tool sequence', async () => {
  const conversationHistory = buildAgentConversation({
    initialUserRequest: 'Get user profile and recent orders for user-001',
    toolCallHistory: [
      {
        toolName: 'get_user',
        toolInput: { userId: 'user-001' },
        toolResult: JSON.stringify({ id: 'user-001', name: 'Alice', tier: 'premium' }),
      },
      {
        toolName: 'get_orders',
        toolInput: { userId: 'user-001', limit: 5 },
        toolResult: JSON.stringify([{ id: 'ord-1', status: 'delivered', totalCents: 4999 }]),
      },
    ],
  });

  const result = await AgentOrchestrator.continueConversation(conversationHistory);

  // After two successful tool calls, agent should synthesise a summary
  expect(result.action).toBe('respond');
  expect(result.content).toContain('Alice');
  expect(result.content).toContain('premium');
});
```

**Key patterns for agentic test data:**

| Scenario | Factory approach |
|---|---|
| Agent succeeds on first tool call | `buildToolCallRoundTrip()` with `isError: false` — one round-trip |
| Agent retries after tool failure | Two `buildToolCallRoundTrip()` entries with first `isError: true` |
| Agent asks clarifying question | `AssistantMessage` with `type: 'text'` content block instead of `type: 'tool_use'` |
| Agent uses parallel tool calls | Single `AssistantMessage` with multiple `ToolUseBlock` entries; one `ToolResultMessage` with multiple `ToolResultBlock` entries |
| Agent reaches max turns limit | `buildAgentConversation()` with `toolCallHistory` at the tool call limit threshold |

**Community gotcha #41 [community]:** Tool call IDs must be unique within a conversation
AND must match exactly between the `ToolUseBlock.id` and the `ToolResultBlock.tool_use_id`.
Factories that generate static IDs (e.g., `id: 'toolu_001'`) cause silent failures when
two tool calls in the same conversation share the same ID — the model API returns an error
that most test setups misattribute to the model response parser rather than the conversation
factory. Fix: always use `faker.string.alphanumeric(20)` to generate unique IDs and capture
them as variables before building the result message.
