### Community Gotchas #42–#43  [community]

**42. [community] `context.setStorageState()` (Playwright v1.59) does not propagate to already-open pages — navigate after setting state.**

`browserContext.setStorageState()` updates the context's internal auth state, but any
page that is already open has its own copy of storage (from the previous page load).
Calling `setStorageState()` and then asserting on the current page's content without
a navigation step will still see the OLD auth state in the page's JavaScript context.

```typescript
// WRONG — page still sees old auth state (tokens already loaded in page JS context)
await context.setStorageState(AuthStates.admin);
await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="admin-menu"]')).toBeVisible();
// ↑ Fails if current page loaded before setStorageState() was called

// CORRECT — navigate after switching state (loads page JS context fresh)
await context.setStorageState(AuthStates.admin);
await page.goto(page.url());  // reload current URL with new auth state
await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="admin-menu"]')).toBeVisible();
```

This is particularly subtle in `describe` blocks that reuse a `page` fixture across
multiple `test` calls with different auth states. Each test that switches auth state
must navigate to force the page JS context to reload.

**43. [community] `buildAgentConversation()` factories that truncate history at the AI context window limit silently change agent behaviour.**

When testing long multi-turn agent conversations, factories that generate 50+ turns
of conversation history may exceed the AI model's context window. Many model APIs
silently truncate the beginning of the conversation rather than throwing an error —
the agent then "forgets" earlier tool call results and makes different decisions.
The test still passes (no error is thrown), but it is testing different agent behaviour
than intended.

Fix: add a `conversationTokenEstimate()` utility that estimates the token count of the
generated conversation and warns (or throws) if it exceeds the model's context window:

```typescript
// factories/agentic-conversation.factory.ts — token count guard
const ROUGH_TOKENS_PER_CHAR = 0.25; // ~4 chars per token (GPT-4/Claude approximation)
const MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS = 200_000;  // Claude 3.7 / GPT-4o context window

export function estimateConversationTokens(messages: ConversationMessage[]): number {
  const totalChars = JSON.stringify(messages).length;
  return Math.ceil(totalChars * ROUGH_TOKENS_PER_CHAR);
}

// Call in test setup — warns if factory-generated conversation is too long
export function buildAgentConversationWithGuard(
  options: Parameters<typeof buildAgentConversation>[0]
): ConversationMessage[] {
  const messages = buildAgentConversation(options);
  const tokens = estimateConversationTokens(messages);

  if (tokens > MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS * 0.8) {
    console.warn(
      `[factory-guard] Agent conversation factory estimated ~${tokens} tokens ` +
      `(80% of ${MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS} limit). Conversation may be truncated by the model API.`
    );
  }

  return messages;
}
```

### faker `helpers.fromRegExp()` — Pattern-Constrained Test Data  [community]

`faker.helpers.fromRegExp(pattern)` generates a random string that satisfies a given
regular expression. Introduced in faker v8.1 and stable through v10.x, it is the
recommended replacement for ad hoc string concatenation when the test requires data
in a specific format but still needs variance between test runs.

**Why it matters:** Test data that is too uniform reveals only one code path. A factory
that always returns `"REF-001"` cannot expose off-by-one errors in reference number
parsing. `fromRegExp()` lets you specify *structure* (e.g., `REF-\d{3}`) while
randomising the content — so each test run gets structurally valid but distinct values.

```typescript
// factories/reference-numbers.factory.ts
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

// Generate reference numbers matching the app's expected format: REF-YYYYMMDD-NNN
export function buildReferenceNumber(): string {
  const year = faker.date.past({ years: 1 }).getFullYear().toString();
  // fromRegExp generates a string matching the regex — each call returns a distinct value
  return faker.helpers.fromRegExp(
    new RegExp(`REF-${year}[01]\\d[0-3]\\d-\\d{3}`)
  );
  // e.g. "REF-20261015-472" or "REF-20260302-089"
}

// ISBN-13 format: 978 or 979, then 10 digits
export function buildISBN13(): string {
  return faker.helpers.fromRegExp(/97[89]-\d-\d{3}-\d{5}-\d/);
}

// UK postcode format: AA9 9AA
export function buildUKPostcode(): string {
  return faker.helpers.fromRegExp(/[A-Z]{2}[1-9] [0-9][A-Z]{2}/);
}

// Vehicle registration: UK format (AA12 AAA)
export function buildUKVehicleReg(): string {
  return faker.helpers.fromRegExp(/[A-Z]{2}\d{2} [A-Z]{3}/);
}
```

**Limitation:** `fromRegExp()` supports character classes, quantifiers, alternation, and
anchors but NOT lookaheads, backreferences, or named capture groups. Complex constraint
logic (e.g., "the year in the reference number must be within the last 3 years") requires
a wrapper that validates or regenerates the output.

### faker `helpers.weightedArrayElement()` — Distribution-Aware Test Data  [community]

`faker.helpers.weightedArrayElement(values)` selects a random element from an array
where each element has an explicit `weight` — higher weight means higher probability of
selection. This is essential when your test suite needs a realistic distribution of
data states rather than a uniform one.

**Why it matters:** In a realistic order dataset, 70% of orders are `completed`, 20%
are `pending`, and 10% are `cancelled`. A factory using `faker.helpers.arrayElement()`
gives each state equal probability — producing a test population where one third of
orders are cancelled, which is unrealistic. This can hide bugs that only manifest in
production where `completed` orders dominate.

```typescript
// factories/order.factory.ts
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

type OrderStatus = 'completed' | 'pending' | 'cancelled' | 'refunded';

// buildOrderStatus() — reflects real production distribution
export function buildOrderStatus(): OrderStatus {
  return faker.helpers.weightedArrayElement<OrderStatus>([
    { weight: 70, value: 'completed' },   // 70% of orders complete successfully
    { weight: 20, value: 'pending' },      // 20% are still in progress
    { weight: 7,  value: 'cancelled' },    // 7% are cancelled by users
    { weight: 3,  value: 'refunded' },     // 3% result in refunds
  ]);
}

// buildSubscriptionTier() — freemium distribution
type Tier = 'free' | 'pro' | 'enterprise';
export function buildSubscriptionTier(): Tier {
  return faker.helpers.weightedArrayElement<Tier>([
    { weight: 80, value: 'free' },
    { weight: 15, value: 'pro' },
    { weight: 5,  value: 'enterprise' },
  ]);
}

// In a buildList() scenario — generates 100 orders with realistic status distribution
// (approximately 70 completed, 20 pending, 7 cancelled, 3 refunded)
export function buildOrderList(count: number) {
  return faker.helpers.multiple(
    () => ({ id: faker.string.uuid(), status: buildOrderStatus() }),
    { count }
  );
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Weighted distributions make tests non-deterministic at the status level.
If a specific test needs to cover the rare `refunded` case reliably, use an explicit
override (`buildOrder({ status: 'refunded' })`) rather than relying on weighted selection
— treat weighted selection only for population-level statistics tests.

### faker `helpers.multiple()` — Bulk Factory Generation  [community]

`faker.helpers.multiple(fn, { count })` calls a generator function `count` times and
returns an array. It replaces hand-rolled `Array.from({ length: n }, () => buildFoo())`
patterns and integrates naturally with seed-based reproducibility since the internal
loop is deterministic given a fixed `faker.seed()`.

**Why it matters:** Bulk data generation for performance tests, pagination tests, and
aggregate query tests is a common need. `helpers.multiple()` is the canonical faker
v8.4+ way to express this intent without a utility function.

```typescript
// factories/bulk-factories.ts
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';
import { buildUser } from './user.factory';
import { buildProduct } from './product.factory';

// Generate a list of N users for pagination tests
export function buildUserList(count: number) {
  return faker.helpers.multiple(() => buildUser(), { count });
}

// Seeded bulk generation — same count + seed always produces same data
// Useful for snapshot tests that assert on collections
export function buildDeterministicProductList(count: number, seed = 42) {
  faker.seed(seed);
  return faker.helpers.multiple(
    () => ({
      id: faker.string.uuid(),
      name: faker.commerce.productName(),
      priceCents: faker.number.int({ min: 100, max: 99_900 }),
      category: faker.commerce.department(),
    }),
    { count }
  );
  // Always returns the same products for a given seed — safe for snapshot assertions
}

// Mixed-count generation for table tests
// Generates the data shapes needed for each row in a test.each table
export function buildTestEachData<T>(
  factory: () => T,
  labels: string[],
): Array<[string, T]> {
  return labels.map(label => [label, factory()]);
}
```

### faker `food` Module — Dietary and Restaurant Test Scenarios  [community]

`faker.food` (introduced in faker v9.1 and expanded in v10.x) provides realistic food
data for applications involving dietary preferences, restaurant management, menus, and
food delivery services. Relevant additions in v10.4: plant-based ingredient lists,
extended Finnish food locale, and `faker.food.ethnicCategory()`.

**Why it matters:** Before the `food` module, factories for food-domain applications
resorted to `faker.word.noun()` or hardcoded arrays for ingredient names — producing
test data that doesn't look like food. Realistic food data catches bugs in UI rendering
(long ingredient names, special characters in dish descriptions, allergy labels).

```typescript
// factories/menu.factory.ts — using faker.food for restaurant/food-delivery apps
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

type DietaryLabel = 'vegan' | 'vegetarian' | 'gluten-free' | 'halal' | 'kosher' | 'none';

export function buildMenuItem() {
  const ingredientCount = faker.number.int({ min: 2, max: 8 });
  return {
    id: faker.string.uuid(),
    name: faker.food.dish(),                           // "Margherita Pizza", "Pad Thai"
    description: faker.food.description(),             // realistic dish description
    ingredients: faker.helpers.multiple(
      () => faker.food.ingredient(),                   // "Basil", "Coconut Milk", "Tahini"
      { count: ingredientCount }
    ),
    spiceLevel: faker.number.int({ min: 0, max: 5 }),
    dietaryLabel: faker.helpers.weightedArrayElement<DietaryLabel>([
      { weight: 60, value: 'none' },
      { weight: 15, value: 'vegetarian' },
      { weight: 10, value: 'vegan' },
      { weight: 8,  value: 'gluten-free' },
      { weight: 4,  value: 'halal' },
      { weight: 3,  value: 'kosher' },
    ]),
    allergens: faker.helpers.arrayElements(
      ['nuts', 'dairy', 'gluten', 'shellfish', 'eggs', 'soy'],
      { min: 0, max: 3 }
    ),
    priceCents: faker.number.int({ min: 500, max: 4500 }),
  };
}

export function buildMenu(itemCount = 12) {
  return {
    restaurantId: faker.string.uuid(),
    name: `${faker.food.ethnicCategory()} Kitchen`,   // "Italian Kitchen", "Thai Kitchen"
    currency: 'USD',
    items: faker.helpers.multiple(() => buildMenuItem(), { count: itemCount }),
  };
}
```

### drizzle-seed — Schema-Driven Declarative Database Seeding  [community]

`drizzle-seed` (part of the Drizzle ORM ecosystem, stable as of 2025) generates test
data directly from Drizzle schema definitions. Unlike manually maintained factory
functions, `drizzle-seed` derives column types, constraints, and relationships from
the schema — meaning it stays in sync with migrations automatically.

**Why it matters:** When you add a non-nullable column to a Drizzle schema, manually
maintained factories break at runtime (missing required field). With `drizzle-seed`, the
seeder regenerates from the updated schema definition — no factory update required.
This reduces the factory maintenance burden on teams that iterate rapidly on the schema.

```typescript
// db/test-seeder.ts — drizzle-seed schema-driven seeding for integration tests
import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/node-postgres';
import { seed, reset } from 'drizzle-seed';
import * as schema from './schema';

const db = drizzle(process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL!);

// Seed with default auto-generated data (derived from schema types and constraints)
export async function seedTestDatabase(options?: {
  users?: number;
  products?: number;
  orders?: number;
}) {
  await seed(db, schema, {
    count: options?.users ?? 10,  // default 10 of each entity
  });
}

// Seed with refinements — override specific columns with custom generators
export async function seedWithRefinements() {
  await seed(db, schema).refine(f => ({
    users: {
      count: 20,
      columns: {
        // Override email with a custom pattern to ensure uniqueness in tests
        email: f.email(),
        status: f.valuesFromArray({
          values: ['active', 'suspended', 'pending'],
          isUnique: false,
        }),
        createdAt: f.date({ minDate: '2024-01-01', maxDate: '2026-01-01' }),
      },
    },
    products: {
      count: 50,
      columns: {
        priceCents: f.int({ minValue: 100, maxValue: 99_900 }),
        inStock: f.boolean({ probability: 0.85 }),  // 85% in stock
      },
    },
  }));
}

// Reset test database between test runs (truncates all seeded tables)
export async function resetTestDatabase() {
  await reset(db, schema);
}
```

**Vitest integration — global setup and teardown:**

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — run seed/reset around integration test suite
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    globalSetup: './db/vitest-global-setup.ts',
  },
});

// db/vitest-global-setup.ts
import { seedTestDatabase, resetTestDatabase } from './test-seeder';

export async function setup() {
  await seedTestDatabase({ users: 20, products: 100, orders: 50 });
}

export async function teardown() {
  await resetTestDatabase();
}
```

**Tradeoff vs factory functions:** `drizzle-seed` works best for integration tests that
need a populated database baseline. For unit tests and tests requiring precise control
over specific field values, explicit factory functions (`buildUser({ status: 'suspended' })`)
remain more expressive. Use both: `drizzle-seed` for baseline population, factory functions
for test-specific scenarios.

### Vitest `toMatchFileSnapshot()` — Golden-File Test Data Contracts  [community]

`expect(output).toMatchFileSnapshot(filepath)` (Vitest 1.x+) compares serialised output
against an on-disk file and updates it when run with `--update`. Unlike `toMatchSnapshot()`
(which stores snapshots in `__snapshots__/` `.snap` files), `toMatchFileSnapshot()` stores
each snapshot in a named file with a human-readable extension — making it reviewable in
pull requests without decoding Vitest's snapshot format.

**Why it matters for test data:** Golden-file snapshots are the ideal contract test for
factory output. They assert that a factory's shape is stable across refactors, that schema
migrations haven't silently dropped fields, and that serialised API response fixtures
still match the expected structure. The external file format (JSON, HTML, XML) means
reviewers can read the diff directly.

```typescript
// tests/factories/user-factory.contract.test.ts
// Contract test: asserts the shape of buildUser() output is stable
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { buildUser, buildUserWithAddress } from '../../factories/user.factory';

// Use a fixed seed to make the snapshot deterministic
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

describe('UserFactory contract', () => {
  it('buildUser() shape matches golden file', async () => {
    faker.seed(1234);  // fixed seed — always produces the same data
    const user = buildUser();

    // Stored in tests/factories/__snapshots__/user-shape.json
    // Committed to VCS — diff is visible in PRs
    await expect(JSON.stringify(user, null, 2)).toMatchFileSnapshot(
      './__snapshots__/user-shape.json'
    );
  });

  it('buildUserWithAddress() shape matches golden file', async () => {
    faker.seed(5678);
    const userWithAddress = buildUserWithAddress();

    await expect(JSON.stringify(userWithAddress, null, 2)).toMatchFileSnapshot(
      './__snapshots__/user-with-address-shape.json'
    );
  });
});
```

**Golden file update workflow:**
```bash
# Update all golden files after intentional schema change
npx vitest run --update tests/factories/

# In CI — golden file mismatch fails the build (do NOT pass --update in CI)
npx vitest run tests/factories/
```

**Tradeoff:** Golden-file snapshots are brittle for randomly-generated data (without
`faker.seed()`). Always pair `toMatchFileSnapshot()` with a fixed `faker.seed()` call
immediately before the factory call to ensure the snapshot is deterministic.

### TypeScript Discriminated Union Factory Type Guards  [community]

When a domain entity has a discriminated union type (e.g., `PaymentMethod` is either
a `CardPayment` or a `BankTransferPayment`), factories should produce type-narrowed
instances and TypeScript tests can use the union discriminant as a type guard. This
pattern enforces that test data is typed at the narrowed level — preventing tests from
accessing `card.last4` on a `BankTransferPayment`.

**Why it matters:** Generic `Partial<PaymentMethod>` overrides allow callers to set
`type: 'card'` but accidentally omit `last4` — which TypeScript can't catch without
narrowing. Discriminated union factories make the type contract explicit and enable
exhaustive branch tests that the TypeScript compiler verifies.

```typescript
// domain/payment.ts — discriminated union domain type
type CardPayment = {
  type: 'card';
  last4: string;
  expiryMonth: number;
  expiryYear: number;
  brand: 'visa' | 'mastercard' | 'amex';
};

type BankTransferPayment = {
  type: 'bank_transfer';
  accountNumberLast4: string;
  routingNumber: string;
  bankName: string;
};

type WalletPayment = {
  type: 'wallet';
  provider: 'paypal' | 'apple_pay' | 'google_pay';
  walletEmail?: string;
};

export type PaymentMethod = CardPayment | BankTransferPayment | WalletPayment;

// factories/payment-method.factory.ts
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';
import type { PaymentMethod, CardPayment, BankTransferPayment, WalletPayment } from '../domain/payment';

export function buildCardPayment(overrides: Partial<CardPayment> = {}): CardPayment {
  return {
    type: 'card',   // discriminant is always 'card' — never overridable
    last4: faker.finance.creditCardNumber('####'),
    expiryMonth: faker.number.int({ min: 1, max: 12 }),
    expiryYear: faker.number.int({ min: 2026, max: 2031 }),
    brand: faker.helpers.arrayElement(['visa', 'mastercard', 'amex'] as const),
    ...overrides,
  };
}

export function buildBankTransferPayment(
  overrides: Partial<BankTransferPayment> = {}
): BankTransferPayment {
  return {
    type: 'bank_transfer',
    accountNumberLast4: faker.finance.accountNumber(4),
    routingNumber: faker.finance.routingNumber(),
    bankName: faker.company.name(),
    ...overrides,
  };
}

export function buildWalletPayment(
  overrides: Partial<WalletPayment> = {}
): WalletPayment {
  return {
    type: 'wallet',
    provider: faker.helpers.arrayElement(['paypal', 'apple_pay', 'google_pay'] as const),
    walletEmail: faker.internet.email(),
    ...overrides,
  };
}

// Exhaustive switch — TypeScript forces you to handle ALL union members
export function describePaymentMethod(pm: PaymentMethod): string {
  switch (pm.type) {
    case 'card':
      return `Card ending in ${pm.last4}`;          // TS knows pm.last4 exists here
    case 'bank_transfer':
      return `Bank transfer (${pm.bankName})`;      // TS knows pm.bankName exists here
    case 'wallet':
      return `Wallet via ${pm.provider}`;           // TS knows pm.provider exists here
    // No default — TypeScript verifies exhaustion at compile time
  }
}
```

**Exhaustive test pattern using the discriminant:**
```typescript
// tests/payment-method.test.ts
import { buildCardPayment, buildBankTransferPayment, buildWalletPayment } from '../factories/payment-method.factory';

describe.each([
  ['card',          () => buildCardPayment()],
  ['bank_transfer', () => buildBankTransferPayment()],
  ['wallet',        () => buildWalletPayment()],
] as const)('PaymentMethod: %s', (type, factory) => {
  it('serialises to JSON without undefined fields', () => {
    const pm = factory();
    expect(pm.type).toBe(type);
    expect(JSON.stringify(pm)).not.toContain('undefined');
  });
});
```

### GDPR-Safe Test Data — Pseudonymization and Anonymization Patterns  [community]

GDPR Article 4(5) defines pseudonymisation as replacing direct identifiers (name, email,
national ID) with pseudonyms that can be reversed only with a separately held key.
For test data, *anonymisation* (irreversible) is preferred — test environments should
never hold real PII, even in pseudonymised form.

**The correct approach:** Generate fully synthetic data using `@faker-js/faker` for all
PII fields. If test data originates from production exports, apply a scrubbing step
before it enters the test environment.

**Why it matters:** GDPR Article 83 fines reach 4% of global annual turnover for PII
leaks via improperly sanitised test environments. Several high-profile data breaches
originated from leaked staging or test databases containing production-copied data.

```typescript
// utils/pii-scrubber.ts — anonymise production exports before they enter test environments
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';
import { createHash } from 'crypto';

type UserRecord = {
  id: string;
  email: string;
  firstName: string;
  lastName: string;
  phoneNumber: string;
  ipAddress: string;
  dateOfBirth: string;
};

// Deterministic anonymisation: same input ID always produces same fake PII
// Useful when FK relationships must remain consistent across tables
function deterministicSeed(id: string): number {
  const hash = createHash('sha256').update(id).digest('hex');
  return parseInt(hash.slice(0, 8), 16);  // first 8 hex chars as a 32-bit integer
}

export function scrubUserRecord(real: UserRecord): UserRecord {
  faker.seed(deterministicSeed(real.id));  // same ID → same fake data → FK consistency
  return {
    id: real.id,  // preserve ID for FK references
    email: faker.internet.email(),
    firstName: faker.person.firstName(),
    lastName: faker.person.lastName(),
    phoneNumber: faker.phone.number(),
    ipAddress: faker.internet.ipv4(),
    // Age-preserve DOB: keep the year to maintain age-related business rules,
    // but randomise month/day to prevent re-identification
    dateOfBirth: `${new Date(real.dateOfBirth).getFullYear()}-${
      String(faker.number.int({ min: 1, max: 12 })).padStart(2, '0')
    }-${String(faker.number.int({ min: 1, max: 28 })).padStart(2, '0')}`,
  };
}

// Bulk scrub — process a production export batch
export function scrubUserBatch(records: UserRecord[]): UserRecord[] {
  return records.map(scrubUserRecord);
}
```

**Automation: scrub at pipeline boundary, not at test time:**
```typescript
// scripts/prepare-test-data.ts — run as a pre-test-run step in CI
// Input: production-exported users.json (from a secure staging extract)
// Output: scrubbed-users.json committed to test fixtures (no real PII)
import { readFileSync, writeFileSync } from 'fs';
import { scrubUserBatch } from './pii-scrubber';

const raw: UserRecord[] = JSON.parse(readFileSync('./export/users.json', 'utf-8'));
const scrubbed = scrubUserBatch(raw);
writeFileSync('./test/fixtures/users.json', JSON.stringify(scrubbed, null, 2));
console.log(`[pii-scrubber] Scrubbed ${raw.length} records — no PII in output`);
```

**Anti-pattern checklist — test data PII violations:**
| Anti-pattern | Risk | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Copying prod DB to test env | GDPR violation — full PII exposure | Use `scrubUserBatch()` first |
| Using real employee emails in fixtures | Internal PII leak | Use `faker.internet.email()` |
| Storing real phone numbers in CI env vars | PII in logs/artifacts | Use `faker.phone.number()` |
| Hardcoded "real-looking" names (e.g. `John Smith`) | May match real person | Use `faker.person.fullName()` |
| Commit `users.json` from prod export | Git history PII leak | Commit only scrubbed output |

### fishery Trait-Based Factory Composition with `afterCreate` Hooks  [community]

fishery v2.x supports **traits** via factory subclassing — reusable named variants of
a factory expressed as methods that return a new factory configured for that variant.
Combined with `afterCreate` hooks, traits can set up relational data (e.g., creating
child records) that depend on the parent entity's resolved `id`.

**Why it matters:** Without traits, tests that need a "premium subscribed user with
billing address" duplicate override objects across many test files. A trait centralises
that configuration, and the `afterCreate` hook ensures the related billing record is
created atomically.

```typescript
// factories/user.factory.ts — fishery Factory subclass with traits and afterCreate
import { Factory, type DeepPartialObject } from 'fishery';
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';
import type { User, Subscription, BillingAddress } from '../domain';
import { db } from '../db';

class UserFactory extends Factory<User> {
  // Trait: suspended user — status is locked to 'suspended'
  suspended() {
    return this.params({ status: 'suspended', suspendedAt: new Date() });
  }

  // Trait: premium user — overrides subscription tier and sets quota
  premium() {
    return this.params({ subscriptionTier: 'premium', storageQuotaGb: 100 });
  }

  // Trait: admin user — has admin flag and elevated permissions
  admin() {
    return this.params({ isAdmin: true, permissions: ['read', 'write', 'delete', 'admin'] });
  }

  // Compound trait: premium admin — chains two traits
  premiumAdmin() {
    return this.premium().admin();
  }

  // Trait with afterCreate: pro user WITH billing address (created in DB after user insert)
  withBillingAddress(addressOverrides: DeepPartialObject<BillingAddress> = {}) {
    return this.afterCreate(async (user) => {
      await db.billingAddresses.create({
        userId: user.id,           // uses the resolved user.id from the just-created row
        street: faker.location.streetAddress(),
        city: faker.location.city(),
        country: faker.location.countryCode(),
        ...addressOverrides,
      });
    });
  }
}

export const userFactory = UserFactory.define(({ sequence }) => ({
  id: faker.string.uuid(),
  email: faker.internet.email(),
  firstName: faker.person.firstName(),
  lastName: faker.person.lastName(),
  status: 'active' as const,
  isAdmin: false,
  subscriptionTier: 'free' as const,
  storageQuotaGb: 5,
  permissions: ['read'] as string[],
  createdAt: faker.date.past(),
  sequence,  // auto-incrementing number for unique sequences
}));

// Usage
const suspendedUser   = await userFactory.suspended().create();
const premiumAdmin    = await userFactory.premiumAdmin().create();
const userWithBilling = await userFactory.premium().withBillingAddress({ country: 'DE' }).create();
```

**`afterCreate` ordering rule:** Multiple `afterCreate` hooks are executed in definition
order, after `onCreate`. If your factory has both a `withBillingAddress` `afterCreate` and
a global `afterCreate` in the base factory, the global one runs first — which can matter
if the `withBillingAddress` hook reads data that the global hook sets up.

### Playwright `page.requests()` — Asserting Factory-Driven API Requests  [community]

`page.requests()` (Playwright v1.56+) returns an array of `Request` objects for all
network requests made since the page was created (or since the last navigation). It is
the complement to `page.responses()` — and together they let you assert that the
factory-seeded test data caused exactly the expected API calls.

**Why it matters:** When a test seeds a user with `status: 'suspended'`, the assertion
`await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="blocked"]')).toBeVisible()` only verifies the
UI output. `page.requests()` lets you additionally verify that the checkout API call was
*not* made (the front-end correctly blocked it pre-request) — a tighter assertion that
catches bugs where the UI shows an error but still submits the form.

```typescript
// specs/checkout-blocked.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { userFactory } from '../factories/user.factory';
import { seedTestUser } from '../fixtures/db-seed';

test('suspended user sees blocked message and no checkout API call is made', async ({ page }) => {
  // Arrange: seed a suspended user via factory
  const user = await userFactory.suspended().create();
  await seedTestUser(user);

  // Act: log in and attempt checkout
  await page.goto('/login');
  await page.fill('[data-testid="email"]', user.email);
  await page.fill('[data-testid="password"]', 'test-password-123');
  await page.click('[data-testid="submit"]');
  await page.goto('/checkout');

  // Assert UI: blocked message visible
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="account-suspended"]')).toBeVisible();

  // Assert network: no POST to /api/checkout was made
  // page.requests() returns ALL requests since page creation
  const checkoutRequests = page.requests()
    .filter(r => r.url().includes('/api/checkout') && r.method() === 'POST');

  expect(checkoutRequests).toHaveLength(0);  // factory-seeded status blocked the request
});
```

**Combining with `page.consoleMessages()` and `page.pageErrors()`** (also v1.56+):
```typescript
// Assert no JS errors occurred while processing factory-generated data
const errors = page.pageErrors();
expect(errors).toHaveLength(0);

// Assert a specific factory-triggered analytics event was logged to console
const consoleMsgs = page.consoleMessages()
  .filter(m => m.text().includes('analytics:checkout_blocked'));
expect(consoleMsgs).toHaveLength(1);
```

### fast-check `fc.record()` — Property-Based Factory Testing  [community]

`fc.record(recordModel)` (fast-check) generates objects matching a structure where each
key is an independent `Arbitrary`. Combined with Vitest's `test.prop()` integration
(via `@fast-check/vitest`), it enables *property-based testing* — testing invariants
across a space of inputs rather than a set of hand-crafted examples.

**Why it matters:** A factory might be wrong about what constitutes a valid `User`. If
`buildUser()` always sets `email` to a valid RFC 5322 email, tests that use the factory
never exercise what happens with an empty string or a malformed email. Property-based
tests with `fc.record()` expose these blind spots.

```typescript
// tests/user-validation.prop.test.ts — property-based test using fast-check + Vitest
import { describe, it } from 'vitest';
import { test as fcTest } from '@fast-check/vitest';
import fc from 'fast-check';
import { validateUser } from '../domain/user-validation';

// Property: any record with a non-empty email and a valid status always passes validation
fcTest.prop([
  fc.record({
    id: fc.uuidV(4),
    email: fc.emailAddress(),              // fast-check generates valid RFC emails
    firstName: fc.string({ minLength: 1, maxLength: 50 }),
    lastName: fc.string({ minLength: 1, maxLength: 50 }),
    status: fc.constantFrom('active', 'suspended', 'pending'),
    createdAt: fc.date({ min: new Date('2020-01-01') }),
  }),
])('valid user records always pass validateUser()', (user) => {
  const result = validateUser(user);
  expect(result.valid).toBe(true);
});

// Property: any record with an empty email always fails validation
fcTest.prop([
  fc.record({
    id: fc.uuidV(4),
    email: fc.constant(''),               // always empty string
    firstName: fc.string({ minLength: 1 }),
    lastName: fc.string({ minLength: 1 }),
    status: fc.constantFrom('active', 'suspended'),
    createdAt: fc.date(),
  }),
])('empty email always fails validateUser()', (user) => {
  const result = validateUser(user);
  expect(result.valid).toBe(false);
  expect(result.errors).toContain('email: required');
});

// Property: validateUser() is idempotent — calling it twice returns the same result
fcTest.prop([
  fc.record({
    id: fc.uuidV(4),
    email: fc.emailAddress(),
    firstName: fc.string({ minLength: 1 }),
    lastName: fc.string({ minLength: 1 }),
    status: fc.constantFrom('active', 'suspended', 'pending'),
    createdAt: fc.date(),
  }),
])('validateUser() is idempotent', (user) => {
  const result1 = validateUser(user);
  const result2 = validateUser(user);
  expect(result1).toEqual(result2);
});
```

**Tradeoff vs example-based factories:** Property-based tests explore the *input space*
but don't produce readable "story" tests. Use example-based factories
(`buildUser({ status: 'suspended' })`) for business-rule documentation and property-based
tests for invariant verification. They are complementary, not competing.

### Lazy-Evaluation Async Factory — Deferred Expensive Test Data  [community]

Some test data is expensive to generate (database inserts, network calls, image
processing). When a factory always eagerly creates the data in `beforeEach`, tests that
don't need it pay the creation cost anyway. A lazy factory defers creation to the first
access — and caches the result for subsequent accesses within the same test.

**Why it matters:** In a test suite with 50 tests where only 10 need a full user hierarchy
(user + subscription + 3 child accounts), eager creation wastes 40× the DB insert cost.
Lazy factories make the opt-in cost explicit.

```typescript
// factories/lazy-factory.ts — deferred factory creation pattern
type LazyFactory<T> = {
  get: () => Promise<T>;
  reset: () => void;
};

export function lazyFactory<T>(factory: () => Promise<T>): LazyFactory<T> {
  let cached: Promise<T> | null = null;

  return {
    get: () => {
      if (!cached) {
        cached = factory();
      }
      return cached;
    },
    reset: () => {
      cached = null;
    },
  };
}

// Usage in a test file
import { userFactory } from '../factories/user.factory';
import { lazyFactory } from '../factories/lazy-factory';

// Declared once per describe block — only created if a test calls .get()
const lazyAdmin = lazyFactory(async () => {
  const user = await userFactory.admin().create();
  // Expensive: also creates subscription, billing, permissions records
  await setupAdminPermissions(user.id);
  return user;
});

describe('admin dashboard', () => {
  afterEach(() => lazyAdmin.reset());  // clear cache between tests to prevent leakage

  it('admin sees user management panel', async ({ page }) => {
    const admin = await lazyAdmin.get();  // created on first call only
    await loginAs(page, admin);
    await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="user-management"]')).toBeVisible();
  });

  it('unauthenticated user does not see admin panel', async ({ page }) => {
    // admin is NOT called here — no DB insert happens
    await page.goto('/admin');
    await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="login-redirect"]')).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```

### Worker-Scoped Parallel DB Seeding with Playwright Fixtures  [community]

In Playwright's parallel execution model, each worker process is independent. Worker-scoped
fixtures (`scope: 'worker'`) run once per worker — making them ideal for expensive
database seeding that is shared across all tests in that worker, but isolated from
other workers. This pattern avoids both the overhead of per-test DB seeding and the
data-leakage risk of a single shared global seed.

**Why it matters:** Per-test DB seeding (in `beforeEach`) is correct but slow for
suites with 100+ tests. A single global seed (in `globalSetup`) is fast but creates
cross-worker data sharing that causes flakiness. Worker-scoped seeding is the middle
ground: each worker seeds its own isolated data set once, and all tests in that worker
share it safely (they all run in the same worker process, sequentially).

```typescript
// fixtures/worker-db.fixture.ts — worker-scoped database seeding
import { test as base, WorkerInfo } from '@playwright/test';
import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/node-postgres';
import { seed, reset } from 'drizzle-seed';
import * as schema from '../../db/schema';

type WorkerDbFixtures = {
  workerDb: ReturnType<typeof drizzle>;
  seededWorkerData: {
    users: { id: string; email: string }[];
    products: { id: string; name: string }[];
  };
};

export const test = base.extend<{}, WorkerDbFixtures>({
  // worker-scoped: created once per Playwright worker, torn down when worker exits
  workerDb: [async ({}, use, workerInfo: WorkerInfo) => {
    // Each worker gets its own schema (schema_worker_0, schema_worker_1, …)
    const workerSchema = `test_worker_${workerInfo.workerIndex}`;
    const db = drizzle(`${process.env.TEST_DB_BASE_URL}/${workerSchema}`);
    await use(db);
    // Teardown: clean up this worker's schema when the worker exits
    await reset(db, schema);
  }, { scope: 'worker' }],

  seededWorkerData: [async ({ workerDb }, use, workerInfo: WorkerInfo) => {
    // Seed using deterministic seed based on worker index — reproducible but isolated
    const workerSeed = 1000 + workerInfo.workerIndex;
    await seed(workerDb, schema, { seed: workerSeed, count: 30 });

    const users = await workerDb.select().from(schema.users).limit(30);
    const products = await workerDb.select().from(schema.products).limit(30);

    await use({ users, products });
  }, { scope: 'worker' }],
});

// specs/product-list.spec.ts — uses worker-seeded data
import { test } from '../fixtures/worker-db.fixture';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('product list shows seeded products', async ({ page, seededWorkerData }) => {
  await page.goto('/products');
  // Worker's seeded products are visible — other workers have their own isolated set
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="product-item"]'))
    .toHaveCount(seededWorkerData.products.length);
});
```

### MSW v2.14 `ws.onUpgrade()` — Node.js WebSocket Upgrade Handler  [community]

`ws.onUpgrade(handler)` (MSW v2.14.0) intercepts HTTP-to-WebSocket upgrade requests in
Node.js (server-side / Vitest) before a connection is established. This enables test data
injection *at the handshake level* — rejecting connections based on auth headers,
injecting mock session data into the upgrade response, or routing different upgrade
requests to different mock WebSocket servers.

**Why it matters:** `ws.link()` (the existing MSW WS API) intercepts *messages* after
a connection is established. `ws.onUpgrade()` operates at the HTTP upgrade layer —
allowing you to test authentication checks that happen before the WebSocket connection
is accepted, and to set connection-level metadata (e.g., session tokens passed as
query parameters in the upgrade URL).

```typescript
// mocks/websocket-handlers.ts — upgrade-level authentication test data injection
import { ws } from 'msw';
import { setupServer } from 'msw/node';

const chatWs = ws.link('ws://localhost:3001/chat');

const handlers = [
  // Intercept upgrade requests — reject unauthenticated connections at the handshake
  chatWs.onUpgrade((upgradeRequest) => {
    const token = new URL(upgradeRequest.url).searchParams.get('token');

    if (!token || token === 'invalid-token') {
      // Reject the upgrade — client will receive HTTP 401 instead of 101 Switching Protocols
      return new Response('Unauthorized', { status: 401 });
    }
    // Return undefined (or nothing) to allow the upgrade to proceed
  }),

  // After upgrade succeeds — intercept messages as usual
  chatWs.addEventListener('connection', ({ client }) => {
    client.addEventListener('message', ({ data }) => {
      const parsed = JSON.parse(data as string);
      if (parsed.type === 'join_room') {
        // Send factory-generated room state to the client
        client.send(JSON.stringify({
          type: 'room_state',
          members: [
            { id: 'user-1', name: 'Alice', online: true },
            { id: 'user-2', name: 'Bob',   online: false },
          ],
        }));
      }
    });
  }),
];

export const server = setupServer(...handlers);
```

**`onUpgrade` vs `link` — when to use each:**

| Need | API |
|---|---|
| Test auth checks before connection | `ws.onUpgrade()` — runs at HTTP upgrade |
| Test message-level behaviour | `ws.link()` + `addEventListener('connection')` |
| Test reconnection logic | `ws.link()` + `client.close()` in handler |
| Test subprotocol negotiation | `webSocketRoute.protocols()` (Playwright) |

**Important:** `ws.onUpgrade()` is **not available in browser/service worker context**
(MSW browser runtime does not intercept upgrade requests at the HTTP level). It is
Node.js-only (Vitest, Jest, integration tests). [community]

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 23

**44. [community] `faker.helpers.fromRegExp()` with anchored patterns (`^$`) generates
the literal characters `^` and `$` rather than treating them as anchors.**

`fromRegExp()` does not strip regex anchors — it treats `^` and `$` as literal characters
to include in the output. A pattern like `new RegExp('^[A-Z]{3}$')` will produce strings
that include literal caret and dollar sign characters (e.g., `"^ABC$"`), not a clean
three-uppercase-letter string.

Fix: always pass unanchored patterns to `fromRegExp()`:
```typescript
// WRONG — anchors become literal characters in output
faker.helpers.fromRegExp(/^[A-Z]{3}$/)  // → "^ABC$"

// CORRECT — remove anchors; fromRegExp() always generates a full match
faker.helpers.fromRegExp(/[A-Z]{3}/)    // → "ABC"
```

**45. [community] drizzle-seed `seed()` is not idempotent — calling it twice without
`reset()` first duplicates rows rather than replacing them.**

`seed(db, schema)` inserts new rows on each call. It does not check for existing data
or truncate tables first. In a Vitest global setup that calls `seed()` without a
preceding `reset()`, a second test run (without restarting the process) doubles all
seed data — causing `UNIQUE constraint` failures on seeded emails and IDs.

Fix: always call `reset(db, schema)` before `seed()` in global setup:
```typescript
// vitest-global-setup.ts — always reset before seeding
export async function setup() {
  await reset(db, schema);   // ← required; otherwise duplicates accumulate
  await seed(db, schema, { count: 30 });
}
```

**46. [community] `faker.seed()` state is shared across the module — seeding in one
factory affects the sequence of all subsequent factories in the same test run.**

`faker.seed(N)` sets the global faker instance's seed. If `buildDeterministicProduct()`
calls `faker.seed(42)` and then `buildDeterministicUser()` is called *immediately after*,
the user factory inherits the post-product state of the PRNG — not a fresh seed. Only
the first factory after `seed()` is guaranteed to produce the seeded sequence.

Fix: either use `faker.seed()` at the test level (before all factory calls in the test),
or create a dedicated `Faker` instance per factory:
```typescript
import { Faker, en } from '@faker-js/faker';

// Dedicated instance — does not affect the global faker instance
const productFaker = new Faker({ locale: [en] });
productFaker.seed(42);
```

**47. [community] fishery `afterCreate` hooks do NOT run when `build()` is called — only
when `create()` is called.**

`afterCreate` runs only after the `onCreate` callback (the DB persistence step). Calling
`userFactory.withBillingAddress().build()` builds the user object in memory but never
triggers the billing address creation hook. Tests that verify relational data set up by
`afterCreate` must use `create()`, not `build()`.

This distinction matters in unit tests (which typically avoid DB calls): if a unit test
calls `.build()` expecting the full relational tree from `afterCreate` to be present,
the billing address will be `undefined` and the test assertion will silently fail with
a misleading error rather than a clear "billing address was not created" message.

**48. [community] `toMatchFileSnapshot()` in Vitest produces a diff of the FULL file
when any factory field changes — even one unrelated field — making PR reviews noisy on
large snapshot files.**

When a factory adds a new optional field with a default value, ALL tests using
`toMatchFileSnapshot()` for that factory will fail with a diff showing the new field.
On a large team, this creates a "snapshot churn" problem where every schema iteration
requires updating dozens of golden files in CI.

Fix: use field-specific inline snapshots for critical fields rather than snapshotting
the entire factory output:
```typescript
// More targeted than full-object toMatchFileSnapshot()
// Only assert the fields that matter for this contract
faker.seed(1234);
const user = buildUser();
expect(user.status).toBe('active');
expect(user.subscriptionTier).toBe('free');
expect(user.email).toMatchInlineSnapshot('"Colt.Simonis@yahoo.com"');
// Adding new fields to buildUser() does NOT break this assertion
```

| faker.js food module | Official | https://fakerjs.dev/api/food.html | `faker.food.dish()`, `faker.food.ingredient()`, `faker.food.ethnicCategory()` for realistic food-domain test data |
| MSW ws.onUpgrade() API | Official | https://mswjs.io/docs/api/ws | WebSocket upgrade-level HTTP interception for Node.js — auth rejection and connection-metadata injection before WS handshake |
| fast-check `fc.record()` for domain models | Official | https://fast-check.dev/docs/core-blocks/arbitraries/combiners/record/ | `fc.record(model)` — property-based factory generation for invariant testing across input spaces |
| Vitest `toMatchFileSnapshot()` | Official | https://vitest.dev/api/expect#tomatchfilesnapshot | Golden-file contract testing for factory output — human-readable external snapshot files that diff cleanly in PRs |

### faker `internet.jwt()` — Auth Token Test Data

`faker.internet.jwt(options?)` (added in faker v9.1) generates a syntactically valid
JSON Web Token containing a Base64URL-encoded header, payload, and a random signature.
The payload embeds `iat` (issued-at) and `exp` (expiry) timestamps, making it immediately
usable as a realistic auth token without running an actual signing key.

**Why it matters:** Tests that use hardcoded JWT strings (`"eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9..."`)
fail or produce misleading assertion diffs when the application reads claim values (e.g.,
`exp`, `sub`, `role`) from the token. `faker.internet.jwt()` lets you generate tokens
with controlled claim values so tests verify the correct business behaviour rather than
treating the token as an opaque string.

```typescript
// factories/auth.factory.ts
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

interface JwtClaims {
  sub?: string;
  role?: 'admin' | 'user' | 'guest';
  exp?: number;  // unix seconds
}

// Build a realistic Bearer token with controllable claims
export function buildJwt(claims: JwtClaims = {}): string {
  const now = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000);
  return faker.internet.jwt({
    header: { alg: 'HS256', typ: 'JWT' },
    payload: {
      sub:  claims.sub  ?? faker.string.uuid(),
      role: claims.role ?? 'user',
      iat:  now,
      exp:  claims.exp  ?? now + 3600,   // default: 1 hour
    },
  });
}

// Build an expired token — triggers 401 handling in the SUT
export function buildExpiredJwt(sub?: string): string {
  const past = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) - 7200; // 2 hours ago
  return faker.internet.jwt({
    payload: { sub: sub ?? faker.string.uuid(), iat: past - 3600, exp: past },
  });
}

// Usage in test
it('returns 401 when token is expired', async () => {
  const token = buildExpiredJwt();
  const response = await request(app)
    .get('/api/protected')
    .set('Authorization', `Bearer ${token}`);
  expect(response.status).toBe(401);
});
```

**Key limitation:** `faker.internet.jwt()` generates a token with a *random* signature
— it is NOT cryptographically valid. If your application verifies the signature (e.g.,
`jwt.verify(token, secret)`), the verification will fail. Use `jsonwebtoken.sign()`
or your auth library's signing function for tests that exercise the verification path.

### faker `string.ulid()` — Time-Ordered Identifier Test Data

`faker.string.ulid()` (added in faker v9.1, stable through v10.x) generates a Universally
Unique Lexicographically Sortable Identifier (ULID). Unlike UUID v4 (random), a ULID
encodes a 48-bit millisecond timestamp prefix, making it naturally sortable by creation
time.

**Why it matters for test data:** Applications that use ULIDs as primary keys derive
implicit ordering guarantees (e.g., pagination cursors, audit log queries ordered by
insertion time). Tests that use UUIDs as stand-ins for ULID fields break these ordering
invariants — pagination tests pass with random UUIDs locally but fail against real data
in CI where ordering matters.

```typescript
// factories/identifiers.factory.ts
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

// Build a ULID with a controlled timestamp — ensures deterministic ordering in tests
export function buildUlid(at: Date = new Date()): string {
  // faker.string.ulid() uses current time by default
  // Pass a seed time to produce a ULID that sorts correctly relative to others
  return faker.string.ulid(at.getTime());  // pass ms timestamp
}

// Build a sequence of ULIDs that are guaranteed to be in ascending order
export function buildUlidSequence(count: number, startDate = new Date()): string[] {
  return Array.from({ length: count }, (_, i) => {
    // Increment by 1ms per entry — ULIDs are ms-precision so this guarantees sort order
    const ms = startDate.getTime() + i;
    return faker.string.ulid(ms);
  });
}

// In a test — pagination that depends on insertion order
it('returns events in ULID order (most recent last)', async () => {
  const base = new Date('2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z');
  const ids = buildUlidSequence(3, base);  // ['01H...', '01H...', '01H...'] sorted asc

  // Seed the DB with events in the given order
  await Promise.all(ids.map((id, i) => createEvent({ id, payload: `event-${i}` })));

  const events = await getEventsAscending();
  expect(events.map(e => e.id)).toEqual(ids);  // strict order assertion
});
```

**ULID vs UUID v7 decision:**

| Criterion | ULID | UUID v7 |
|---|---|---|
| Standard | De-facto (unofficial spec) | IETF RFC 9562 (official) |
| Sortable | Yes — ms-precision prefix | Yes — ms-precision prefix |
| URL-safe | Yes — Crockford Base32 | No — hyphenated hex |
| DB index efficiency | High (B-tree friendly) | High (B-tree friendly) |
| Ecosystem support | `ulid` npm package | PostgreSQL 16 native |
| faker support | `faker.string.ulid()` | `faker.string.uuid({version: 7})` |

Use ULID when your codebase already uses the `ulid` npm package. Use UUID v7 when
targeting PostgreSQL 16+ or any runtime where `crypto.randomUUID()` is the foundation.

### Vitest `test.for()` — Data-Driven Test Data Tables

`test.for(cases)(name, fn)` (introduced in Vitest 3.x, refined in 4.x) is the idiomatic
Vitest approach for **data-driven testing**: running the same assertion over a table of
inputs and expected outputs. Unlike `test.each()`, `test.for()` preserves the array
structure and provides `TestContext` as the second callback argument — enabling
concurrent snapshot testing.

**Why it matters:** Data-table driven tests (ISTQB CTFL 4.0 Section 4.4 — "Decision
Table Testing") are a core test design technique. They express test conditions in tabular
form: each row is a test case, each column is a variable. `test.for()` maps directly onto
this model while keeping factory logic out of the test cases.

```typescript
// tests/pricing.test.ts
import { test, expect } from 'vitest';
import { buildUser }     from '../factories/user.factory';
import { calculatePrice } from '../src/pricing';

// Decision table: subscription tier × currency × expected price
const pricingTable = [
  { tier: 'free',    currency: 'USD', expected: 0 },
  { tier: 'basic',   currency: 'USD', expected: 9.99 },
  { tier: 'basic',   currency: 'EUR', expected: 9.49 },
  { tier: 'premium', currency: 'USD', expected: 29.99 },
  { tier: 'premium', currency: 'EUR', expected: 27.99 },
  { tier: 'premium', currency: 'GBP', expected: 24.99 },
] as const;

test.for(pricingTable)(
  'calculatePrice($tier, $currency) = $expected',
  async ({ tier, currency, expected }, { expect: localExpect }) => {
    // Build a factory-generated user with the given subscription tier
    const user = buildUser({ subscriptionTier: tier });
    const price = await calculatePrice(user, currency);
    localExpect(price).toBeCloseTo(expected, 2);
  }
);

// test.concurrent.for() — parallel execution with per-test expect context
// Snapshot testing works correctly because each test gets its own expect instance
test.concurrent.for([
  ['admin',   ['read', 'write', 'delete']],
  ['editor',  ['read', 'write']],
  ['viewer',  ['read']],
] as const)(
  '%s role permissions',
  ([role, perms], { expect: localExpect }) => {
    const user = buildUser({ role });
    const actual = getUserPermissions(user);
    // toMatchSnapshot() is safe with concurrent because localExpect is test-scoped
    localExpect(actual).toMatchSnapshot();
  }
);
```

**`test.for()` vs `test.each()` decision:**

| Need | Use |
|---|---|
| Spread array args into separate params | `test.each([[a, b, expected]])` |
| Access `TestContext` (fixtures, per-test `expect`) | `test.for([[a, b]])` |
| Concurrent snapshot tests | `test.concurrent.for()` — required for correctness |
| Template literal test names with `$variable` | Both — same interpolation syntax |

### Vitest 4.1 `test.aroundEach()` — Transaction-Scoped Test Data

`test.aroundEach(callback)` (Vitest 4.1) registers a hook that *wraps* each test — the
hook calls the provided `runTest` function to invoke the test itself. This enables
patterns like wrapping every test in a database transaction that is rolled back after
the assertion, providing automatic test data isolation without explicit teardown.

**Why it matters:** Transaction-rollback isolation is the cleanest strategy for
integration tests that write to a real database: the factory creates rows, the test
runs assertions, and the transaction is rolled back — leaving the database clean without
a `DELETE` or `TRUNCATE` step. `aroundEach` removes the boilerplate of
`beforeEach`/`afterEach` pairs that manage the transaction context.

```typescript
// vitest.setup.ts — applied globally via setupFiles
import { test as baseTest } from 'vitest';
import { db } from './src/db';

// Extend test with a transaction-wrapped database client
export const test = baseTest.extend({
  // tx: a Drizzle/Prisma transaction client — all factories use this inside the test
  tx: async ({}, use) => {
    await db.transaction(async (tx) => {
      await use(tx);
      // Vitest will call tx.rollback() when use() returns
      tx.rollback();
    });
  },
});

// Alternative: aroundEach for a global rollback without needing the fixture
// (applies to all tests in the file)
import { afterEach, beforeEach } from 'vitest';
let txContext: { rollback: () => Promise<void> } | null = null;

test.aroundEach(async (runTest, context) => {
  // Start a transaction before the test
  await db.transaction(async (tx) => {
    // Attach tx to the test context so factories can use it
    Object.assign(context, { db: tx });
    await runTest();
    // Explicit rollback — ensures the test data never hits the DB permanently
    tx.rollback();
  });
});

// In a test — factories create rows inside the rolled-back transaction
test('factory creates user in transaction', async ({ db: tx }) => {
  // Insert via factory; row exists only for this test's duration
  const user = await userFactory.create({ db: tx });
  const found = await tx.select().from(users).where(eq(users.id, user.id));
  expect(found).toHaveLength(1);
  // after test: tx.rollback() fires — 'found' row no longer exists in the real DB
});
```

**When to use `aroundEach` vs `beforeEach`/`afterEach`:**

| Pattern | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| `aroundEach` with tx rollback | One hook, clean lifecycle, no state bleed | Requires DB support for savepoints if tests nest transactions |
| `beforeEach` + `afterEach` pair | Widely understood | State leaks if `afterEach` throws before cleanup |
| `scope: 'file'` fixture with transaction | Reusable across test files | Must import custom `test` in every file |

### Vitest 4.1 `vi.defineHelper()` — Clean Factory Assertion Stack Traces

`vi.defineHelper(fn)` (Vitest 4.1) wraps a helper function so that its internal
implementation frames are stripped from stack traces. When a factory-based assertion
helper fails, the error points to the *caller* in the test file rather than to the
helper's internals — making failures immediately actionable without manual stack
trace archaeology.

**Why it matters:** As factory assertion helpers grow in sophistication (e.g.,
`expectValidOrder(order)` that checks 8 fields), stack traces become hard to read:
the error appears inside the helper rather than on the test line that called it.
`vi.defineHelper()` fixes this while keeping the helper DRY.

```typescript
// test-helpers/order-assertions.ts
import { vi, expect } from 'vitest';

// Without vi.defineHelper — stack trace shows line inside helper, not the test
export function assertValidOrder(order: Order) {
  expect(order.id).toBeDefined();
  expect(order.status).toMatch(/^(pending|completed|cancelled)$/);
  expect(order.items).toHaveLength.greaterThan(0);
  expect(order.total).toBeGreaterThan(0);
  expect(order.createdAt).toBeInstanceOf(Date);
}

// WITH vi.defineHelper — stack trace shows the test file line that called this
export const assertValidOrder = vi.defineHelper((order: Order) => {
  expect(order.id).toBeDefined();
  expect(order.status).toMatch(/^(pending|completed|cancelled)$/);
  expect(order.items.length).toBeGreaterThan(0);  // Note: .length for type safety
  expect(order.total).toBeGreaterThan(0);
  expect(order.createdAt).toBeInstanceOf(Date);
  // If ANY of these fail, the stack trace points to the test, not this helper
});

// Usage in test — failure message says "at test.ts:12" not "at order-assertions.ts:5"
test('buildOrder() produces a valid order', () => {
  const order = buildOrder({ status: 'pending' });
  assertValidOrder(order);   // ← stack trace points HERE on failure
});
```

**Composing helpers:** `vi.defineHelper()` can wrap helpers that call other helpers.
The outermost helper's call site is preserved in the trace:

```typescript
export const assertValidCheckout = vi.defineHelper((result: CheckoutResult) => {
  assertValidOrder(result.order);  // nested helper — outer call site is preserved
  expect(result.paymentId).toBeDefined();
});
```

### Vitest 4.1 Builder Pattern for `test.extend()` — Return-Based Fixtures

Vitest 4.1 introduces a **return-based fixture builder API** for `test.extend()`. Instead
of calling the `use()` callback, you return the fixture value directly. TypeScript infers
the fixture's type automatically from the return type — eliminating the need for explicit
generic type annotations on `test.extend<{ myFixture: MyType }>()`.

**Why it matters:** The `use()` callback pattern requires TypeScript generics to type
the fixture map, which creates verbose boilerplate for large factory fixture sets. The
return-based API is shorter, more readable, and lets TypeScript do the typing work.

```typescript
// fixtures/db-fixtures.ts — return-based fixture builder (Vitest 4.1+)
import { test as baseTest } from 'vitest';
import { PGlite } from '@electric-sql/pglite';

// .extend() with return — no use() callback, no explicit generic
export const test = baseTest
  // Simple value fixture — return the value directly
  .extend('testId', () => `test-${Math.random().toString(36).slice(2)}`)

  // Async fixture — return a Promise; resolved value becomes the fixture
  .extend('db', async () => {
    const db = new PGlite();
    await db.exec(schema);
    return db;   // ← return instead of use(db)
    // Teardown: use onCleanup for async cleanup (see below)
  })

  // Fixture with cleanup — use onCleanup instead of wrapping with try/finally
  .extend('seededDb', async ({ db }, { onCleanup }) => {
    await seed(db, { users: 10, orders: 30 });
    onCleanup(async () => {
      await reset(db);
    });
    return db;   // fixtures can depend on other fixtures via destructuring
  })

  // Fixture that depends on another fixture
  .extend('adminUser', async ({ seededDb }) => {
    const user = await seededDb.query.users.findFirst({
      where: (u, { eq }) => eq(u.role, 'admin'),
    });
    if (!user) throw new Error('No admin user in seeded DB');
    return user;  // TypeScript infers: { id: string; email: string; role: 'admin'; ... }
  });

// In a test — TypeScript knows the types without any explicit annotation
test('admin can delete any order', async ({ adminUser, seededDb }) => {
  const order = await seededDb.query.orders.findFirst();
  const result = await deleteOrder(seededDb, adminUser.id, order!.id);
  expect(result.deleted).toBe(true);
});
```

**Migration from `use()` callback pattern:**

```typescript
// Old pattern (Vitest < 4.1)
export const test = baseTest.extend<{ db: PGlite }>({
  db: async ({}, use) => {
    const db = new PGlite();
    await db.exec(schema);
    await use(db);
    await reset(db);  // teardown after use()
  },
});

// New pattern (Vitest 4.1)
export const test = baseTest
  .extend('db', async ({}, { onCleanup }) => {
    const db = new PGlite();
    await db.exec(schema);
    onCleanup(() => reset(db));  // teardown registered separately
    return db;
  });
```

### Playwright HAR Replay as Self-Initialising Fake for E2E Test Data

Playwright's `routeFromHAR()` implements the **Self-Initialising Fake** pattern (Fowler)
for E2E test data: on first run against a real backend, all API responses are recorded
into an HTTP Archive (HAR) file; subsequent runs replay those responses without a backend.
This is particularly effective for APIs that are slow, rate-limited, or require complex
infrastructure (payment gateways, third-party enrichment APIs).

**Why it matters:** E2E tests that hit real external APIs are slow, brittle (depends on
network and third-party uptime), and violate test isolation. Recording real responses
once gives you realistic data that covers all the edge cases a factory would miss
(pagination metadata, embedded hypermedia links, versioned schemas) while keeping
tests deterministic.

```typescript
// tests/payment.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';

const HAR_FILE = path.resolve(__dirname, '__hars__/payment-gateway.har');

test.describe('Stripe checkout flow', () => {
  test.use({
    // On CI: update: false — replays recorded responses
    // During recording: update: 'minimal' — re-records only new/changed requests
    // During full re-record: update: true — records all requests
  });

  test('successful payment creates an order', async ({ page, context }) => {
    // Route all Stripe API traffic through the HAR fixture
    await context.routeFromHAR(HAR_FILE, {
      url:    /api\.stripe\.com/,     // only Stripe calls go through HAR
      update: process.env.CI ? false : 'minimal',
      // notFound: 'abort' — fail the test if a new Stripe request has no HAR entry
      notFound: 'abort',
    });

    await page.goto('/checkout');
    await page.fill('[data-testid="card-number"]', '4242424242424242');
    await page.fill('[data-testid="expiry"]',      '12/28');
    await page.fill('[data-testid="cvc"]',         '123');
    await page.click('[data-testid="pay-button"]');

    await expect(page.getByTestId('order-confirmation')).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```

**HAR file lifecycle management:**

| Trigger | `update` setting | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| First time recording | `true` | Records ALL matching requests |
| Adding a new user journey | `'minimal'` | Re-records only unmatched requests; preserves existing entries |
| CI runs | `false` | Replays only; fails if a new request has no entry |
| Schema change in 3rd-party API | Delete HAR + `true` | Full re-record; check into version control |

**Important:** HAR files can contain sensitive data (auth tokens, API keys in headers).
Add a HAR scrubbing step before committing — replace `Authorization` headers with
`Bearer REDACTED` and cookie values with `REDACTED`.

### Playwright `route.fetch()` + Factory Enrichment Pattern

Playwright's `route.fetch()` fetches the real response, then lets you enrich it with
factory-generated data before fulfilling the request. This is the recommended approach
when you need realistic test data that builds on production-like responses rather than
fully replacing them.

**Why it matters:** Pure factory mocks can drift from the real API schema — new fields
are added to the real response but the mock factory is never updated. The
`route.fetch()` enrichment pattern keeps the base response structure in sync with the
real API while allowing targeted factory overrides for the fields relevant to the test.

```typescript
// tests/product-detail.spec.ts — enrich real response with test-specific factory data
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { buildProductReview } from '../factories/product.factory';

test('renders injected review data alongside real product data', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.route('**/api/products/*/reviews', async (route) => {
    // Fetch the real response (with real product base data, pagination, etc.)
    const realResponse  = await route.fetch();
    const realData      = await realResponse.json();

    // Inject factory-generated reviews alongside the real ones
    const factoryReviews = Array.from({ length: 3 }, () =>
      buildProductReview({ rating: 5, verified: true })
    );

    await route.fulfill({
      response: realResponse,  // preserves headers, status, etc. from real response
      json: {
        ...realData,
        reviews: [...factoryReviews, ...realData.reviews.slice(0, 2)],
        totalCount: factoryReviews.length + 2,
      },
    });
  });

  await page.goto('/products/phone-x');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('review-count')).toContainText('5 reviews');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('average-rating')).toContainText('5.0');
});
```

**Schema drift detection:** If the real API adds a required field that the enrichment
drops, the assertion will catch it rather than silently returning incorrect data.
Compare this with a pure mock factory that would silently omit the new field.

### MSW Streaming Response Factory — LLM / AI Feature Test Data

Applications that integrate LLM APIs (Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini) receive responses as
**Server-Sent Event (SSE) streams**. MSW's `ReadableStream` integration lets you build
a streaming response factory that delivers token-by-token data to your test, validating
that the UI handles partial renders, loading states, and stream termination correctly.

**Why it matters:** LLM-integrated UIs have several test-data-specific failure modes
that synchronous factories cannot cover: the UI must handle partial content while the
stream is open, update progressively as tokens arrive, and clean up correctly when the
stream ends or errors. Streaming factories reproduce these exact conditions in
unit/integration tests without requiring a real LLM API call.

```typescript
// factories/llm-stream.factory.ts
// Builds a ReadableStream that emits an LLM response token-by-token

interface StreamChunk {
  id:    string;
  delta: { type: 'text_delta'; text: string };
  type:  'content_block_delta';
}

// Build an Anthropic-compatible SSE stream from a string response
export function buildAnthropicStream(fullText: string, chunkSize = 10): ReadableStream<Uint8Array> {
  const encoder = new TextEncoder();
  const chunks  = fullText.match(new RegExp(`.{1,${chunkSize}}`, 'g')) ?? [];
  let index = 0;

  return new ReadableStream<Uint8Array>({
    pull(controller) {
      if (index >= chunks.length) {
        // Emit stream_end event and close
        controller.enqueue(encoder.encode('data: {"type":"message_stop"}\n\n'));
        controller.close();
        return;
      }

      const chunk: StreamChunk = {
        id:    `chunk-${index}`,
        type:  'content_block_delta',
        delta: { type: 'text_delta', text: chunks[index++] },
      };

      controller.enqueue(encoder.encode(`data: ${JSON.stringify(chunk)}\n\n`));
    },
  });
}

// MSW handler using the streaming factory
// handlers/ai-handlers.ts
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw';
import { buildAnthropicStream } from '../factories/llm-stream.factory';

export const aiHandlers = [
  http.post('https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages', async ({ request }) => {
    const body = await request.json() as { messages: { content: string }[] };
    const prompt = body.messages.at(-1)?.content ?? '';

    // Generate a contextual fake response
    const responseText = prompt.includes('summarize')
      ? 'This document discusses three key themes: ...'
      : 'I can help you with that. Here is what I found: ...';

    return new HttpResponse(buildAnthropicStream(responseText, 15), {
      headers: {
        'Content-Type':  'text/event-stream',
        'Cache-Control': 'no-cache',
      },
    });
  }),
];

// In Vitest test
import { setupServer } from 'msw/node';
import { aiHandlers }  from './handlers/ai-handlers';

const server = setupServer(...aiHandlers);
beforeAll(() => server.listen());
afterAll(() => server.close());

test('renders streaming response progressively', async () => {
  render(<AiSummaryWidget />);
  await userEvent.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: /summarize/i }));

  // Stream is still open — partial content visible
  await waitFor(() =>
    expect(screen.getByTestId('ai-output')).toHaveTextContent(/This document/i)
  );

  // Stream complete — full response visible
  await waitFor(() =>
    expect(screen.getByTestId('ai-output')).toHaveTextContent(/three key themes/i)
  );

  // Loading indicator should be gone after stream completes
  expect(screen.queryByTestId('loading-spinner')).not.toBeInTheDocument();
});
```

**Common streaming test scenarios:**

| Scenario | Factory configuration |
|---|---|
| Happy path | `buildAnthropicStream(responseText)` |
| Mid-stream error | `controller.error(new Error('stream_error'))` after N chunks |
| Empty response | `buildAnthropicStream('')` — triggers loading-state cleanup test |
| Very slow stream | Wrap `pull()` in `await delay(200)` — tests timeout/cancel UI |

---

### `@anatine/zod-mock` — Schema-Driven Mock Generation

`@anatine/zod-mock` (`npm i -D @anatine/zod-mock @faker-js/faker`) generates a faker.js-backed
mock object from any Zod schema. It traverses the schema's type graph and produces a realistic
value for each field type: `z.string()` → fake sentence, `z.email()` → fake email,
`z.number()` → random number, `z.enum()` → random enum member, `z.date()` → faker date.

**Why it matters:** When your domain model is already expressed as a Zod schema (e.g., the
request body schema for an API endpoint), `generateMock(schema)` derives a valid factory
from that schema automatically. The factory is always in sync with the schema — if a required
field is added to the Zod schema, `generateMock()` immediately includes it in the output
without any factory update.

```typescript
// factories/schema-driven.factory.ts
import { z }            from 'zod';
import { generateMock } from '@anatine/zod-mock';

// Domain schema (source of truth)
const OrderSchema = z.object({
  id:        z.string().uuid(),
  status:    z.enum(['pending', 'completed', 'cancelled']),
  total:     z.number().min(0).max(10_000),
  createdAt: z.date(),
  customer: z.object({
    id:    z.string().uuid(),
    email: z.string().email(),
    tier:  z.enum(['free', 'basic', 'premium']).default('free'),
  }),
  items: z.array(
    z.object({
      sku:      z.string(),
      quantity: z.number().int().min(1),
      price:    z.number().min(0),
    })
  ).min(1),
});

type Order = z.infer<typeof OrderSchema>;

// Factory derived directly from the schema — stays in sync automatically
export function buildMockOrder(overrides: Partial<Order> = {}): Order {
  const base = generateMock(OrderSchema);
  return { ...base, ...overrides };
}

// Build a list of schema-driven mocks
export function buildMockOrderList(count: number): Order[] {
  return Array.from({ length: count }, () => generateMock(OrderSchema));
}

// In test — schema-driven factory, no manual field maintenance
it('renders order summary correctly', () => {
  // All fields populated from schema; overrides only the fields relevant to the test
  const order = buildMockOrder({ status: 'completed', total: 99.99 });
  render(<OrderSummary order={order} />);
  expect(screen.getByText('$99.99')).toBeInTheDocument();
  expect(screen.getByText('completed')).toBeInTheDocument();
});
```

**When schema-driven mocks are NOT enough:**

| Limitation | Symptom | Workaround |
|---|---|---|
| No business-rule constraints | `z.number().min(0)` may produce `0` — not a realistic price | Use `overrides` for the field or add `.min(0.01).max(9999.99)` to schema |
| `z.string()` without refinements generates lorem ipsum | Email field without `.email()` refinement = fake sentence | Add `.email()`, `.url()`, `.uuid()` Zod refinements to constrain generation |
| No cross-field relationships | `quantity: 3` but `total: 0.07` — inconsistent | Use schema-driven mock as base; compute derived fields in override |
| Nested factories ignored | `generateMock` creates random nested objects — may not be persisted to DB | For DB-backed tests, use fishery's `create()` after schema-driven build |

### TypeScript `satisfies` Operator for Narrowed Factory Defaults

The TypeScript `satisfies` operator (TS 4.9+) validates that an expression satisfies
a type constraint while **preserving the narrowest literal type** of the value — rather
than widening it to the base type. This lets factory default objects retain specific
literal types for discriminated unions while still being type-checked against the full
interface.

**Why it matters:** Factory defaults typically need to satisfy `Partial<T>` for flexibility,
but the defaults themselves should have *narrow* types so TypeScript can narrow the return
type correctly. Without `satisfies`, `defaults.status = 'active'` widens to `string` and
the factory loses the ability to discriminate on the status field in the test assertion.

```typescript
// factories/user.factory.ts
interface User {
  id:       string;
  status:   'active' | 'suspended' | 'deleted';
  role:     'admin' | 'editor' | 'viewer';
  email:    string;
  metadata: { createdAt: Date; loginCount: number };
}

import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

// WITHOUT satisfies — status widens to string; TypeScript loses narrow type info
const defaultsWide: Partial<User> = {
  status: 'active',   // type: string (widened to Partial<User>['status'] = string | undefined)
  role:   'viewer',
};

// WITH satisfies — status retains literal type 'active'; validated against Partial<User>
const defaults = {
  status:   'active',   // type: 'active' (literal preserved)
  role:     'viewer',   // type: 'viewer' (literal preserved)
  metadata: {
    createdAt:  new Date(),
    loginCount: 0,
  },
} satisfies Partial<User>;
// ^ TypeScript error if a field is wrong type (e.g., status: 'inactive' → error)

export function buildUser(overrides: Partial<User> = {}): User {
  return {
    id:       faker.string.uuid(),
    email:    faker.internet.email(),
    ...defaults,
    ...overrides,
  } satisfies User;  // second satisfies: ensures the merged result is a complete User
}

// Usage — TypeScript narrows correctly with satisfies defaults
const user = buildUser();
if (user.status === 'active') {
  // TypeScript knows user.status is 'active' here — discriminated union narrows correctly
  console.log(user.role); // type narrowing works as expected
}
```

**`satisfies` vs `as const` vs explicit annotation:**

| Technique | Literal preserved | Type-checked | Override-friendly |
|---|---|---|---|
| `const obj: Partial<T> = { ... }` | No — widens | Yes | Yes |
| `const obj = { ... } as const` | Yes — readonly | No | No (all fields readonly) |
| `const obj = { ... } satisfies Partial<T>` | Yes | Yes | Yes — not readonly |
| `const obj = { ... } satisfies T` | Yes | Yes (all required fields) | Only with spread |
