### Discriminated-Union Conditional Factory  [community]

TypeScript discriminated unions (e.g., `type Result = { kind: 'success'; data: T } | { kind: 'error'; code: string }`) require factories that produce structurally correct variants — a `success` result must include `data`, an `error` result must never include it. A **conditional factory** uses TypeScript overloads or a `kind`-keyed dispatch map to enforce this invariant at compile time.

**Why it matters:** A factory that accepts `Partial<Result>` allows callers to pass `{ kind: 'success' }` without `data`, producing a structurally invalid object that passes TypeScript type checks (because `data` is present on `Partial<Result>`) but fails at runtime when downstream code reads `result.data`. Discriminated-union factories enforce the per-variant field requirements with TypeScript overloads.

**When to use:** API response factories, command/event result factories, and any union type where different members have different required fields. **When NOT to use:** Simple string unions where all variants have the same shape — plain `buildUser({ status: 'suspended' })` suffices. Named alternative: separate factory functions per variant (`buildSuccessResult`, `buildErrorResult`).

```typescript
// factories/result.factory.ts — discriminated-union conditional factory with overloads
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

type ApiResult<T> =
  | { kind: 'success'; data: T; requestId: string; durationMs: number }
  | { kind: 'error'; code: string; message: string; requestId: string; retryable: boolean }
  | { kind: 'partial'; data: Partial<T>; warnings: string[]; requestId: string };

// Convenience factory map — callers use named constructors, not the raw `kind` argument
export const ApiResultFactory = {
  success: <T>(data: T): ApiResult<T> => ({
    kind: 'success',
    data,
    requestId: faker.string.uuid(),
    durationMs: faker.number.int({ min: 10, max: 500 }),
  }),

  rateLimitError: (): ApiResult<never> => ({
    kind: 'error',
    code: 'ERR_RATE_LIMIT',
    message: 'Rate limit exceeded. Retry after 60s.',
    requestId: faker.string.uuid(),
    retryable: true,
  }),

  notFoundError: (): ApiResult<never> => ({
    kind: 'error',
    code: 'ERR_NOT_FOUND',
    message: 'The requested resource was not found.',
    requestId: faker.string.uuid(),
    retryable: false,
  }),

  serverError: (message = 'Internal server error'): ApiResult<never> => ({
    kind: 'error',
    code: 'ERR_INTERNAL',
    message,
    requestId: faker.string.uuid(),
    retryable: false,
  }),

  partialWithWarnings: <T>(data: Partial<T>, warnings: string[]): ApiResult<T> => ({
    kind: 'partial',
    data,
    warnings,
    requestId: faker.string.uuid(),
  }),
};
```

```typescript
// specs/api-client.test.ts — typed result factory usage
import { test, expect } from 'vitest';
import { ApiResultFactory } from '../factories/result.factory';
import { apiClient } from '../clients/api.client';

test('client retries on rate-limit error (retryable: true)', () => {
  const error = ApiResultFactory.rateLimitError();
  // TypeScript narrows: error.kind === 'error', so error.retryable is accessible
  expect(error.retryable).toBe(true);
  expect(error.code).toBe('ERR_RATE_LIMIT');
});

test('client does not retry on 404 (retryable: false)', () => {
  const error = ApiResultFactory.notFoundError();
  expect(error.retryable).toBe(false);
});
```

### Factory Mutation Testing — Verifying Factories Detect Real Bugs  [community]

**Mutation testing** verifies that your test suite detects injected bugs. Applied to factories, it answers: "if I intentionally corrupt this factory output, does at least one test fail?" A factory whose mutations all pass undetected means the test suite is not exercising the affected field — the factory is providing a field that tests ignore.

**Why it matters:** Factories can quietly produce fields that are never asserted on. Removing a field, changing its type, or inverting a boolean in the factory output should cause at least one test to fail. If no test fails, the factory field is dead test infrastructure — it adds maintenance cost but zero test value.

**When to use:** As a quarterly factory audit to find dead factory fields and remove them. **When NOT to use:** As part of every CI run — mutation testing is expensive (O(fields × test runs)). Use Stryker.js for automated mutation testing; the pattern below is a manual spot-check technique. Named alternative: `ts-morph` AST mutation for TypeScript-aware field removal.

```typescript
// specs/factory-mutation-audit/user-status.mutation.test.ts
// Run in isolation: vitest run --project mutation (NOT part of the standard test suite)
// Purpose: verify that a mutation to factory output is detected by at least one test
import { test, expect, vi } from 'vitest';
import { buildUser } from '../../factories/user.factory';
import { checkoutService } from '../../services/checkout.service';
import { authService } from '../../services/auth.service';

// Mutation: always produce 'suspended' status regardless of override
// If ALL tests below pass with this mutation, the test suite has a coverage gap
vi.mock('../../factories/user.factory', async (importOriginal) => {
  const original = await importOriginal<typeof import('../../factories/user.factory')>();
  return {
    ...original,
    // Mutation applied: override status to always be 'suspended'
    buildUser: (overrides: Parameters<typeof original.buildUser>[0] = {}) =>
      original.buildUser({ ...overrides, status: 'suspended' }),
  };
});

// This test MUST fail when the mutation is applied (suspended user cannot checkout)
// If it passes, our test suite never asserts that active users can checkout
test('[mutation-coverage] suspended-status mutation is detected by checkout test', async () => {
  const user = buildUser({ status: 'active' });  // mutation overrides this to 'suspended'
  const result = checkoutService.isEligible(user);
  // With the mutation: result === false, this assertion FAILS — mutation is detected ✓
  // Without mutation:  result === true,  this assertion PASSES — coverage confirmed ✓
  expect(result).toBe(true);
});

test('[mutation-coverage] suspended-status mutation is detected by login test', async () => {
  const user = buildUser({ status: 'active' });
  const result = authService.canLogin(user);
  expect(result).toBe(true);  // must fail when mutation applies suspended status
});
```

### `fc.modelRun()` — Model-Based Property Testing with Factories  [official]

`fast-check`'s `fc.modelRun()` and `fc.commands()` implement *model-based testing*: a reference model (simple correct implementation) runs alongside the system under test (SUT). For every command generated by fast-check, both the model and SUT execute it; the model's output is compared to the SUT's output. Factories generate the initial state and command payloads.

**Why it matters:** Unit tests verify individual operations. Model-based tests verify that arbitrary *sequences* of operations leave the SUT in a consistent state. A shopping cart that handles individual add/remove correctly may fail when add → remove → add produces incorrect totals. `fc.modelRun()` exhaustively generates command sequences to find these multi-step invariant violations.

**When to use:** Stateful domain objects with complex operation sequences (carts, subscriptions, account balances, editor histories). **When NOT to use:** Stateless functions where `fc.property()` suffices. Named alternative: `fc.asyncProperty()` with a manually maintained model (less structured but simpler for small state machines).

```typescript
// specs/cart.model-based.test.ts — model-based testing of shopping cart operations
import * as fc from 'fast-check';
import { test } from 'vitest';

// Reference model: the "correct" cart (kept simple — this is the spec, not the SUT)
interface CartModel {
  items: Map<string, { price: number; quantity: number }>;
}

// SUT interface: the real CartService under test
interface CartSUT {
  addItem(productId: string, price: number, quantity: number): void;
  removeItem(productId: string): void;
  getTotal(): number;
}

// Command: add an item to both model and SUT, then check totals agree
class AddItemCommand implements fc.Command<CartModel, CartSUT> {
  constructor(
    private readonly productId: string,
    private readonly price: number,
    private readonly quantity: number,
  ) {}

  check(_m: CartModel) { return this.quantity > 0 && this.price > 0; }

  run(m: CartModel, sut: CartSUT): void {
    m.items.set(this.productId, { price: this.price, quantity: this.quantity });
    sut.addItem(this.productId, this.price, this.quantity);

    // Invariant: model total === SUT total after every operation
    const modelTotal = [...m.items.values()]
      .reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price * i.quantity, 0);
    if (Math.abs(modelTotal - sut.getTotal()) >= 0.01) {
      throw new Error(`Total mismatch: model=${modelTotal}, sut=${sut.getTotal()}`);
    }
  }

  toString() {
    return `AddItem(${this.productId}, price=${this.price}, qty=${this.quantity})`;
  }
}

// Command: remove an item that exists in the model
class RemoveItemCommand implements fc.Command<CartModel, CartSUT> {
  constructor(private readonly productId: string) {}
  check(m: CartModel) { return m.items.has(this.productId); }
  run(m: CartModel, sut: CartSUT): void {
    m.items.delete(this.productId);
    sut.removeItem(this.productId);
  }
  toString() { return `RemoveItem(${this.productId})`; }
}

test('cart operations maintain total consistency under arbitrary command sequences', () => {
  fc.assert(
    fc.property(
      fc.commands(
        [
          // Command factory: arbitrary add-item commands with factory-generated product data
          fc.record({
            productId: fc.uuid(),
            price: fc.integer({ min: 1, max: 50_000 }),
            quantity: fc.integer({ min: 1, max: 10 }),
          }).map(({ productId, price, quantity }) =>
            new AddItemCommand(productId, price, quantity)
          ),
          // Command factory: remove a known item (check() guards against unknown IDs)
          fc.uuid().map(id => new RemoveItemCommand(id)),
        ],
        { maxCommands: 100 }
      ),
      (commands) => {
        const model: CartModel = { items: new Map() };
        const sut = new CartService();  // real implementation under test
        fc.modelRun(() => ({ model, real: sut }), commands);
      }
    ),
    { numRuns: 500 }
  );
});
```

### WebSocket / SSE Push Factory Pattern  [community]

End-to-end tests for real-time features (live dashboards, collaborative editing, chat) require factories that *push* data to the client over WebSocket or SSE connections, not just seed the database. Playwright's `page.routeWebSocket()` combined with factories creates a controllable push channel that avoids the need for a live WebSocket server in tests.

**Why it matters:** A live order-tracking dashboard that receives WebSocket updates cannot be tested with a static DB fixture — the test must push a sequence of status updates and assert that the UI re-renders correctly. Without a factory-driven WebSocket mock, teams either skip real-time tests entirely or require a live server, adding flakiness.

**When to use:** E2E tests for any feature that consumes real-time data (order status, live prices, notifications, presence indicators). **When NOT to use:** Unit tests for the event handler logic — mock the WebSocket at the module level instead. Named alternative: `msw`'s `ws` handler for Node.js WebSocket interception in Vitest integration tests.

```typescript
// fixtures/websocket-fixtures.ts — Playwright WebSocket push factory
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';
import type { WebSocketRoute } from '@playwright/test';

// Factory for server-sent order status messages
function buildOrderStatusMessage(orderId: string, status: string): string {
  return JSON.stringify({
    type: 'ORDER_STATUS_UPDATED',
    orderId,
    status,
    updatedAt: new Date().toISOString(),
    estimatedDelivery: faker.date.soon({ days: 3 }).toISOString(),
  });
}

type WsFixtures = {
  orderWebSocket: { push: (orderId: string, status: string) => Promise<void> };
};

export const test = base.extend<WsFixtures>({
  orderWebSocket: async ({ page }, use) => {
    let wsRoute: WebSocketRoute;

    // Route all WebSocket connections to /api/ws/orders through our factory mock
    await page.routeWebSocket('/api/ws/orders', (ws) => {
      wsRoute = ws;
      // Send a connection-confirmed message on connect
      ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: 'CONNECTED', timestamp: new Date().toISOString() }));
    });

    // Expose a push() helper: tests call this to inject factory-generated events
    const push = async (orderId: string, status: string): Promise<void> => {
      wsRoute.send(buildOrderStatusMessage(orderId, status));
    };

    await use({ push });
    // Playwright auto-closes route when the page closes; explicit close for clarity
    await wsRoute!.close();
  },
});

export { expect } from '@playwright/test';
```

```typescript
// specs/order-tracking.e2e.spec.ts — real-time UI test with factory-pushed events
import { test, expect } from '../fixtures/websocket-fixtures';

test('order tracking page updates status when WebSocket pushes update', async ({ page, orderWebSocket }) => {
  const orderId = 'ord-e2e-001';
  await page.goto(`/orders/${orderId}`);
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="order-status"]')).toHaveText('Pending');

  // Push a factory-generated status update over the mocked WebSocket
  await orderWebSocket.push(orderId, 'shipped');

  // Assert the UI re-renders with the new status from the factory event
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="order-status"]')).toHaveText('Shipped', {
    timeout: 3000,
  });
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="delivery-estimate"]')).toBeVisible();
});
```

### React Server Component Test Data with `renderToString`  [community]

React Server Components (RSC) cannot be tested with `@testing-library/react`'s `render()` (which expects a client render environment). Test data for RSC integration tests is injected via `renderToString()` or RSC-aware test utilities combined with factories that produce the *DB state* the server component reads at render time — not component props.

**Why it matters:** RSC test factories must produce *DB state* that the server component reads at render time, not prop objects passed to the component. The factory is a DB seed, not a props builder. This is a fundamental shift from client component testing. Tests that mock props directly for an RSC miss the data-fetching logic entirely — the most important thing an RSC does.

**When to use:** Integration tests for RSC-based routes in Next.js App Router or Remix. **When NOT to use:** Client component tests where factory-generated props are still correct. Named alternative: Playwright E2E tests (always exercise the full RSC render pipeline, but slower and harder to set up for unit-style assertions).

```typescript
// factories/rsc.factory.ts — DB state factories for React Server Component tests
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';
import { db } from '../db';
import { users, posts } from '../db/schema';
import { eq } from 'drizzle-orm';

// Seed DB state that the RSC's data-fetching logic (db.query) will read
export async function seedRscUserProfile(options: {
  userId?: string;
  postCount?: number;
} = {}): Promise<{ userId: string; cleanup: () => Promise<void> }> {
  const userId = options.userId ?? faker.string.uuid();

  // Create the user record — RSC fetches this via db.query.users.findFirst()
  await db.insert(users).values({
    id: userId,
    email: faker.internet.email(),
    name: faker.person.fullName(),
    status: 'active',
    subscriptionTier: 'free',
  });

  // Create N posts — RSC fetches these via db.query.posts.findMany()
  const postCount = options.postCount ?? 3;
  for (let i = 0; i < postCount; i++) {
    await db.insert(posts).values({
      id: faker.string.uuid(),
      userId,
      title: faker.lorem.sentence(),
      body: faker.lorem.paragraphs(2),
      publishedAt: faker.date.past(),
    });
  }

  return {
    userId,
    cleanup: async () => {
      await db.delete(posts).where(eq(posts.userId, userId));
      await db.delete(users).where(eq(users.id, userId));
    },
  };
}
```

```typescript
// specs/rsc/user-profile.rsc.test.tsx — RSC integration test with factory-seeded DB
import { test, expect, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { renderToString } from 'react-dom/server';
import { seedRscUserProfile } from '../../factories/rsc.factory';
import { UserProfilePage } from '../../app/users/[userId]/page';

let cleanup: (() => Promise<void>) | undefined;
afterEach(async () => { await cleanup?.(); });

test('UserProfilePage renders user name and post count from seeded DB state', async () => {
  // Factory seeds DB — RSC will read from it at render time
  const { userId, cleanup: cleanupFn } = await seedRscUserProfile({ postCount: 5 });
  cleanup = cleanupFn;

  // RSC render: component fetches from the seeded DB, not from injected props
  const html = await renderToString(<UserProfilePage params={{ userId }} />);

  expect(html).toContain('5 posts');
  expect(html).toMatch(/aria-label="user profile"/);
});
```

### Database View / Read-Model Seeding  [community]

Materialised views, SQL views, and CQRS read-models present a seeding challenge: you cannot insert directly into a view. The correct factory pattern seeds the *underlying base tables* in the right combination to produce the desired view row, rather than attempting to mock the view. This forces the factory to exercise the same projection logic that the view uses.

**Why it matters:** Tests that mock a database view (via ORM `vi.mock()`) pass even when the view's SQL query is wrong. Tests that seed the base tables and read through the actual view catch view definition bugs — the most dangerous class of silent failure in analytics and reporting code.

**When to use:** Integration tests for reporting queries, dashboard endpoints, or CQRS read-model projections. **When NOT to use:** Unit tests for business logic that does not read from views — use plain object factories. Named alternative: seed the view table directly in databases that support `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY` (only for snapshot-style tests where staleness is acceptable; see community gotcha #73).

```typescript
// factories/read-model.factory.ts — seed base tables to produce desired view rows
// Target view: monthly_revenue_by_user (aggregates orders + items + products)
// We cannot INSERT into this view — we seed the 4 underlying base tables.
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';
import { db } from '../db';
import { users, orders, orderItems, products } from '../db/schema';
import { eq, sql } from 'drizzle-orm';

interface MonthlyRevenueScenario {
  userId: string;
  month: string;           // 'YYYY-MM'
  expectedRevenueCents: number;
  cleanup: () => Promise<void>;
}

export async function seedMonthlyRevenueScenario(
  targetMonth = '2026-01',
  revenueTargetCents = 10_000
): Promise<MonthlyRevenueScenario> {
  const userId = faker.string.uuid();
  const productId = faker.string.uuid();
  const orderId = faker.string.uuid();

  // 1. User (FK anchor for orders)
  await db.insert(users).values({
    id: userId, email: faker.internet.email(), name: faker.person.fullName(),
    status: 'active', subscriptionTier: 'premium',
  });

  // 2. Product (FK anchor for order items)
  await db.insert(products).values({
    id: productId, name: 'Test Product', priceCents: revenueTargetCents, category: 'test',
  });

  // 3. Order in the target month (the revenue period)
  const orderDate = new Date(`${targetMonth}-15T12:00:00Z`);
  await db.insert(orders).values({
    id: orderId, userId, status: 'paid', paidAt: orderDate, createdAt: orderDate,
  });

  // 4. Order item — this is the revenue row the view aggregates
  await db.insert(orderItems).values({
    orderId, productId, quantity: 1, unitPriceCents: revenueTargetCents,
  });

  // 5. Refresh the materialised view (PostgreSQL)
  //    CONCURRENTLY requires a unique index; omit if not available — see gotcha #73
  await db.execute(sql`REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY monthly_revenue_by_user`);

  return {
    userId,
    month: targetMonth,
    expectedRevenueCents: revenueTargetCents,
    cleanup: async () => {
      await db.delete(orderItems).where(eq(orderItems.orderId, orderId));
      await db.delete(orders).where(eq(orders.id, orderId));
      await db.delete(products).where(eq(products.id, productId));
      await db.delete(users).where(eq(users.id, userId));
      await db.execute(sql`REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY monthly_revenue_by_user`);
    },
  };
}
```

```typescript
// specs/revenue-report.test.ts — tests the view via base-table factory seeding
import { test, expect, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { seedMonthlyRevenueScenario } from '../factories/read-model.factory';
import { revenueReportService } from '../services/revenue-report.service';

let cleanup: (() => Promise<void>) | undefined;
afterEach(async () => { await cleanup?.(); });

test('monthly revenue view reflects correct total for seeded orders', async () => {
  const scenario = await seedMonthlyRevenueScenario('2026-01', 15_000);
  cleanup = scenario.cleanup;

  const report = await revenueReportService.getMonthlyBreakdown(scenario.userId, '2026-01');

  expect(report.totalCents).toBe(15_000);
  expect(report.month).toBe('2026-01');
});
```

### gRPC / Protobuf Contract-Driven Factories  [community]

In microservices using gRPC, the `.proto` file is the single source of truth for message shapes. TypeScript factories derived from protobuf-generated types (via `ts-proto` or `@grpc/proto-loader`) stay in sync with the service contract — when the `.proto` changes, the generated types change, the factory fails to compile, and drift is caught immediately.

**Why it matters:** Teams that maintain hand-written TypeScript interfaces for gRPC message types in their test factories diverge from the `.proto` file over time — especially when the proto evolves through field additions (backwards compatible at the wire level but type-incompatible in TypeScript). Using generated types eliminates this entire class of contract drift.

**When to use:** Any TypeScript project consuming a gRPC service with a `.proto` definition. **When NOT to use:** REST-based services (use OpenAPI-generated types instead). Named alternative: `protobufjs` with compiled descriptors for dynamic factory generation without a `ts-proto` codegen step.

```typescript
// factories/grpc-order.factory.ts — protobuf-typed gRPC factory
// Run first: npx ts-proto --ts_proto_out=./generated ./protos/order.proto
// This generates ./generated/order.ts with exact TypeScript types from the proto

import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';
// These types ARE the protobuf message types — generated by ts-proto
import type { CreateOrderRequest, CreateOrderResponse, OrderItem } from '../generated/order';

// Sub-factory for the nested OrderItem message
function buildOrderItem(overrides: Partial<OrderItem> = {}): OrderItem {
  return {
    productId: faker.string.uuid(),
    quantity: faker.number.int({ min: 1, max: 10 }),
    unitPriceCents: faker.number.int({ min: 100, max: 50_000 }),
    productName: faker.commerce.productName(),
    ...overrides,
  };
}

// CreateOrderRequest factory — type derived from ts-proto generated type, not hand-written
export function buildCreateOrderRequest(
  overrides: Partial<CreateOrderRequest> = {}
): CreateOrderRequest {
  return {
    userId: faker.string.uuid(),
    tenantId: faker.string.uuid(),
    currency: 'USD',
    items: [buildOrderItem(), buildOrderItem()],
    shippingAddressLine1: faker.location.streetAddress(),
    shippingCity: faker.location.city(),
    shippingPostalCode: faker.location.zipCode(),
    shippingCountryCode: 'US',
    // Idempotency key is critical for gRPC retry safety — always generate per-call
    idempotencyKey: faker.string.uuid(),
    ...overrides,
  };
}

// CreateOrderResponse factory — for gRPC client mock setup in tests
export function buildCreateOrderResponse(
  overrides: Partial<CreateOrderResponse> = {}
): CreateOrderResponse {
  return {
    orderId: faker.string.uuid(),
    status: 'PENDING',
    totalCents: faker.number.int({ min: 500, max: 100_000 }),
    // protobuf Timestamp — NOT a JavaScript Date; see community gotcha #72
    createdAt: { seconds: BigInt(Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000)), nanos: 0 },
    ...overrides,
  };
}
```

```typescript
// specs/order-grpc-client.test.ts — gRPC client test with proto-typed factory
import { test, expect, vi } from 'vitest';
import { buildCreateOrderRequest, buildCreateOrderResponse } from '../factories/grpc-order.factory';
import { orderGrpcClient } from '../clients/order.grpc-client';

test('gRPC client sends correctly shaped CreateOrderRequest with idempotency key', async () => {
  const mockCall = vi.spyOn(orderGrpcClient, 'createOrder').mockResolvedValue(
    buildCreateOrderResponse({ status: 'PENDING' })
  );

  const request = buildCreateOrderRequest({ currency: 'EUR' });
  const response = await orderGrpcClient.createOrder(request);

  // idempotencyKey is generated per-call — verify it is a valid UUID
  expect(mockCall).toHaveBeenCalledWith(expect.objectContaining({
    currency: 'EUR',
    idempotencyKey: expect.stringMatching(/^[0-9a-f-]{36}$/),
  }));
  expect(response.status).toBe('PENDING');
});
```

### Storybook Interaction Test Data  [community]

Storybook's `play()` function (interaction testing via `@storybook/addon-interactions`) runs user interactions against a Story's rendered component and asserts on the outcome. The Story's `args` are the factory output — making Storybook stories the *visual documentation* of your factory variants and the *interaction test specification* simultaneously.

**Why it matters:** Without interaction tests, Storybook stories are documentation only — they verify that a component renders without crashing but don't assert behavior. Adding `play()` functions that use `@testing-library/user-event` to simulate user actions on factory-generated data turns stories into executable test cases that run in both the browser (Storybook UI) and CI (Storybook test runner).

**When to use:** React component libraries, design systems, and components with complex interactive states (forms, modals, dropdowns). **When NOT to use:** Simple presentational components with no interaction logic — snapshot tests are sufficient. Named alternative: `@playwright/test` component tests (lower story reuse but stronger E2E integration).

```typescript
// stories/CheckoutForm.stories.tsx — factory-driven Storybook interaction tests
import type { Meta, StoryObj } from '@storybook/react';
import { within, userEvent, expect } from '@storybook/test';
import { CheckoutForm } from '../components/CheckoutForm';
import { UserMother } from '../factories/user.mother';
import { buildCart } from '../factories/cart.factory';

const meta: Meta<typeof CheckoutForm> = {
  component: CheckoutForm,
  title: 'Checkout/CheckoutForm',
};
export default meta;
type Story = StoryObj<typeof CheckoutForm>;

// Story: happy path — active premium user with payment method
export const ActivePremiumUser: Story = {
  args: {
    // Factory produces the props — story IS the factory documentation
    user: UserMother.premiumWithPayment().build(),
    cart: buildCart(2),
    onSuccess: () => {},
    onError: () => {},
  },
  play: async ({ canvasElement }) => {
    const canvas = within(canvasElement);
    await expect(canvas.getByTestId('cart-total')).toBeInTheDocument();
    // Simulate form submission — factory provides a valid paymentMethodId
    await userEvent.click(canvas.getByRole('button', { name: /place order/i }));
    await expect(canvas.getByTestId('order-confirmation')).toBeVisible();
  },
};

// Story: suspended user — blocked checkout interaction test
export const SuspendedUser: Story = {
  args: {
    user: UserMother.suspended().build(),  // UserMother returns Builder; .build() gives User
    cart: buildCart(1),
    onSuccess: () => {},
    onError: () => {},
  },
  play: async ({ canvasElement }) => {
    const canvas = within(canvasElement);
    await expect(canvas.getByRole('alert')).toHaveTextContent(/account suspended/i);
    // Suspended users must not see the checkout button
    expect(canvas.queryByRole('button', { name: /place order/i })).toBeNull();
  },
};

// Story: empty cart — boundary condition interaction test
export const EmptyCart: Story = {
  args: {
    user: UserMother.default(),
    cart: buildCart(0),   // 0-item cart is a valid boundary case
    onSuccess: () => {},
    onError: () => {},
  },
  play: async ({ canvasElement }) => {
    const canvas = within(canvasElement);
    await expect(canvas.getByTestId('empty-cart-message')).toBeVisible();
    // Submit button must be disabled for empty carts
    expect(canvas.getByRole('button', { name: /place order/i })).toBeDisabled();
  },
};
```

### Factory Health-Check CI Gate  [community]

A **factory health-check** is a dedicated CI job that runs before the full test suite. It instantiates every registered factory with default arguments and validates the output against its schema (Zod, Prisma type, or `satisfies` assertion). If any factory produces a schema-invalid object — due to a domain model change, a faker API deprecation, or a missing required field — the health-check fails loudly before any test even runs.

**Why it matters:** Without a health-check, factory regressions manifest as mysterious failures deep in the test suite: a Prisma constraint error at line 847, a null-dereference in an unrelated test, or a flaky schema validation failure in CI. The health-check makes factory failures fast, explicit, and actionable.

**When to use:** Any project with 10+ factories. Run it as the first job in CI, blocking all downstream test jobs. **When NOT to use:** Projects with fewer than 10 factories — `expect.schemaMatching()` smoke tests in the test suite itself are sufficient at that scale.

```typescript
// test/factory-health-check.test.ts — CI gate: all factories must produce valid output
import { test, expect, describe } from 'vitest';
import { UserSchema } from '../schemas/user.schema';
import { OrderSchema } from '../schemas/order.schema';
import { ProductSchema } from '../schemas/product.schema';
import { SubscriptionSchema } from '../schemas/subscription.schema';
import { buildUser } from '../factories/user.factory';
import { buildDraftOrder, buildPaidOrder, buildShippedOrder } from '../factories/order-state-machine.factory';
import { buildProduct } from '../factories/product.factory';
import { SubscriptionFactory } from '../factories/subscription.factory';

describe('factory health checks — all factories must produce schema-valid output', () => {
  test('buildUser() satisfies UserSchema', () => {
    expect(buildUser()).toEqual(expect.schemaMatching(UserSchema));
  });

  test('buildDraftOrder() satisfies OrderSchema', () => {
    expect(buildDraftOrder()).toEqual(expect.schemaMatching(OrderSchema));
  });

  test('buildPaidOrder() satisfies OrderSchema and has required paid-state fields', () => {
    const order = buildPaidOrder();
    expect(order).toEqual(expect.schemaMatching(OrderSchema));
    // State-machine invariant: paid orders always have paidAt and paymentIntentId
    expect(order.paidAt).toBeInstanceOf(Date);
    expect(order.paymentIntentId).toBeTruthy();
  });

  test('buildShippedOrder() satisfies OrderSchema and has required shipped-state fields', () => {
    const order = buildShippedOrder();
    expect(order).toEqual(expect.schemaMatching(OrderSchema));
    expect(order.shippedAt).toBeInstanceOf(Date);
    expect(order.trackingNumber).toBeTruthy();
  });

  test('buildProduct() satisfies ProductSchema', () => {
    expect(buildProduct()).toEqual(expect.schemaMatching(ProductSchema));
  });

  test('SubscriptionFactory.activeTrial() satisfies SubscriptionSchema', () => {
    expect(SubscriptionFactory.activeTrial()).toEqual(expect.schemaMatching(SubscriptionSchema));
  });

  test('SubscriptionFactory.expiredTrial() satisfies SubscriptionSchema', () => {
    expect(SubscriptionFactory.expiredTrial()).toEqual(expect.schemaMatching(SubscriptionSchema));
  });

  test('SubscriptionFactory.pastDue() satisfies SubscriptionSchema', () => {
    expect(SubscriptionFactory.pastDue()).toEqual(expect.schemaMatching(SubscriptionSchema));
  });
});
```

```json
// package.json — factory health check blocks all downstream CI test jobs
{
  "scripts": {
    "test:factory-health": "vitest run --reporter=verbose test/factory-health-check.test.ts",
    "test:ci": "npm run test:factory-health && npm run test:unit && npm run test:integration && npm run test:e2e"
  }
}
```

### Stream-Based `Readable` Factory for Large Dataset Testing  [community]

For tests that validate streaming pipelines, CSV export endpoints, or large file-generation services, a **stream factory** produces a Node.js `Readable` stream of factory-generated objects instead of an in-memory array. This enables testing of backpressure handling, chunk-size constraints, and partial-read behavior that `buildList(N)` cannot expose.

**Why it matters:** A `buildList(100_000)` call allocates all 100,000 objects in memory before the first byte is processed. A stream factory yields one object at a time, allowing tests to verify that the consuming code respects backpressure (`highWaterMark` limits) and correctly handles partial reads. Streaming CSV exporters that serialize row-by-row will silently corrupt data at chunk boundaries if the factory always provides perfectly-sized batches.

**When to use:** Tests for streaming exports, ETL pipelines, S3/GCS bulk-upload handlers, and any code that reads from a `Readable` stream. **When NOT to use:** Tests that need all data available upfront for assertion (use `buildList()` with a modest count instead). Named alternative: `AsyncGenerator`-based factory (simpler but less compatible with Node.js stream tooling like `pipeline()`).

```typescript
// factories/stream.factory.ts — Node.js Readable stream of factory-generated rows
import { Readable } from 'stream';
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';
import { User } from '../domain/user';

interface StreamFactoryOptions {
  count: number;
  highWaterMark?: number;   // objects to buffer before backpressure (default: 16)
  delayMs?: number;         // simulate slow upstream (e.g., DB cursor latency)
}

// Create a Readable stream in object mode that yields `count` factory-generated Users
export function createUserStream(options: StreamFactoryOptions): Readable {
  const { count, highWaterMark = 16, delayMs = 0 } = options;
  let emitted = 0;

  return new Readable({
    objectMode: true,
    highWaterMark,
    async read() {
      if (emitted >= count) {
        this.push(null);   // end of stream signal
        return;
      }

      if (delayMs > 0) {
        await new Promise<void>(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
      }

      const user: User = {
        id: faker.string.uuid(),
        email: `stream-user-${emitted}@${faker.internet.domainName()}`,
        name: faker.person.fullName(),
        status: 'active',
        subscriptionTier: 'free',
        createdAt: faker.date.past({ years: 2 }),
        paymentMethodId: null,
      };

      emitted++;
      this.push(user);
    },
  });
}

// Collect all stream items into an array (for count/content assertions in tests)
export async function collectStream<T>(stream: Readable): Promise<T[]> {
  const items: T[] = [];
  for await (const item of stream) {
    items.push(item);
  }
  return items;
}
```

```typescript
// specs/csv-export.stream.test.ts — stream factory for export pipeline testing
import { test, expect } from 'vitest';
import { pipeline } from 'stream/promises';
import { Writable } from 'stream';
import { createUserStream } from '../factories/stream.factory';
import { csvExportTransform } from '../transforms/csv-export.transform';

test('CSV export pipeline produces correct row count for 10,000 streamed users', async () => {
  // Small highWaterMark deliberately tests backpressure behaviour
  const source = createUserStream({ count: 10_000, highWaterMark: 50 });
  const outputLines: string[] = [];

  const sink = new Writable({
    objectMode: false,
    write(chunk, _enc, cb) {
      outputLines.push(...chunk.toString().split('\n').filter(Boolean));
      cb();
    },
  });

  await pipeline(source, csvExportTransform, sink);

  // 1 header row + 10,000 data rows
  expect(outputLines.length).toBe(10_001);
  expect(outputLines[0]).toMatch(/^id,email,name,status/);  // header format verified
});
```

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 28

**69. [community] `fc.scheduler()` tests that use `await scheduler.waitAll()` inside a
`finally` block surface dangling scheduled tasks when an assertion inside a task throws —
the `finally` runs while the fast-check error handler has already captured the failure,
leaving orphaned tasks that pollute the next `numRuns` iteration.**

When a property assertion throws inside a scheduled task (e.g., `expect(model.total).toBe(sut.getTotal())`), fast-check captures the exception and begins shrinking. If `await scheduler.waitAll()` is inside a `try/finally`, the `finally` block executes after fast-check has already reported the counterexample and the scheduler is in an indeterminate state. Unresolved tasks from the failed run bleed into the next iteration's scheduler, producing false secondary failures that don't correspond to any counterexample. Fix: always place `scheduler.waitAll()` as the final step after all assertions, outside any `try/finally` block. WHY: every `fc.scheduler()` bug report involving "counterexample doesn't reproduce" on GitHub fast-check issues from 2025 traces back to this pattern.

**70. [community] Storybook `play()` functions that consume `UserMother` factories with
faker calls at module load time produce identical data across Storybook hot-module-replacement
reloads in dev mode — but different data in CI builds — causing snapshot tests to fail in
CI while passing locally.**

When `UserMother.default()` calls `faker.person.fullName()` at the module level (as an initializer value rather than inside a function), the faker RNG advances at import time. In Storybook dev mode with HMR, each reload re-imports the module from the same seed position — producing identical names. In production builds (CI), modules load once in sequence across all stories — the RNG has advanced further by story N than in dev mode. Snapshot tests of stories fail in CI but pass locally. Fix: never call faker inside module-level object initializers; always wrap in `() => faker.person.fullName()` function calls. WHY: this is the most common cause of "passes locally, fails in CI" reports in Storybook + Vitest snapshot test issue trackers.

**71. [community] Redis cache-layer factories that don't specify `db: parseInt(process.env.REDIS_TEST_DB ?? '1')` write to the application's default `db: 0` in environments where no test Redis is configured — overwriting real application cache entries in local dev environments and causing the application to return factory-generated test objects to real users.**

The default `new Redis()` client connects to `db: 0`. If the application service also uses `db: 0` (common when Redis is used only for caching with no DB separation), a test factory that writes to Redis overwrites real application cache entries in development environments. The next request to the service returns the factory-generated test object instead of a freshly computed value. Fix: always configure the test Redis client with `db: parseInt(process.env.REDIS_TEST_DB ?? '1')`, and add a health-check assertion: `if (parseInt(process.env.REDIS_TEST_DB ?? '1') === 0) throw new Error('[factory-guard] REDIS_TEST_DB must not be 0')`. WHY: invisible in CI (where Redis is spun up fresh per run) but silently corrupts local dev environments when integration tests run without a Redis sandbox.

**72. [community] `ts-proto` generated types encode Protobuf `Timestamp` fields as `{ seconds: bigint, nanos: number }` — NOT as JavaScript `Date` — causing factory assertions of the form `expect(response.createdAt).toBeInstanceOf(Date)` to always fail, and causing `JSON.stringify(response)` to throw `TypeError: Do not know how to serialize a BigInt` in test output helpers.**

A factory that builds `createdAt: new Date()` for a gRPC response type compiled by `ts-proto` will cause `expect(response.createdAt).toBeInstanceOf(Date)` to always fail — the actual type is `{ seconds: BigInt(1748000000), nanos: 0 }`. Additionally, any test helper that calls `JSON.stringify(response)` (e.g., for logging the factory output on failure) throws `TypeError: Do not know how to serialize a BigInt`. Fix: assert on `response.createdAt.seconds` (BigInt) for raw gRPC types, or call `ts-proto`'s generated `toJSON()` method before serialization. For factory construction, set `createdAt: { seconds: BigInt(Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000)), nanos: 0 }` — not `new Date()`. WHY: this surprises developers coming from REST-style test factories where `createdAt: new Date()` is idiomatic, and the BigInt serialization error adds a second confusing failure on top of the first.

**73. [community] DB view / materialised-view factories that call `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW` (without `CONCURRENTLY`) in `beforeEach` or factory setup contend with concurrent Vitest workers — two workers refreshing the same view simultaneously produce a PostgreSQL `ERROR: canceling statement due to conflict with recovery` or an `AccessExclusiveLock` timeout, failing both tests with a database error rather than a meaningful assertion failure.**

`REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW` (without `CONCURRENTLY`) takes an `AccessExclusiveLock` — no reads or writes to the view can proceed while the refresh runs. With `maxWorkers: 4`, four workers each calling `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW` in parallel will deadlock or timeout. `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY` uses a weaker lock but requires a unique index on the view and is only available in PostgreSQL ≥ 9.4. Fix: (a) use `CONCURRENTLY` and add the required unique index, or (b) run all materialised-view integration tests in a single worker (`pool: 'forks', maxWorkers: 1, isolate: false`). WHY: manifests only in parallel CI runs with ≥2 workers and is invisible in local sequential `vitest run` — a classic "works locally, fails in CI" deadlock that wastes hours to diagnose without knowing about the lock type.

### OpenAPI Schema-Diffing for Factory Drift Detection  [community]

As APIs evolve, factories silently go stale: new required fields are added to the OpenAPI spec but never added to the factory, causing tests to pass against the old contract while the real API now rejects the payload. Schema-diffing on CI catches this class of drift automatically by comparing the factory's output shape to the live OpenAPI spec at test time.

**Why it matters:** Factory drift is the single most common reason tests "pass in CI but fail in staging" — the factory produces a valid-looking payload that satisfies the test's `expect()` but would be rejected by the server running the latest spec.

**When to use:** Any integration or E2E test suite that communicates with an API governed by an OpenAPI spec. **When NOT to use:** Pure unit tests that do not exercise an API boundary; adds latency from spec fetch. Named alternative: `zod-openapi` (generates a Zod schema from the spec and validates factory output against it — more type-safe, but requires OpenAPI spec to be stored locally).

```typescript
// factories/api-drift-check.ts — OpenAPI schema-diff guard for factory output
import Ajv from 'ajv';
import addFormats from 'ajv-formats';
import type { OpenAPIV3 } from 'openapi-types';

const ajv = new Ajv({ allErrors: true, strict: false });
addFormats(ajv);

let schemaCache: OpenAPIV3.Document | null = null;

export async function loadOpenApiSpec(url: string): Promise<OpenAPIV3.Document> {
  if (schemaCache) return schemaCache;
  const response = await fetch(url);
  schemaCache = (await response.json()) as OpenAPIV3.Document;
  return schemaCache;
}

export async function assertFactoryMatchesSchema(
  factoryOutput: unknown,
  schemaRef: string,   // e.g. '#/components/schemas/CreateOrderRequest'
  specUrl: string,
): Promise<void> {
  const spec = await loadOpenApiSpec(specUrl);
  const parts = schemaRef.replace('#/', '').split('/');
  const schema = parts.reduce<unknown>((acc, key) => (acc as Record<string, unknown>)[key], spec);

  const validate = ajv.compile(schema as object);
  const valid = validate(factoryOutput);

  if (!valid) {
    const errors = ajv.errorsText(validate.errors, { separator: '\n  ' });
    throw new Error(
      `[factory-drift] Factory output does not match OpenAPI schema "${schemaRef}":\n  ${errors}`,
    );
  }
}
```

```typescript
// specs/order-factory-drift.test.ts
import { describe, it, beforeAll } from 'vitest';
import { buildCreateOrderRequest } from '../factories/order.factory';
import { assertFactoryMatchesSchema } from '../factories/api-drift-check';

const SPEC_URL = process.env.OPENAPI_SPEC_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3000/api-docs/openapi.json';

describe('Factory → OpenAPI schema conformance', () => {
  it('CreateOrderRequest factory output matches current OpenAPI spec', async () => {
    const payload = buildCreateOrderRequest();
    await assertFactoryMatchesSchema(
      payload,
      '#/components/schemas/CreateOrderRequest',
      SPEC_URL,
    );
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Requires the spec server to be running (or the spec to be bundled). In CI, use a `globalSetup` to fetch and cache the spec once. Set `schemaCache = null` between spec-version upgrades.

[community]

### Hono / Edge-Runtime Factory Adapters  [community]

Factories written for Node.js use `Buffer`, `fs`, `crypto`, and other Node-only APIs that do not exist in the Cloudflare Workers or Vercel Edge Runtime environments. An edge-runtime factory adapter wraps those calls behind an abstraction so the same factory can run in both environments.

**Why it matters:** Teams running integration tests for Hono or Next.js edge routes discover — often at the point of CI failure — that `crypto.randomBytes()`, `Buffer.from()`, or `Date.now()` behave differently or are unavailable. Building the adapter at factory-authoring time prevents the problem.

**When to use:** Projects deploying to Cloudflare Workers, Deno Deploy, or Vercel Edge Runtime, where integration tests use Miniflare, `@hono/testing`, or similar edge-faithful runtimes. **When NOT to use:** Pure Node.js server projects — the abstraction layer adds unnecessary indirection. Named alternative: replace `crypto.randomBytes()` with `globalThis.crypto.getRandomValues()` (Web Crypto — available in all environments).

```typescript
// factories/edge-compat.factory.ts — edge-runtime-safe factory primitives
//
// Miniflare (Cloudflare Workers test runtime) does not expose Node's 'crypto' module.
// All factories should import from this module, NOT from 'node:crypto'.

/** Generate a UUID v4 using the Web Crypto API (available in all runtimes). */
export function randomUUID(): string {
  // globalThis.crypto is available in Node ≥ 19, Cloudflare Workers, Deno, and Bun.
  return globalThis.crypto.randomUUID();
}

/** Base64-encode a string using only Web APIs (no Buffer). */
export function toBase64(input: string): string {
  // btoa is available in browsers, Workers, Deno, Node ≥ 16, and Bun.
  return btoa(unescape(encodeURIComponent(input)));
}

/** Generate a timestamp-based numeric sequence seed — no Date.now() in Workers. */
export function nowMs(): number {
  // performance.now() is available in Workers; Date.now() is NOT reliable in Miniflare.
  return Math.floor(performance.now());
}

// Example factory that uses edge-compat primitives
export function buildEdgeRequest(overrides: Partial<{ id: string; auth: string }> = {}) {
  return {
    id: overrides.id ?? randomUUID(),
    auth: overrides.auth ?? `Bearer ${toBase64(`token:${randomUUID()}`)}`,
    timestamp: nowMs(),
  };
}
```

```typescript
// specs/edge-route.test.ts — Hono + Miniflare integration test
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { app } from '../src/app';        // Hono app
import { buildEdgeRequest } from '../factories/edge-compat.factory';

describe('POST /api/orders (Edge Runtime)', () => {
  it('accepts a valid edge-compat factory request', async () => {
    const req = buildEdgeRequest();
    const res = await app.request('/api/orders', {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: { Authorization: req.auth, 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      body: JSON.stringify({ requestId: req.id }),
    });
    expect(res.status).toBe(200);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `globalThis.crypto.randomUUID()` is slightly slower than `node:crypto.randomUUID()` in Node.js because it goes through the platform abstraction layer. Profile if generating >100,000 IDs per test run.

[community]

### `@effect/schema` / `Schema.make()` — Effect-TS Factory Integration  [community]

The Effect ecosystem's `@effect/schema` library (now `effect/Schema` in Effect 3.x) provides a composable schema system that doubles as a factory input validator. When a service layer is built on Effect, factories should produce `Schema`-valid objects and test failures should surface as Effect `ParseError` values rather than raw TypeScript errors — preserving the full Effect error channel.

**Why it matters:** Projects adopting Effect-TS often find that plain factory functions bypass the Effect schema layer entirely, producing objects that satisfy TypeScript's type checker but fail `Schema.decode` at runtime. Using `Schema.make()` as the factory constructor ensures the factory output is always schema-valid and the error messages are Effect-native.

**When to use:** Service codebases that use Effect for domain modeling and dependency injection. **When NOT to use:** Projects not using Effect — `@effect/schema` adds a heavyweight dependency for marginal benefit outside the Effect ecosystem. Named alternative: `zod` + `zod-fixture` (lighter weight, comparable schema-driven generation without Effect).

```typescript
// factories/user.effect.factory.ts — Effect Schema-driven factory
import { Schema } from 'effect';
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

// 1. Define the schema once — the factory derives its type from it automatically
const UserSchema = Schema.Struct({
  id:    Schema.UUID,
  email: Schema.String.pipe(Schema.pattern(/^[^@]+@[^@]+\.[^@]+$/)),
  role:  Schema.Literal('admin', 'editor', 'viewer'),
  age:   Schema.Number.pipe(Schema.between(18, 120)),
  createdAt: Schema.DateFromSelf,
});

type User = Schema.Schema.Type<typeof UserSchema>;

// 2. Factory function — build a valid object then decode through the schema
export function buildUser(overrides: Partial<User> = {}): User {
  const raw = {
    id:        faker.string.uuid(),
    email:     faker.internet.email(),
    role:      faker.helpers.arrayElement(['admin', 'editor', 'viewer'] as const),
    age:       faker.number.int({ min: 18, max: 80 }),
    createdAt: faker.date.past({ years: 2 }),
    ...overrides,
  };

  // Schema.decodeUnknownSync throws an Effect ParseError if the raw object is invalid.
  // This catches factory drift immediately at construction time, not at assertion time.
  return Schema.decodeUnknownSync(UserSchema)(raw);
}

// 3. Usage in test
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';

describe('buildUser() factory', () => {
  it('produces a schema-valid user', () => {
    const user = buildUser({ role: 'admin' });
    expect(user.role).toBe('admin');
    expect(user.age).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(18);
  });

  it('throws ParseError when an invalid override is passed', () => {
    // age: -1 violates Schema.between(18, 120) — test documents the constraint
    expect(() => buildUser({ age: -1 })).toThrow();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `Schema.decodeUnknownSync` throws synchronously, which is appropriate for factory construction but incompatible with async Effect workflows that expect `Either` or `Effect` return types. For async factories, use `Schema.decodeUnknown(UserSchema)(raw)` and `Effect.runPromise`.

### PostgreSQL Savepoint Isolation — Sub-Transaction Test Cleanup  [community]

The standard transaction-rollback isolation pattern (begin a transaction in `beforeEach`, roll it back in `afterEach`) fails when the code under test itself opens nested transactions or calls stored procedures that issue `COMMIT`. PostgreSQL savepoints offer a more granular alternative: each test begins inside a savepoint, and `ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT` undoes only that test's mutations without touching the outer transaction.

**Why it matters:** ORMs like Prisma use `$transaction()` internally, which issues a real `BEGIN`/`COMMIT`. Rolling back the outer test transaction then tries to roll back a transaction that is already committed — producing `"ERROR: there is no transaction in progress"` failures. Savepoints nest cleanly around ORM-managed inner transactions.

**When to use:** Integration tests against a real PostgreSQL database where the code under test uses nested transactions or ORM transaction helpers. **When NOT to use:** SQLite (limited savepoint support) or when the test workload spans multiple database connections (savepoints are connection-scoped). Named alternative: `testcontainers` with a fresh database per test (full isolation, much higher overhead).

```typescript
// test/helpers/savepoint.ts — savepoint-based sub-transaction isolation
import { sql } from 'drizzle-orm';
import { db } from '../../src/db';

let savepointCounter = 0;

export async function withSavepoint<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
  const name = `sp_test_${++savepointCounter}`;

  await db.execute(sql.raw(`SAVEPOINT ${name}`));
  try {
    const result = await fn();
    // Release the savepoint on success — mutations visible within the outer transaction
    // but will be rolled back when the outer test transaction itself rolls back.
    await db.execute(sql.raw(`RELEASE SAVEPOINT ${name}`));
    return result;
  } catch (err) {
    await db.execute(sql.raw(`ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT ${name}`));
    throw err;
  }
}
```

```typescript
// specs/order.service.test.ts — savepoint isolation with Drizzle + Prisma inner txn
import { beforeAll, afterAll, beforeEach, afterEach, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { db } from '../../src/db';
import { sql } from 'drizzle-orm';
import { withSavepoint } from '../helpers/savepoint';
import { buildOrder } from '../factories/order.factory';
import { orderService } from '../../src/services/order.service';

beforeAll(() => db.execute(sql`BEGIN`));    // outer transaction wrapping all tests
afterAll(()  => db.execute(sql`ROLLBACK`)); // rolls back everything after the suite

it('creates an order and charges payment (uses nested ORM transaction internally)', async () => {
  const order = buildOrder({ status: 'pending', totalCents: 4999 });

  // withSavepoint lets the inner COMMIT inside orderService.create() succeed,
  // but the savepoint rollback undoes it after the test.
  await withSavepoint(async () => {
    const created = await orderService.create(order);
    expect(created.id).toBeDefined();
    expect(created.status).toBe('confirmed');
  });
  // Order rows no longer exist in DB — next test starts clean
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Savepoint names are connection-scoped; tests that run in parallel on different connections each need their own outer transaction. Use `maxWorkers: 1` or per-worker database connections when applying this pattern to parallel Vitest runs.

[community]

### Pact.js Contract-State Factories — Consumer-Driven Contract Test Data  [official]

Pact.js consumer-driven contract tests require "provider states" — named preconditions that tell the provider how to set up data before replaying a specific interaction. Factories are the canonical way to implement provider states: each state name maps to a factory call that seeds exactly the data the consumer assumed exists.

**Why it matters:** Without factories, provider states are implemented with hardcoded SQL or fixture files. When the domain model changes, the fixture file is out of sync with the schema and the pact verification fails with a cryptic DB error rather than a meaningful contract violation message. Factories make provider states self-maintaining.

**When to use:** Microservice teams using Pact or PactFlow for contract testing. Every provider state in a consumer contract should map to a named factory function. **When NOT to use:** Monoliths or services that do not publish/consume Pact contracts — the overhead of maintaining provider states is unjustified. Named alternative: `msw` handler factories (mock the provider entirely in the consumer test — no real provider state needed, but at the cost of contract fidelity).

```typescript
// pact/provider-states.ts — factory-backed provider state setup for Pact.js
import { buildUser } from '../factories/user.factory';
import { buildSubscription } from '../factories/subscription.factory';
import { userRepository } from '../src/repositories/user.repository';
import { subscriptionRepository } from '../src/repositories/subscription.repository';

// Maps Pact provider state names to factory calls.
// The Pact verifier calls this before replaying each consumer interaction.
export const providerStates: Record<string, () => Promise<void>> = {
  'user with active subscription exists': async () => {
    const user = await userRepository.create(buildUser({ status: 'active' }));
    await subscriptionRepository.create(
      buildSubscription({ userId: user.id, tier: 'pro', status: 'active' }),
    );
  },

  'user with no payment method exists': async () => {
    await userRepository.create(
      buildUser({ status: 'active', paymentMethodId: null }),
    );
  },

  'suspended user exists': async () => {
    await userRepository.create(buildUser({ status: 'suspended' }));
  },
};
```

```typescript
// pact/provider.verifier.test.ts — Pact verifier wired to factory states
import { Verifier } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
import { providerStates } from './provider-states';
import { app } from '../src/app';
import { server } from '../src/server';

describe('Pact Provider Verification', () => {
  it('satisfies all consumer contracts', async () => {
    const verifier = new Verifier({
      provider: 'UserService',
      providerBaseUrl: 'http://localhost:3001',
      pactBrokerUrl: process.env.PACT_BROKER_URL!,
      stateHandlers: providerStates,     // factory-backed state setup
      publishVerificationResult: true,
      providerVersion: process.env.GIT_SHA,
    });

    await verifier.verifyProvider();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Provider state factories must be kept in sync with both the consumer contract and the domain model. Add a CI job that runs provider verification against the latest pact from the broker on every provider deploy.

[official]

### `worker_threads` Parallel Database Seeding  [community]

`globalSetup` in Vitest and Playwright runs in a single thread. For test suites that require seeding large datasets (10,000+ rows), moving the seeding work to a pool of `worker_threads` reduces suite startup time from minutes to seconds by parallelising insert batches across CPU cores.

**Why it matters:** A suite that takes 3 minutes to seed before any test runs will be skipped in local development ("I'll just run the tests manually") — defeating the purpose of integration testing. Parallel seeding makes large dataset integration tests fast enough to run on every save.

**When to use:** Suites that seed ≥10,000 rows as a fixed baseline before tests begin. **When NOT to use:** Small datasets (<1,000 rows) — thread startup overhead dominates at small scales. Named alternative: `pg COPY FROM` / Prisma `createMany()` batch inserts (single-threaded but highly optimised for bulk inserts — often faster than worker_threads for medium datasets).

```typescript
// scripts/seed-workers.ts — parallelise seed across worker_threads
import { Worker, isMainThread, workerData, parentPort } from 'worker_threads';
import * as os from 'os';
import { buildUser } from '../factories/user.factory';
import { db } from '../src/db';
import { users } from '../src/db/schema';

const TOTAL_USERS = 50_000;
const WORKER_COUNT = os.cpus().length;

if (isMainThread) {
  // Coordinator: split work across workers
  const chunkSize = Math.ceil(TOTAL_USERS / WORKER_COUNT);
  const workers: Promise<void>[] = [];

  for (let i = 0; i < WORKER_COUNT; i++) {
    const start = i * chunkSize;
    const count = Math.min(chunkSize, TOTAL_USERS - start);

    workers.push(
      new Promise<void>((resolve, reject) => {
        const w = new Worker(__filename, { workerData: { start, count } });
        w.on('exit', code => (code === 0 ? resolve() : reject(new Error(`Worker exited with code ${code}`))));
        w.on('error', reject);
      }),
    );
  }

  await Promise.all(workers);
  console.log(`Seeded ${TOTAL_USERS} users across ${WORKER_COUNT} workers.`);
} else {
  // Worker: insert its assigned chunk
  const { start, count } = workerData as { start: number; count: number };
  const batch = Array.from({ length: count }, (_, i) =>
    buildUser({ email: `seed-user-${start + i}@example.com` }),
  );
  await db.insert(users).values(batch);
  parentPort?.postMessage('done');
  process.exit(0);
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Each worker opens its own DB connection. Ensure your connection pool size is at least `WORKER_COUNT`. For PgBouncer-limited environments, reduce `WORKER_COUNT` or use a single connection with batched `INSERT` (Prisma `createMany` with `skipDuplicates`).

[community]

### `fc.statistics()` — Distribution Assertions for Randomly Generated Test Data  [official]

`fc.statistics()` (fast-check) collects frequency histograms over arbitrary values across all `numRuns` iterations and emits them as a formatted report. This verifies that a factory's random output is distributed as expected — catching biased generators that over-produce certain values and under-represent edge cases.

**Why it matters:** A `faker.helpers.arrayElement()` call that weights toward the first element (due to a seeding bug) will produce test data that exercises the "first case" path far more than others, giving false confidence that branch coverage is achieved when many branches are never exercised. `fc.statistics()` makes the distribution visible in the test output.

**When to use:** Any factory that uses randomness to select between multiple variants (status values, roles, tiers) and where even distribution is semantically required. **When NOT to use:** Factories with intentionally skewed distributions (e.g., `faker.helpers.weightedArrayElement`) — the distribution will appear uneven by design. Named alternative: manual histogram test with `Array.from({ length: 1000 })` and `expect` on frequency counts (more verbose, no shrinking).

```typescript
// specs/user-status-distribution.prop.test.ts — fc.statistics() distribution check
import * as fc from 'fast-check';
import { test } from 'vitest';
import { buildUser } from '../factories/user.factory';

test('buildUser() distributes statuses roughly evenly across 1000 runs', () => {
  // fc.statistics() does NOT assert — it logs a histogram to the console.
  // Set VERBOSE=true in CI to capture it. Pair with fc.assert to catch imbalance.
  fc.statistics(
    fc.constant(null),          // arbitrary placeholder — we don't need generated values
    () => buildUser().status,   // label function: maps each run to a histogram bucket
    { numRuns: 1000, verbose: true },
  );

  // Paired assertion: verify all statuses appear at least once
  const statuses = new Set<string>();
  fc.assert(
    fc.property(fc.constant(null), () => {
      statuses.add(buildUser().status);
      return true;
    }),
    { numRuns: 500 },
  );

  const expected = new Set(['active', 'suspended', 'pending', 'deleted']);
  for (const s of expected) {
    if (!statuses.has(s)) {
      throw new Error(`[distribution] buildUser() never produced status "${s}" in 500 runs`);
    }
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `fc.statistics()` output is printed to `stdout`, not captured by Vitest's reporter. In `--reporter=verbose` mode it is visible; in silent CI it is lost. For machine-readable distribution assertions, use the paired `fc.assert` approach above.

[official]

### `structuredClone()` — Deep Copy in Factory Overrides  [community]

Factory functions that return object references allow tests to mutate the "canonical" factory output unintentionally. When `buildUser()` returns the same reference (or a shallowly spread copy) and a test mutates a nested field, subsequent uses of the same factory within the test produce a modified object. Using `structuredClone()` — available natively in Node ≥ 17, browsers, and all modern edge runtimes — deep copies the factory output with zero dependencies.

**Why it matters:** Shallow spread (`{ ...defaults, ...overrides }`) does not clone nested objects. A test that mutates `user.address.city = 'Berlin'` modifies the address object that is shared with other users created from the same factory call. `structuredClone()` prevents this class of test interference without adding Lodash, `immer`, or `rfdc` as dependencies.

**When to use:** Factories that return objects with nested mutable references (address, settings, metadata, arrays). **When NOT to use:** Factories that return objects containing non-cloneable types (`Date` objects cloned correctly, but `Map`, `Set`, `undefined`, functions, and class instances with custom prototypes are cloned with caveats or dropped). Named alternative: `rfdc` (Really Fast Deep Clone) for cases where `structuredClone` performance or prototype-preservation is insufficient.

```typescript
// factories/user.factory.ts — structuredClone for safe deep-copy of nested objects
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

interface Address { street: string; city: string; country: string; }
interface User {
  id: string; email: string; role: 'admin' | 'user';
  address: Address;
  tags: string[];
}

const DEFAULT_USER: User = {
  id:      'usr-default',
  email:   'default@example.com',
  role:    'user',
  address: { street: '1 Main St', city: 'London', country: 'GB' },
  tags:    ['new'],
};

export function buildUser(overrides: Partial<User> = {}): User {
  // structuredClone produces a fresh deep copy on every call — no shared references.
  const base = structuredClone(DEFAULT_USER);

  return {
    ...base,
    id:    faker.string.uuid(),
    email: faker.internet.email(),
    // Deep-merge nested address override rather than replacing the whole object
    address: { ...base.address, ...overrides.address },
    tags:    overrides.tags ? [...overrides.tags] : [...base.tags],
    ...overrides,
    // Re-apply after spread to prevent overrides from clobbering the merged nested fields
    address: { ...base.address, ...overrides.address },
  };
}

// Test demonstrating the isolation guarantee
import { it, expect } from 'vitest';
it('mutation of one factory result does not affect another', () => {
  const user1 = buildUser();
  const user2 = buildUser();
  user1.address.city = 'Berlin';   // mutate user1's address
  expect(user2.address.city).not.toBe('Berlin');  // user2 is unaffected
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `structuredClone()` is ~2–5x slower than a manual shallow spread for simple flat objects. For flat-object factories (no nested objects), prefer shallow spread. Apply `structuredClone` only to factories that have nested mutable references.

[community]

---

### `crypto.randomUUID()` vs `faker.string.uuid()` — Performance Trade-off  [community]

Both `globalThis.crypto.randomUUID()` and `faker.string.uuid()` generate RFC 4122 v4 UUIDs, but they have different performance profiles, seeding characteristics, and runtime availability. Choosing the wrong one for the wrong use case causes either non-reproducible test failures (unseeded `crypto.randomUUID()` in snapshot tests) or unexpectedly slow test data generation at scale (faker overhead for millions of IDs).

**Why it matters:** Factories that generate 1,000,000 IDs during load tests (e.g., seeding a large dataset) spend measurably more time in `faker.string.uuid()` than in `crypto.randomUUID()` because faker adds format validation, seeding state tracking, and locale overhead. Conversely, snapshot tests that use `crypto.randomUUID()` never produce stable UUIDs, breaking snapshot assertions on every run.

**When to use `crypto.randomUUID()`:** High-volume factory scenarios (>100,000 IDs), edge runtimes, or anywhere Faker is not already a dependency and reproducibility is not required. **When NOT to use:** Snapshot tests, golden-file tests, or any test that asserts on the exact value of a generated ID. Named alternative: `nanoid()` (shorter IDs, URL-safe alphabet, comparable performance to `crypto.randomUUID()`).

```typescript
// factories/id-strategy.factory.ts — performance-aware ID generation
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

// Strategy 1: Faker UUID — reproducible with faker.seed(), locale-aware, slightly slower
export const fakerUUID = () => faker.string.uuid();

// Strategy 2: Web Crypto UUID — non-reproducible, fastest available, no dependencies
export const cryptoUUID = () => globalThis.crypto.randomUUID();

// Strategy 3: Deterministic sequential ID — fully reproducible, zero runtime cost
let counter = 0;
export const sequentialID = (prefix = 'id') => `${prefix}-${String(++counter).padStart(6, '0')}`;
export const resetSequentialCounter = () => { counter = 0; };

// Benchmark comparison (approximate, Node 20, M1 MacBook):
// fakerUUID():     ~1.2µs per call
// cryptoUUID():   ~0.3µs per call
// sequentialID():  ~0.05µs per call

// Load test factory — uses cryptoUUID for speed
export function buildUserForLoadTest(index: number) {
  return {
    id:    cryptoUUID(),   // speed prioritised over reproducibility
    email: `load-user-${index}@perf-test.local`,
    role:  'user' as const,
  };
}

// Snapshot test factory — uses sequentialID for stability
export function buildUserForSnapshot(index: number) {
  return {
    id:    sequentialID('usr'),  // stable across runs
    email: `snapshot-user-${index}@example.com`,
    role:  'user' as const,
  };
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Sequential IDs are fast and stable but expose test coupling when tests assert on ordering (e.g., `expect(users[0].id).toBe('usr-000001')`). Always call `resetSequentialCounter()` in `beforeEach` to prevent counter drift across test files when using `isolate: false`.

[community]

---

### `json-schema-faker` — JSON Schema–Driven Test Data Generation  [community]

`json-schema-faker` (JSF) generates random-but-valid data from any JSON Schema (draft-04 through draft-07). Unlike `zod-fixture` (which requires a Zod schema) or `@anatine/zod-mock`, JSF works directly from raw JSON Schema documents — making it the natural choice for projects that publish their data model as JSON Schema (OpenAPI schemas, AsyncAPI message schemas, AWS EventBridge schema registry exports).

**Why it matters:** Teams that publish their event schemas to AWS EventBridge or an AsyncAPI registry have a canonical JSON Schema available. `json-schema-faker` turns that schema into an executable factory with zero manual factory code — schema changes automatically produce updated factory output without touching the factory file.

**When to use:** Projects that already have a JSON Schema (from OpenAPI, AsyncAPI, or JSON Schema Store) and want zero-maintenance factories derived from that schema. **When NOT to use:** Projects that need full domain control over factory output (e.g., specific business rule combinations) — JSF generates structurally valid but semantically arbitrary data, missing domain-level invariants. Named alternative: `zod-fixture` (Zod schema-driven, more TypeScript-idiomatic for projects already using Zod).

```typescript
// factories/jsf.factory.ts — json-schema-faker for AsyncAPI schema-driven generation
import jsf from 'json-schema-faker';
import { faker as fakerInstance } from '@faker-js/faker';

// Wire JSF to use Faker as its underlying data generator for realistic values
jsf.extend('faker', () => fakerInstance);
jsf.option({ alwaysFakeOptionals: true, useDefaultValue: true });

// Raw JSON Schema (e.g., exported from EventBridge schema registry or OpenAPI spec)
const OrderCreatedEventSchema = {
  type: 'object',
  required: ['orderId', 'userId', 'totalCents', 'createdAt'],
  properties: {
    orderId:    { type: 'string', format: 'uuid' },
    userId:     { type: 'string', format: 'uuid' },
    totalCents: { type: 'integer', minimum: 1, maximum: 1_000_000 },
    currency:   { type: 'string', enum: ['USD', 'EUR', 'GBP'] },
    createdAt:  { type: 'string', format: 'date-time' },
    items: {
      type: 'array',
      minItems: 1,
      maxItems: 5,
      items: {
        type: 'object',
        required: ['sku', 'quantity', 'unitCents'],
        properties: {
          sku:       { type: 'string', pattern: '^[A-Z]{3}-\\d{6}$' },
          quantity:  { type: 'integer', minimum: 1, maximum: 10 },
          unitCents: { type: 'integer', minimum: 1 },
        },
      },
    },
  },
};

export async function buildOrderCreatedEvent(
  overrides: Partial<Record<string, unknown>> = {},
): Promise<Record<string, unknown>> {
  const generated = await jsf.resolve(OrderCreatedEventSchema);
  return { ...generated, ...overrides };
}
```

```typescript
// specs/order-event.test.ts
import { it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { buildOrderCreatedEvent } from '../factories/jsf.factory';

it('generates a valid OrderCreatedEvent from JSON Schema', async () => {
  const event = await buildOrderCreatedEvent({ currency: 'EUR' });
  expect(event.currency).toBe('EUR');
  expect(typeof event.totalCents).toBe('number');
  expect((event.items as unknown[]).length).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(1);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `jsf.resolve()` is asynchronous and slower than synchronous factory functions due to schema traversal. Cache resolved schemas with `jsf.generate()` (synchronous, less accurate) for performance-sensitive seeding loops.

[community]
