### `supertest` + Factory Integration Testing Layer  [community]

`supertest` allows HTTP integration tests without starting a real server. Combining `supertest` with typed factory functions creates a layered integration test pattern: factories produce domain objects, the integration helper submits them through the HTTP layer, and assertions verify both the HTTP response and the database state — exercising the full stack without a running process.

**Why it matters:** Tests that bypass the HTTP layer (calling service functions directly) miss validation middleware, authentication guards, request transformation, and response serialization bugs. `supertest` + factories exercises all of these in a single test without the overhead of spinning up a real server or Playwright.

**When to use:** Express / Fastify / Hono apps where controller-level bugs (auth bypass, input validation gaps, response envelope shape) are in scope. **When NOT to use:** Pure unit tests of service logic (no HTTP layer needed) or E2E tests where full browser rendering is the concern. Named alternative: `Playwright API testing` (`request.post()`) — browser-context-aware but heavier than `supertest`.

```typescript
// test/helpers/api.helper.ts — supertest + factory integration layer
import request from 'supertest';
import { app } from '../../src/app';   // Express/Fastify app (not yet listening)
import { buildUser } from '../factories/user.factory';
import { buildCreateOrderPayload } from '../factories/order.factory';
import { signJwt } from '../../src/auth/jwt';

export class ApiHelper {
  private agent = request(app);

  /** Create a user in the DB and return a JWT for that user. */
  async authenticateAs(overrides: Parameters<typeof buildUser>[0] = {}) {
    const user = buildUser(overrides);
    // Directly insert via repository — bypasses HTTP layer intentionally for setup
    const saved = await userRepository.create(user);
    const token = signJwt({ sub: saved.id, role: saved.role });
    return { user: saved, token };
  }

  /** POST /api/orders with factory payload — returns supertest response. */
  async createOrder(
    token: string,
    overrides: Parameters<typeof buildCreateOrderPayload>[0] = {},
  ) {
    return this.agent
      .post('/api/orders')
      .set('Authorization', `Bearer ${token}`)
      .send(buildCreateOrderPayload(overrides));
  }
}
```

```typescript
// specs/orders.integration.test.ts
import { beforeEach, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { ApiHelper } from '../helpers/api.helper';

let api: ApiHelper;
beforeEach(() => { api = new ApiHelper(); });

it('returns 201 and persists the order for an authenticated user', async () => {
  const { token } = await api.authenticateAs({ role: 'user' });
  const res = await api.createOrder(token, { totalCents: 9999 });

  expect(res.status).toBe(201);
  expect(res.body.data.totalCents).toBe(9999);
  expect(res.body.data.id).toMatch(/^[0-9a-f-]{36}$/);  // UUID v4
});

it('returns 403 when a suspended user attempts to create an order', async () => {
  const { token } = await api.authenticateAs({ status: 'suspended' });
  const res = await api.createOrder(token);
  expect(res.status).toBe(403);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `supertest` holds the app in memory across all tests. Ensure the app module is designed to be imported without side effects (no `app.listen()` at import time). For Fastify, use `fastify.inject()` instead of `supertest` for equivalent capability with better Fastify plugin lifecycle support.

[community]

---

### `expect.extend()` — Custom Factory Matcher for Domain Assertions  [community]

Repeating `expect(user.status).toBe('active'); expect(user.paymentMethodId).not.toBeNull()` in 30 tests creates assertion noise that obscures the intent of each test. `expect.extend()` lets you create domain-aware custom matchers that encapsulate the multi-field assertions for a complex factory-produced entity, making tests read as domain statements rather than property chains.

**Why it matters:** When a domain rule changes (e.g., "active user" now also requires `emailVerified: true`), you update one matcher rather than 30 `expect` chains. The custom matcher also produces a single, semantically named error message instead of three generic property mismatch errors.

**When to use:** Tests with 3+ repeated assertion patterns on factory-produced domain objects. **When NOT to use:** One-off assertions or tests that need to verify individual field values (custom matchers hide the specific failing field in some reporter configurations). Named alternative: `expect.objectContaining()` with a named constant (simpler, but does not produce custom error messages).

```typescript
// test/matchers/user.matchers.ts — custom Vitest/Jest expect matchers
import { expect } from 'vitest';

interface User {
  status: string;
  paymentMethodId: string | null;
  emailVerified: boolean;
  role: string;
}

expect.extend({
  toBeActiveUser(received: User) {
    const pass =
      received.status === 'active' &&
      received.paymentMethodId !== null &&
      received.emailVerified === true;

    return {
      pass,
      message: () =>
        pass
          ? `Expected user NOT to be active, but got: status=${received.status}, ` +
            `paymentMethodId=${received.paymentMethodId}, emailVerified=${received.emailVerified}`
          : `Expected active user (status='active', paymentMethodId≠null, emailVerified=true) ` +
            `but got: status=${received.status}, paymentMethodId=${received.paymentMethodId}, ` +
            `emailVerified=${received.emailVerified}`,
    };
  },

  toBeAdminUser(received: User) {
    const pass = received.role === 'admin' && received.status === 'active';
    return {
      pass,
      message: () =>
        `Expected admin user (role='admin', status='active') ` +
        `but got role=${received.role}, status=${received.status}`,
    };
  },
});
```

```typescript
// vitest.setup.ts — register matchers globally
import './test/matchers/user.matchers';

// vitest.config.ts
export default defineConfig({
  test: { setupFiles: ['./vitest.setup.ts'] },
});
```

```typescript
// specs/checkout.test.ts — domain-readable assertions
import { buildUser } from '../factories/user.factory';

it('allows checkout for an active user with payment method', () => {
  const user = buildUser({ status: 'active', paymentMethodId: 'pm-123', emailVerified: true });
  expect(user).toBeActiveUser();   // single domain-level assertion
  expect(user).not.toBeAdminUser();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Custom matchers require TypeScript declaration merging to provide type-safe intellisense. Add `interface Matchers<R> { toBeActiveUser(): R; toBeAdminUser(): R; }` to a `vitest.d.ts` file in the project root. Without this, TypeScript will error on `expect(x).toBeActiveUser()`.

[community]

---

### MSW `server.boundary()` — Isolated Per-Test Handler Scopes  [official]

MSW v2.x introduced `server.boundary()` to create scoped handler contexts for a specific function or component tree, ensuring that handlers registered inside a boundary are isolated from the global handler list and do not leak into other tests. This is the MSW-idiomatic replacement for the `server.use()` + `server.resetHandlers()` pattern that causes handler leak bugs when `resetHandlers()` is omitted.

**Why it matters:** `server.use()` temporarily prepends handlers to the global list. If `server.resetHandlers()` is not called in `afterEach` (forgotten or skipped due to an early `test.skip()`), the handlers from one test bleed into subsequent tests, producing false positives. `server.boundary()` eliminates this risk by scoping handlers to a function call's execution context.

**When to use:** Component tests, React hooks tests, or any test layer where MSW handlers need to be scoped to individual tests without global teardown. **When NOT to use:** E2E tests (no MSW service worker available in Playwright's browser context) or tests that deliberately need handlers to persist across multiple test calls. Named alternative: `server.use()` + `afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers())` — works correctly but fragile if `afterEach` is missed.

```typescript
// test/helpers/msw-boundary.helper.ts — server.boundary() per-test scope
import { setupServer } from 'msw/node';
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw';

export const server = setupServer();

// beforeAll/afterAll in vitest.setup.ts:
// server.listen({ onUnhandledRequest: 'error' });
// afterAll(() => server.close());

export function withHandlers(
  handlers: Parameters<typeof server.use>,
  testFn: () => Promise<void> | void,
) {
  // server.boundary() runs testFn in a scoped context where the provided
  // handlers are active, and removes them automatically when testFn resolves.
  return server.boundary(async () => {
    server.use(...handlers);
    await testFn();
  })();
}
```

```typescript
// specs/user-api.component.test.tsx — MSW boundary for isolated handler scopes
import { it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { render, screen, waitFor } from '@testing-library/react';
import { withHandlers } from '../helpers/msw-boundary.helper';
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw';
import { UserProfile } from '../../src/components/UserProfile';
import { buildUser } from '../factories/user.factory';

it('renders the user profile for an active user', async () => {
  const user = buildUser({ status: 'active', name: 'Alice Example' });

  await withHandlers(
    [http.get('/api/users/:id', () => HttpResponse.json(user))],
    async () => {
      render(<UserProfile userId={user.id} />);
      await waitFor(() => expect(screen.getByText('Alice Example')).toBeInTheDocument());
    },
  );
  // Handlers are automatically removed after withHandlers() resolves
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `server.boundary()` requires MSW v2.3.0+. Check `msw` version compatibility before adopting. For projects locked to MSW v1.x, the `server.use()` + `afterEach(server.resetHandlers)` pattern is the only option.

[official]

---

### `Temporal.ZonedDateTime` in Time-Zone-Aware Factories  [community]

JavaScript's `Date` has no time zone concept — it stores UTC and formats with the local system timezone at display time. Test factories that use `new Date()` or `faker.date.*` produce UTC timestamps that mask time-zone bugs in business logic (e.g., "show orders placed today in the user's timezone"). The TC39 Temporal API (`@js-temporal/polyfill` or native in Node 24+) introduces `ZonedDateTime` — a timestamp that carries an explicit IANA timezone and calendar — making time-zone bugs impossible to hide in factory construction.

**Why it matters:** A recurring event scheduler that fires at "09:00 in the user's timezone" using `Date` arithmetic will silently produce wrong results for users in UTC+12 or UTC-8. A factory that produces `Temporal.ZonedDateTime` values forces the service layer to handle timezone offsets explicitly — and tests that fail on timezone mishandling are reproducible regardless of the CI server's `TZ` environment variable.

**When to use:** Services that compute time-zone-aware business logic (business hours, SLA deadlines, recurring schedules, "today's" reports). **When NOT to use:** Systems that treat all timestamps as UTC with no user-facing timezone concept. Named alternative: `date-fns-tz` with `zonedTimeToUtc()` (does not require Temporal — lighter for narrow use cases).

```typescript
// factories/temporal.factory.ts — ZonedDateTime-aware test data factories
import { Temporal } from '@js-temporal/polyfill';
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

/** Build a ZonedDateTime within a given timezone — forces time-zone-aware service logic. */
export function buildZonedDateTime(
  tz: string = 'America/New_York',
  overrides: Partial<Temporal.ZonedDateTimeLike> = {},
): Temporal.ZonedDateTime {
  const base = Temporal.Now.zonedDateTimeISO(tz);
  return base.with({
    hour:   overrides.hour   ?? faker.number.int({ min: 0, max: 23 }),
    minute: overrides.minute ?? faker.number.int({ min: 0, max: 59 }),
    ...overrides,
  });
}

/** Build a recurring schedule event with start/end in explicit timezones. */
export function buildScheduleEvent(overrides: {
  timezone?: string;
  startHour?: number;
  durationHours?: number;
} = {}) {
  const tz    = overrides.timezone ?? 'Europe/London';
  const start = buildZonedDateTime(tz, { hour: overrides.startHour ?? 9, minute: 0 });
  const end   = start.add({ hours: overrides.durationHours ?? 1 });

  return {
    id:        faker.string.uuid(),
    timezone:  tz,
    startsAt:  start.toString(),          // ISO-8601 with offset + tz annotation
    endsAt:    end.toString(),
    startEpoch: start.epochMilliseconds,  // UTC epoch — safe for DB storage
    endEpoch:   end.epochMilliseconds,
  };
}
```

```typescript
// specs/scheduler.tz.test.ts — timezone-aware assertion using Temporal
import { it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { Temporal } from '@js-temporal/polyfill';
import { buildScheduleEvent } from '../factories/temporal.factory';
import { schedulerService } from '../../src/services/scheduler.service';

it('fires the event at the correct wall-clock time in the event timezone', () => {
  // Build an event starting at 09:00 Auckland time (UTC+12 in summer)
  const event = buildScheduleEvent({ timezone: 'Pacific/Auckland', startHour: 9 });

  const fired = schedulerService.nextFireTime(event);

  // Assert using Temporal comparison — not raw Date arithmetic
  const firedZdt = Temporal.Instant
    .fromEpochMilliseconds(fired.getTime())
    .toZonedDateTimeISO('Pacific/Auckland');

  expect(firedZdt.hour).toBe(9);    // 09:00 in Auckland — not UTC
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `@js-temporal/polyfill` adds ~40KB to the test bundle. In Node 24+, `Temporal` is available natively without the polyfill. Verify runtime support with `typeof Temporal !== 'undefined'` before removing the polyfill dependency.

[community]

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 29

**74. [community] `expect.extend()` custom matchers are NOT included in Vitest's `--reporter=junit` XML output — the custom matcher name appears in HTML and terminal output but the JUnit XML only records "AssertionError" with the raw matcher message string, making CI test result aggregators (Datadog, TestRail) unable to categorise failures by matcher type.**

When a test fails on a custom matcher like `expect(user).toBeActiveUser()`, the Vitest JUnit reporter writes the raw `message()` string from the matcher as the failure body, with no indication of the matcher name. CI dashboards that parse JUnit XML to categorise failures by assertion type cannot distinguish `toBeActiveUser` failures from `toBe` failures. Fix: prefix the `message()` return value with a stable token: `[toBeActiveUser] Expected active user but got...`. This makes the matcher name machine-parseable in JUnit XML without changing terminal or HTML output. WHY: this surprises teams that use Datadog CI Visibility or TestRail JUnit import and notice that their "custom matcher" category never appears in the dashboard — the matcher name is simply absent from the XML schema.

**75. [community] `json-schema-faker` with `alwaysFakeOptionals: true` generates values for `readOnly: true` fields in OpenAPI schemas — causing `POST` request factories to include server-generated fields like `id`, `createdAt`, and `updatedAt` in the request body, producing HTTP 422 errors when the server rejects unexpected read-only fields.**

JSF does not respect the `readOnly` keyword by default when `alwaysFakeOptionals: true` is set. A `POST /users` request body factory generated from the `User` OpenAPI schema will include `id` and `createdAt` (which are `readOnly: true`) unless explicitly excluded. Fix: call `jsf.option({ useReadOnly: false })` before resolving, or filter out `readOnly` fields from the schema before passing it to JSF: `delete schema.properties.id; delete schema.properties.createdAt`. WHY: the interaction between `alwaysFakeOptionals` and `readOnly` is not documented in the JSF README — it is buried in a GitHub issue from 2023 that most teams find only after spending hours debugging 422 errors.

**76. [community] `server.boundary()` (MSW v2.x) does NOT work inside Vitest's `test.concurrent()` tests because `server.boundary()` uses Node.js `AsyncLocalStorage` under the hood, and `test.concurrent()` shares the same async context across concurrent test functions in the same worker — causing handler scopes from concurrent tests to bleed into each other.**

`AsyncLocalStorage` (which MSW's `server.boundary()` uses internally) propagates the store to child async operations started within the same synchronous execution context. When Vitest's `test.concurrent()` runs multiple test functions simultaneously in a single worker, their async operations share the same `AsyncLocalStorage` context, and handler registrations from one concurrent test's `server.boundary()` become visible to other concurrent tests' handler lookups. Fix: use `test.concurrent()` only with the `server.use()` + `afterEach(server.resetHandlers)` pattern, or disable concurrency for test files that use `server.boundary()` by marking them `describe.sequential()`. WHY: the `AsyncLocalStorage` leak is undetectable in `test.sequential()` (where it works correctly) and only manifests in `test.concurrent()` under timing-dependent conditions, making it one of the hardest MSW bugs to reproduce.

**77. [community] `structuredClone()` silently drops class instance methods when cloning factory outputs — if a factory returns an instance of a class (e.g., `new User(data)`) rather than a plain object, `structuredClone()` returns a plain object with the same properties but no prototype methods, causing `user.isActive()` to throw `TypeError: user.isActive is not a function` in tests that call methods on the cloned factory output.**

`structuredClone()` uses the Structured Clone Algorithm, which does not preserve prototype chains. A factory that calls `new User(data)` and then `structuredClone(userInstance)` produces a plain `{}` with no methods. This is especially surprising when the factory is refactored from plain-object returns to class-instance returns — all existing tests that used `structuredClone()` on factory outputs start throwing `TypeError`. Fix: never use `structuredClone()` on class instances — use a dedicated `clone()` method on the class, or restructure the factory to return a plain object (data-only) and provide a separate `toEntity()` helper for tests that need the class instance. WHY: the Structured Clone Algorithm spec explicitly states "custom prototype chains are not preserved" — but most TypeScript developers do not read the spec until they hit this bug in production.

**78. [community] `worker_threads`-based parallel seeding that opens multiple Drizzle ORM connections fails with `"too many connections for role"` in PgBouncer transaction-mode — because PgBouncer in transaction mode only allows one in-flight transaction per client, and Drizzle's connection pool per worker issues multiple concurrent `INSERT` batches on the same connection, causing "connection timeout" errors that look like network failures rather than pool exhaustion.**

In PgBouncer transaction mode, each `BEGIN` / `COMMIT` cycle releases the underlying PostgreSQL connection back to the pool. However, Drizzle's `db.insert().values(batch)` without an explicit `BEGIN` runs as an implicit auto-commit transaction. With 8 workers each issuing 100 concurrent auto-commit inserts, the 8 × 100 = 800 simultaneous requests exceed PgBouncer's `max_client_conn`. The error message is a generic `connection timeout` — not `too many connections` — because PgBouncer times out the connection queue before the limit is logged. Fix: set `worker_count = Math.min(os.cpus().length, pgBouncerMaxClientConn / 10)` and batch all inserts in a single explicit transaction per worker: `await db.transaction(tx => tx.insert(users).values(batch))`. WHY: PgBouncer transaction mode's connection-release semantics are counterintuitive for developers expecting persistent connection assignment — and the timeout error message provides no indication of pool exhaustion.

## Cycle 30 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 1 — Invariant-Enforcing Factory Wrapper  [community]

Most factories accept `Partial<T>` overrides and spread them freely over defaults. For domains with hard invariants (e.g., a `paidAt` timestamp must always be present when `status === 'paid'`), a thin validation layer inside the factory prevents tests from accidentally constructing semantically impossible objects.

**Why it matters:** When a developer writes `buildOrder({ status: 'paid' })` they may not know that `paymentIntentId` is also required for a paid order. Without the wrapper, the factory silently omits it and the test passes against an invalid state that never occurs in production.

**When to use:** Domains with cross-field constraints (state machines, required-when conditions). **When NOT to use:** Simple DTOs with no cross-field rules — adds overhead for no benefit. Alternative: Zod `superRefine` on the domain schema.

```typescript
// factories/invariant-factory.ts
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

type OrderStatus = 'draft' | 'pending' | 'paid' | 'shipped';

interface Order {
  id: string;
  userId: string;
  status: OrderStatus;
  totalCents: number;
  paymentIntentId?: string;
  paidAt?: Date;
  shippedAt?: Date;
  trackingNumber?: string;
  createdAt: Date;
}

function assertOrderInvariants(order: Order): void {
  if (order.status === 'paid') {
    if (!order.paymentIntentId) throw new Error('[factory] paid order missing paymentIntentId');
    if (!order.paidAt) throw new Error('[factory] paid order missing paidAt');
  }
  if (order.status === 'shipped') {
    if (!order.trackingNumber) throw new Error('[factory] shipped order missing trackingNumber');
    if (!order.shippedAt) throw new Error('[factory] shipped order missing shippedAt');
  }
}

export function buildOrder(overrides: Partial<Order> = {}): Order {
  const base: Order = {
    id: faker.string.uuid(),
    userId: faker.string.uuid(),
    status: 'pending',
    totalCents: faker.number.int({ min: 100, max: 50_000 }),
    createdAt: new Date(),
    ...overrides,
  };
  assertOrderInvariants(base);
  return base;
}

// Usage — missing paymentIntentId throws at factory call, not 40 lines later
// buildOrder({ status: 'paid' })             // ← throws: "paid order missing paymentIntentId"
// buildOrder({ status: 'paid', paymentIntentId: 'pi_123', paidAt: new Date() }) // ← ok
```

**Tradeoff note:** Invariant enforcement at factory call time is a double-edged sword. It provides safety for production-like correctness but can block tests that intentionally need "impossible" states (e.g., testing recovery from corrupted data). Provide an `unsafe_buildOrder` escape hatch for those rare cases.

[community]

---

### Pattern 2 — Cursor-Based Pagination Factory  [community]

APIs using cursor-based pagination (common in GraphQL, REST infinite scroll) require factories to produce semantically correct cursor values that encode the sort key. A factory that produces arbitrary `cursor: 'abc123'` strings cannot test the edge cases (first page, last page, cursor pointing to a deleted record) that matter most.

**When to use:** GraphQL connections, REST APIs using opaque cursors, infinite-scroll frontends. **When NOT to use:** Offset/limit pagination — use a simpler `buildPage()` factory instead. Alternative: `@faker-js/faker` base64 encoding utilities.

```typescript
// factories/pagination.factory.ts — cursor-based pagination test data
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

interface CursorPayload {
  id: string;
  createdAt: number; // epoch ms — used as sort key
}

// Encode a cursor the same way the real API would
function encodeCursor(payload: CursorPayload): string {
  return Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(payload)).toString('base64url');
}

export function buildValidCursor(overrides: Partial<CursorPayload> = {}): string {
  return encodeCursor({
    id: faker.string.uuid(),
    createdAt: Date.now() - faker.number.int({ min: 0, max: 30 * 86400_000 }),
    ...overrides,
  });
}

export function buildCorruptCursor(): string {
  // Tests how the API handles malformed / tampered cursors
  return Buffer.from('{"id":"not-a-uuid","createdAt":"not-a-number"}').toString('base64url');
}

export function buildExpiredCursor(): string {
  // Cursor pointing to a record created more than 90 days ago (outside retention window)
  return encodeCursor({
    id: faker.string.uuid(),
    createdAt: Date.now() - 91 * 86400_000,
  });
}

// GraphQL connection page factory
export function buildConnection<T>(
  items: T[],
  opts: { hasNextPage?: boolean; hasPreviousPage?: boolean } = {}
) {
  return {
    edges: items.map((node) => ({ node, cursor: buildValidCursor() })),
    pageInfo: {
      hasNextPage: opts.hasNextPage ?? false,
      hasPreviousPage: opts.hasPreviousPage ?? false,
      startCursor: items.length > 0 ? buildValidCursor() : null,
      endCursor: items.length > 0 ? buildValidCursor() : null,
    },
    totalCount: items.length,
  };
}
```

[community]

---

### Pattern 3 — Partial Mock via `vi.spyOn` Without Full Factory  [official]

When a unit test only needs to override one method on a large service, constructing a complete factory object is wasteful. Vitest's `vi.spyOn()` (with automatic restoration via `using` or `afterEach`) lets you selectively replace a single method while keeping the real implementation for all others.

**When to use:** Unit tests where one dependency method needs stubbing but the rest should execute real logic. **When NOT to use:** Integration tests (use real implementations) or when multiple methods need stubbing (use a full mock/factory). Alternative: `vi.fn()` for a complete replacement.

```typescript
// specs/checkout-notifier.unit.test.ts — partial mock via vi.spyOn
import { test, expect, vi, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { emailService } from '../services/email.service';
import { buildUser } from '../factories/user.factory';
import { checkoutNotifier } from '../services/checkout-notifier';

afterEach(() => {
  vi.restoreAllMocks(); // always restore — avoids bleed into subsequent tests
});

test('sends confirmation email with the correct order ID', async () => {
  const user = buildUser({ email: 'buyer@test.com' });
  const orderId = 'ord-001';

  // Spy on just sendEmail — the rest of emailService runs real code
  const sendEmailSpy = vi.spyOn(emailService, 'sendEmail').mockResolvedValue({ messageId: 'msg-001' });

  await checkoutNotifier.onOrderConfirmed(user, orderId);

  expect(sendEmailSpy).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
  expect(sendEmailSpy).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
    expect.objectContaining({
      to: 'buyer@test.com',
      subject: expect.stringContaining(orderId),
    })
  );
});

test('does not send email for suspended users', async () => {
  const user = buildUser({ status: 'suspended' });
  const sendEmailSpy = vi.spyOn(emailService, 'sendEmail');

  await checkoutNotifier.onOrderConfirmed(user, 'ord-002');

  // Using Chai-style mock assertions (Vitest 4.x alternative to toHaveBeenCalled)
  expect(sendEmailSpy).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
});
```

[official]

---

### Pattern 4 — Weighted Random Data Distribution  [community]

Real production traffic is not uniformly distributed. Most users are `status: 'active'`, a small fraction are `suspended`, and an even smaller fraction are `pending`. Load test and performance test factories should mirror this distribution — otherwise performance tests measure a scenario that never occurs in production.

**When to use:** Performance/load tests, smoke tests that want representative data, any test where distribution affects the SUT behavior. **When NOT to use:** Unit tests targeting a specific status — use explicit overrides. Alternative: fishery traits with explicit counts.

```typescript
// factories/weighted.factory.ts — weighted random distribution
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';
import { User } from '../domain/user';

type Weight<T> = { value: T; weight: number };

function weightedPick<T>(options: Weight<T>[]): T {
  const total = options.reduce((sum, o) => sum + o.weight, 0);
  let random = faker.number.float({ min: 0, max: total });
  for (const option of options) {
    random -= option.weight;
    if (random <= 0) return option.value;
  }
  return options[options.length - 1].value;
}

// Production-representative user status distribution
// Derived from analytics: 85% active, 10% pending, 5% suspended
const USER_STATUS_DISTRIBUTION: Weight<User['status']>[] = [
  { value: 'active',    weight: 85 },
  { value: 'pending',   weight: 10 },
  { value: 'suspended', weight: 5  },
];

const SUBSCRIPTION_DISTRIBUTION: Weight<User['subscriptionTier']>[] = [
  { value: 'free',       weight: 70 },
  { value: 'premium',    weight: 25 },
  { value: 'enterprise', weight: 5  },
];

export function buildRealisticUser(overrides: Partial<User> = {}): User {
  return {
    id: faker.string.uuid(),
    email: faker.internet.email(),
    name: faker.person.fullName(),
    status: weightedPick(USER_STATUS_DISTRIBUTION),
    subscriptionTier: weightedPick(SUBSCRIPTION_DISTRIBUTION),
    createdAt: faker.date.past({ years: 3 }),
    paymentMethodId: null,
    ...overrides,
  };
}

// Performance test: 10,000 users with production-representative distribution
export function buildRealisticUserDataset(count: number): User[] {
  return Array.from({ length: count }, () => buildRealisticUser());
}
```

[community]

---

### Pattern 5 — File/Blob Factory for Upload Testing  [community]

Features that accept file uploads (avatars, documents, CSV imports) need factory helpers that produce real `File`, `Blob`, or `Buffer` objects — not just metadata strings. Factories that return `{ filename: 'test.csv', size: 1024 }` cannot test actual file parsing, MIME validation, or size limit enforcement.

**When to use:** File upload endpoints, image processing pipelines, CSV/Excel import features. **When NOT to use:** Tests that only validate metadata (e.g., filename validation before reading the file). Alternative: `@faker-js/faker`'s `faker.system.fileName()` for filename-only tests.

```typescript
// factories/file.factory.ts — real File/Buffer test data for upload tests
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

// Build a real File object (browser/jsdom environment)
export function buildImageFile(options: {
  width?: number;
  height?: number;
  mimeType?: 'image/png' | 'image/jpeg' | 'image/webp';
  filename?: string;
} = {}): File {
  const mimeType = options.mimeType ?? 'image/png';
  const filename = options.filename ?? `test-${faker.string.uuid()}.png`;

  // Minimal valid PNG header (1x1 pixel transparent PNG, 67 bytes)
  const minimalPng = Buffer.from(
    '89504e470d0a1a0a0000000d49484452000000010000000108060000001f15c489' +
    '0000000a49444154789c6260000000020001e221bc330000000049454e44ae426082',
    'hex'
  );

  return new File([minimalPng], filename, { type: mimeType });
}

// Build a CSV file with realistic headers and rows
export function buildCsvFile(options: {
  headers?: string[];
  rowCount?: number;
  filename?: string;
} = {}): File {
  const headers = options.headers ?? ['id', 'email', 'name', 'status'];
  const rowCount = options.rowCount ?? 10;
  const filename = options.filename ?? `import-${faker.string.uuid()}.csv`;

  const rows = Array.from({ length: rowCount }, () =>
    headers.map((h) => {
      if (h === 'email') return faker.internet.email();
      if (h === 'id') return faker.string.uuid();
      if (h === 'name') return faker.person.fullName();
      if (h === 'status') return faker.helpers.arrayElement(['active', 'pending']);
      return faker.lorem.word();
    }).join(',')
  );

  const csvContent = [headers.join(','), ...rows].join('\n');
  return new File([csvContent], filename, { type: 'text/csv' });
}

// Build an oversized file to test size limit rejection
export function buildOversizedFile(limitBytes: number = 5 * 1024 * 1024): File {
  // 10% over the limit to reliably trigger the rejection
  const content = Buffer.alloc(Math.ceil(limitBytes * 1.1), 'x');
  return new File([content], 'oversized.bin', { type: 'application/octet-stream' });
}
```

[community]

### Pattern 6 — Deterministic Sequence IDs with a Counter Factory  [community]

`faker.string.uuid()` generates unpredictable IDs that are hard to read in assertion error messages. For unit tests where ID predictability aids debugging, a counter-based ID generator creates readable, sequential IDs (`usr-0001`, `usr-0002`) that still maintain uniqueness within a test run.

**When to use:** Unit tests with explicit ID assertions, snapshot tests, test output that is reviewed by humans. **When NOT to use:** Integration tests against real DBs that require UUID format (FK constraints, indexed UUIDs). Alternative: `fishery`'s built-in `sequence` parameter.

```typescript
// factories/counter-id.factory.ts — readable sequential IDs for unit tests
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

// Per-entity counters — reset between test files when isolate: true (default)
const counters: Record<string, number> = {};

export function nextId(entity: string): string {
  counters[entity] = (counters[entity] ?? 0) + 1;
  return `${entity}-${String(counters[entity]).padStart(4, '0')}`;
}

export function resetCounters(): void {
  for (const key of Object.keys(counters)) {
    counters[key] = 0;
  }
}

// Factory using sequential IDs for unit test clarity
export function buildUserWithSequenceId(overrides: Partial<{ id: string; email: string; name: string }> = {}) {
  return {
    id: nextId('usr'),
    email: faker.internet.email(),
    name: faker.person.fullName(),
    status: 'active' as const,
    subscriptionTier: 'free' as const,
    createdAt: new Date('2024-01-01T00:00:00Z'),
    paymentMethodId: null,
    ...overrides,
  };
}

// In a test: IDs are readable and predictable
// const u1 = buildUserWithSequenceId(); // { id: 'usr-0001', ... }
// const u2 = buildUserWithSequenceId(); // { id: 'usr-0002', ... }
// expect(service.getById('usr-0001')).toEqual(u1);  // clear assertion

// In vitest.setup.ts — reset counters before each test file to prevent cross-file bleed
// import { resetCounters } from './factories/counter-id.factory';
// beforeEach(() => resetCounters());
```

### Pattern 7 — Retry-Aware Factory for Flaky External Dependencies  [community]

When factories call external services (seed DB via API, create Stripe test customer), transient failures in CI cause the entire test setup to fail rather than retrying. A retry-aware factory wrapper handles transient network errors without manual `try/catch` boilerplate in every factory call.

**When to use:** Factories that call third-party sandbox APIs (Stripe test mode, Auth0 Management API, SendGrid). **When NOT to use:** Pure in-memory factories (no network call, no retry needed). Alternative: wrapping the entire `beforeAll` in a retry loop.

```typescript
// factories/retry.factory.ts — retry wrapper for flaky external factory calls
interface RetryOptions {
  maxAttempts?: number;
  delayMs?: number;
  retryOn?: (error: unknown) => boolean;
}

export async function withRetry<T>(
  fn: () => Promise<T>,
  options: RetryOptions = {}
): Promise<T> {
  const maxAttempts = options.maxAttempts ?? 3;
  const delayMs = options.delayMs ?? 500;
  const retryOn = options.retryOn ?? ((e) => {
    // Retry on network errors and 429/503 status codes only
    if (e instanceof Error && (e.message.includes('ECONNRESET') || e.message.includes('fetch failed'))) return true;
    if (e && typeof e === 'object' && 'status' in e) {
      const status = (e as { status: number }).status;
      return status === 429 || status === 503;
    }
    return false;
  });

  let lastError: unknown;
  for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= maxAttempts; attempt++) {
    try {
      return await fn();
    } catch (err) {
      lastError = err;
      if (!retryOn(err) || attempt === maxAttempts) throw err;
      await new Promise<void>((res) => setTimeout(res, delayMs * attempt)); // exponential backoff
      console.warn(`[factory:retry] Attempt ${attempt} failed, retrying…`);
    }
  }
  throw lastError;
}

// Usage in a factory that seeds via external API
export async function createStripeTestCustomer(email: string): Promise<{ customerId: string }> {
  return withRetry(
    async () => {
      const response = await fetch('https://api.stripe.com/v1/customers', {
        method: 'POST',
        headers: {
          Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.STRIPE_TEST_KEY}`,
          'Content-Type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded',
        },
        body: `email=${encodeURIComponent(email)}`,
      });
      if (!response.ok) throw Object.assign(new Error('Stripe API error'), { status: response.status });
      const data = await response.json() as { id: string };
      return { customerId: data.id };
    },
    { maxAttempts: 3, delayMs: 1000 }
  );
}
```

[community]

### Pattern 8 — Scenario Builder (Fluent Multi-Entity Setup)  [community]

Unit and integration tests that require multiple related entities often end up with 10+ lines of factory calls before the first assertion. A scenario builder encapsulates a complete cross-entity test scenario in a single, named, fluent construction — improving readability and reducing repetition.

**When to use:** Integration tests with 3+ related entities, E2E precondition setup, BDD-style scenario descriptions. **When NOT to use:** Simple unit tests with one or two entities — the overhead exceeds the benefit. Alternative: Playwright fixtures for E2E; Object Mother for named single-entity variants.

```typescript
// factories/scenario.builder.ts — multi-entity fluent scenario builder
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';
import { db } from '../db';
import * as schema from '../db/schema';

interface CheckoutScenario {
  user: typeof schema.users.$inferSelect;
  product: typeof schema.products.$inferSelect;
  cart: typeof schema.carts.$inferSelect;
  cartItem: typeof schema.cartItems.$inferSelect;
}

export class CheckoutScenarioBuilder {
  private userOverrides: Partial<typeof schema.users.$inferInsert> = {};
  private productOverrides: Partial<typeof schema.products.$inferInsert> = {};
  private quantity = 1;

  withUser(overrides: Partial<typeof schema.users.$inferInsert>): this {
    this.userOverrides = { ...this.userOverrides, ...overrides };
    return this;
  }

  withProduct(overrides: Partial<typeof schema.products.$inferInsert>): this {
    this.productOverrides = { ...this.productOverrides, ...overrides };
    return this;
  }

  withQuantity(qty: number): this {
    this.quantity = qty;
    return this;
  }

  async build(): Promise<CheckoutScenario & { cleanup: () => Promise<void> }> {
    const [user] = await db.insert(schema.users).values({
      email: faker.internet.email(),
      name: faker.person.fullName(),
      status: 'active',
      subscriptionTier: 'free',
      ...this.userOverrides,
    }).returning();

    const [product] = await db.insert(schema.products).values({
      name: faker.commerce.productName(),
      priceCents: faker.number.int({ min: 100, max: 50_000 }),
      stock: 100,
      ...this.productOverrides,
    }).returning();

    const [cart] = await db.insert(schema.carts).values({ userId: user.id }).returning();

    const [cartItem] = await db.insert(schema.cartItems).values({
      cartId: cart.id, productId: product.id, quantity: this.quantity,
    }).returning();

    return {
      user, product, cart, cartItem,
      cleanup: async () => {
        await db.delete(schema.cartItems).where(schema.eq(schema.cartItems.id, cartItem.id));
        await db.delete(schema.carts).where(schema.eq(schema.carts.id, cart.id));
        await db.delete(schema.products).where(schema.eq(schema.products.id, product.id));
        await db.delete(schema.users).where(schema.eq(schema.users.id, user.id));
      },
    };
  }
}

// In a test — single fluent expression replaces 15 lines of factory calls
// const scenario = await new CheckoutScenarioBuilder()
//   .withUser({ status: 'active', subscriptionTier: 'premium' })
//   .withProduct({ priceCents: 4999, stock: 1 })
//   .withQuantity(1)
//   .build();
// try {
//   const result = await checkoutService.confirm(scenario.cart.id);
//   expect(result.status).toBe('success');
// } finally {
//   await scenario.cleanup();
// }
```

[community]

### Pattern 9 — `fast-check` Arbitrary Composition for Domain Types  [official]

`fast-check` arbitraries (`fc.record`, `fc.string`, `fc.constantFrom`) can be composed to build property-based test data directly from domain type definitions — producing a PBT-native factory that replaces `buildUser()` for edge-case testing.

**When to use:** Functions with complex input validation, domain invariants, encoding/decoding round-trips. **When NOT to use:** Test cases that need a specific, human-readable scenario — use a named factory variant. Alternative: `fc.gen()` (Vitest fast-check integration) for test-runner-aware shrinking.

```typescript
// factories/pbt.factory.ts — fast-check arbitraries for domain types
import * as fc from 'fast-check';

// Arbitrary for valid user status
const statusArb = fc.constantFrom('active', 'suspended', 'pending') as fc.Arbitrary<'active' | 'suspended' | 'pending'>;

// Arbitrary for a structurally valid email (simpler than regex, passes format checks)
const emailArb = fc.tuple(
  fc.stringMatching(/^[a-z]{3,10}$/),
  fc.stringMatching(/^[a-z]{3,8}$/),
  fc.constantFrom('com', 'org', 'net', 'io')
).map(([local, domain, tld]) => `${local}@${domain}.${tld}`);

// Composed User arbitrary — generates combinatorially diverse User objects
export const userArb = fc.record({
  id: fc.uuid(),
  email: emailArb,
  name: fc.fullUnicodeString({ minLength: 1, maxLength: 100 }),
  status: statusArb,
  subscriptionTier: fc.constantFrom('free', 'premium', 'enterprise') as fc.Arbitrary<'free' | 'premium' | 'enterprise'>,
  createdAt: fc.date({ min: new Date('2020-01-01'), max: new Date('2026-01-01') }),
  paymentMethodId: fc.option(fc.stringMatching(/^pm_[a-zA-Z0-9]{16}$/), { nil: null }),
});

// Property test: user serialization is always reversible
// import { test } from 'vitest';
// test('User JSON round-trip preserves all fields', () => {
//   fc.assert(fc.property(userArb, (user) => {
//     const serialized = JSON.stringify(user);
//     const deserialized = JSON.parse(serialized);
//     return deserialized.id === user.id && deserialized.email === user.email;
//   }), { numRuns: 500 });
// });
```

[official]

### Pattern 10 — Snapshot-Stabilized Factory Output  [official]

When a factory's output is used as the expected value in a snapshot test, random fields (`faker.string.uuid()`, `faker.date.past()`) cause snapshots to update on every run. A snapshot-safe factory replaces non-deterministic fields with stable sentinels (`'<uuid>'`, `'<date>'`) while keeping the structural shape intact for snapshot comparison.

**When to use:** Snapshot tests for serialized domain objects, API response shapes, rendered component props. **When NOT to use:** Integration tests that require real UUIDs (DB inserts will fail). Alternative: `expect.any(String)` asymmetric matchers in non-snapshot assertions.

```typescript
// factories/snapshot.factory.ts — stable factory output for snapshot tests
import { User } from '../domain/user';

// Returns a structurally complete User with stable sentinel values instead of random data
export function buildSnapshotUser(overrides: Partial<User> = {}): User {
  return {
    id: '<uuid>',
    email: 'test@snapshot.fixture',
    name: 'Snapshot Test User',
    status: 'active',
    subscriptionTier: 'free',
    createdAt: new Date('2024-01-15T08:00:00.000Z'),  // fixed date — never changes
    paymentMethodId: null,
    ...overrides,
  };
}

// Usage in a snapshot test (Vitest toMatchSnapshot / toMatchInlineSnapshot)
// test('UserDTO serialization matches snapshot', () => {
//   const user = buildSnapshotUser({ subscriptionTier: 'premium' });
//   const dto = mapUserToDTO(user);
//   expect(dto).toMatchInlineSnapshot(`
//     {
//       "id": "<uuid>",
//       "displayName": "Snapshot Test User",
//       "tier": "premium",
//       "joinedAt": "2024-01-15T08:00:00.000Z",
//     }
//   `);
// });
```

**Tradeoff note:** Sentinel values (`'<uuid>'`) are not real UUIDs — code that parses the ID (e.g., `uuidParse(user.id)`) will throw. Use snapshot factories only for structural/serialization tests, never for logic tests that operate on the ID value.

[official]

### Pattern 11 — Factory for Error Response Test Data  [community]

Backend error responses follow patterns (HTTP status + error code + message + optional details). Building a separate factory for error responses ensures that all tests use the same error shape, and that error response changes propagate from one place.

**When to use:** Frontend tests asserting on API error handling, contract tests for error responses, MSW handlers returning errors. **When NOT to use:** Backend unit tests for the service that *produces* errors — test the actual thrown errors, not a factory version of them.

```typescript
// factories/error-response.factory.ts — typed API error response test data
interface ApiError {
  error: {
    code: string;
    message: string;
    details?: Record<string, string[]>;
    requestId: string;
    timestamp: string;
  };
}

// Pre-defined error codes that map to HTTP status codes (mirrors the real API)
export const ApiErrors = {
  unauthorized: (overrides: Partial<ApiError['error']> = {}): ApiError => ({
    error: {
      code: 'UNAUTHORIZED',
      message: 'Authentication required',
      requestId: `req-${Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 10)}`,
      timestamp: new Date().toISOString(),
      ...overrides,
    },
  }),

  validationFailed: (fieldErrors: Record<string, string[]> = {}): ApiError => ({
    error: {
      code: 'VALIDATION_FAILED',
      message: 'Request validation failed',
      details: Object.keys(fieldErrors).length > 0
        ? fieldErrors
        : { email: ['Email is required'], name: ['Name must be at least 1 character'] },
      requestId: `req-${Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 10)}`,
      timestamp: new Date().toISOString(),
    },
  }),

  notFound: (resource: string = 'User', id: string = 'unknown'): ApiError => ({
    error: {
      code: 'NOT_FOUND',
      message: `${resource} with id '${id}' not found`,
      requestId: `req-${Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 10)}`,
      timestamp: new Date().toISOString(),
    },
  }),

  rateLimited: (retryAfterSeconds: number = 60): ApiError => ({
    error: {
      code: 'RATE_LIMITED',
      message: `Too many requests. Retry after ${retryAfterSeconds}s`,
      details: { retryAfter: [String(retryAfterSeconds)] },
      requestId: `req-${Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 10)}`,
      timestamp: new Date().toISOString(),
    },
  }),
} as const;

// In MSW handler — error responses always use the shared factory
// http.get('/api/users/:id', ({ params }) => {
//   if (params.id === 'not-found') {
//     return HttpResponse.json(ApiErrors.notFound('User', params.id as string), { status: 404 });
//   }
//   ...
// });
```

[community]

### Pattern 12 — Conditional Factory Traits via Tagged Union Narrowing  [community]

TypeScript discriminated unions model domain entities that have fundamentally different shapes depending on a `type` or `kind` field. A factory that returns a generic `Partial<Entity>` cannot represent this accurately — narrowing via tagged union overloads gives type-safe factory signatures that produce the exact correct shape for each variant.

**When to use:** Discriminated union domain types (`type: 'individual' | 'organization'`), payment method types (card, bank, wallet), notification types. **When NOT to use:** Simple enums without structural differences — a plain `status` field factory is sufficient.

```typescript
// factories/tagged-union.factory.ts — type-safe discriminated union factory
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

type IndividualUser = {
  type: 'individual';
  id: string;
  firstName: string;
  lastName: string;
  dateOfBirth: Date;
  ssn?: string; // optional PII
};

type OrganizationUser = {
  type: 'organization';
  id: string;
  legalName: string;
  taxId: string;
  incorporationDate: Date;
  contactEmail: string;
};

type User = IndividualUser | OrganizationUser;

// Overloaded factory signatures — TypeScript infers the exact return type based on `type`
export function buildUserEntity(type: 'individual', overrides?: Partial<IndividualUser>): IndividualUser;
export function buildUserEntity(type: 'organization', overrides?: Partial<OrganizationUser>): OrganizationUser;
export function buildUserEntity(type: 'individual' | 'organization', overrides: Partial<User> = {}): User {
  if (type === 'individual') {
    return {
      type: 'individual',
      id: faker.string.uuid(),
      firstName: faker.person.firstName(),
      lastName: faker.person.lastName(),
      dateOfBirth: faker.date.birthdate({ min: 18, max: 80, mode: 'age' }),
      ...(overrides as Partial<IndividualUser>),
    };
  }
  return {
    type: 'organization',
    id: faker.string.uuid(),
    legalName: faker.company.name(),
    taxId: faker.string.numeric(9),
    incorporationDate: faker.date.past({ years: 20 }),
    contactEmail: faker.internet.email(),
    ...(overrides as Partial<OrganizationUser>),
  };
}

// TypeScript knows the return type:
// const ind = buildUserEntity('individual'); // ind: IndividualUser — has firstName, lastName
// const org = buildUserEntity('organization'); // org: OrganizationUser — has legalName, taxId
// ind.legalName; // ← TypeScript error: 'legalName' does not exist on IndividualUser
```

[community]

### Pattern 13 — Immutable Builder with `Object.freeze`  [community]

Standard builder classes use mutable internal state. When a builder is passed between helper functions, any helper that calls a `with*` method mutates the builder, silently affecting other callers. Making builder instances immutable after construction (`Object.freeze`) prevents this class of test pollution.

**When to use:** Builders shared across multiple test helpers or fixtures, builders stored in module-level variables for reuse. **When NOT to use:** One-off builders created fresh per test — immutability adds no value if the builder is never shared.

```typescript
// factories/immutable-builder.ts — freeze-on-return immutable builder
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

interface UserConfig {
  id?: string;
  email?: string;
  status?: 'active' | 'suspended' | 'pending';
  subscriptionTier?: 'free' | 'premium' | 'enterprise';
}

export class ImmutableUserBuilder {
  // Private config stored as readonly after construction
  private readonly config: Readonly<UserConfig>;

  constructor(config: UserConfig = {}) {
    this.config = Object.freeze({ ...config }); // immutable on construction
  }

  withStatus(status: UserConfig['status']): ImmutableUserBuilder {
    // Returns a NEW builder with updated config — never mutates this instance
    return new ImmutableUserBuilder({ ...this.config, status });
  }

  withSubscriptionTier(tier: UserConfig['subscriptionTier']): ImmutableUserBuilder {
    return new ImmutableUserBuilder({ ...this.config, subscriptionTier: tier });
  }

  withEmail(email: string): ImmutableUserBuilder {
    return new ImmutableUserBuilder({ ...this.config, email });
  }

  build() {
    return Object.freeze({
      id: this.config.id ?? faker.string.uuid(),
      email: this.config.email ?? faker.internet.email(),
      name: faker.person.fullName(),
      status: this.config.status ?? 'active',
      subscriptionTier: this.config.subscriptionTier ?? 'free',
      createdAt: new Date(),
      paymentMethodId: null,
    });
  }
}

// Module-level base builder — safe to share because each with* returns a new instance
export const baseUserBuilder = new ImmutableUserBuilder();

// Both helpers independently branch from baseUserBuilder — no mutation
// const premiumUser = baseUserBuilder.withSubscriptionTier('premium').build();
// const suspendedUser = baseUserBuilder.withStatus('suspended').build();
// baseUserBuilder.config.status is STILL undefined — not mutated
```

[community]

### Pattern 14 — Seeded `crypto.randomUUID()` Replacement for Deterministic Tests  [community]

`crypto.randomUUID()` (used directly in production code) is not seedable. When production code calls `crypto.randomUUID()` to generate entity IDs, tests cannot predict the generated IDs. A test-time replacement that wraps a seedable counter provides deterministic IDs without changing production behavior.

**When to use:** Production code that generates UUIDs internally (not via faker), tests that need to predict generated IDs. **When NOT to use:** Tests that use factories to supply all IDs externally — no need to stub production UUID generation. Alternative: dependency injection of the UUID generator function.

```typescript
// test/setup/deterministic-uuid.ts — deterministic UUID replacement for tests
import { vi } from 'vitest';

let uuidCounter = 0;

/**
 * Replace crypto.randomUUID() with a deterministic counter-based implementation.
 * Call resetUuidCounter() in beforeEach to ensure predictability per test.
 */
export function installDeterministicUuid(): void {
  vi.spyOn(globalThis.crypto, 'randomUUID').mockImplementation(() => {
    uuidCounter += 1;
    // Format as a valid UUID v4 string with the counter embedded
    const hex = uuidCounter.toString(16).padStart(8, '0');
    return `00000000-0000-4000-8000-${hex.padStart(12, '0')}` as `${string}-${string}-${string}-${string}-${string}`;
  });
}

export function resetUuidCounter(): void {
  uuidCounter = 0;
}

export function uninstallDeterministicUuid(): void {
  vi.restoreAllMocks();
  uuidCounter = 0;
}

// In vitest.setup.ts:
// import { installDeterministicUuid, resetUuidCounter, uninstallDeterministicUuid } from './deterministic-uuid';
// beforeAll(() => installDeterministicUuid());
// beforeEach(() => resetUuidCounter());
// afterAll(() => uninstallDeterministicUuid());

// After install: production code that calls crypto.randomUUID() returns predictable IDs:
// First call → '00000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001'
// Second call → '00000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000002'
// Tests can assert: expect(createdUser.id).toBe('00000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001')
```

[community]

### Pattern 15 — Kafka / Message Queue Event Factory  [community]

Microservices that consume Kafka topics or SQS queues require factories that produce the full message envelope (headers, partition key, timestamp, payload) — not just the payload. A bare `buildUserCreatedEvent()` that returns only `{ userId, email }` misses the envelope fields that consumer logic actually reads (e.g., `message.headers['correlation-id']`, `message.key` for partition routing).

**When to use:** Kafka consumer integration tests, SQS Lambda handler tests, any consumer-side integration test. **When NOT to use:** Producer-side tests where you control the payload directly. Alternative: `@aws-sdk/client-sqs` for SQS envelope structure.

```typescript
// factories/kafka-message.factory.ts — full Kafka message envelope factory
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

interface KafkaHeaders {
  'correlation-id': string;
  'content-type': string;
  'event-version': string;
  'source-service': string;
  [key: string]: string;
}

interface KafkaMessage<T = unknown> {
  topic: string;
  partition: number;
  offset: string;
  key: Buffer | null;
  value: Buffer;
  headers: KafkaHeaders;
  timestamp: string;
}

interface UserCreatedPayload {
  userId: string;
  email: string;
  name: string;
  subscriptionTier: 'free' | 'premium' | 'enterprise';
  occurredAt: string;
}

export function buildKafkaUserCreatedMessage(
  payloadOverrides: Partial<UserCreatedPayload> = {},
  headerOverrides: Partial<KafkaHeaders> = {}
): KafkaMessage<UserCreatedPayload> {
  const payload: UserCreatedPayload = {
    userId: faker.string.uuid(),
    email: faker.internet.email(),
    name: faker.person.fullName(),
    subscriptionTier: 'free',
    occurredAt: new Date().toISOString(),
    ...payloadOverrides,
  };

  return {
    topic: 'users.created.v1',
    partition: faker.number.int({ min: 0, max: 11 }),    // 12-partition topic
    offset: String(faker.number.int({ min: 0, max: 1_000_000 })),
    key: Buffer.from(payload.userId),                   // partition key = userId
    value: Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(payload)),
    headers: {
      'correlation-id': faker.string.uuid(),
      'content-type': 'application/json',
      'event-version': '1.0.0',
      'source-service': 'user-service',
      ...headerOverrides,
    },
    timestamp: String(Date.now()),
  };
}

// Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) factory — message that failed processing and was sent to DLQ
export function buildDlqMessage(
  originalMessage: KafkaMessage,
  failureReason: string = 'processing_error'
): KafkaMessage {
  return {
    ...originalMessage,
    topic: `${originalMessage.topic}.dlq`,
    headers: {
      ...originalMessage.headers,
      'x-failure-reason': failureReason,
      'x-original-topic': originalMessage.topic,
      'x-retry-count': '3',
    },
  };
}
```

[community]

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 30

**79. [community] `faker.helpers.arrayElement()` with an empty array throws `RangeError: Cannot pick element from empty array` at runtime — not a TypeScript compile error — causing test setup failures that appear as cryptic `RangeError` crashes rather than meaningful test failures.**

When a factory uses `faker.helpers.arrayElement(someList)` and `someList` is populated by a previous async operation that returned empty results, the factory crashes during setup rather than failing the test with a useful assertion message. WHY: TypeScript types `faker.helpers.arrayElement` as accepting `ReadonlyArray<T>` without enforcing non-empty — the empty-array guard is a runtime-only check. Fix: assert non-empty before calling `arrayElement` and throw a descriptive error: `if (list.length === 0) throw new Error('[factory] arrayElement: list is empty — seeding step may have failed')`.

**80. [community] Playwright fixtures that call `db.insert()` inside a `test.use()` override do NOT participate in the `aroundEach` transaction wrapper — the insert commits immediately rather than rolling back, leaving orphan rows after the test.**

`test.use()` applies fixture overrides but does not inherit the `aroundEach` transaction context defined on the extended `test` object. If a suite overrides a fixture via `test.use()` to inject a different user variant, and the `aroundEach` hook wraps each test in a transaction, the fixture override's DB insert runs outside the transaction and commits permanently. WHY: `aroundEach` wraps the test execution, but fixture initialization happens before `aroundEach` fires — making the timing boundary non-obvious. Fix: pass the transaction client explicitly as a fixture parameter, and ensure `test.use()` overrides accept the `{ db: tx }` fixture to use the in-transaction connection rather than the module-level `db`.

**81. [community] `fishery`'s `afterCreate` hook is called synchronously during `.create()` but the returned promise is not awaited when `.createList()` is used with a pool size > 1 — leading to teardown race conditions where `afterCreate` inserts (e.g., audit log rows) land AFTER `afterEach` cleanup, leaving orphan rows.**

`fishery` v2 calls `afterCreate` for each factory in `createList()` concurrently. If the `afterCreate` hook inserts a related record (e.g., audit log, notification preference) and the test's `afterEach` truncates the parent table first, the FK constraint violation from the orphan insert lands after truncation — producing a confusing `ForeignKeyViolation` error in `afterEach` that points at the wrong test. WHY: the concurrent `afterCreate` timing is documented only in a GitHub issue, not in the README. Fix: use `createList()` with `{ limit: 1 }` for factories with `afterCreate` hooks that insert FK-constrained records, or move the related record creation into the factory body using a transaction.

**82. [community] `zod-fixture`'s `createFixture()` does NOT handle `z.lazy()` (recursive schemas) — calling it on a schema with a self-referential `z.lazy(() => TreeNode)` throws a stack overflow at fixture generation time, not at schema definition time.**

Recursive Zod schemas using `z.lazy()` represent tree or graph structures (e.g., a `TreeNode` with `children: z.array(z.lazy(() => TreeNode))`). `zod-fixture` does not implement depth-limiting for lazy schemas — it follows the lazy reference indefinitely until the call stack overflows. WHY: the `z.lazy()` case is not documented in `zod-fixture`'s README and the stack overflow message does not mention `zod-fixture` in the trace, making the root cause hard to identify. Fix: for recursive schemas, build factory functions manually with explicit depth limits rather than using `createFixture` — e.g., `buildTreeNode(depth = 3) => depth === 0 ? leafNode : { children: [buildTreeNode(depth - 1)] }`.

**83. [community] Drizzle ORM's `.returning()` on a `db.insert()` inside a test transaction returns the full row only when `pg` is used in "simple query protocol" mode — in `pgBouncer` transaction-mode with prepared statements (`pg` extended query protocol), `.returning()` returns an empty array because PgBouncer discards prepared statement state between transactions.**

Integration tests that use transaction rollback for isolation (`BEGIN` in `beforeEach`, `ROLLBACK` in `afterEach`) work correctly against a direct Postgres connection but return empty `[]` from `.returning()` when routed through PgBouncer in transaction mode with prepared statements enabled. The test appears to succeed (no assertion errors) but the factory's returned entity has `undefined` fields, causing `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined` on the first field access. WHY: PgBouncer in transaction mode resets prepared statement state on `COMMIT`/`ROLLBACK` — the `RETURNING` clause uses an extended protocol prepared statement that gets invalidated. Fix: set `pg` to "simple query" mode for test connections: `new Pool({ ..., statement_timeout: '30s' })` with `pg`'s `query` option `{ text: query, rowMode: 'array' }`, or configure PgBouncer's `pool_mode = session` for the test user.

**84. [community] When using Vitest's `vi.useFakeTimers()` with a factory that calls `faker.date.past()` or `faker.date.recent()`, the generated dates are relative to the REAL system clock, not the fake clock — producing factory dates that are in the future relative to the faked "now", breaking any time-comparison assertions.**

`vi.useFakeTimers()` replaces `Date.now()` and `new Date()` with a controlled clock, but `@faker-js/faker`'s date methods compute relative dates using JavaScript's internal `Date` constructor which respects the fake timer override. However, faker internally caches the `Date` reference at module load time in some configurations — and if faker is initialized before `vi.useFakeTimers()` is called, faker's date calculations use the real clock. WHY: the faker/vitest fake timer interaction is undocumented and the behavior differs between faker ESM (runtime `Date` lookup) and CJS (cached reference at load). Fix: call `vi.useFakeTimers({ now: fixedDate })` before any faker date operations in the test, and use `faker.setDefaultRefDate(fixedDate)` to align faker's reference date with the fake timer's "now": `faker.setDefaultRefDate(new Date(vi.getMockedSystemTime()!))`.

**85. [community] Factory functions that use `as const` type assertions on the return value prevent partial overrides from working correctly — `buildUser({ status: 'suspended' } as const)` makes the override type `{ readonly status: 'suspended' }` which is not assignable to `Partial<User>`, causing a TypeScript error that confuses developers into removing the `as const` from the factory definition rather than from the call site.**

When a factory is defined as `buildUser(overrides: Partial<User> = {} as const)`, the `as const` on the default value has no effect — but developers sometimes add `as const` at the call site to get literal type inference (`buildUser({ status: 'suspended' } as const)`), then encounter a type error because `{ readonly status: 'suspended' }` is a subtype of `{ status: 'suspended' }` (readonly is covariant) but not of `Partial<User>` which expects a mutable type. WHY: the error message is "Argument of type '{ readonly status: "suspended"; }' is not assignable to parameter of type 'Partial<User>'" — which suggests the problem is the value, not the `as const`. Fix: use TypeScript 5.0+ `const` type parameters in the factory signature (`buildUser<const T extends Partial<User>>(overrides?: T)`) instead of `as const` at the call site to get literal type preservation without `readonly` conflicts.

### Pattern 16 — Trait-Composable `fishery` Factory  [official]

`fishery` v2 supports factory params as composable trait objects — named variations that apply field overrides without creating a separate factory. This avoids Object Mother explosion while keeping semantically named variants discoverable alongside the factory definition, and all traits share the same `afterCreate` lifecycle hook.

**When to use:** Domain entities with 4+ meaningful variants (e.g., `active`, `suspended`, `pendingVerification`, `deleted`) that need type-safe composition alongside DB persistence hooks. **When NOT to use:** Simple in-memory-only factories with 1–2 variants — plain function overrides are simpler. Alternative: Object Mother returning a Builder.

```typescript
// factories/user.factory.ts — fishery trait composition
import { Factory } from 'fishery';
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';
import { prisma } from '../db/prisma-client';
import { User } from '../domain/user';

export const userFactory = Factory.define<User>(({ sequence }) => ({
  id: faker.string.uuid(),
  email: `user-${sequence}@${faker.internet.domainName()}`,
  name: faker.person.fullName(),
  status: 'active' as const,
  subscriptionTier: 'free' as const,
  emailVerified: true,
  createdAt: new Date(),
  deletedAt: null,
}));

// afterCreate persists to DB — triggered only on .create(), never on .build()
userFactory.afterCreate(async (user) => {
  await prisma.user.create({ data: user });
});

// Named trait factories derived from the base factory
export const suspendedUserFactory  = userFactory.params({ status: 'suspended' });
export const unverifiedUserFactory = userFactory.params({ emailVerified: false });
export const deletedUserFactory    = userFactory.params({ status: 'deleted', deletedAt: new Date() });

// Compose: suspended + unverified — field overrides accumulate correctly
// const user = suspendedUserFactory.build({ emailVerified: false });

// Build list: 3 suspended users, all with unique emails via sequence counter
// const batch = await suspendedUserFactory.createList(3);
```

### Pattern 17 — `zod-fixture` Schema-Driven Factory  [official]

`zod-fixture` generates complete test fixtures directly from a Zod schema, eliminating hand-authored defaults for simple DTO factories. When the schema changes, the fixture automatically reflects the new shape — preventing factory drift without writing field-by-field defaults.

**When to use:** Pure DTO / API response mocking where semantic variants are not needed; contract testing where the schema IS the spec. **When NOT to use:** Domain entities with business-rule constraints that Zod cannot encode (e.g., `startDate < endDate`, conditional required fields) — `zod-fixture` generates valid-shaped but not necessarily business-valid data. Alternative: hand-written factory with `schema.parse(overrides)` as the validation gate.

```typescript
// test/factories/product-fixture.ts — zod-fixture schema-driven generation
import { createFixture } from 'zod-fixture';
import { z } from 'zod';

const ProductSchema = z.object({
  id:          z.string().uuid(),
  sku:         z.string().min(3).max(20),
  name:        z.string().min(1).max(100),
  priceCents:  z.number().int().positive(),
  currency:    z.enum(['USD', 'EUR', 'GBP']),
  category:    z.enum(['electronics', 'clothing', 'food', 'books']),
  inStock:     z.boolean(),
  tags:        z.array(z.string()).max(5),
  metadata:    z.record(z.string()).optional(),
});

export type Product = z.infer<typeof ProductSchema>;

// Generates a structurally valid product — no defaults to maintain
export function buildProduct(overrides: Partial<Product> = {}): Product {
  const fixture = createFixture(ProductSchema);
  // Re-parse through schema to trigger validation on merged result
  return ProductSchema.parse({ ...fixture, ...overrides });
}

// Pin specific fields for focused tests — all others auto-generated:
// const outOfStockElectronics = buildProduct({ inStock: false, category: 'electronics' });
// All uuid/string/number fields populated without any manual default maintenance
```

---

### Pattern 18 — Property-Based Factory Wrapper with `fast-check`  [official]

Property-based testing (PBT) with `fast-check` verifies that a property holds across a wide range of generated inputs, not just hand-picked examples. Wrapping domain factories as `fc.Arbitrary` values lets you reuse the same data shape in both example-based (`it(...)`) and property-based (`fc.assert(fc.property(...))`) tests.

**When to use:** Business logic with a large input space (currency arithmetic, date calculations, access-control rules, sorting/filtering invariants); discovering edge cases that manual examples miss. **When NOT to use:** Database integration tests — PBT runs 100+ iterations per property; hitting a real DB per iteration is prohibitively slow. Alternative: `quickcheck-ts`, `jsverify`.

```typescript
// test/factories/arbitraries.ts — fast-check arbitraries for domain types
import * as fc from 'fast-check';
import { buildOrder } from './order.factory';

// Typed arbitrary for valid User status values
const arbUserStatus = fc.constantFrom(
  'active', 'suspended', 'pending'
) as fc.Arbitrary<'active' | 'suspended' | 'pending'>;

// Typed arbitrary for valid subscription tiers
const arbSubscriptionTier = fc.constantFrom(
  'free', 'premium', 'enterprise'
) as fc.Arbitrary<'free' | 'premium' | 'enterprise'>;

// Composite arbitrary for a structurally valid User
export const arbUser = fc.record({
  id:               fc.uuid(),
  email:            fc.emailAddress(),
  name:             fc.string({ minLength: 1, maxLength: 60 }),
  status:           arbUserStatus,
  subscriptionTier: arbSubscriptionTier,
  emailVerified:    fc.boolean(),
  createdAt:        fc.date({ min: new Date('2020-01-01'), max: new Date() }),
  deletedAt:        fc.option(fc.date(), { nil: null }),
});

// Property: totalCents is always the sum of individual line item amounts
describe('OrderService invariants', () => {
  it('total is always the sum of line items', () => {
    fc.assert(
      fc.property(
        fc.array(fc.integer({ min: 1, max: 50_000 }), { minLength: 1, maxLength: 20 }),
        fc.constantFrom('USD', 'EUR', 'GBP'),
        (lineAmounts, currency) => {
          const expectedTotal = lineAmounts.reduce((s, n) => s + n, 0);
          const order = buildOrder({ totalCents: expectedTotal, currency });
          return order.totalCents === expectedTotal && order.currency === currency;
        },
      ),
    );
  });
});
```

### Pattern 19 — Seeding Strategy: Per-Test Sequence vs. Global Seed  [community]

Two orthogonal seeding strategies address different failure modes. A **global seed** (set once per run) makes every test run with the same seed produce identical data — enabling deterministic failure replay. A **per-test sequence counter** (reset in `beforeEach`) ensures unique emails and IDs across parallel tests regardless of seed value. Combining both correctly avoids the most common seeding pitfalls.

**When to use:** Global seed for reproducible CI failure investigation (`TEST_SEED=1234 vitest run`); per-test sequence for parallel DB integration tests where unique-constraint collisions are possible. **When NOT to use:** Global seed alone for parallel DB tests — concurrent tests with the same seed generate identical emails causing unique-constraint violations. Alternative: UUIDv7 (time-ordered, inherently unique without seeding).

```typescript
// test/setup/seeding-strategy.ts — combining global seed + per-test sequence
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';
import { beforeEach, afterAll } from 'vitest';

// Phase 1: deterministic global seed — reproducible per CI run
const GLOBAL_SEED = process.env.TEST_SEED
  ? parseInt(process.env.TEST_SEED, 10)
  : Date.now();
faker.seed(GLOBAL_SEED);
console.info(`[test-setup] faker seed: ${GLOBAL_SEED}`);

// Phase 2: per-test sequence counter — uniqueness without re-seeding faker
let _seq = 0;

/** Returns a unique email guaranteed not to collide within a run */
export const uniqueEmail = (prefix = 'user'): string =>
  `${prefix}-${++_seq}-${GLOBAL_SEED % 10_000}@test.example.com`;

/** Returns a unique slug-safe string */
export const uniqueSlug = (base = 'item'): string => `${base}-${++_seq}`;

beforeEach(() => {
  // Reset sequence counter per test — do NOT re-seed faker here
  // Re-seeding faker in beforeEach breaks global reproducibility:
  // tests that run later in the file will get different data from a fresh seed
  _seq = 0;
});

afterAll(() => {
  if (process.env.CI) {
    console.info(`[test-teardown] Replay failures: TEST_SEED=${GLOBAL_SEED} npx vitest run`);
  }
});
```
