### Pattern 20 — MSW Handler Factory for API Response Test Data  [official]

MSW (Mock Service Worker) v2 handler factories produce typed, schema-consistent API response mocks without a real backend. Wrapping `http.get`/`http.post` handlers in factory functions makes handler setup composable and avoids copy-pasted `HttpResponse.json(...)` literals across test files.

**When to use:** Frontend unit/integration tests that call `fetch`/`axios`; component tests with TanStack Query or SWR; Playwright component test suites. **When NOT to use:** Full E2E tests that must exercise the real API contract — use a real test environment instead. Alternative: `nock` (Node.js interceptor, no service worker), `json-server` (static file-based mock server).

```typescript
// test/mocks/handlers/user-handlers.factory.ts — MSW v2 handler factory
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw';
import { buildUser } from '../factories/user.factory';
import { User } from '../../domain/user';

interface UserHandlerOptions {
  userOverrides?: Partial<User>;
  status?: 200 | 401 | 403 | 404 | 500;
}

// IMPORTANT: buildUser() must be called INSIDE the callback (not outside)
// to generate a fresh object per request — see Gotcha #91
export function makeGetUserHandler(userId: string, opts: UserHandlerOptions = {}) {
  const { userOverrides = {}, status = 200 } = opts;
  return http.get(`/api/users/${userId}`, () => {
    if (status !== 200) {
      return HttpResponse.json(
        { error: 'User not found', code: 'USER_NOT_FOUND' },
        { status }
      );
    }
    // Called per request — fresh faker data each time
    return HttpResponse.json(buildUser({ id: userId, ...userOverrides }));
  });
}

export function makeListUsersHandler(count = 5, opts: UserHandlerOptions = {}) {
  return http.get('/api/users', () => {
    const users = Array.from({ length: count }, (_, i) =>
      buildUser({ ...opts.userOverrides, id: `user-${i + 1}` })
    );
    return HttpResponse.json({ users, total: count, page: 1, pageSize: count });
  });
}

// Usage: server.use(makeGetUserHandler('usr-123', { userOverrides: { status: 'suspended' } }));
```

---

### Pattern 21 — Idempotent Upsert Seeding for Shared Baseline Data  [community]

Test database seeds that use unconditional `INSERT` fail when run twice (e.g., after a partial CI failure or during watch-mode reruns). Structuring seeds as idempotent upserts (`INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`) allows re-running without cleanup, making seed scripts composable and safe to call in `beforeAll` of multiple test files.

**When to use:** Shared baseline data that multiple test files read but never modify (roles, permission codes, country codes, feature flags); `beforeAll` setup in E2E suites. **When NOT to use:** Per-test dynamic data where upsert semantics could mask logic errors (the upsert might silently "succeed" with stale data from a previous run). Alternative: truncate-and-reseed strategy for full reproducibility.

```typescript
// test/seed/permissions.seed.ts — idempotent upsert seeding
import { prisma } from '../../src/db/prisma-client';

const BASELINE_PERMISSIONS = [
  { code: 'users:read',   description: 'Read user records' },
  { code: 'users:write',  description: 'Create and update users' },
  { code: 'orders:read',  description: 'Read order records' },
  { code: 'orders:write', description: 'Create and update orders' },
  { code: 'admin:all',    description: 'Full administrative access' },
] as const;

export async function seedPermissions(): Promise<void> {
  await prisma.$transaction(
    BASELINE_PERMISSIONS.map((p) =>
      prisma.permission.upsert({
        where:  { code: p.code },
        update: { description: p.description }, // idempotent: refresh description if changed
        create: p,
      })
    )
  );
  console.info(`[seed] Upserted ${BASELINE_PERMISSIONS.length} permissions`);
}

// Call in globalSetup (runs once per test run) or in a file-scoped beforeAll
// import { seedPermissions } from './seed/permissions.seed';
// beforeAll(() => seedPermissions());
```

---

### Pattern 22 — GraphQL Variable Factory Aligned with Codegen Types  [community]

GraphQL mutations and queries require typed variable objects that match the generated operation types. A dedicated variable factory derived from `graphql-codegen` output ensures test variables are always structurally compatible with the schema — schema changes surface as TypeScript compile errors in the factory file before tests even run.

**When to use:** GraphQL API integration tests and E2E tests using Apollo Client, urql, or URQL; Playwright tests that submit GraphQL mutations. **When NOT to use:** REST API tests — use plain object factories instead. Alternative: `@graphql-codegen/testing` plugin that generates mock resolver factories automatically from the schema.

```typescript
// test/factories/graphql-variables.factory.ts — codegen-aligned GQL variable factories
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

// Types imported from graphql-codegen output — any schema change causes a TS error here
import type {
  CreateUserMutationVariables,
  UpdateUserStatusMutationVariables,
  ListUsersQueryVariables,
} from '../../src/graphql/generated/types';

export function buildCreateUserVariables(
  overrides: Partial<CreateUserMutationVariables['input']> = {}
): CreateUserMutationVariables {
  return {
    input: {
      email:            faker.internet.email(),
      name:             faker.person.fullName(),
      subscriptionTier: 'FREE',
      ...overrides,
    },
  };
}

export function buildUpdateUserStatusVariables(
  userId: string,
  status: 'ACTIVE' | 'SUSPENDED'
): UpdateUserStatusMutationVariables {
  return { userId, status };
}

export function buildListUsersVariables(
  overrides: Partial<ListUsersQueryVariables> = {}
): ListUsersQueryVariables {
  return {
    page:         1,
    pageSize:     10,
    statusFilter: null,
    ...overrides,
  };
}

// Usage:
// const vars = buildCreateUserVariables({ subscriptionTier: 'PREMIUM' });
// const result = await apolloClient.mutate({ mutation: CREATE_USER, variables: vars });
```

---

### Pattern 23 — Multi-Tenant Fixture Isolation via Tenant Context Factory  [community]

Multi-tenant applications require all test entities to be scoped to an isolated tenant. A tenant context factory wraps every domain factory — injecting a shared `tenantId` into every created entity — preventing cross-tenant data leakage in integration tests that run concurrently.

**When to use:** Multi-tenant SaaS applications; tests that run in parallel against a shared DB; any system where `tenantId` is a foreign key on every table. **When NOT to use:** Single-tenant applications, or tests that spin up isolated DB instances per test — tenant scoping adds complexity without benefit. Alternative: per-test PostgreSQL schema isolation using `SET search_path TO test_schema_$testId`.

```typescript
// test/factories/tenant-context.factory.ts — tenant-scoped factory wrapper
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';
import { buildUser } from './user.factory';
import { buildOrder } from './order.factory';
import { buildProduct } from './product.factory';
import type { User, Order, Product } from '../../src/domain/types';

export interface TenantContext {
  tenantId: string;
  buildUser(overrides?: Partial<User>): User;
  buildOrder(overrides?: Partial<Order>): Order;
  buildProduct(overrides?: Partial<Product>): Product;
}

/**
 * Creates a factory context bound to a specific tenant.
 * All entities produced within this context carry the same tenantId,
 * ensuring parallel tests cannot produce cross-tenant row leakage.
 * The tenantId is a random UUID unless explicitly provided.
 */
export function createTenantContext(tenantId?: string): TenantContext {
  const id = tenantId ?? faker.string.uuid();
  return {
    tenantId: id,
    buildUser:    (overrides = {}) => buildUser({ ...overrides, tenantId: id }),
    buildOrder:   (overrides = {}) => buildOrder({ ...overrides, tenantId: id }),
    buildProduct: (overrides = {}) => buildProduct({ ...overrides, tenantId: id }),
  };
}

// In a parallel integration test:
// const tenant = createTenantContext();   // unique tenantId per test
// const admin  = tenant.buildUser({ role: 'admin' });
// const order  = tenant.buildOrder({ userId: admin.id });
// Both carry the same tenantId — no cross-tenant FK violations in parallel runs
```

---

### Pattern 24 — Relative Date Factory for Time-Sensitive Business Logic  [community]

Tests involving date-sensitive business logic (expiry windows, grace periods, subscription renewals) commonly hard-code `new Date('2024-01-01')` literals that silently drift as calendar time advances past the hard-coded date. Relative date factories compute all dates from a configurable `referenceNow` — making tests valid indefinitely and compatible with `vi.useFakeTimers`.

**When to use:** Subscription expiry, billing cycles, cooldown periods, reminder scheduling, any "is this X days from now?" logic. **When NOT to use:** Historical reporting queries where absolute dates are semantically meaningful to the test assertion. Alternative: `date-fns` `addDays`/`subDays` utilities for inline one-off expressions.

```typescript
// test/factories/temporal.factory.ts — relative date helpers
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

type DateOffsetMs = { days?: number; hours?: number; minutes?: number; seconds?: number };

function offset(base: Date, delta: DateOffsetMs): Date {
  const ms =
    (delta.days    ?? 0) * 86_400_000 +
    (delta.hours   ?? 0) * 3_600_000  +
    (delta.minutes ?? 0) * 60_000     +
    (delta.seconds ?? 0) * 1_000;
  return new Date(base.getTime() + ms);
}

/**
 * Returns a named set of dates relative to `referenceNow`.
 * Pass `referenceNow` explicitly when using vi.useFakeTimers to align with the fake clock:
 *   vi.useFakeTimers({ now: new Date('2025-06-01') });
 *   faker.setDefaultRefDate(new Date('2025-06-01'));
 *   const d = buildTemporalDates({ referenceNow: new Date('2025-06-01') });
 */
export function buildTemporalDates(opts: { referenceNow?: Date } = {}) {
  const now = opts.referenceNow ?? new Date();
  return {
    yesterday:          offset(now, { days: -1 }),
    tomorrow:           offset(now, { days: 1 }),
    in7Days:            offset(now, { days: 7 }),
    in30Days:           offset(now, { days: 30 }),
    expired30DaysAgo:   offset(now, { days: -30 }),
    justExpired:        offset(now, { minutes: -1 }),
    expiresInOneHour:   offset(now, { hours: 1 }),
    withinGracePeriod:  offset(now, { days: -3 }),   // inside typical 7-day grace
    beyondGracePeriod:  offset(now, { days: -10 }),  // outside 7-day grace
    randomPast:         faker.date.past({ years: 1, refDate: now }),
    randomFuture:       faker.date.future({ years: 1, refDate: now }),
  };
}

// Subscription factory using temporal helpers:
export function buildExpiredSubscription(referenceNow?: Date) {
  const d = buildTemporalDates({ referenceNow });
  return {
    id: faker.string.uuid(), tier: 'premium' as const,
    startedAt: d.expired30DaysAgo, expiresAt: d.justExpired, graceEndsAt: d.in7Days,
  };
}
```

### Pattern 25 — `toMatchFileSnapshot` for Factory Output Shape Validation  [official]

Rather than asserting individual fields on a factory's output, snapshot the entire serialized output to a fixture file. This validates structural completeness (no missing fields), acts as a change-detector when the domain model is refactored, and provides a living example of exactly what a "real" API response looks like.

**When to use:** API response factories, serialization layer tests, factories for complex nested DTOs where asserting every field individually is noise. **When NOT to use:** Factories with non-deterministic fields (`uuid`, `Date.now()`) unless those fields are normalized before snapshotting — otherwise the snapshot diffs on every run. Alternative: `toMatchObject` for partial structural assertions without snapshot maintenance.

```typescript
// test/factories/__snapshots__/factory-shape.test.ts — snapshot-based factory validation
import { describe, it, expect, beforeAll } from 'vitest';
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';
import { buildUser } from '../factories/user.factory';
import { buildOrder } from '../factories/order.factory';

// Pin faker seed ONCE for the entire snapshot file — same output every run
beforeAll(() => { faker.seed(12345); });

// Field normalizer: replace runtime-random values with stable placeholders
function normalise(obj: unknown): unknown {
  return JSON.parse(
    JSON.stringify(obj, (key, value) => {
      if (key === 'id' || key.endsWith('Id')) return '[uuid]';
      if (value instanceof Date) return '[date]';
      return value;
    })
  );
}

describe('factory output shape validation', () => {
  it('buildUser matches expected shape', async () => {
    const user = buildUser({ id: 'usr-snap-001', createdAt: new Date('2025-01-01T00:00:00Z') });
    await expect(JSON.stringify(normalise(user), null, 2))
      .toMatchFileSnapshot('./__snapshots__/user-factory-output.json');
  });

  it('buildOrder matches expected shape', async () => {
    const order = buildOrder({ id: 'ord-snap-001', createdAt: new Date('2025-01-01T00:00:00Z') });
    await expect(JSON.stringify(normalise(order), null, 2))
      .toMatchFileSnapshot('./__snapshots__/order-factory-output.json');
  });
});
```

### Pattern 26 — HAR-Based Self-Initializing Fake for External API Test Data  [official]

Playwright's `routeFromHAR` turns a recorded HTTP Archive (HAR) file into a replay fixture — the canonical Self-Initializing Fake (Fowler) applied to E2E test data. The first run records real API responses; subsequent runs replay them without a live network call.

**When to use:** E2E tests against external APIs (payment gateways, address validation, SMS providers) where each call costs money, has rate limits, or requires credentials. **When NOT to use:** Internal APIs you control and can run locally — HAR fixtures drift silently when the real API changes (see Gotcha #26 from Cycle 38). Alternative: MSW handler factories for internal API mocking with explicit schema validation.

```typescript
// test/e2e/checkout.spec.ts — Playwright HAR-based self-initializing fake
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';

const HAR_PATH = path.join(__dirname, 'fixtures/stripe-checkout.har');

test.beforeEach(async ({ page }) => {
  // update: false = replay mode (default for CI)
  // Set UPDATE_HAR=true to re-record against the live Stripe sandbox
  await page.routeFromHAR(HAR_PATH, {
    url:           '**/api.stripe.com/**',
    update:        process.env.UPDATE_HAR === 'true',
    updateContent: 'embed',    // inline response bodies in the HAR file
  });
});

test('processes payment with recorded Stripe response', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.fill('[data-testid="card-number"]', '4242 4242 4242 4242');
  await page.fill('[data-testid="card-expiry"]', '12/26');
  await page.fill('[data-testid="card-cvc"]', '123');
  await page.click('[data-testid="pay-now"]');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('confirmation-banner')).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('order-id')).not.toBeEmpty();
});

// Refresh HAR when Stripe API changes: UPDATE_HAR=true npx playwright test checkout.spec.ts
// Commit the updated HAR file so CI uses the new recording
```

### Pattern 27 — PII Scrubbing Factory for Production-Data Seeding  [community]

When integration or performance tests require realistic data volumes, teams may use a production database snapshot. A PII scrubbing factory transforms production records in-place — replacing real names, emails, phone numbers, and addresses with faker-generated equivalents while preserving referential integrity (IDs, relationships, and cardinality remain intact).

**When to use:** Performance tests requiring realistic data volume; staging environments seeded from production snapshots; GDPR Article 25 (privacy by design) compliance for test environments. **When NOT to use:** Unit/integration tests — generate synthetic data from factories instead; never store un-scrubbed PII in any non-production environment. Alternative: `faker.helpers.replaceSymbols` for format-preserving tokenized scrubbing.

```typescript
// scripts/scrub-prod-dump.ts — PII scrubbing factory for production snapshot rows
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

interface RawUserRow {
  id: string;
  email: string;
  full_name: string;
  phone_number: string | null;
  address_line1: string | null;
  address_city: string | null;
  ip_address: string | null;
  stripe_customer_id: string | null;
}

// Deterministic per-user scrub: same userId always yields the same fake email
// Prevents assertion mismatches when the scrub script is run multiple times
function deterministicEmail(userId: string): string {
  const savedSeed = Math.random() * 2 ** 32;       // capture current state (approximate)
  faker.seed(stableHash(userId));
  const email = faker.internet.email();
  faker.seed(Date.now());                           // restore entropy for subsequent calls
  return email;
}

function stableHash(s: string): number {
  return s.split('').reduce((h, c) => (Math.imul(31, h) + c.charCodeAt(0)) | 0, 0);
}

export function scrubUserRow(row: RawUserRow): RawUserRow {
  return {
    ...row,
    email:               deterministicEmail(row.id),
    full_name:           faker.person.fullName(),
    phone_number:        row.phone_number  ? faker.phone.number()           : null,
    address_line1:       row.address_line1 ? faker.location.streetAddress() : null,
    address_city:        row.address_city  ? faker.location.city()          : null,
    ip_address:          row.ip_address    ? faker.internet.ipv4()          : null,
    stripe_customer_id:  row.stripe_customer_id
      ? `cus_scrubbed_${row.id.slice(0, 8)}`  // preserve format and length
      : null,
  };
}

// Batch-scrub 1000 rows at a time to bound memory usage:
export async function scrubUserBatch(rows: RawUserRow[]): Promise<RawUserRow[]> {
  return rows.map(scrubUserRow);
}
```

### Pattern 28 — Vitest `scope: 'file'` Fixture for Expensive Seed Setup  [official]

Vitest 3.2+ introduced `scope: 'file'` for `test.extend()` fixtures, providing lazy `beforeAll` semantics: the fixture initializes once per test file, and teardown runs after all tests in the file complete. This is ideal for expensive DB seed fixtures that all tests in a file share as read-only baseline data.

**When to use:** Integration test files where all tests read from the same seed data (e.g., a product catalogue seeded once and queried by 20 tests). **When NOT to use:** Fixtures that hold mutable state modified by tests — use the default `scope: 'test'` to get fresh state per test. Alternative: `beforeAll`/`afterAll` with shared module-level variables (less ergonomic, no automatic teardown type safety).

```typescript
// test/fixtures/db-seed.fixture.ts — Vitest 3.2+ file-scoped DB seed fixture
import { test as baseTest } from 'vitest';
import { prisma } from '../../src/db/prisma-client';
import { buildProduct } from '../factories/product.factory';

interface SeedFixtures {
  seededProducts: Array<{ id: string; name: string; priceCents: number }>;
}

export const test = baseTest.extend<SeedFixtures>({
  seededProducts: [
    async ({}, use) => {
      // Setup: insert 10 products once for the entire test file
      const products = Array.from({ length: 10 }, () => buildProduct());
      await prisma.product.createMany({ data: products });

      await use(products);   // hand baseline data to all tests in this file

      // Teardown: remove only this file's rows — no cross-file pollution
      const ids = products.map((p) => p.id);
      await prisma.product.deleteMany({ where: { id: { in: ids } } });
    },
    { scope: 'file' },   // Vitest 3.2+ — single setup/teardown per file, not per test
  ],
});

// In a test file:
// import { test } from '../fixtures/db-seed.fixture';
// test('lists all seeded products', async ({ seededProducts }) => {
//   expect(seededProducts).toHaveLength(10);
// });
```

### Pattern 29 — `faker.helpers.fromRegExp` for Format-Constrained Identifiers  [official]

`@faker-js/faker` v8+ includes `faker.helpers.fromRegExp(pattern)` which generates strings matching a given regular expression. This is the idiomatic way to generate format-constrained identifiers (product SKUs, tracking numbers, postal codes, structured reference numbers) without writing custom character-by-character generators.

**When to use:** Input validation tests that assert specific format rules; factories for third-party system identifiers (IBAN, EAN, UPC, tracking numbers) with known regex formats. **When NOT to use:** Strings longer than ~256 characters — `fromRegExp` caps output at 256 chars silently (see Gotcha #86 below). Alternative: `faker.helpers.replaceSymbols('#-??-##')` for simple alphanumeric placeholder templates.

```typescript
// factories/identifiers.factory.ts — format-constrained ID generation
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

// Product SKU: 2 uppercase letters + 4 digits + 1 uppercase letter (e.g., "AB1234C")
export const buildSku = (): string =>
  faker.helpers.fromRegExp(/[A-Z]{2}[0-9]{4}[A-Z]{1}/);

// IBAN-like format for European bank account test data (simplified)
export const buildTestIban = (): string =>
  faker.helpers.fromRegExp(/[A-Z]{2}[0-9]{2}[A-Z]{4}[0-9]{14}/);

// US ZIP+4 format: e.g., "94105-1234"
export const buildZipPlusFour = (): string =>
  faker.helpers.fromRegExp(/[0-9]{5}-[0-9]{4}/);

// UPS-style tracking number
export const buildTrackingNumber = (): string =>
  faker.helpers.fromRegExp(/1Z[A-Z0-9]{16}/);

// Combine into a shipment factory using format-constrained fields
export function buildShipment(overrides: Record<string, unknown> = {}) {
  return {
    id:              faker.string.uuid(),
    trackingNumber:  buildTrackingNumber(),
    recipientZip:    buildZipPlusFour(),
    productSku:      buildSku(),
    weight:          faker.number.float({ min: 0.1, max: 70.0, fractionDigits: 2 }),
    dispatchedAt:    faker.date.recent({ days: 5 }),
    ...overrides,
  };
}
```

### Pattern 30 — Transaction-Per-Test Isolation with Drizzle ORM  [community]

The transaction-per-test pattern wraps each test in a database transaction that is unconditionally rolled back in teardown — ensuring zero row leakage without the cost of full table truncation. The same transaction client is injected into both the factory (for inserts) and the service under test (for queries), guaranteeing both operations see the same in-progress state.

**When to use:** Drizzle ORM integration tests against PostgreSQL or MySQL where test run time is important and truncation is too slow. **When NOT to use:** Tests that must verify `COMMIT` semantics (e.g., "does the row survive after the function returns?") — unconditional rollback prevents that assertion. Alternative: per-test PostgreSQL schema creation using `CREATE SCHEMA test_$id; SET search_path TO test_$id`.

```typescript
// test/fixtures/transaction-isolation.ts — rollback-per-test with Drizzle ORM
import { test as baseTest } from 'vitest';
import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/postgres-js';
import postgres from 'postgres';
import * as schema from '../../src/db/schema';

type DrizzleDb = ReturnType<typeof drizzle<typeof schema>>;

const pool = postgres(process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL!, { max: 5 });

interface TxFixtures {
  db: DrizzleDb;  // always a transaction-scoped client — never commits
}

export const test = baseTest.extend<TxFixtures>({
  db: async ({}, use) => {
    let triggerRollback!: () => void;

    // Open a long-lived transaction — resolve the drizzle client into the test
    const txClientPromise = new Promise<DrizzleDb>((resolve) => {
      pool.begin(async (txRaw) => {
        resolve(drizzle(txRaw, { schema }));
        // Block the transaction open until the test calls triggerRollback()
        await new Promise<void>((_, reject) => {
          triggerRollback = () => reject(new Error('__rollback__'));
        });
      }).catch((e) => {
        if ((e as Error).message !== '__rollback__') throw e;  // suppress expected rollback
      });
    });

    await use(await txClientPromise);  // run the test with the tx-scoped DB client
    triggerRollback();                 // unconditionally roll back all changes
  },
});

// In an integration test:
// import { test } from '../fixtures/transaction-isolation';
// test('createUser inserts a row', async ({ db }) => {
//   await db.insert(schema.users).values(buildUser());
//   const rows = await db.select().from(schema.users);
//   expect(rows).toHaveLength(1);
// });  // ← row is rolled back; next test starts clean
```

---

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 31

**86. [community] `faker.helpers.fromRegExp()` silently caps output at 256 characters for quantifier ranges — a pattern like `/[a-z]{1,500}/` produces at most 256 characters, not up to 500. WHY: faker's regex generator has an undocumented hard cap of 256 characters as a safety measure against regex denial-of-service; the cap does not throw an error and is not documented in the API reference, so factories that need large strings (e.g., rich-text field overflow tests) silently produce undersized data, causing tests to pass when the production system would have rejected a larger input.**

Fix: for strings longer than 256 characters, use `faker.string.alpha({ length: { min: 300, max: 500 } })` directly. For format-constrained long strings, concatenate multiple `fromRegExp` calls and join them.

**87. [community] Vitest `scope: 'file'` fixtures do NOT re-initialize cleanly in `--ui` watch mode when a test file is triggered multiple times in rapid succession — the async teardown from run N can overlap with the setup of run N+1, causing the fixture to be in a partially torn-down state when the second run's tests start. WHY: the Vitest UI watch mode triggers re-runs before awaiting the previous run's file-scope teardown; the teardown is async (DB cleanup) and the watch mode does not serialize them.**

Fix: for watch-mode DB integration suites using `scope: 'file'`, add an explicit idempotent `afterAll` cleanup that completes before the file-scoped fixture teardown, or switch to `scope: 'test'` during active development and reserve `scope: 'file'` for CI-only runs.

**88. [community] `fishery` factory `sequence` counters are module-level state that persists across test files within the same Vitest worker — factories defined at the module level share the same counter across all files executed in that worker, causing `user-1@example.com`, `user-2@example.com`... to continue counting upward across files instead of resetting per file. WHY: Vitest worker mode re-uses the same module registry across test files unless `isolate: true` is configured, and fishery's sequence counter is a closure-scoped mutable variable captured at `Factory.define()` time.**

Fix: either enable `isolate: true` in `vitest.config.ts` (performance cost per file), call `userFactory.rewindSequence()` in `beforeEach` if available (fishery v2 API), or incorporate `process.pid` and a per-test nonce into the email template: `` `user-${process.pid}-${sequence}@example.com` `` to guarantee uniqueness without resetting.

**89. [community] `zod-fixture` generates `undefined` (not `null`) for `z.optional()` fields — but JSON serialization via `JSON.stringify` drops `undefined` values entirely, so factory output serialized to JSON and then deserialized loses the optional field altogether rather than retaining a `null` placeholder. WHY: `z.optional()` means "may be absent" which zod-fixture represents as `undefined`; `null` requires explicit `z.nullable()` or `z.nullish()`. Developers using `z.optional()` as a shorthand for "nullable in the API" silently get `undefined` in their fixture, which serializes to `{}` instead of `{ field: null }`, breaking assertion like `expect(response.middleName).toBeNull()`.**

Fix: use `z.nullable()` or `z.string().nullish()` in schemas where the API contract sends `null` rather than omitting the field. Add a snapshot test on factory output (Pattern 25) to catch this semantic mismatch at fixture authoring time.

**90. [community] `fast-check`'s `fc.date()` arbitrary generates `Date` objects that include time components — when the system under test stores dates in a `DATE` (date-only) column in PostgreSQL, the ORM silently truncates the time on write and returns `2025-06-15T00:00:00.000Z` on read, causing `expect(result.startDate).toEqual(input.startDate)` to fail because `2025-06-15T14:32:00Z` (written) !== `2025-06-15T00:00:00Z` (read). WHY: `fc.date()` has no `dateOnly` option; the truncation is invisible in the ORM layer and produces no error — the test silently fails on the value comparison.**

Fix: normalise PBT date arbitraries for date-only columns by mapping to midnight UTC: `fc.date().map(d => new Date(Date.UTC(d.getUTCFullYear(), d.getUTCMonth(), d.getUTCDate())))`. For range-bounded date-only arbitraries, use `fc.integer({ min: 0, max: 36500 }).map(days => addDays(new Date('2020-01-01'), days))`.

**91. [community] MSW handler factories that call `buildUser()` outside the request callback generate a single object at handler registration time — all requests to that handler return the same stale faker-generated data for the lifetime of the test file, not a fresh object per request. WHY: `HttpResponse.json(buildUser())` eagerly calls `buildUser()` at the moment `server.use(makeGetUserHandler())` is called; the resulting `HttpResponse` object captures the serialized bytes, not a factory reference. Developers expect each request to produce fresh data because the handler "looks like" a function, but the factory is only called once during `server.use()`.**

Fix: move the factory call inside the handler callback arrow function: `http.get('/api/users/:id', () => HttpResponse.json(buildUser()))` — the arrow function is invoked per request, so `buildUser()` generates a new object each time. See Pattern 20 for the idiomatic handler factory structure.

## Cycle 32 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 31 — `fishery` `afterBuild` Hook for Computed Derived Fields  [official]

`fishery` exposes an `afterBuild` hook that fires synchronously after the factory assembles the base object but before it is returned to the caller. Use it to compute derived fields (e.g., `fullName` from `firstName`/`lastName`, `slug` from `title`, tax-inclusive `totalCents` from `subtotalCents`) without repeating derivation logic in every `buildX()` call site.

**When to use:** Domain objects where one field is always deterministically derived from another — keeping derivation inside the factory ensures test data never has an inconsistent computed field. **When NOT to use:** Derivations that require async operations (e.g., reading from DB) — use `afterCreate` instead, which is async-capable. Alternative: a standalone `deriveOrderTotals(partial)` pure function called by callers explicitly, which keeps the factory simple at the cost of consistency enforcement.

```typescript
// factories/product.factory.ts — fishery afterBuild for slug derivation
import { Factory } from 'fishery';
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

interface Product {
  id: string;
  title: string;
  slug: string;        // always derived from title — must never diverge
  priceCents: number;
  taxCents: number;
  totalCents: number;  // always priceCents + taxCents
  inStock: boolean;
}

const toSlug = (title: string): string =>
  title.toLowerCase().replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, '-').replace(/^-|-$/g, '');

export const productFactory = Factory.define<Product>(({ sequence, afterBuild }) => {
  afterBuild((product) => {
    // Enforce derived fields unconditionally — overrides to title are reflected here
    product.slug       = toSlug(product.title);
    product.totalCents = product.priceCents + product.taxCents;
  });

  return {
    id:         faker.string.uuid(),
    title:      faker.commerce.productName(),
    slug:       '',          // overwritten by afterBuild — placeholder only
    priceCents: faker.number.int({ min: 100, max: 50_000 }),
    taxCents:   faker.number.int({ min: 0, max: 5_000 }),
    totalCents: 0,           // overwritten by afterBuild
    inStock:    faker.datatype.boolean(),
  };
});

// Usage — even when title is overridden, slug and totalCents stay consistent:
// const p = productFactory.build({ title: 'Standing Desk Pro' });
// p.slug       → 'standing-desk-pro'
// p.totalCents → priceCents + taxCents  (never 0)
```

### Pattern 32 — `fast-check` Model-Based Testing for Stateful Factories  [official]

Property-based testing with `fast-check` supports *model-based testing* via `fc.commands()` + `fc.modelRun()`. Instead of testing individual inputs, you define a set of commands (create, update, delete) that a model and the real system must agree on after every step. This is the gold standard for testing stateful factory pipelines — shopping carts, event sourcing, or CQRS projections.

**When to use:** Stateful domain logic where a sequence of mutations must always leave the system in a consistent state — entity lifecycle tests, projection rebuilds, shopping cart invariants. **When NOT to use:** Simple CRUD with no shared state between commands — plain `fc.record()` arbitraries (Pattern 18) are sufficient and much faster. Alternative: `@fast-check/vitest` integration with `test.prop()` for simpler property tests without the command machinery.

```typescript
// test/cart.model-based.test.ts — fc model-based testing for cart mutations
import { test, expect } from 'vitest';
import * as fc from 'fast-check';
import { Cart } from '../../src/domain/cart';

// ---------- Model (pure in-memory reference implementation) ----------
interface CartModel {
  items: Map<string, { quantity: number; priceCents: number }>;
}

// ---------- Commands ----------
class AddItemCommand implements fc.Command<CartModel, Cart> {
  constructor(private readonly productId: string, private readonly qty: number) {}
  check = (_m: CartModel) => true;
  run(model: CartModel, cart: Cart): void {
    cart.addItem(this.productId, this.qty, 1000);
    const existing = model.items.get(this.productId);
    model.items.set(this.productId, {
      quantity:   (existing?.quantity ?? 0) + this.qty,
      priceCents: 1000,
    });
    const modelTotal = [...model.items.values()].reduce(
      (s, i) => s + i.quantity * i.priceCents, 0
    );
    expect(cart.totalCents).toBe(modelTotal);
  }
  toString = () => `AddItem(${this.productId}, qty=${this.qty})`;
}

class ClearCommand implements fc.Command<CartModel, Cart> {
  check = (_m: CartModel) => true;
  run(model: CartModel, cart: Cart): void {
    cart.clear();
    model.items.clear();
    expect(cart.totalCents).toBe(0);
  }
  toString = () => 'Clear()';
}

// ---------- Test ----------
test('cart model-based: real cart always matches reference model', () => {
  const allCommands = fc.commands([
    fc.record({ productId: fc.uuidV(4), qty: fc.integer({ min: 1, max: 10 }) })
      .map(({ productId, qty }) => new AddItemCommand(productId, qty)),
    fc.constant(new ClearCommand()),
  ]);
  fc.assert(fc.property(allCommands, (cmds) => {
    const model: CartModel = { items: new Map() };
    const cart             = new Cart();
    fc.modelRun(() => ({ model, real: cart }), cmds);
  }));
});
```

---

### Pattern 33 — Schema-Version–Tagged Factory with Zod Discriminated Union  [community]

When your API or event schema evolves across versions, factories must produce version-correct payloads. Encode the schema version as a discriminated union literal in Zod and build a per-version factory that the shared dispatcher switches on. This makes it impossible to accidentally pass a v1 payload to a v2 handler in tests.

**When to use:** Microservices or event-driven systems with multiple live schema versions (e.g., Kafka topics receiving events from old and new producers simultaneously). **When NOT to use:** Single-version systems where a plain factory with an optional `version` field is sufficient — discriminated unions add ceremony that is not justified for a single active version. Alternative: a `schemaVersion` field on a plain object factory with a runtime assertion that the version matches the endpoint.

```typescript
// factories/order-event.factory.ts — versioned event factory via Zod discriminated union
import { z } from 'zod';
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

const OrderEventV1 = z.object({
  version:     z.literal('v1'),
  orderId:     z.string().uuid(),
  totalAmount: z.number(),            // v1 sends total as a float
  status:      z.enum(['created', 'paid', 'shipped']),
});

const OrderEventV2 = z.object({
  version:      z.literal('v2'),
  orderId:      z.string().uuid(),
  totalCents:   z.number().int(),     // v2 sends total as integer cents
  currencyCode: z.string().length(3),
  status:       z.enum(['created', 'paid', 'shipped', 'returned']),
});

type OrderEventV1 = z.infer<typeof OrderEventV1>;
type OrderEventV2 = z.infer<typeof OrderEventV2>;

export function buildOrderEventV1(overrides: Partial<OrderEventV1> = {}): OrderEventV1 {
  return OrderEventV1.parse({
    version:     'v1',
    orderId:     faker.string.uuid(),
    totalAmount: faker.number.float({ min: 1.0, max: 9999.99, fractionDigits: 2 }),
    status:      faker.helpers.arrayElement(['created', 'paid', 'shipped']),
    ...overrides,
  });
}

export function buildOrderEventV2(overrides: Partial<OrderEventV2> = {}): OrderEventV2 {
  return OrderEventV2.parse({
    version:      'v2',
    orderId:      faker.string.uuid(),
    totalCents:   faker.number.int({ min: 100, max: 999_900 }),
    currencyCode: faker.finance.currencyCode(),
    status:       faker.helpers.arrayElement(['created', 'paid', 'shipped', 'returned']),
    ...overrides,
  });
}
// Zod.parse() throws ZodError at factory call time if overrides violate the schema —
// immediately surfacing version-field mismatches instead of at assertion time.
```

---

### Pattern 34 — UUID v7 Factory for Time-Ordered Database Test Data  [community]

UUID v7 embeds a Unix timestamp in the first 48 bits, making UUIDs monotonically increasing when inserted in order. This matters for test data in systems that rely on UUID-ordered cursor pagination or that use UUID primary keys as a proxy for insertion order. Generating UUID v7 values in factories prevents subtle ordering bugs that only surface when test data is inserted out of chronological order.

**When to use:** Factories for entities with UUID v7 primary keys where tests assert on cursor-based pagination order, range scans, or "latest N items" queries. **When NOT to use:** Systems using UUID v4 or ULID — mixing UUID versions in the same column breaks ordering guarantees silently. Alternative: ULID (via the `ulid` npm package) which achieves the same time-ordered property but with a Crockford base-32 encoding that sorts correctly as a string without a UUID library.

```typescript
// factories/blog-post.factory.ts — UUID v7 for time-ordered DB test data
// Requires: npm install uuid  (v9+ ships uuidv7)
import { v7 as uuidv7 } from 'uuid';
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

interface BlogPost {
  id: string;          // UUID v7 — encodes creation timestamp in first 48 bits
  title: string;
  body: string;
  authorId: string;
  publishedAt: Date;
}

// Produce N posts published at 1-second intervals — IDs sort in insertion order
export function buildBlogPostSequence(count: number, baseDate = new Date()): BlogPost[] {
  return Array.from({ length: count }, (_, i) => {
    const publishedAt = new Date(baseDate.getTime() + i * 1_000);
    return {
      id:          uuidv7(),     // monotonically increasing per call
      title:       faker.lorem.sentence(),
      body:        faker.lorem.paragraphs(2),
      authorId:    faker.string.uuid(),
      publishedAt,
    };
  });
}

// Assert cursor pagination returns posts in UUID order:
// const posts = buildBlogPostSequence(5);
// await db.insert(schema.blogPosts).values(posts);
// const page = await getPostsAfterCursor(posts[1].id, { limit: 3 });
// expect(page.map((p) => p.id)).toEqual(posts.slice(2).map((p) => p.id));
```

### Pattern 35 — Neon DB Branch-Per-Test-Suite for Isolated PostgreSQL Fixtures  [community]

Neon Serverless PostgreSQL supports copy-on-write branching that creates a full database clone in milliseconds. Each test suite (or CI job) provisions a branch, runs migrations and seeds, then deletes the branch on teardown — providing true PostgreSQL isolation without Docker Compose or shared schemas.

**When to use:** Integration or E2E suites that need a real PostgreSQL instance with production-like constraints (foreign keys, triggers, stored procedures) and cannot tolerate shared schema isolation. **When NOT to use:** Unit tests or suites that run in under 10 seconds — the branch creation overhead (~200ms) and network latency add up; use the transaction-per-test pattern (Pattern 30) for lightweight isolation instead. Alternative: Testcontainers with PostgreSQL image for fully local isolation that does not require a Neon account.

```typescript
// test/setup/neon-branch.ts — per-suite Neon branch provisioning
import { createApiClient } from '@neondatabase/api-client';
import { neon } from '@neondatabase/serverless';

const neonApi    = createApiClient({ apiKey: process.env.NEON_API_KEY! });
const PROJECT_ID = process.env.NEON_PROJECT_ID!;

export async function createTestBranch(suiteName: string) {
  const branchName = `test/${suiteName}-${Date.now()}`;
  const { data: branch } = await neonApi.createProjectBranch(PROJECT_ID, {
    branch:    { name: branchName },
    endpoints: [{ type: 'read_write' }],
  });
  const connectionString = branch.connection_uris[0].connection_uri;
  const sql = neon(connectionString);
  return { sql, branchId: branch.branch.id, connectionString };
}

export async function deleteTestBranch(branchId: string) {
  await neonApi.deleteProjectBranch(PROJECT_ID, branchId);
}

// Usage in a Vitest globalSetup file:
// export async function setup() {
//   const { connectionString, branchId } = await createTestBranch('checkout-suite');
//   process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL    = connectionString;
//   process.env.NEON_TEST_BRANCH_ID  = branchId;
// }
// export async function teardown() {
//   await deleteTestBranch(process.env.NEON_TEST_BRANCH_ID!);
// }
```

### Pattern 36 — `fc.letrec` for Recursive Domain Object Arbitraries  [official]

`fast-check`'s `fc.letrec()` defines mutually recursive arbitraries — essential for domain objects with tree-shaped or nested structures (comment threads, category hierarchies, JSON-like documents, AST nodes). Without `letrec`, hand-rolling recursive arbitraries causes stack overflows or requires depth-limiting boilerplate in every factory.

**When to use:** Domain types that are genuinely recursive — nested comments, folder/file trees, expression ASTs, organizational hierarchies, JSON Schema documents. **When NOT to use:** Flat domain objects — `fc.record()` is simpler and faster. Alternative: `fc.oneof(fc.constant(leafNode), fc.lazy(() => treeArbitrary))` for simple binary recursion without the full `letrec` machinery.

```typescript
// test/arbitraries/comment-tree.arbitrary.ts — recursive arbitrary with fc.letrec
import * as fc from 'fast-check';

interface Comment {
  id: string;
  body: string;
  depth: number;
  replies: Comment[];
}

// letrec ties the knot: 'comment' references itself via the tie callback
const { comment } = fc.letrec((tie) => ({
  comment: fc.record({
    id:      fc.uuidV(4),
    body:    fc.string({ minLength: 10, maxLength: 200 }),
    depth:   fc.integer({ min: 0, max: 4 }),
    replies: fc.array(tie('comment'), { maxLength: 3 }),
  }),
}));

function computeMaxDepth(c: Comment, d = 0): number {
  if (c.replies.length === 0) return d;
  return Math.max(...c.replies.map((r) => computeMaxDepth(r, d + 1)));
}

function normalizeDepths(c: Comment, d = 0): Comment {
  return { ...c, depth: d, replies: c.replies.map((r) => normalizeDepths(r, d + 1)) };
}

// Depth-limited export to avoid exponential size blowup in large runs
export const commentTreeArbitrary: fc.Arbitrary<Comment> = comment
  .filter((c) => computeMaxDepth(c) <= 4)
  .map((c) => normalizeDepths(c));

// Usage in a property test:
// import { test } from '@fast-check/vitest';
// test.prop([commentTreeArbitrary])('render never throws for any comment tree', (root) => {
//   expect(() => renderCommentThread(root)).not.toThrow();
// });
```

### Pattern 37 — Per-Environment Seeding Strategy with Environment-Keyed Factories  [community]

A single factory definition often needs to produce subtly different data for different environments: `local` (human-readable, low volume), `ci` (deterministic, seeded, high volume), and `staging` (production-like, realistic). Centralising the environment switch inside the factory prevents copy-paste drift across environment-specific seed scripts.

**When to use:** Projects with multiple seed targets — local dev, CI pipeline, staging QA baseline — each with different data volume and realism requirements. **When NOT to use:** Projects with a single seed target — an environment switch inside the factory adds ceremony that is not justified. Alternative: separate factory files per environment, selected by the seed script — simpler but requires keeping multiple files in sync.

```typescript
// factories/order.factory.ts — environment-keyed factory behaviour
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

type EnvTier = 'local' | 'ci' | 'staging';
const ENV_TIER: EnvTier = (process.env.ENV_TIER as EnvTier) ?? 'local';

interface OrderSeedOptions { count?: number; tier?: EnvTier; }

export function buildOrderBatch({ count, tier = ENV_TIER }: OrderSeedOptions = {}) {
  const targetCount = count ?? { local: 20, ci: 200, staging: 5_000 }[tier];
  const localeMap:  Record<EnvTier, string> = { local: 'en', ci: 'en', staging: 'de' };

  faker.setLocale(localeMap[tier]);
  if (tier === 'ci') faker.seed(42);  // deterministic for CI snapshot assertions

  return Array.from({ length: targetCount }, () => ({
    id:           faker.string.uuid(),
    customerName: faker.person.fullName(),
    amountCents:  faker.number.int({ min: 500, max: 100_000 }),
    currency:     tier === 'staging' ? 'EUR' : 'USD',
    status:       faker.helpers.arrayElement(['pending', 'paid', 'shipped', 'cancelled']),
    createdAt:    faker.date.recent({ days: tier === 'staging' ? 365 : 30 }),
  }));
}

// Seed runner:
// ENV_TIER=staging npx tsx scripts/seed-orders.ts
// ENV_TIER=ci     npx vitest run --reporter=verbose
```

### Pattern 38 — Vitest 4.1 Return-Based Fixture Builder  [official]

Vitest 4.1 introduced a return-based syntax for `test.extend()` fixtures as an alternative to the `use()` callback style. The fixture function simply returns the value (or a Promise), and Vitest handles the lifecycle. This is more ergonomic for read-only, non-teardown fixtures — particularly factory-produced seed objects — and enables better TypeScript type inference without manual generic annotations.

**When to use:** Fixtures that produce a value but need no teardown — factory-produced objects, computed configuration, one-time seed records. **When NOT to use:** Fixtures that require teardown (DB cleanup, server shutdown) — those must use the `use()` callback pattern so Vitest can run teardown code after the test. Alternative: the classic `use()` callback style, which remains fully supported and is required for any fixture with teardown logic.

```typescript
// test/fixtures/order-fixtures.ts — Vitest 4.1 return-based fixture syntax
import { test as baseTest } from 'vitest';
import { buildUser  } from '../factories/user.factory';
import { buildOrder } from '../factories/order.factory';

interface OrderFixtures {
  buyer:        ReturnType<typeof buildUser>;
  pendingOrder: ReturnType<typeof buildOrder>;
  paidOrder:    ReturnType<typeof buildOrder>;
}

export const test = baseTest.extend<OrderFixtures>({
  // Return-based (Vitest 4.1+): no use() callback, TypeScript infers the type
  buyer: () => buildUser({ status: 'active', subscriptionTier: 'premium' }),

  pendingOrder: ({ buyer }) =>
    buildOrder({ customerId: buyer.id, status: 'pending' }),

  paidOrder: ({ buyer }) =>
    buildOrder({ customerId: buyer.id, status: 'paid', paidAt: new Date() }),
});

// In a test file:
// import { test } from '../fixtures/order-fixtures';
// test('paid order shows receipt link', ({ paidOrder }) => {
//   expect(getReceiptUrl(paidOrder)).toMatch(/^https:\/\/receipts\./);
// });
```

### Pattern 39 — `vi.defineHelper()` for Factory Assertion Stack Traces  [official]

Vitest 4.1 introduced `vi.defineHelper()` to mark utility functions as test helpers, causing failure stack traces to point to the test call site rather than inside the helper. For factory assertion wrappers — functions that call `expect()` internally to validate factory output — this dramatically improves debuggability by surfacing *which test* produced invalid data rather than a generic line inside the factory module.

**When to use:** Any factory utility that contains `expect()` assertions — invariant validators, schema-shape checkers, contract assertion helpers. **When NOT to use:** Pure factory functions that return data without assertions — `vi.defineHelper()` has no effect on non-assertion helpers. Alternative: inline the assertion directly in the test (avoids the issue entirely at the cost of repetition), or use `expect.assertions(n)` to verify assertion count.

```typescript
// test/helpers/order-assertions.ts — vi.defineHelper() for clean stack traces
import { vi, expect } from 'vitest';
import { z }          from 'zod';

const OrderSchema = z.object({
  id:          z.string().uuid(),
  customerId:  z.string().uuid(),
  amountCents: z.number().int().positive(),
  status:      z.enum(['pending', 'paid', 'shipped', 'cancelled']),
  createdAt:   z.date(),
});

// Without vi.defineHelper(), a failure here points to this file, not the calling test.
// With vi.defineHelper(), the stack trace skips this frame entirely.
export const assertValidOrder = vi.defineHelper(function assertValidOrder(order: unknown) {
  const result = OrderSchema.safeParse(order);
  if (!result.success) {
    expect(result.success, `Invalid order shape: ${result.error.message}`).toBe(true);
  }
});

// In a test:
// import { assertValidOrder } from '../helpers/order-assertions';
// test('buildOrder produces a valid order', () => {
//   const order = buildOrder();
//   assertValidOrder(order);  // failure stack → points here, not inside assertValidOrder
// });
```

### Pattern 40 — Playwright `mergeTests()` for Modular E2E Fixture Composition  [official]

Playwright's `mergeTests()` utility composes independent fixture modules into a single `test` object without inheritance chains or a single mega-fixture file. Each domain (auth, database, payments) owns its own fixture file, and tests import the exact composed surface they need.

**When to use:** E2E suites with many orthogonal fixture domains — auth tokens, DB seeds, API mocks, payment sandbox state — where a single `fixtures.ts` file would become a thousand-line monolith. **When NOT to use:** Small suites with 2-3 fixtures — `mergeTests()` adds indirection that is not justified. Alternative: direct `baseTest.extend()` chaining, which is simpler but requires fixtures to be defined in a single call chain and can cause tight coupling between unrelated domains.

```typescript
// test/fixtures/index.ts — Playwright mergeTests() fixture composition
import { mergeTests }               from '@playwright/test';
import { test as authFixtures }     from './auth.fixtures';
import { test as dbFixtures }       from './db-seed.fixtures';
import { test as mswFixtures }      from './msw-network.fixtures';

// Each fixture module is independently defined via its own test.extend() call.
// mergeTests() combines them without cross-module imports or coupling.
export const test = mergeTests(authFixtures, dbFixtures, mswFixtures);
export { expect } from '@playwright/test';

// auth.fixtures.ts (abbreviated):
// export const test = base.extend<{ authToken: string }>({
//   authToken: async ({ request }, use) => {
//     const token = await loginAndGetToken(request);
//     await use(token);
//   },
// });

// db-seed.fixtures.ts (abbreviated):
// export const test = base.extend<{ seededUser: User }>({
//   seededUser: async ({}, use) => {
//     const user = await db.users.create(buildUser());
//     await use(user);
//     await db.users.delete(user.id);
//   },
// });

// In a test — gets authToken AND seededUser from the composed fixture:
// import { test, expect } from '../fixtures';
// test('profile page shows seeded user name', async ({ page, authToken, seededUser }) => {
//   await page.setExtraHTTPHeaders({ Authorization: `Bearer ${authToken}` });
//   await page.goto(`/profile/${seededUser.id}`);
//   await expect(page.getByText(seededUser.name)).toBeVisible();
// });
```

### Pattern 41 — `faker.helpers.weightedArrayElement` for Realistic Distribution Testing  [official]

`@faker-js/faker` v8.3+ includes `faker.helpers.weightedArrayElement()` which selects from an array using probability weights. This enables factories that produce data with realistic business distributions — most orders are `'paid'`, a small fraction are `'refunded'`, and very few are `'fraudulent'` — matching real-world frequency without manual probability math.

**When to use:** Load testing, analytics pipelines, and reporting test suites where the distribution of status values affects aggregate results. **When NOT to use:** Tests that need to assert on a specific status — use a plain override instead of weighted random; randomness in assertion-specific tests creates flakiness. Alternative: `faker.helpers.arrayElement()` for uniform distribution, or a manual `Math.random()` threshold check for simple two-outcome distributions.

```typescript
// factories/order.factory.ts — weighted distribution for realistic order test data
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

type OrderStatus = 'pending' | 'paid' | 'shipped' | 'refunded' | 'fraudulent';

// Weights approximate a real-world production distribution from analytics
const STATUS_WEIGHTS: Array<{ weight: number; value: OrderStatus }> = [
  { weight: 5,  value: 'pending'    },
  { weight: 65, value: 'paid'       },
  { weight: 25, value: 'shipped'    },
  { weight: 4,  value: 'refunded'   },
  { weight: 1,  value: 'fraudulent' },
];

export function buildRealisticOrder(overrides: Record<string, unknown> = {}) {
  return {
    id:          faker.string.uuid(),
    customerId:  faker.string.uuid(),
    amountCents: faker.number.int({ min: 500, max: 150_000 }),
    status:      faker.helpers.weightedArrayElement(STATUS_WEIGHTS),
    currency:    faker.helpers.arrayElement(['USD', 'EUR', 'GBP']),
    createdAt:   faker.date.recent({ days: 90 }),
    ...overrides,
  };
}

// Build a 1000-order batch where ~65% are 'paid' — for analytics pipeline assertions:
// const orders = Array.from({ length: 1000 }, () => buildRealisticOrder());
// const paidCount = orders.filter((o) => o.status === 'paid').length;
// expect(paidCount).toBeGreaterThan(550);  // statistically ~650 with tolerance
```

### Pattern 42 — Playwright `testInfo.abort()` for Fixture Precondition Enforcement  [official]

Playwright 1.60 introduced `testInfo.abort()` which immediately terminates a test and marks it as `skipped` (not failed) from within a fixture. This is the idiomatic way to enforce fixture preconditions — if a DB seed fails or an auth token cannot be obtained, the test is skipped with a clear reason rather than failing with a cryptic assertion error deep inside test code.

**When to use:** E2E fixtures with external dependencies (auth services, DB seeds, third-party sandboxes) that may be unavailable in certain CI environments or during local development without required secrets. **When NOT to use:** Conditions that represent actual test failures — use `expect().toBe()` for those. A fixture using `testInfo.abort()` silently hides real failures if overused. Alternative: `test.skip()` inside the test body with an explicit condition check, but that requires the test to be aware of fixture availability, breaking fixture encapsulation.

```typescript
// test/fixtures/payment-sandbox.fixture.ts — abort() for precondition enforcement
import { test as baseTest } from '@playwright/test';

interface PaymentSandboxFixtures { stripeCustomerId: string; }

export const test = baseTest.extend<PaymentSandboxFixtures>({
  stripeCustomerId: async ({ request }, use, testInfo) => {
    if (!process.env.STRIPE_TEST_SECRET_KEY) {
      // Marks the test as skipped with an explicit reason — not as a failure
      await testInfo.abort('STRIPE_TEST_SECRET_KEY not set — skipping payment E2E test');
      return;
    }
    const response = await request.post('https://api.stripe.com/v1/customers', {
      form:    { description: `E2E test customer — ${testInfo.title}` },
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.STRIPE_TEST_SECRET_KEY}` },
    });
    const { id } = await response.json() as { id: string };
    await use(id);
    // Cleanup: delete the test customer after the test regardless of outcome
    await request.delete(`https://api.stripe.com/v1/customers/${id}`, {
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.STRIPE_TEST_SECRET_KEY}` },
    });
  },
});
```

---

### Pattern 43 — Self-Initializing Fake with MSW and JSON File Replay  [community]

The Self-Initializing Fake pattern (Martin Fowler) records real API responses on first run and replays them on subsequent runs. Implemented with MSW in Node.js, the recorder intercepts real responses and persists them to a JSON file. On replay, MSW serves the cached responses deterministically — without network access — bridging the gap between pure mocking and live API calls.

**When to use:** External APIs with stable response shapes that are expensive or rate-limited — payment confirmations, geocoding, address validation. The recorded responses give realistic data without test-time network calls. **When NOT to use:** APIs with rapidly changing schemas or real-time state (stock prices, live inventory). Recorded responses go stale silently and have no automatic re-recording signal. Alternative: HAR-based replay via Playwright's `routeFromHAR` (Pattern 26) for E2E tests; this MSW variant is better suited to component/integration tests.

```typescript
// test/msw/self-initializing-fake.ts — MSW record/replay for Node.js tests
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw';
import * as fs   from 'node:fs';
import * as path from 'node:path';

const CACHE_DIR = path.join(__dirname, '__msw-cache__');

function cachePath(key: string): string {
  return path.join(CACHE_DIR, `${key.replace(/[^a-z0-9]/gi, '_')}.json`);
}

export function createSelfInitializingHandler(url: string, cacheKey: string) {
  return http.get(url, async ({ request }) => {
    const cached = cachePath(cacheKey);
    if (fs.existsSync(cached)) {
      // REPLAY: return the recorded response directly
      return HttpResponse.json(JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(cached, 'utf8')));
    }
    // RECORD: pass through to the real network, then persist the response
    const real = await fetch(request.url);
    const data = await real.json();
    fs.mkdirSync(CACHE_DIR, { recursive: true });
    fs.writeFileSync(cached, JSON.stringify(data, null, 2), 'utf8');
    return HttpResponse.json(data);
  });
}

// Usage in a test file:
// const server = setupServer(
//   createSelfInitializingHandler(
//     'https://api.geocode.earth/v1/autocomplete',
//     'geocode-london-search'
//   )
// );
// beforeAll(() => server.listen({ onUnhandledRequest: 'error' }));
// afterAll(() => server.close());
// First run hits the network and writes __msw-cache__/geocode_london_search.json.
// All subsequent runs serve the cached file. Commit __msw-cache__/ to version control.
```

---

### Pattern 44 — Testing Resource Pool with Pool-Size-1 Schema Isolation  [official]

Martin Fowler's Testing Resource Pools pattern isolates tests that share a limited external resource by managing the resource as an explicit pool. The pool-size-1 technique provisions exactly one resource per Vitest worker — a PostgreSQL schema per worker — eliminating resource contention without requiring full mocking. Parallelism is tuned by setting `maxWorkers` to the number of available DB connections.

**When to use:** Integration tests against a finite set of external resources (N DB connections, M sandbox accounts) where each worker needs its own isolated resource for full test independence. **When NOT to use:** Tests that can run fully in-process with mocks — the pool machinery adds overhead and external dependency that mocks eliminate. Alternative: per-test resource provisioning (more isolation, higher cost) or a single shared resource with mutex locking (serializes tests, kills parallelism).

```typescript
// test/fixtures/db-pool.fixture.ts — pool-size-1: one PostgreSQL schema per worker
import { test as baseTest } from 'vitest';
import postgres from 'postgres';

const WORKER_ID   = process.env.VITEST_WORKER_ID ?? '0';
const SCHEMA_NAME = `test_worker_${WORKER_ID}`;

interface PoolFixtures {
  sql:    ReturnType<typeof postgres>;
  schema: string;
}

const pool = postgres(process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL!, { max: 1 });

export const test = baseTest.extend<PoolFixtures>({
  sql: async ({}, use) => {
    await pool.unsafe(`CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS ${SCHEMA_NAME}`);
    await pool.unsafe(`SET search_path TO ${SCHEMA_NAME}, public`);
    await use(pool);
    // Drop only this worker's schema — sibling workers are completely unaffected
    await pool.unsafe(`DROP SCHEMA IF EXISTS ${SCHEMA_NAME} CASCADE`);
  },
  schema: async ({}, use) => {
    await use(SCHEMA_NAME);
  },
});

// vitest.config.ts: match maxWorkers to available DB connections
// export default defineConfig({ test: { maxWorkers: 4 } })
// Each worker operates in its own schema — no locks, no contention, full parallelism.
```

---

### Pattern 45 — `expect.schemaMatching` for Inline Factory Output Validation  [official]

Vitest 4.0 introduced `expect.schemaMatching(schema)` which accepts any Zod, Valibot, or ArkType schema and asserts that the received value matches it. Applied to factory output, this gives a single-line assertion that validates the entire shape of a factory-produced object — without writing a custom matcher or calling `schema.parse()` manually.

**When to use:** Factory smoke tests in a dedicated `factories.spec.ts` file; any test that receives a factory-produced object and needs to assert its full shape before drilling into individual fields. **When NOT to use:** Replacing per-field `expect(x.field).toBe(y)` assertions — schema matching verifies shape, not exact values. Use it as a precondition check, then assert specific fields separately. Alternative: `schema.safeParse(factory()).success` with a manual `expect` — works but gives a less readable diff on failure.

```typescript
// test/factories/order.factory.spec.ts — expect.schemaMatching inline validation
import { test, expect } from 'vitest';
import { z }            from 'zod';
import { buildOrder, buildOrderList } from '../factories/order.factory';

const LineItemSchema = z.object({
  productId: z.string().uuid(),
  quantity:  z.number().int().positive(),
  unitCents: z.number().int().positive(),
});

const OrderSchema = z.object({
  id:          z.string().uuid(),
  customerId:  z.string().uuid(),
  amountCents: z.number().int().positive(),
  status:      z.enum(['pending', 'paid', 'shipped', 'cancelled']),
  createdAt:   z.date(),
  lineItems:   z.array(LineItemSchema).min(1),
});

test('buildOrder output matches OrderSchema', () => {
  // Vitest 4.0 expect.schemaMatching — fails with a Zod diff on mismatch
  expect(buildOrder()).toEqual(expect.schemaMatching(OrderSchema));
});

test('buildOrderList produces N schema-valid orders', () => {
  const orders = buildOrderList(5);
  expect(orders).toHaveLength(5);
  for (const order of orders) {
    expect(order).toEqual(expect.schemaMatching(OrderSchema));
  }
});

test('status override is preserved in schema-valid output', () => {
  const paidOrder = buildOrder({ status: 'paid' });
  expect(paidOrder).toEqual(expect.schemaMatching(OrderSchema));
  expect(paidOrder.status).toBe('paid');
});
```

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 32

## Community Gotcha #92 — `fishery` `afterBuild` hook receives a shallow copy — mutating a nested object inside `afterBuild` mutates the factory's internal default array  [community]

**WHY: `fishery` passes a shallow copy of the assembled object to `afterBuild`. For flat objects this is safe, but if the factory default contains a nested array or object (e.g., `tags: []`), the shallow copy shares the same reference. Mutating `product.tags.push('sale')` inside `afterBuild` modifies the original default array, causing every subsequent `build()` call to accumulate tags from all previous calls — tests that pass in isolation fail when run together because factory state leaks across calls.**

Fix: deep-clone nested defaults in the factory definition using `structuredClone()`, or use arrow-function defaults — fishery re-evaluates function defaults on each `build()` call: `tags: () => []` instead of `tags: []`. Alternatively, use spread syntax on every nested field inside `afterBuild`: `product.tags = [...(product.tags ?? [])]` before pushing.

---

## Community Gotcha #93 — `fc.commands()` model-based shrinking may produce a minimal sequence that hides the root cause by removing prerequisite state-setup commands  [community]

**WHY: `fast-check`'s shrinking algorithm reduces a failing command sequence to the shortest sequence that still fails. For model-based tests, the minimal sequence is correct but can be misleading: if the bug only manifests after `AddItem` → `ApplyDiscount` → `RemoveItem`, but `RemoveItem` on an empty cart also throws, shrinking may stop at `[RemoveItem]` alone — masking the three-step interaction bug. Developers fix the wrong (empty-cart) path and the original discount+remove bug persists.**

Fix: add `check()` method guards to commands that require preconditions (e.g., `RemoveItemCommand.check = (model) => model.items.size > 0`). This prevents fast-check from generating or shrinking to sequences where a command is logically invalid, keeping the shrunk reproducer semantically meaningful and pointing at the real bug.

---

## Community Gotcha #94 — `faker.setLocale()` is global mutable state — calling it inside a factory function changes the locale for all subsequent faker calls across all factories in the same worker process  [community]

**WHY: `faker` in `@faker-js/faker` v8 and earlier exposes a singleton whose locale is globally mutable. When a factory calls `faker.setLocale('de')` to generate a German address, all faker calls in the same worker process after that point use the German locale — including completely unrelated factories like `buildUser()`. This causes non-deterministic test failures where `buildUser()` returns German-looking names in some files but English names in others, depending on execution order within the worker.**

Fix: use locale-scoped faker instances instead of the global singleton: `const deFaker = new Faker({ locale: [de, base] })`. Import `deFaker` only in the factory that needs German data. Never mutate the global `faker` import. In faker v10+, the locale-specific package imports (`import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker/locale/de'`) also provide isolated instances without affecting the default `faker`.

---

## Community Gotcha #95 — Vitest 4.1 return-based fixtures silently skip teardown — developers use the concise return syntax for fixtures that create DB rows, leaving orphaned rows that cause unique-constraint violations in later tests  [community]

**WHY: The Vitest 4.1 return-based fixture syntax (`myFixture: () => buildUser()`) is designed for pure value fixtures with no teardown. Vitest accepts the return-based form without warning even when the fixture is a DB-backed object, but the teardown code is never executed — the row is never deleted. Over a full CI run, orphaned rows accumulate and eventually cause unique-constraint violations or pollute query results in tests that run after the offending fixture.**

Fix: any fixture that creates an external side effect (DB insert, file creation, server start) must use the `use()` callback form: `async ({}, use) => { const row = await db.insert(...); await use(row); await db.delete(row.id); }`. Reserve the return-based syntax strictly for pure in-memory factory values with zero external side effects. Document this rule in the project's fixture authoring guide.

---

## Community Gotcha #96 — `zod-fixture` ignores `z.default()` — it generates its own value and discards the default, making fixtures diverge from what production Zod parsing would produce for missing fields  [community]

**WHY: `zod-fixture` generates values by traversing the Zod schema's internal `_def` structure and synthesizing a value for every field. It never calls `z.parse(undefined)`, so `z.default()` wrappers are traversed past rather than applied. As a result, `z.string().default('N/A')` in the schema produces a random string from zod-fixture, not `'N/A'`. Tests that rely on fixture objects having the same default values as production Zod parsing silently receive different data, causing assertion mismatches that are hard to trace to the fixture generation layer.**

Fix: after calling `createFixture(Schema)`, apply a merge with the schema's Zod-parsed defaults: `const defaults = Schema.parse({})` (triggers all defaults for an empty input) then `{ ...defaults, ...createFixture(Schema) }`. This ensures default values are present while zod-fixture fills non-defaulted fields. Add a snapshot test on factory output (Pattern 25 / Pattern 45) to catch this mismatch at fixture authoring time.

---

## Community Gotcha #97 — calling `faker.seed()` inside a factory function re-seeds the global RNG on every invocation — two calls to the same batch factory in one test produce identical data, causing duplicate-key violations on DB insert  [community]

**WHY: A common mistake when implementing deterministic factories is placing `faker.seed(42)` inside the factory function body for reproducibility rather than in global test setup. Every time the factory is called, faker's RNG is reset to the same seed, so `buildOrderBatch(10)` called twice in the same test produces the same 10 objects both times. Uniqueness-constrained DB inserts succeed on the first call and fail with duplicate-key violations on the second — but only when both calls happen in the same test or worker, producing intermittent CI failures that are difficult to reproduce locally.**

Fix: call `faker.seed()` exactly once per test suite in `globalSetup` or `beforeAll`, never inside a factory function body. For factories that must be reproducible in isolation (e.g., snapshot tests), use a locally-seeded faker instance: `const localFaker = new Faker({ locale: [en] }); localFaker.seed(42)` — this does not affect the global seed. Document the seeding strategy in the factory file's JSDoc comment so future contributors do not re-introduce the anti-pattern.

## Cycle 33 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 46 — `faker.internet.jwt()` for Realistic Auth Token Test Data  [official]

Faker.js v9 introduced `faker.internet.jwt()`, which generates structurally valid but unsigned JWT strings with realistic headers and payloads. Tests that validate token parsing, token-boundary logic, or middleware that inspects JWT shape now have a first-class faker primitive instead of hand-rolled base64 strings or hardcoded fixture constants. The method accepts an optional `options` object allowing overrides for `header`, `payload`, and `algorithm` fields, making it easy to produce tokens with specific claims like `exp`, `sub`, or custom scopes. Because the generated JWT is unsigned, never use it to test actual cryptographic verification — the signature segment is a random base64url string that will fail real `jwt.verify()` calls.

**Use when:** testing middleware, route guards, or parsers that read JWT claims without verifying the signature — for example, extracting a user role from an Authorization header in a unit test of a permission-checking function. **Do NOT use when:** the test exercises real `jsonwebtoken.verify()` or `jose.jwtVerify()` paths; use `jsonwebtoken.sign()` with a known test secret instead. **Alternative:** `jsonwebtoken.sign({ sub: 'u_123', role: 'admin' }, 'test-secret', { expiresIn: '1h' })` for tests that must validate the signature.

```typescript
// test/factories/auth.factory.ts
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

interface TokenOptions {
  sub?: string;
  role?: 'admin' | 'editor' | 'viewer';
  expiresIn?: number; // seconds from now
}

export function buildJwtFixture(options: TokenOptions = {}): string {
  const now = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000);
  return faker.internet.jwt({
    payload: {
      sub:  options.sub  ?? faker.string.uuid(),
      role: options.role ?? faker.helpers.arrayElement(['admin', 'editor', 'viewer']),
      iat:  now,
      exp:  now + (options.expiresIn ?? 3600),
    },
  });
}

// usage in a unit test for a permission middleware:
test('middleware rejects viewer role on admin route', () => {
  const token = buildJwtFixture({ role: 'viewer' });
  const req   = { headers: { authorization: `Bearer ${token}` } };
  expect(checkAdminPermission(req)).toBe(false);
});
```

---

### Pattern 47 — `faker.string.ulid()` for Lexicographically Sortable Test IDs  [official]

Faker.js v9 added `faker.string.ulid()`, which generates a 26-character ULID (Universally Unique Lexicographically Sortable Identifier). ULIDs embed a millisecond timestamp in the first 10 characters, making them naturally sortable and time-ordered — unlike random UUIDs. Test factories for event-sourced systems, audit logs, or cursor-paginated APIs benefit from ULIDs because ordering assertions like `expect(events[0].id < events[1].id).toBe(true)` work correctly without additional sorting logic. The method optionally accepts a `refDate` parameter so factories can produce deterministically ordered IDs anchored to a known timestamp.

**Use when:** the system under test stores entities in a key-value store or uses cursors based on ULID ordering, and you need test data whose natural ID ordering reflects insertion time. **Do NOT use when:** the system uses UUID v4 primary keys backed by a UUID index in PostgreSQL — switching the test data to ULIDs diverges from production key shape and can mask collation or type-cast bugs. **Alternative:** `faker.string.uuid({ version: 7 })` (added in v9) produces a UUID v7 with embedded timestamp and is directly compatible with UUID-typed columns.

```typescript
// test/factories/event.factory.ts
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

export interface DomainEvent {
  id:        string;
  type:      string;
  payload:   Record<string, unknown>;
  createdAt: Date;
}

export function buildDomainEvent(overrides: Partial<DomainEvent> = {}): DomainEvent {
  const createdAt = overrides.createdAt ?? faker.date.recent({ days: 7 });
  return {
    id:        faker.string.ulid({ refDate: createdAt }),
    type:      faker.helpers.arrayElement(['UserCreated', 'OrderPlaced', 'PaymentReceived']),
    payload:   {},
    createdAt,
    ...overrides,
  };
}

// Verify cursor-pagination contract — IDs must be ascending with time:
test('events returned in ULID order match chronological insertion order', () => {
  const events = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4].map(i =>
    buildDomainEvent({ createdAt: new Date(Date.now() + i * 1000) })
  );
  const sorted = [...events].sort((a, b) => a.id.localeCompare(b.id));
  expect(sorted.map(e => e.id)).toEqual(events.map(e => e.id));
});
```

---

### Pattern 48 — Faker.js v9 `faker.string.uuid({ version: 7 })` for Time-Ordered UUID Primary Keys  [official]

Faker.js v9 extended `faker.string.uuid()` to accept a `version` option, including `7` for UUID v7 — a time-ordered UUID variant defined by RFC 9562. UUID v7 encodes a Unix millisecond timestamp in the most-significant bits, producing naturally sortable strings that look like standard UUIDs and are compatible with UUID-typed database columns. Test factories that previously relied on a separate `uuid` npm package for v7 generation can now use the built-in faker API, reducing dependencies. Because the timestamp is real, two `faker.string.uuid({ version: 7 })` calls within the same millisecond may produce the same first 48 bits — use `await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 1))` or a sequence counter when strict ordering is required in a synchronous factory loop.

**Use when:** the production schema uses UUID v7 primary keys and tests must verify pagination, timeline queries, or range-scan logic that depends on UUID sort order. **Do NOT use when:** the column type is `uuid` but the production code generates v4 random UUIDs — using v7 in tests changes the statistical distribution and can mask bugs in code that assumes no correlation between UUID values and insertion time. **Alternative:** `crypto.randomUUID()` (Node.js 19+) generates v4 UUIDs natively and is always available without any import; use it for pure-random-ID test factories that do not need ordering.

```typescript
// test/factories/subscription.factory.ts
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

export interface Subscription {
  id:        string; // UUID v7
  userId:    string;
  planId:    string;
  startedAt: Date;
  status:    'active' | 'cancelled' | 'paused';
}

export function buildSubscription(overrides: Partial<Subscription> = {}): Subscription {
  const startedAt = overrides.startedAt ?? faker.date.past({ years: 1 });
  return {
    id:        faker.string.uuid({ version: 7 }),
    userId:    faker.string.uuid({ version: 4 }),
    planId:    faker.helpers.arrayElement(['plan_free', 'plan_pro', 'plan_enterprise']),
    startedAt,
    status:    'active',
    ...overrides,
  };
}

test('subscriptions list is returned in creation order by UUID v7 sort', () => {
  const subs = Array.from({ length: 5 }, (_, i) =>
    buildSubscription({ startedAt: new Date(2024_000_000_000 + i * 60_000) })
  );
  const ids = subs.map(s => s.id);
  expect([...ids].sort()).toEqual(ids); // v7 IDs should already be ordered
});
```
