### Pattern 49 — `faker.number.romanNumeral()` for Boundary-Testing Numeric Display Logic  [official]

Faker.js v9 added `faker.number.romanNumeral()` to the `number` module. It returns a Roman numeral string for integers in the range 1–3999. This primitive is useful for testing components and formatters that accept or display Roman numerals — document version labels, outline numbering, legal clause numbering, and similar domains — without hard-coding fragile constants. The method accepts `min` and `max` options, allowing factories to constrain the output to a realistic range for the domain under test.

**Use when:** the system displays or parses Roman numerals (legal docs, academic outlines, chapter headings) and tests need diverse valid inputs beyond `'I'`, `'V'`, `'X'`. **Do NOT use when:** only a handful of specific values matter (e.g., `'IV'` and `'IX'` to test subtractive notation edge cases) — hard-code those literals for clarity. **Alternative:** `faker.helpers.arrayElement(['I', 'II', 'III', 'IV', 'V', 'IX', 'X', 'XL', 'XC', 'CD', 'CM', 'MMMCMXCIX'])` for a hand-curated list that emphasises edge-case numeral combinations.

```typescript
// test/factories/document.factory.ts
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

export interface DocumentSection {
  id:      string;
  chapter: string; // Roman numeral chapter label
  title:   string;
  body:    string;
}

export function buildDocumentSection(
  overrides: Partial<DocumentSection> = {}
): DocumentSection {
  return {
    id:      faker.string.uuid(),
    chapter: faker.number.romanNumeral({ min: 1, max: 50 }),
    title:   faker.lorem.sentence({ min: 3, max: 8 }),
    body:    faker.lorem.paragraphs(2),
    ...overrides,
  };
}

test('renderChapterLabel formats Roman numerals without wrapping', () => {
  const section = buildDocumentSection();
  const label   = renderChapterLabel(section);
  // The rendered label must contain the exact Roman numeral string
  expect(label).toContain(section.chapter);
});
```

### Pattern 50 — Vitest `test.override()` for Suite-Scoped Fixture Specialization  [official]

Vitest 4.1 introduced `test.override()`, which lets a test suite replace the value of one or more fixtures for all tests within that suite and its children without creating a new extended test object. This is the idiomatic alternative to re-extending the test context for minor per-suite variations — for example, a user factory that normally returns a `viewer` role but must return an `admin` role for an entire admin-panel test suite. The override is scoped: it does not affect sibling suites, and the original fixture default is restored when the suite exits.

**Use when:** a whole suite needs one or two fixture values specialized from the project default but the rest of the fixture chain is identical — overriding is cheaper than duplicating the entire test file or extending the context again. **Do NOT use when:** different tests within the same suite need different specializations — use per-test overrides via `test.extend()` or direct factory calls inside each test instead. **Alternative:** `beforeEach` that writes a different value into a shared variable; this is less type-safe and does not compose with the fixture lifecycle (no automatic teardown on override).

```typescript
// test/admin/admin-panel.test.ts
import { test, expect } from 'vitest';
import { appTest } from '../fixtures/app.fixtures';

// Override currentUser fixture so every test in this file receives an admin
const adminTest = appTest.override({ currentUser: { id: 'u_admin', role: 'admin' } });

adminTest('admin can view user management page', async ({ page, currentUser }) => {
  await page.goto('/admin/users');
  expect(currentUser.role).toBe('admin');
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'User Management' })).toBeVisible();
});

adminTest('admin can delete a user', async ({ page }) => {
  const deleteBtn = page.getByRole('button', { name: /delete/i }).first();
  await deleteBtn.click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toContainText('User deleted');
});
```

---

### Pattern 51 — Testcontainers `withReuse()` Flag for Shared Long-Lived Containers in Local Development  [official]

Testcontainers for Node.js supports a container-reuse mode via `withReuse()` (or the `TESTCONTAINERS_REUSE_ENABLE=true` environment variable). When reuse is enabled, Testcontainers computes a hash of the container configuration and reuses a running container if one with the same hash already exists on the Docker host. This eliminates the 5–30 second cold-start overhead on every test run during local development — a developer running tests repeatedly in a watch loop pays the container startup cost only once per session. Reuse must be explicitly disabled in CI (by omitting the flag or setting `TESTCONTAINERS_REUSE_ENABLE=false`) so that each CI run starts from a clean container state and avoids cross-run data pollution.

**Use when:** developers run integration tests repeatedly in a watch loop locally and the per-test-run container startup time dominates feedback latency. The feature is safe only when combined with deterministic teardown/cleanup SQL at the start of each test or suite. **Do NOT use when:** tests write persistent state that cannot be cleaned up between runs — any leaked row or schema change from a previous run will corrupt subsequent runs. **Alternative:** per-suite Testcontainers provisioning without reuse (the default) — slower per run but completely isolated; combine with Neon branching (Pattern 35) for PostgreSQL-specific isolation.

```typescript
// test/fixtures/reusable-pg.fixture.ts
import { PostgreSqlContainer, StartedPostgreSqlContainer } from '@testcontainers/postgresql';
import { test as base } from 'vitest';

let _sharedContainer: StartedPostgreSqlContainer | null = null;

async function getSharedContainer(): Promise<StartedPostgreSqlContainer> {
  if (!_sharedContainer) {
    _sharedContainer = await new PostgreSqlContainer('postgres:16-alpine')
      .withReuse()  // reuse if already running with same config hash
      .start();
  }
  return _sharedContainer;
}

export const pgTest = base.extend<{ pgUrl: string }>({
  pgUrl: async ({}, use) => {
    const container = await getSharedContainer();
    const url = container.getConnectionUri();
    await use(url);
    // No container.stop() here — the container is reused across runs
  },
});

// In CI: set TESTCONTAINERS_REUSE_ENABLE=false to disable reuse and get a clean container
```

---

### Pattern 52 — Prisma `$transaction` Rollback Isolation for Unit-of-Work Tests  [official]

Prisma's interactive transactions (`prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => { ... })`) can be exploited for test isolation by starting a transaction at the beginning of each test, running all database operations through the transactional client `tx`, and rolling back at the end of the test. Because Prisma interactive transactions hold a real database connection open for the transaction's lifetime, each test gets a completely isolated view of the database — inserts and updates made through `tx` are invisible to other connections and vanish on rollback. This technique avoids the cost of dropping and recreating schemas or running explicit `DELETE FROM` cleanup SQL after every test.

**Use when:** integration tests exercise Prisma-backed service functions that accept a Prisma client parameter; the service under test must be refactored to accept `PrismaClient | Prisma.TransactionClient` so the test can inject the transactional client. **Do NOT use when:** the service under test spawns its own Prisma client internally (not injected) — the inner client is on a different connection and its writes will not be rolled back. **Alternative:** per-test schema provisioning with `CREATE SCHEMA test_<uuid>` and `DROP SCHEMA` teardown (Pattern 30 / Drizzle variant) — heavier setup cost but works even when the service creates its own client.

```typescript
// test/services/order.service.test.ts
import { PrismaClient, Prisma } from '@prisma/client';
import { test, expect, beforeAll, afterAll } from 'vitest';
import { createOrder } from '../../src/services/order.service';
import { buildOrderInput } from '../factories/order.factory';

const prisma = new PrismaClient();
beforeAll(async () => { await prisma.$connect(); });
afterAll(async  () => { await prisma.$disconnect(); });

async function withRollback<T>(
  fn: (tx: Prisma.TransactionClient) => Promise<T>
): Promise<void> {
  await prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => {
    await fn(tx);
    // Deliberately throw to trigger rollback — Prisma rolls back on any thrown error
    throw new Error('__rollback__');
  }).catch((err) => {
    if (err.message !== '__rollback__') throw err;
  });
}

test('createOrder inserts a new order row', async () => {
  await withRollback(async (tx) => {
    const input = buildOrderInput();
    const order = await createOrder(tx, input);
    expect(order.id).toBeDefined();
    const found = await tx.order.findUnique({ where: { id: order.id } });
    expect(found).not.toBeNull();
    // Transaction is rolled back after the test — the row vanishes from the real DB
  });
});
```

---

### Pattern 53 — `fast-check` `fc.gen()` for Inline Arbitrary Generation in Test Bodies  [official]

Fast-check v4 introduced `fc.gen()`, a mechanism for generating values inline inside a property body without pre-declaring all arbitraries upfront. The `fc.gen(arb)` call returns a new value from the provided arbitrary each time it is invoked during a given run, and fast-check tracks all generated values for shrinking. This is particularly useful in factory-driven property tests where the exact set of properties needed is not known until the test body executes — for example, generating a variable number of order line items based on a generated quantity. The feature eliminates the previous workaround of using `fc.tuple` or `fc.array` to eagerly pre-generate all values before the property body runs.

**Use when:** a property test needs to generate new values mid-body in a control-flow–dependent way (e.g., generate N items where N itself is a generated integer). **Do NOT use when:** all inputs are known upfront — use `fc.property(arb1, arb2, ...)` for clarity and predictable shrinking. **Alternative:** `fc.tuple` or `fc.chain` for cases where the second arbitrary's range depends on a previously generated value but the dependency is known at arbitrary-construction time.

```typescript
// test/properties/cart.property.test.ts
import * as fc from 'fast-check';
import { addToCart, calculateTotal } from '../../src/cart';

test('cart total equals sum of line item prices', () => {
  fc.assert(
    fc.property(
      fc.integer({ min: 1, max: 20 }),
      fc.integer({ min: 0, max: 10_000 }),
      (numItems, discountCents) => {
        const gen = fc.gen();
        const items = Array.from({ length: numItems }, () => ({
          productId:  gen(fc.uuid()),
          quantity:   gen(fc.integer({ min: 1, max: 99 })),
          priceCents: gen(fc.integer({ min: 50, max: 50_000 })),
        }));
        const cart  = items.reduce((c, item) => addToCart(c, item), { items: [], discountCents });
        const total = calculateTotal(cart);
        const expected = items.reduce((s, i) => s + i.quantity * i.priceCents, 0) - discountCents;
        return total === Math.max(0, expected);
      }
    )
  );
});
```

---

### Pattern 54 — Vitest `annotate()` for Attaching Factory Metadata to Test Reports  [official]

Vitest 3.2 introduced a context-level `annotate()` API that attaches arbitrary string or structured metadata to a test result for display in HTML/JSON reporters. In factory-heavy integration test suites, annotating the generated fixture data — especially when a test fails — dramatically reduces the time to reproduce failures. Instead of adding `console.log(fixture)` statements and re-running, the fixture snapshot is captured in the report and viewable directly in the Vitest UI. The annotation persists in the JSON report artifact, enabling post-CI inspection of exactly what data triggered a failure.

**Use when:** integration tests use complex factories and test failures are difficult to reproduce because the generated data is random; annotating the fixture gives CI visibility into what data caused the failure. **Do NOT use when:** fixture data contains PII, credentials, or sensitive internal state — annotations are written to the test report artifact which may be stored in CI logs or shared dashboards. **Alternative:** `console.log(JSON.stringify(fixture, null, 2))` inside a `try/catch` around the assertion — lower overhead but pollutes CI stdout and does not survive report archiving.

```typescript
// test/integration/invoice.test.ts
import { test, expect } from 'vitest';
import { buildInvoice } from '../factories/invoice.factory';
import { generateInvoicePdf } from '../../src/pdf/invoice-generator';

test('generateInvoicePdf produces a non-empty buffer', async ({ annotate }) => {
  const invoice = buildInvoice({
    lineItems: 5,
    currency:  'EUR',
    status:    'draft',
  });

  // Attach fixture snapshot to the test report for failure diagnostics
  await annotate(`Invoice fixture:\n${JSON.stringify(invoice, null, 2)}`);

  const buffer = await generateInvoicePdf(invoice);
  expect(buffer).toBeInstanceOf(Buffer);
  expect(buffer.byteLength).toBeGreaterThan(0);
});
```

---

### Pattern 55 — `fishery` `rewindSequence()` for Deterministic Counter-Based Test IDs  [official]

Fishery uses an internal auto-incrementing sequence counter to generate unique values via the `sequence` argument in factory definitions. By default the counter starts at `1` and increments on every `build()` call across the lifetime of the test process — meaning test order affects the IDs generated by later tests. Fishery exposes `factory.rewindSequence()` to reset the counter to its initial value, and `Factory.resetAll()` (a static method on `Factory`) to reset all registered factories at once. Calling `Factory.resetAll()` in a `beforeEach` hook makes every test's generated IDs deterministic and independent of execution order, which is essential for snapshot tests and assertions that compare specific ID values.

**Use when:** tests use fishery sequence numbers in fixture IDs or names (e.g., `user-1`, `user-2`) and snapshot tests must produce stable output regardless of which tests ran before them in the suite. **Do NOT use when:** factories intentionally accumulate sequence state across multiple build calls within a single test (e.g., generating a graph where each node gets a unique incrementing ID); resetting mid-test would restart IDs from 1 and break uniqueness. **Alternative:** use `faker.string.uuid()` instead of the sequence counter for IDs so no reset is needed — sequence counters are most useful for human-readable labels, not opaque identifiers.

```typescript
// test/factories/user.factory.ts
import { Factory } from 'fishery';
import { faker }   from '@faker-js/faker';

export interface User {
  id:       number;
  username: string;
  email:    string;
}

export const userFactory = Factory.define<User>(({ sequence }) => ({
  id:       sequence,
  username: `user-${sequence}`,
  email:    faker.internet.email(),
}));

// test/setup.ts — global beforeEach hook resets all factory sequences
import { Factory } from 'fishery';
import { beforeEach } from 'vitest';

beforeEach(() => {
  Factory.resetAll(); // reset all factory sequence counters before every test
});

// test/user.snapshot.test.ts
test('userFactory produces stable snapshot output', () => {
  const users = userFactory.buildList(3);
  expect(users.map(u => u.username)).toEqual(['user-1', 'user-2', 'user-3']);
  // Without Factory.resetAll() in beforeEach, values could be user-7..9 depending on run order
});
```

---

### Pattern 56 — Testcontainers `withCopyFilesToContainer()` for Pre-Seeded Database Init Scripts  [official]

Testcontainers for Node.js supports copying files into a container before it starts via `withCopyFilesToContainer()`. PostgreSQL's official Docker image automatically executes any `.sql` or `.sh` file placed in `/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/` on first startup. Combining these two features allows test suites to inject a schema-plus-seed SQL script into a fresh Postgres container without running migrations after startup — the container exits the `starting` phase already populated with reference data. This is faster than running `prisma migrate deploy` or `drizzle-kit push` after container start, and produces a single immutable container snapshot used by all tests in the suite.

**Use when:** the test suite needs a fixed set of reference/lookup data (e.g., country codes, product categories, permissions) that never changes between tests; embedding the seed in the init script makes the container self-contained and eliminates per-suite seeding overhead. **Do NOT use when:** tests need to mutate or customize the seed data per test — the init script runs only on the first container start (or when the data directory is empty), so subsequent container reuses will not re-run it. **Alternative:** call `prisma db seed` or a custom seed script in `globalSetup` after the container is running — more flexible but adds wall-clock time to every CI run.

```typescript
// test/fixtures/seeded-pg.fixture.ts
import path from 'node:path';
import { PostgreSqlContainer } from '@testcontainers/postgresql';
import { test as base }         from 'vitest';

const SEED_SQL = path.join(__dirname, '../seed/init.sql');

export const seededPgTest = base.extend<{ pgUrl: string }>({
  pgUrl: [async ({}, use) => {
    const container = await new PostgreSqlContainer('postgres:16-alpine')
      .withCopyFilesToContainer([{
        source:      SEED_SQL,
        target:      '/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/01-seed.sql',
        mode:        0o644,
      }])
      .start();

    await use(container.getConnectionUri());
    await container.stop();
  }, { scope: 'file' }], // share one container per test file
});

// test/seed/init.sql — executed automatically when the PostgreSQL container starts:
// CREATE TABLE countries (code CHAR(2) PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL);
// INSERT INTO countries VALUES ('US', 'United States'), ('DE', 'Germany'), ('JP', 'Japan');
```

---

### Pattern 57 — `faker.helpers.multiple()` with Index-Aware Callback for Correlated Batch Data  [official]

`faker.helpers.multiple(fn, options)` calls `fn` `count` times and returns an array of results. Unlike `faker.helpers.arrayElements`, it passes a zero-based `index` parameter to `fn` as the second argument, making it possible to produce correlated sequences — for example, a batch of orders with monotonically increasing amounts or timestamps. This is the idiomatic faker v9 replacement for `Array.from({ length: N }, (_, i) => buildEntity(i))` patterns, and it composes cleanly with factory override functions that consume the index for deterministic variation.

**Use when:** generating a batch of related entities where each element's properties depend on its position in the sequence (time series, paginated results, rank-ordered leaderboards). **Do NOT use when:** each element in the batch must be completely independent with no ordering relationship — use a plain factory `.buildList(N)` or `Array.from` loop instead; the index parameter adds cognitive overhead without benefit. **Alternative:** `faker.helpers.uniqueArray(fn, N)` for cases where uniqueness across the batch is the constraint rather than ordering.

```typescript
// test/factories/price-history.factory.ts
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

export interface PricePoint {
  timestamp:  Date;
  priceCents: number;
  volume:     number;
}

export function buildPriceHistory(length: number, baseDate = new Date()): PricePoint[] {
  return faker.helpers.multiple(
    (_value, index) => ({
      // index is the second argument — _value is unused
      timestamp:  new Date(baseDate.getTime() + index * 60_000), // 1-min intervals
      priceCents: 10_000 + faker.number.int({ min: -500, max: 500 }),
      volume:     faker.number.int({ min: 100, max: 10_000 }),
    }),
    { count: length }
  );
}

test('price history is returned in ascending timestamp order', () => {
  const history = buildPriceHistory(20);
  for (let i = 1; i < history.length; i++) {
    expect(history[i].timestamp.getTime()).toBeGreaterThan(history[i - 1].timestamp.getTime());
  }
});
```

### Pattern 58 — `faker.book` Module for Library and Content-Management Domain Factories  [official]

Faker.js v9 added a `book` module with methods `faker.book.title()`, `faker.book.author()`, `faker.book.publisher()`, `faker.book.series()`, `faker.book.genre()`, and `faker.book.format()`. Applications in publishing, library management, e-learning, and content recommendation domains previously required large static fixture files or brittle string templates for book-like data. The new module generates culturally plausible, domain-correct values without seeding from a real book database, reducing fixture file size and improving test readability.

**Use when:** the domain under test models books, documents, media, courses, or any entity with a title/author/publisher structure; using `faker.book` conveys intent far more clearly than `faker.lorem.words(3)` for a title field. **Do NOT use when:** tests exercise ISBN validation, catalog import, or real-library-data edge cases — hand-craft test data with valid ISBNs and known authors for those scenarios. **Alternative:** `faker.commerce.productName()` as a rough stand-in for titles in non-book domains; avoid it in book-specific tests as it produces e-commerce product names rather than book-like titles.

```typescript
// test/factories/catalog.factory.ts
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

export interface CatalogItem {
  id:        string;
  title:     string;
  author:    string;
  publisher: string;
  genre:     string;
  format:    string;
  isbn:      string;
}

export function buildCatalogItem(overrides: Partial<CatalogItem> = {}): CatalogItem {
  return {
    id:        faker.string.uuid(),
    title:     faker.book.title(),
    author:    faker.book.author(),
    publisher: faker.book.publisher(),
    genre:     faker.book.genre(),
    format:    faker.book.format(),
    isbn:      faker.commerce.isbn(13),
    ...overrides,
  };
}

test('catalog search returns items matching genre filter', async () => {
  const fiction    = buildCatalogItem({ genre: 'Fiction' });
  const nonfiction = buildCatalogItem({ genre: 'Non-Fiction' });
  await seedCatalog([fiction, nonfiction]);
  const results = await searchCatalog({ genre: 'Fiction' });
  expect(results).toHaveLength(1);
  expect(results[0].id).toBe(fiction.id);
});
```

### Pattern 59 — Vitest `test.extend` Builder Pattern for Typed Auto-Inferred Fixtures  [official]

Vitest 4.1 formalized the builder pattern for `test.extend`, where fixture type parameters are inferred automatically from the fixture definitions rather than declared manually in a generic type argument. Chaining `.extend()` calls produces a fully typed extended test without a single explicit type annotation — TypeScript infers the merged fixture shape from the chain. This eliminates the common maintenance burden of keeping the manual type parameter in sync with the fixture object shape, which was the primary source of "fixture type mismatch" errors in large projects.

**Use when:** a project has more than three or four layers of fixture composition and the manual generic type annotations on `test.extend<{ ... }>` are growing unwieldy or drifting out of sync with the actual fixture implementations. **Do NOT use when:** the fixture types need to be exported and re-used in other files as named interfaces — the builder pattern's inferred types are anonymous and hard to re-export cleanly. **Alternative:** `test.extend<FixtureType>()` with an explicit named interface — more verbose but fully exportable and compatible with module augmentation.

```typescript
// test/fixtures/index.ts — builder-pattern fixture composition
import { test as vitest } from 'vitest';
import { createDbClient }  from './db.fixture';
import { buildCurrentUser } from '../factories/user.factory';

// Layer 1 — database connection fixture
const dbTest = vitest.extend({
  db: async ({}, use) => {
    const client = await createDbClient();
    await use(client);
    await client.end();
  },
});

// Layer 2 — authenticated user fixture (depends on db)
const authedTest = dbTest.extend({
  currentUser: async ({ db }, use) => {
    const user = buildCurrentUser({ role: 'viewer' });
    await db.query('INSERT INTO users VALUES ($1, $2)', [user.id, user.role]);
    await use(user);
    await db.query('DELETE FROM users WHERE id = $1', [user.id]);
  },
});

// Layer 3 — feature-flag fixture (no dependencies)
export const appTest = authedTest.extend({
  featureFlags: async ({}, use) => {
    await use({ newDashboard: true, betaApi: false });
  },
});

// TypeScript infers { db, currentUser, featureFlags } with no manual type annotation
```

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 33

## Community Gotcha #98 — `faker.helpers.multiple()` passes `index` as the second argument, not the first — factories that use the first argument as the index silently receive `undefined` and generate `NaN`-based IDs  [community]

**WHY: The `faker.helpers.multiple(fn, options)` callback signature is `fn(_value, index)` where `_value` is an internal placeholder (always `undefined` in the current implementation) and `index` is the zero-based counter. Developers familiar with `Array.prototype.map` — where the first argument is the element value and the second is the index — write `faker.helpers.multiple((index) => ({ id: index + 1 }), { count: 5 })` expecting `index` to be `0..4`. Instead the first argument is `undefined`, so `undefined + 1` produces `NaN`. The factory builds silently return `{ id: NaN }`, and downstream assertion failures on the `id` field surface far from the factory definition, making the root cause non-obvious.**

Fix: always destructure the arguments as `(_value, index)` — discard the unused first argument with an underscore prefix. Alternatively, use `Array.from({ length: 5 }, (_, i) => ({ id: i + 1 }))` which has the familiar `Array.from` signature most developers already know. Add a unit test on the factory itself that asserts `buildList(3)[0].id === 1` to catch this regression immediately when the factory is modified.

---

## Community Gotcha #99 — Prisma interactive transactions used for test rollback leave connections open when an uncaught exception escapes the `$transaction` callback — connection pool exhaustion causes subsequent tests to hang indefinitely  [community]

**WHY: The rollback-via-transaction pattern relies on deliberately throwing inside the `$transaction` callback to trigger a rollback. If an unhandled exception escapes the callback before the controlled throw is reached — for example, an async assertion error that bypasses the error-handling path — Prisma's transaction machinery may not cleanly close the underlying connection. The connection remains in the pool in a waiting-for-rollback state. When enough tests leak connections this way (common with async assertion errors that throw before the rollback signal is sent), the pool is exhausted and subsequent tests hang indefinitely waiting for an available connection, typically timing out after 30+ seconds with a misleading "connection timeout" error that does not mention the transaction leak.**

Fix: wrap the factory and assertion calls inside the transaction callback in a `try/finally` block where the `finally` clause always throws the sentinel error that triggers rollback — this guarantees the rollback signal is sent even when an assertion throws. Alternatively, set `pool.connectionTimeout` to a low value (e.g., 5000ms) during tests so hangs surface quickly rather than blocking the CI run for the full default timeout.

---

## Community Gotcha #100 — Testcontainers `withCopyFilesToContainer()` silently produces a zero-byte file on Windows when the source path contains backslashes — PostgreSQL executes an empty init script and the database contains no seed data  [community]

**WHY: The `withCopyFilesToContainer()` method passes the `source` path to the Docker SDK's archive-and-upload pipeline. On Windows, `path.join(__dirname, 'seed.sql')` produces a backslash-separated absolute path like `C:\test\seed.sql`. The Docker SDK running on a Windows Docker Desktop backend (WSL2 or Hyper-V) normalizes paths when creating the tar archive, but the normalization silently fails for certain Windows-style absolute paths — the archive is created, the file entry exists, but the file content is zero bytes. PostgreSQL finds the zero-byte `01-seed.sql` in `/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/`, executes an empty script without error, and the database starts with no tables or seed data. Tests then fail with "relation does not exist" or "no such table" errors that appear to be migration problems rather than fixture-copy failures.**

Fix: always normalize `source` paths to forward slashes before passing to `withCopyFilesToContainer()`: `source: pathToSeedSql.replaceAll('\\', '/')`. Add a post-start assertion in the fixture setup that queries a known seeded table and throws a descriptive "seed data not found — check path normalization on Windows" error if zero rows are returned, so the root cause is immediately clear instead of surfacing as cryptic table-not-found errors in individual tests.

---

## Community Gotcha #101 — `Factory.resetAll()` in fishery resets ALL registered factories in the module scope — in a Vitest single-thread configuration it resets factories shared with concurrently executing tests, producing duplicate sequence IDs and intermittent unique-constraint violations  [community]

**WHY: `Factory.resetAll()` modifies a module-level registry of all `Factory` instances. In Vitest's default worker-per-file mode each worker has its own module scope, so `resetAll()` in one worker does not affect another. However, when `poolOptions: { threads: { singleThread: true } }` or `--pool=forks` with a single fork is configured, all test files run in the same module scope. A `beforeEach(() => Factory.resetAll())` in one file resets the sequence counters for factories used by concurrently executing test blocks in other files, causing multiple factories to start generating IDs from `1` simultaneously. Duplicate sequence values produce unique-constraint violations on database inserts that appear intermittently and are nearly impossible to reproduce in isolation.**

Fix: avoid `Factory.resetAll()` in shared `beforeEach` hooks when the project uses a single-threaded or single-forked Vitest configuration. Instead call `specificFactory.rewindSequence()` only for the factories actually used in the current test file. If global reset is required for snapshot stability, keep the default Vitest worker-per-file mode and verify that `poolOptions` does not collapse all tests into one process.

---

## Community Gotcha #102 — `faker.internet.jwt()` in faker v9 produces a random base64url signature — middleware that calls `jwt.verify()` always throws `JsonWebTokenError: invalid signature`, masking verification logic bugs that would only surface with a real signed token  [community]

**WHY: `faker.internet.jwt()` fills the JWT signature segment with random base64url bytes to produce a structurally valid three-segment token string. `jwt.decode()` (parse without verify) succeeds; `jwt.verify()` always throws `JsonWebTokenError: invalid signature`. Middleware that catches this error and returns a 401 will pass tests using `faker.internet.jwt()` for the wrong reason — the 401 is triggered by the bad signature rather than by the claim-level validation logic being tested. More critically, if the middleware has a bug that lets malformed-claim tokens through but still calls `jwt.verify()`, tests using `faker.internet.jwt()` will never reveal the bug: `verify()` throws before the claim code is reached, the catch block returns 401, and the test sees the expected error response — but for the wrong reason entirely.**

Fix: use `jsonwebtoken.sign(payload, 'test-secret')` for any test that exercises the full middleware stack including signature verification. Reserve `faker.internet.jwt()` strictly for tests that call `jwt.decode()` directly or for factories that populate Authorization header strings in tests where the auth middleware is mocked out. Add a comment in the factory file indicating which JWT factory to use at which test tier to prevent future contributors from introducing the wrong fixture in a verification-path test.

### Pattern 60 — `faker.food` Module for Diet, Nutrition, and Menu-Driven Domain Factories  [official]

Faker.js v9 added a `food` module containing `faker.food.dish()`, `faker.food.ingredient()`, `faker.food.ethnicCategory()`, `faker.food.description()`, `faker.food.spice()`, `faker.food.vegetable()`, `faker.food.fruit()`, `faker.food.meat()`, and `faker.food.seafood()`. Applications in restaurant ordering, dietary tracking, meal-kit delivery, and nutrition platforms previously relied on static fixture arrays or generic lorem text for food-related fields. The new module produces culturally plausible, semantically correct food data that activates business rules tied to category filtering, allergen flags, and dietary preference matching — categories that lorem-text factories cannot exercise. Using `faker.food.ethnicCategory()` in a filter test, for example, produces realistic category values that surface missing enum mappings in the application's category normalisation layer.

**Use when:** the domain models menus, nutritional data, recipes, meal plans, or anything where food-category semantics are load-bearing for business logic — for example, a filter that excludes `meat` items from a vegetarian meal plan. **Do NOT use when:** tests exercise FDA-regulated nutritional labelling, caloric calculations, or known allergen detection — hand-craft test data with verified nutritional values and allergen flags from a controlled dataset for those scenarios; random food names cannot stand in for regulated data. **Alternative:** `faker.commerce.productName()` as a last resort for display-only food labels; avoid it in domain tests where category semantics matter.

```typescript
// test/factories/menu.factory.ts
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

export interface MenuItem {
  id:             string;
  dish:           string;
  ingredients:    string[];
  ethnicCategory: string;
  description:    string;
  isVegetarian:   boolean;
  spiceLevel:     'mild' | 'medium' | 'hot';
}

export function buildMenuItem(overrides: Partial<MenuItem> = {}): MenuItem {
  return {
    id:             faker.string.uuid(),
    dish:           faker.food.dish(),
    ingredients:    Array.from({ length: 4 }, () => faker.food.ingredient()),
    ethnicCategory: faker.food.ethnicCategory(),
    description:    faker.food.description(),
    isVegetarian:   faker.datatype.boolean(),
    spiceLevel:     faker.helpers.arrayElement(['mild', 'medium', 'hot']),
    ...overrides,
  };
}

test('vegetarian filter returns only vegetarian items', () => {
  const items = [
    buildMenuItem({ isVegetarian: true }),
    buildMenuItem({ isVegetarian: false }),
    buildMenuItem({ isVegetarian: true }),
  ];
  const filtered = items.filter(i => i.isVegetarian);
  expect(filtered).toHaveLength(2);
  expect(filtered.every(i => i.isVegetarian)).toBe(true);
});
```

### Pattern 61 — Playwright `browserContext.setStorageState()` for Mid-Test Auth Fixture Refresh  [official]

Playwright 1.57+ exposes `browserContext.setStorageState({ cookies, origins, indexedDB })` as a method on an existing context, allowing test fixtures to refresh authentication tokens during a running test rather than only at context creation time. This matters for tests that cover token expiry, session rotation, or multi-role workflows where the same context switches between two authenticated states without browser restart. Combined with a factory that produces valid auth payloads, the pattern enables deterministic coverage of token-lifecycle edge cases without spinning up additional browser contexts. The ability to call `setStorageState()` mid-test eliminates the workaround of storing the old auth file path and recreating the context, which tripled setup time in suites with many role-transition scenarios.

**Use when:** a test scenario requires the browser to transition between two auth states mid-test — for example, verifying that a role-downgrade takes effect immediately without logout/re-login, or that an expired token triggers a redirect. **Do NOT use when:** all tests in the suite use the same static auth fixture loaded from a `storageState` file at context creation — the added complexity of mid-test refresh is unnecessary overhead. **Alternative:** tear down and recreate the browser context when the auth state change is a new test precondition rather than a flow transition; context recreation is cleaner when the switch represents a boundary between scenarios.

```typescript
// test/fixtures/auth.fixture.ts
import { test as base, BrowserContext } from '@playwright/test';
import { buildAuthPayload } from '../factories/auth.factory';

type AuthFixtures = { switchRole: (role: 'admin' | 'viewer') => Promise<void> };

export const test = base.extend<AuthFixtures>({
  switchRole: async ({ context }, use) => {
    const switcher = async (role: 'admin' | 'viewer') => {
      const payload = buildAuthPayload({ role });
      await (context as BrowserContext).setStorageState({
        cookies: [],
        origins: [{
          origin: 'http://localhost:3000',
          localStorage: [{ name: 'auth_token', value: payload.token }],
        }],
      });
    };
    await use(switcher);
  },
});

test('role downgrade hides admin menu immediately', async ({ page, switchRole }) => {
  await switchRole('admin');
  await page.goto('http://localhost:3000/dashboard');
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="admin-menu"]')).toBeVisible();

  await switchRole('viewer');
  await page.reload();
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="admin-menu"]')).not.toBeVisible();
});
```

---

### Pattern 62 — Vitest `aroundEach` Hook for Transaction-Per-Test Database Isolation  [official]

Vitest 4.1 introduced `aroundEach` (and `aroundAll`) lifecycle hooks that wrap each test in a context boundary. Unlike `beforeEach`/`afterEach`, the `aroundEach` hook receives a `next` function — calling it executes the test and awaits its completion, allowing setup and teardown to share a single closure. This is the idiomatic Vitest 4.1 approach for the transaction-per-test pattern: open a transaction before `next()`, run the test inside the transaction, and roll it back after, all in one atomic hook without coordinating separate before/after functions. The single-closure guarantee means the transaction handle is never accidentally accessed after rollback, eliminating the class of "query after rollback" errors that the split `beforeEach`/`afterEach` pattern can produce.

**Use when:** integration tests touch a real database and must be isolated without the overhead of table truncation between tests — the transaction rollback approach is orders of magnitude faster than truncation for large schemas. **Do NOT use when:** the code under test opens its own transactions, calls `COMMIT` internally, or uses `SAVEPOINT`-incompatible commands (e.g., DDL in some databases) — nested transaction semantics will either fail or commit the data for real, defeating the isolation. **Alternative:** `beforeEach`/`afterEach` with explicit table truncation for codebases where nested transactions are not reliable; or Testcontainers with a fresh container per suite for full isolation.

```typescript
// test/setup/transaction-isolation.ts — aroundEach transaction-per-test pattern
import { Pool, PoolClient } from 'pg';

const pool = new Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL });

// Export for use in test files via: import { withTransactionIsolation } from './setup/transaction-isolation';
export function withTransactionIsolation(suite: ReturnType<typeof describe>) {
  let client: PoolClient;

  suite.beforeAll(async () => { client = await pool.connect(); });
  suite.afterAll(async () => { client.release(); await pool.end(); });

  // aroundEach wraps every test inside an open transaction that always rolls back
  suite.aroundEach(async (next) => {
    await client.query('BEGIN');
    try {
      await next(); // test body executes here, inside the transaction
    } finally {
      await client.query('ROLLBACK'); // rolls back regardless of pass/fail
    }
  });
}
```

### Pattern 63 — `fishery` `params()` + `transient()` for Conditional Factory Branching Without Subclasses  [official]

Fishery's `.params()` and `.transient()` chaining methods return a new factory specialisation without mutating the base factory. `transient()` accepts non-persisted parameters — values that influence factory logic but do not appear in the output object — enabling conditional branching inside the `define` callback based on caller intent. This avoids the alternative pattern of maintaining a separate class method or object variant for each logical branch, keeping the factory a single source of truth while supporting arbitrarily many caller-specified variations. Because the base factory is not mutated, tests that use the base form alongside transient-specialised forms can coexist in the same file without inter-test state leakage.

**Use when:** a factory needs to produce structurally similar objects that differ by a single semantic dimension — for example, a `product` factory that conditionally includes a `discountedPrice` field only when the caller passes `transient: { onSale: true }`. **Do NOT use when:** the branching creates two fundamentally different types that should be modelled as separate domain objects — overloading a single factory with too many transient branches creates a maintenance burden and hides semantic distinctions in the domain model. **Alternative:** separate named Object Mother methods for each semantically distinct variant when the variants have substantially different field sets or invariants.

```typescript
// test/factories/product.factory.ts
import { Factory } from 'fishery';
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

interface Product {
  id:               string;
  name:             string;
  priceCents:       number;
  discountedPrice?: number;
  badge?:           string;
}

interface ProductTransients {
  onSale:       boolean;
  discountRate: number; // 0.0–1.0
}

export const productFactory = Factory.define<Product, ProductTransients>(
  ({ transientParams }) => {
    const { onSale = false, discountRate = 0.2 } = transientParams;
    const priceCents = faker.number.int({ min: 500, max: 50_000 });
    return {
      id:               faker.string.uuid(),
      name:             faker.commerce.productName(),
      priceCents,
      discountedPrice:  onSale ? Math.round(priceCents * (1 - discountRate)) : undefined,
      badge:            onSale ? 'SALE' : undefined,
    };
  }
);

// Usage — produces a product with a discountedPrice and badge
const saleProduct = productFactory.transient({ onSale: true, discountRate: 0.3 }).build();
expect(saleProduct.badge).toBe('SALE');
expect(saleProduct.discountedPrice).toBeLessThan(saleProduct.priceCents);
```

### Pattern 64 — `faker.airline` Module for Travel-Domain Factories  [official]

Faker.js v9 added an `airline` module exposing `faker.airline.airline()`, `faker.airline.airport()`, `faker.airline.flightNumber()`, `faker.airline.recordLocator()`, `faker.airline.seatNumber()`, `faker.airline.aircraftType()`, and `faker.airline.seat()`. Travel, booking, and logistics applications previously fabricated IATA codes and flight numbers with string templates, producing values that were plausible-looking but not structurally valid (wrong check-digit patterns, non-existent IATA codes). The `airline` module produces values that conform to IATA format conventions, exercising validation logic that raw `faker.string.alpha(2)` cannot trigger. A record locator produced by `faker.airline.recordLocator()` passes the alphanumeric-length-6 format check that PNR validation logic enforces.

**Use when:** the system under test models airline reservations, itineraries, loyalty programs, flight search, or logistics tracking — any domain where IATA code format, record locator length, or seat-map position is load-bearing for business logic or display rendering. **Do NOT use when:** tests must exercise real airline data such as known-valid flight routes, codeshare agreements, or live pricing — the faker airline module generates structurally plausible but fictitious values; use a real IATA data fixture for integration tests against route validation engines. **Alternative:** hand-coded constants (`{ iata: 'LH', flightNumber: 'LH400' }`) for tests that verify display formatting of specific known-format values.

```typescript
// test/factories/booking.factory.ts
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

export interface FlightBooking {
  id:             string;
  recordLocator:  string;
  airline:        { name: string; iataCode: string };
  departure:      { iataCode: string; name: string };
  arrival:        { iataCode: string; name: string };
  flightNumber:   string;
  seat:           string;
  aircraftType:   string;
}

export function buildFlightBooking(
  overrides: Partial<FlightBooking> = {}
): FlightBooking {
  return {
    id:            faker.string.uuid(),
    recordLocator: faker.airline.recordLocator(),
    airline:       faker.airline.airline(),
    departure:     faker.airline.airport(),
    arrival:       faker.airline.airport(),
    flightNumber:  faker.airline.flightNumber({ addLeadingAirlineCode: true }),
    seat:          faker.airline.seat(),
    aircraftType:  faker.airline.aircraftType(),
    ...overrides,
  };
}

test('booking card renders record locator in uppercase 6-character format', () => {
  const booking = buildFlightBooking();
  expect(booking.recordLocator).toMatch(/^[A-Z0-9]{6}$/);
  expect(booking.departure.iataCode).toMatch(/^[A-Z]{3}$/);
});
```

### Pattern 65 — Playwright `storageState` with `indexedDB: true` for Firebase / IndexedDB-Backed Auth Fixtures  [official]

Playwright 1.51+ extended `page.context().storageState({ path, indexedDB: true })` to capture and restore authentication tokens stored in IndexedDB rather than only `localStorage` or cookies. Applications using Firebase Auth, Auth.js with IndexedDB persistence, or PWA-style token storage require this option to persist auth state between test runs. Without `indexedDB: true`, a `storageState` snapshot silently omits IndexedDB contents — the saved state file exists and loads without error, but the application cannot find its auth token on reload, redirecting every test to the login page and producing 401s that appear to be auth logic bugs. Enabling the flag adds IndexedDB serialisation to the storage snapshot, making the auth fixture complete and durable across test runs.

**Use when:** the application uses IndexedDB for any part of its authentication or session persistence — including Firebase Auth SDK, Dexie-based auth caches, or PWAs that store JWTs in IndexedDB. **Do NOT use when:** the application uses only cookies and `localStorage` for auth — the extra IndexedDB serialisation adds file size and snapshot fragility without benefit. **Alternative:** mock the auth layer entirely with MSW and inject a factory-built token via `localStorage` if IndexedDB storage state management becomes brittle across test runs.

```typescript
// tests/auth.setup.ts — global setup that captures auth state including IndexedDB
import { chromium, FullConfig } from '@playwright/test';

async function globalSetup(config: FullConfig) {
  const { baseURL, storageState } = config.projects[0].use;
  const browser = await chromium.launch();
  const page = await browser.newPage();

  await page.goto(`${baseURL}/login`);
  await page.fill('[data-testid="email"]', process.env.TEST_USER_EMAIL!);
  await page.fill('[data-testid="password"]', process.env.TEST_USER_PASSWORD!);
  await page.click('[data-testid="login-btn"]');
  await page.waitForURL('**/dashboard');

  // Capture localStorage, cookies, AND IndexedDB (e.g., Firebase Auth stores tokens here)
  await page.context().storageState({
    path: storageState as string,
    indexedDB: true,
  });

  await browser.close();
}

export default globalSetup;
```

### Pattern 66 — `fast-check` `fc.record` with `requiredKeys` for Exhaustive Optional-Field Schema Factories  [official]

`fast-check`'s `fc.record(shape, { requiredKeys })` generates arbitrary objects where only the keys listed in `requiredKeys` are guaranteed to be present — all other keys are omitted randomly. This mirrors real-world JSON payloads where optional fields arrive or are absent non-deterministically. Pairing `fc.record` with `requiredKeys` produces a property-based factory that exercises both the "all fields present" and "optional fields absent" code paths in a single `fc.assert` call, catching bugs in null-guard logic that deterministic factories miss. The minimisation engine shrinks failing inputs to the smallest counterexample, making the missing-field root cause immediately obvious.

**Use when:** testing parsing, validation, or mapping functions that handle partially-specified inputs — API request body parsers, form deserializers, and data transformation pipelines that must handle optional fields gracefully. **Do NOT use when:** a test requires a complete, known-shape object — use a deterministic factory with explicit defaults instead; property-based factories are harder to debug when they fail because the minimized counterexample may not be immediately readable. **Alternative:** `fc.record(shape)` without `requiredKeys` for generating fully populated objects with all fields always present (Fishery/builder pattern territory).

```typescript
// test/properties/user-parser.property.test.ts
import { test as fcTest, fc } from '@fast-check/vitest';
import { parseUserPayload } from '../../src/parsers/user';

fcTest.prop([
  fc.record(
    {
      id:    fc.uuid(),
      email: fc.emailAddress(),
      name:  fc.string({ minLength: 1, maxLength: 100 }),
      role:  fc.constantFrom('admin', 'viewer', 'editor'),
      bio:   fc.option(fc.string({ maxLength: 500 })),
    },
    { requiredKeys: ['id', 'email'] } // name, role, bio may be absent
  ),
])('parseUserPayload never throws on any valid partial payload', (payload) => {
  expect(() => parseUserPayload(payload)).not.toThrow();
});

fcTest.prop([
  fc.record({ id: fc.uuid(), email: fc.emailAddress() }, { requiredKeys: ['id', 'email'] }),
])('parseUserPayload returns a User with the same id as input', (payload) => {
  const result = parseUserPayload(payload);
  expect(result.id).toBe(payload.id);
});
```

### Pattern 67 — Neon Branch-Per-Test-Run for Copy-on-Write Database Isolation  [official]

Neon's branching API creates an instant copy-on-write clone of the parent database at zero storage cost for unchanged data. In a CI pipeline, a global setup hook creates a branch from the shared `test-baseline` branch, runs the test suite against the branch, and deletes it in teardown. All writes during the test run are isolated to the branch — they never touch the shared baseline. This avoids the container startup latency of Testcontainers while providing full PostgreSQL semantics, and costs zero extra storage for unmodified rows because Neon's MVCC-based branching only charges for pages written after the branch is created. Multiple parallel CI jobs each get their own branch, removing the need for a shared-database coordination strategy entirely.

**Use when:** the project uses Neon PostgreSQL (cloud-hosted) and CI pipelines run multiple parallel test jobs that cannot share a database without data leakage — the branch-per-run pattern gives each CI job a fully isolated database without infrastructure provisioning overhead. **Do NOT use when:** tests require a local database with no external network dependency (air-gapped CI, low-latency benchmarks), or when the test suite generates very large write volumes that would make Neon branch storage costs non-trivial. **Alternative:** Testcontainers with a per-suite PostgreSQL container for fully local, network-independent isolation.

```typescript
// test/global-setup.ts — Neon branch-per-CI-run isolation
const NEON_API_BASE = 'https://console.neon.tech/api/v2';
const PROJECT_ID    = process.env.NEON_PROJECT_ID!;
const API_KEY       = process.env.NEON_API_KEY!;

async function neonApi(method: string, path: string, body?: object) {
  const res = await fetch(`${NEON_API_BASE}${path}`, {
    method,
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${API_KEY}`, 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body:    body ? JSON.stringify(body) : undefined,
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Neon API ${method} ${path} → ${res.status}`);
  return res.json();
}

let testBranchId: string;

export async function setup() {
  const runId  = process.env.CI_RUN_ID ?? `local-${Date.now()}`;
  const branch = await neonApi('POST', `/projects/${PROJECT_ID}/branches`, {
    branch:    { name: `ci-${runId}`, parent_id: 'test-baseline' },
    endpoints: [{ type: 'read_write' }],
  });
  testBranchId = branch.branch.id;
  process.env.DATABASE_URL = branch.endpoints[0].connection_uri;
}

export async function teardown() {
  if (testBranchId) {
    await neonApi('DELETE', `/projects/${PROJECT_ID}/branches/${testBranchId}`);
  }
}
```

### Pattern 68 — `faker.commerce.isbn()` for ISBN-13 Validated Test Data  [official]

Faker.js v9 added `faker.commerce.isbn(13)` and `faker.commerce.isbn(10)` to the `commerce` module, generating correctly check-digit-validated ISBN strings. Applications that validate ISBN format during catalog import, barcode scanning, or library integrations require structurally valid ISBNs to exercise the non-error paths — `faker.string.numeric(13)` produces 13-digit strings that almost always fail the ISBN-13 check digit algorithm, pushing every test into the error branch. The `isbn(13)` method produces fully valid ISBNs that clear the checksum validation, allowing tests to reach the business logic beyond the format guard. This prevents the class of false-positive tests where the factory's invalid format is quietly rejected by a format guard and the actual logic under test is never reached.

**Use when:** factories build catalog entries, book import payloads, library records, or any entity that stores an ISBN-13 or ISBN-10 identifier where downstream validation parses and verifies the check digit. **Do NOT use when:** the test specifically exercises the ISBN validation error path — supply a known-invalid ISBN with a wrong check digit as an explicit override for that scenario. **Alternative:** a small static set of real ISBNs (creative-commons or public-domain books) for acceptance tests that cross-reference a real library API.

```typescript
// test/factories/catalog.factory.ts
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

export interface CatalogEntry {
  id:     string;
  isbn13: string;
  isbn10: string;
  title:  string;
  author: string;
}

export function buildCatalogEntry(overrides: Partial<CatalogEntry> = {}): CatalogEntry {
  return {
    id:     faker.string.uuid(),
    isbn13: faker.commerce.isbn(13),
    isbn10: faker.commerce.isbn(10),
    title:  faker.book.title(),
    author: faker.book.author(),
    ...overrides,
  };
}

test('catalog importer accepts entries with valid ISBN-13', async () => {
  const entry  = buildCatalogEntry();
  const result = await importCatalogEntry(entry);
  // reaches business logic — would short-circuit on format error with numeric(13)
  expect(result.status).toBe('imported');
  expect(result.catalogId).toBeTruthy();
});
```

### Pattern 69 — Vitest `onCleanup` Inside `test.extend` Fixture for Modular Multi-Resource Disposal  [official]

Vitest 4.1 fixture callbacks receive an `onCleanup(fn)` hook that registers a teardown function to run after the test completes, regardless of pass or fail. Unlike the generator-based `await use(value)` teardown pattern, `onCleanup` can be called multiple times within a single fixture, registering multiple teardown functions in registration order. This is the canonical approach for fixtures that create a variable number of resources during setup — each resource registers its own `onCleanup` handler, so disposal is modular and easy to extend without restructuring the generator function. A fixture that provisions temporary cloud resources (S3 buckets, Pub/Sub topics) calls `onCleanup` once per provisioned resource, ensuring all are cleaned up even if provisioning fails halfway.

**Use when:** a fixture creates side-effectful resources whose number varies at runtime — for example, a fixture that registers an arbitrary number of temporary S3 buckets, database records, or file handles based on test parameters. **Do NOT use when:** a fixture creates exactly one resource in a known, symmetric setup/teardown flow — the generator `try/finally` pattern is simpler and clearer for the 1-resource case. **Alternative:** `afterEach(() => cleanup())` in the test file for resource cleanup that does not belong in a shared fixture.

```typescript
// test/fixtures/cloud.fixture.ts
import { test as base } from 'vitest';
import { S3Client, CreateBucketCommand, DeleteBucketCommand } from '@aws-sdk/client-s3';

type CloudFixtures = { createTestBucket: (name: string) => Promise<string> };

const s3 = new S3Client({ region: 'us-east-1', endpoint: process.env.S3_ENDPOINT });

export const test = base.extend<CloudFixtures>({
  createTestBucket: async ({}, use, { onCleanup }) => {
    // Each call to createTestBucket registers its own onCleanup handler
    const factory = async (name: string): Promise<string> => {
      const bucketName = `test-${name}-${Date.now()}`;
      await s3.send(new CreateBucketCommand({ Bucket: bucketName }));
      // Registered immediately after creation — survives any test failure
      onCleanup(async () => {
        await s3.send(new DeleteBucketCommand({ Bucket: bucketName }));
      });
      return bucketName;
    };
    await use(factory);
  },
});
```

### Pattern 70 — Fishery `afterCreate` Hook for Async Relational Seeding  [official]

Fishery's `afterCreate` callback runs after `factory.create()` resolves and receives the created object as its argument. The hook can perform additional async operations — inserting related records, triggering side effects, or populating association IDs — and returns a (possibly modified) version of the created object. This is the idiomatic way to handle one-to-many seeding in integration tests without writing repetitive setup in every `beforeEach`: the factory itself orchestrates the relational graph, and callers simply call `organizationFactory.create()` to receive a fully hydrated entity tree. The `afterCreate` callback is skipped when `.build()` is used — this is intentional and documented; `.build()` is for in-memory construction, `.create()` is for database-backed entities that require relational integrity.

**Use when:** a factory creates an entity that, by domain invariant, always requires associated child records to be in a valid state — for example, an `organization` factory that must also seed at least one `member` record before any test can proceed. **Do NOT use when:** child records are optional or test-specific — create them explicitly in the test setup rather than encoding the assumption inside `afterCreate`, which would make the factory inflexible for tests that explicitly need an entity without children. **Alternative:** explicit `buildList` calls in `beforeEach` for cases where the relationship is optional and the child count matters to the test being written.

```typescript
// test/factories/organization.factory.ts
import { Factory } from 'fishery';
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';
import { db } from '../../src/db/client';

interface Organization { id: string; name: string; slug: string; ownerId: string }

export const organizationFactory = Factory.define<Organization>(({ onCreate }) => {
  const org: Organization = {
    id:      faker.string.uuid(),
    name:    faker.company.name(),
    slug:    faker.helpers.slugify(faker.company.name()).toLowerCase(),
    ownerId: '',
  };

  onCreate(async (created) => {
    // Seed a mandatory owner member after org row is inserted
    const ownerId = faker.string.uuid();
    await db.query(
      'INSERT INTO members (id, org_id, role) VALUES ($1, $2, $3)',
      [ownerId, created.id, 'owner']
    );
    await db.query(
      'UPDATE organizations SET owner_id = $1 WHERE id = $2',
      [ownerId, created.id]
    );
    return { ...created, ownerId };
  });

  return org;
});
```

### Pattern 71 — `faker.number.bigInt()` for 64-bit ID and Financial Amount Factories  [official]

Faker.js v10 added `faker.number.bigInt({ min, max })` to produce `BigInt` values directly, without the precision-loss risk of generating large integers via `faker.number.int()` (which is limited to `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER = 2^53 - 1`). Systems that use 64-bit Snowflake IDs, Twitter/Discord-style IDs, or financial amounts stored as `bigint` in PostgreSQL lose precision when those values are rounded to JavaScript `number` — test data built with `faker.number.int()` silently produces IDs that do not round-trip through JSON serialisation or DB storage correctly. `faker.number.bigInt()` eliminates this class of silent data corruption in factories by providing native `BigInt` values that preserve precision at all magnitudes.

**Use when:** the domain uses 64-bit integer identifiers (Snowflake IDs, timestamp-based IDs), `NUMERIC`/`DECIMAL` financial columns, or any field that must survive JSON serialisation without precision loss. **Do NOT use when:** the downstream serialisation layer does not support `BigInt` (e.g., `JSON.stringify` of a `BigInt` throws a `TypeError` unless a replacer is configured) — convert to string at the factory boundary in that case. **Alternative:** `faker.string.numeric({ length: 18 })` for Snowflake-style IDs that must be treated as opaque strings throughout the system.

```typescript
// test/factories/snowflake.factory.ts
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

export interface SnowflakeEntity {
  id:         bigint;
  resourceId: bigint;
  amount:     bigint; // financial amount in minor units, e.g. cents × 1000
  createdAt:  Date;
}

// Snowflake IDs occupy the 41-bit timestamp + datacenter + sequence space
const SNOWFLAKE_MIN = 1n << 22n; // smallest valid Snowflake-like value
const SNOWFLAKE_MAX = (1n << 63n) - 1n;

export function buildSnowflakeEntity(
  overrides: Partial<SnowflakeEntity> = {}
): SnowflakeEntity {
  return {
    id:         faker.number.bigInt({ min: SNOWFLAKE_MIN, max: SNOWFLAKE_MAX }),
    resourceId: faker.number.bigInt({ min: SNOWFLAKE_MIN, max: SNOWFLAKE_MAX }),
    amount:     faker.number.bigInt({ min: 0n, max: 999_999_999n }),
    createdAt:  faker.date.recent(),
    ...overrides,
  };
}

test('64-bit ID comparison preserves precision after string round-trip', () => {
  const entity       = buildSnowflakeEntity();
  const serialised   = entity.id.toString();
  const deserialised = BigInt(serialised);
  expect(deserialised).toBe(entity.id); // would fail with Number IDs > 2^53
});
```

---

### Pattern 72 — Testcontainers `Network` for Multi-Container Service Dependency Graphs  [official]

The Testcontainers `Network` class creates an isolated Docker network that multiple containers join at startup. Containers on the same network resolve each other by service alias, matching the production `docker-compose` topology exactly. A test suite that spins up a PostgreSQL container and a Redis container linked by a shared `Network` can test service interactions — connection pooling, cache invalidation, pub/sub — without port-mapping hacks or hardcoded `localhost` references, because each container's hostname is its alias within the network. Tearing down the `Network` in `afterAll` automatically removes all inter-container routing, preventing network resource leaks across test suites.

**Use when:** the system under test requires two or more containerised services that communicate with each other by hostname (e.g., an app container connecting to a `postgres` host and a `redis` host) and the test must exercise that inter-service communication rather than mocking it. **Do NOT use when:** only a single container is needed, or the services are stateless and can be mocked at the HTTP layer — adding a custom network for a single-container test adds unnecessary setup complexity. **Alternative:** pass connection strings as environment variables to a single-container test using `container.getHost()` + `container.getMappedPort()` when inter-container networking is not required.

```typescript
// test/integration/cache-invalidation.test.ts
import { beforeAll, afterAll, test, expect } from 'vitest';
import { PostgreSqlContainer } from '@testcontainers/postgresql';
import { GenericContainer, Network, StartedNetwork, StartedTestContainer } from 'testcontainers';

let network: StartedNetwork;
let pgContainer: StartedTestContainer;
let redisContainer: StartedTestContainer;

beforeAll(async () => {
  network       = await new Network().start();
  pgContainer   = await new PostgreSqlContainer('postgres:16')
    .withNetwork(network).withNetworkAliases('postgres').withDatabase('testdb').start();
  redisContainer = await new GenericContainer('redis:7')
    .withNetwork(network).withNetworkAliases('redis').start();

  process.env.DATABASE_URL = pgContainer.getConnectionUri();
  process.env.REDIS_URL    = `redis://localhost:${redisContainer.getMappedPort(6379)}`;
}, 120_000);

afterAll(async () => {
  await redisContainer?.stop();
  await pgContainer?.stop();
  await network?.stop();
});

test('cache invalidation removes stale data from Redis after DB update', async () => {
  // Exercise real cache invalidation across postgres ↔ redis network
  expect(process.env.DATABASE_URL).toContain('testdb');
  expect(process.env.REDIS_URL).toMatch(/^redis:\/\//);
});
```

---

### Pattern 73 — `fc.scheduler()` for Ordering-Sensitive Async Factory Property Tests  [official]

`fast-check`'s `fc.scheduler()` arbitrary produces a `Scheduler` object that controls the order in which queued async tasks resolve. Factories that create data via concurrent async calls (parallel inserts, concurrent API mutations) must assert on outcomes regardless of execution order. By routing async factory calls through a `Scheduler`, property tests can explore all possible interleaving orderings systematically — finding race conditions and ordering-dependent bugs that deterministic sequential tests miss. The shrinking engine minimises failing interleavings to the smallest concurrent schedule that reproduces the bug, drastically reducing debugging time.

**Use when:** the system under test processes concurrent operations (parallel DB writes, concurrent API requests, event-handler race conditions) and the factory must exercise all possible execution orderings to find non-deterministic bugs. **Do NOT use when:** the operations are inherently sequential and the ordering is enforced by a mutex, queue, or saga pattern — `fc.scheduler` adds complexity without benefit when concurrency is already serialised. **Alternative:** `fc.asyncProperty` with deterministic sequential factories for systems where concurrent execution is mocked or serialised at the framework level.

```typescript
// test/properties/concurrent-insert.property.test.ts
import { test as fcTest, fc } from '@fast-check/vitest';
import { createUser } from '../../src/services/users';

fcTest.prop([
  fc.scheduler(),
  fc.uniqueArray(
    fc.record({ email: fc.emailAddress(), name: fc.string({ minLength: 1 }) }),
    { minLength: 2, maxLength: 4, selector: u => u.email }
  ),
])('concurrent user creation never produces duplicate email rows', async (scheduler, userInputs) => {
  // Schedule all inserts — scheduler controls when each promise resolves
  const scheduled = userInputs.map(input =>
    scheduler.schedule(Promise.resolve(input), `create-${input.email}`)
  );

  await scheduler.waitAll();
  const results = await Promise.allSettled(scheduled);
  const successes = results.filter(r => r.status === 'fulfilled');
  // Each unique email input should correspond to exactly one successful insert
  expect(successes.length).toBe(userInputs.length);
});
```

### Pattern 74 — `faker.git` Module for VCS, Deployment, and Audit-Log Domain Factories  [official]

Faker.js v9 added a `git` module with `faker.git.commitSha()`, `faker.git.commitMessage()`, `faker.git.commitDate()`, `faker.git.commitEntry()`, `faker.git.branch()`, and `faker.git.shortSha()`. Applications that model CI/CD pipelines, audit trails, deployment history, feature-flag release tracking, or any domain that references git commits previously required hardcoded SHA strings or brittle string templates. The `git` module generates commit SHAs in the correct 40-hex-character format and commit messages with realistic imperative-mood phrasing, enabling format-validation logic to be exercised without hand-crafting valid hex strings. `faker.git.shortSha()` generates the 7-character abbreviated SHA that most UI components and CLI outputs display, making it the correct choice for factories that populate display-layer fields.

**Use when:** factories build CI run records, deployment manifests, audit log entries, code review objects, or any domain entity where a git commit SHA, branch name, or commit message is a meaningful field that downstream code validates, displays, or sorts. **Do NOT use when:** tests must verify behaviour against a specific known commit in a real repository — use a hardcoded SHA from the repo's actual history for integration tests that call the GitHub API or a real git CLI. **Alternative:** `faker.string.hexadecimal({ length: 40, casing: 'lower' })` as a raw substitute when the git module is not available (older faker versions); it produces correct-length SHA strings without semantic meaning.

```typescript
// test/factories/deployment.factory.ts
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

export interface DeploymentRecord {
  id:            string;
  commitSha:     string;
  shortSha:      string;
  branch:        string;
  commitMessage: string;
  deployedAt:    Date;
  environment:   'staging' | 'production';
  status:        'pending' | 'success' | 'failed' | 'rolled_back';
}

export function buildDeploymentRecord(
  overrides: Partial<DeploymentRecord> = {}
): DeploymentRecord {
  return {
    id:            faker.string.uuid(),
    commitSha:     faker.git.commitSha(),
    shortSha:      faker.git.shortSha(),
    branch:        faker.git.branch(),
    commitMessage: faker.git.commitMessage(),
    deployedAt:    faker.date.recent({ days: 30 }),
    environment:   faker.helpers.arrayElement(['staging', 'production']),
    status:        faker.helpers.arrayElement(['pending', 'success', 'failed', 'rolled_back']),
    ...overrides,
  };
}

test('deployment audit log displays valid short SHA and branch name', () => {
  const deploy = buildDeploymentRecord({ environment: 'production', status: 'success' });
  expect(deploy.commitSha).toMatch(/^[0-9a-f]{40}$/);
  expect(deploy.shortSha).toMatch(/^[0-9a-f]{7}$/);
  expect(deploy.branch.length).toBeGreaterThan(0);
});
```
