### Pattern 255 — `fc.letrec()` for mutually recursive arbitrary trees (AST, JSON, nested comment threads) [official]

`fc.letrec()` declares a set of co-dependent arbitraries that reference each other by name, enabling generation of recursive data structures without stack overflows. Fast-check controls recursion depth automatically via its size parameter, making it safe for CI with the default `"small"` size setting.

```ts
import * as fc from 'fast-check';

type JsonValue =
  | null | boolean | number | string
  | JsonValue[]
  | { [key: string]: JsonValue };

const jsonArbitrary: fc.Arbitrary<JsonValue> = fc.letrec((tie) => ({
  json: fc.oneof(
    { depthFactor: 0.5, withCrossShrink: true },
    fc.constant(null),
    fc.boolean(),
    fc.float({ noNaN: true }),
    fc.string(),
    fc.array(tie('json'), { maxLength: 5 }),
    fc.dictionary(fc.string({ maxLength: 12 }), tie('json'), { maxKeys: 6 }),
  ),
})).json;

fc.assert(
  fc.property(jsonArbitrary, (value) => {
    const roundTripped = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(value));
    expect(roundTripped).toEqual(value);
  }),
);
```

**Tradeoff:** `depthFactor` controls how aggressively recursion is curtailed — higher values generate deeper trees but slow down shrinking dramatically. Keep `depthFactor` at or below `0.5` in CI; raise to `0.9` only in focused stress-test runs. Shrinking recursive structures is inherently slow because fast-check must explore many sub-tree reductions before finding the minimal failing case; set `shrinkingMode: 'bounded'` if shrink time exceeds 10 seconds in practice.

---

### Pattern 256 — MSW `http.all()` wildcard handler for catch-all fixture logging in debugging sessions [official]

`http.all('*', resolver)` matches every HTTP method and every URL pattern, making it useful as a debugging intercept that logs unhandled requests during test authoring. Remove or demote it to `onUnhandledRequest: 'warn'` before committing.

```ts
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw';
import { setupServer } from 'msw/node';

const unhandledLog: string[] = [];

const debugHandler = http.all('*', ({ request }) => {
  unhandledLog.push(`${request.method} ${request.url}`);
  // Let the request fall through to real handlers defined after this one
  return undefined; // passthrough
});

const server = setupServer(
  debugHandler,
  http.get('/api/users', () =>
    HttpResponse.json([{ id: '1', name: 'Alice' }]),
  ),
  http.post('/api/orders', () =>
    HttpResponse.json({ orderId: 'ord-001' }, { status: 201 }),
  ),
);

afterEach(() => {
  if (unhandledLog.length > 0) {
    console.warn('[MSW DEBUG] Intercepted:', unhandledLog);
    unhandledLog.length = 0;
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `http.all('*')` that returns `undefined` (passthrough) works in `msw/node` but behaves differently in browser-mode service workers where returning `undefined` is treated as an error — use the explicit `passthrough()` helper from `msw` for browser contexts. Never leave a wildcard debug handler in production test suites; it adds overhead to every request interception and the `unhandledLog` array grows unboundedly across test files run in the same worker process.

---

### Pattern 257 — Fishery `factory.extend()` for type-safe factory inheritance without prototype pollution [official]

`factory.extend()` creates a new factory that inherits the parent's `build()` strategy and can selectively override fields. This is the preferred pattern over redefining factories for each entity subtype because it preserves TypeScript inference on the full output shape.

```ts
import { Factory } from 'fishery';
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

interface User { id: string; name: string; email: string; role: 'user' | 'admin' | 'moderator' }
interface AdminUser extends User { role: 'admin'; permissions: string[] }

const userFactory = Factory.define<User>(() => ({
  id: faker.string.uuid(),
  name: faker.person.fullName(),
  email: faker.internet.email(),
  role: 'user',
}));

const adminFactory = userFactory.extend<AdminUser>(() => ({
  role: 'admin',
  permissions: faker.helpers.arrayElements(
    ['manage:users', 'manage:content', 'manage:billing', 'view:analytics'],
    { min: 1, max: 4 },
  ),
}));

const moderatorFactory = userFactory.extend<User>(() => ({
  role: 'moderator',
}));

const admin = adminFactory.build({ name: 'Super Admin' });
const moderators = moderatorFactory.buildList(3);
```

**Tradeoff:** `factory.extend()` creates a shallow merge of the parent and child `build()` results — deeply nested objects in the parent are not deep-merged, they are replaced entirely if the child defines the same key. For deeply nested overrides, use `factory.build({ nested: { ...existing, extra: true } })` at call-site rather than baking partial nesting into `extend()`. The TypeScript type of the extended factory is the child's generic parameter, so fields on the parent that are not in the child interface will not appear in type hints — use intersection types (`ParentType & ChildExtras`) to avoid losing parent fields from autocomplete.

---

### Pattern 258 — `faker.helpers.weightedArrayElement()` for realistic probability distributions in fixture datasets [official]

`weightedArrayElement()` selects from an array of `{ weight, value }` objects with probability proportional to weight. Use it to generate realistic data skews (e.g., 80% "active" users, 15% "inactive", 5% "suspended") that trigger edge-case UI branches without manual distribution logic.

```ts
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

type OrderStatus = 'pending' | 'processing' | 'shipped' | 'delivered' | 'cancelled' | 'refunded';

function buildOrder() {
  const status = faker.helpers.weightedArrayElement<OrderStatus>([
    { weight: 10, value: 'pending' },
    { weight: 25, value: 'processing' },
    { weight: 20, value: 'shipped' },
    { weight: 35, value: 'delivered' },
    { weight: 7,  value: 'cancelled' },
    { weight: 3,  value: 'refunded' },
  ]);

  return {
    id: faker.string.uuid(),
    status,
    amount: faker.number.float({ min: 5, max: 2000, multipleOf: 0.01 }),
    createdAt: faker.date.recent({ days: 30 }).toISOString(),
    trackingNumber: ['shipped', 'delivered'].includes(status)
      ? faker.string.alphanumeric(12).toUpperCase()
      : null,
  };
}

const orders = Array.from({ length: 100 }, buildOrder);
// Approximately 35 orders should be 'delivered', ~25 'processing', etc.
```

**Tradeoff:** Weights are relative integers, not percentages — the total does not need to sum to 100, but keeping weights readable (summing to 100 or a round number) makes the intent clear to reviewers. `weightedArrayElement()` uses `faker`'s internal seeded RNG, so distributions are reproducible given a fixed seed but will drift if you reorder elements in the array (since the RNG call sequence changes). Freeze the element order in code review and use `faker.seed(n)` in tests where exact distributions matter.

---

### Pattern 259 — `fc.scheduler()` for testing async concurrency, race conditions, and out-of-order promise resolution [official]

`fc.scheduler()` provides a virtual async scheduler that controls the resolution order of promises. Use it to property-test components or services that must be correct regardless of which concurrent async operation settles first.

```ts
import * as fc from 'fast-check';

async function fetchUserAndProfile(
  userId: string,
  fetchUser: (id: string) => Promise<{ name: string }>,
  fetchProfile: (id: string) => Promise<{ bio: string }>,
) {
  const [user, profile] = await Promise.all([fetchUser(userId), fetchProfile(userId)]);
  return { ...user, ...profile };
}

fc.assert(
  fc.asyncProperty(fc.scheduler(), async (scheduler) => {
    const fetchUser = scheduler.scheduleFunction(
      async (_id: string) => ({ name: 'Alice' }),
    );
    const fetchProfile = scheduler.scheduleFunction(
      async (_id: string) => ({ bio: 'Engineer' }),
    );

    const resultPromise = fetchUserAndProfile('u1', fetchUser, fetchProfile);
    await scheduler.waitAll();
    const result = await resultPromise;

    expect(result).toEqual({ name: 'Alice', bio: 'Engineer' });
    // fast-check tries every resolution order — if result depends on order, it will find it
  }),
);
```

**Tradeoff:** `fc.scheduler()` only controls promises wrapped via `scheduler.scheduleFunction()` or `scheduler.schedule()` — native `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, and `queueMicrotask` calls inside the tested code are not controlled. Mix `fc.scheduler()` with fake timers (`vi.useFakeTimers()` or `jest.useFakeTimers()`) when the code under test uses both promises and timer-based delays. The virtual scheduler makes tests deterministic but much slower than real async tests — limit use to concurrency-critical paths and not to general integration tests.

---

### Pattern 260 — MSW `server.use()` with `{ once: true }` for single-shot error injection fixtures [official]

Passing `{ once: true }` to `server.use()` registers a handler that fires exactly once and is then automatically removed, falling back to the baseline handler on subsequent requests. This is the canonical way to simulate transient errors (network flicker, 503 on first attempt) without permanently overriding the test's success handlers.

```ts
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw';
import { setupServer } from 'msw/node';
import { render, screen, waitFor } from '@testing-library/react';
import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event';

const server = setupServer(
  http.get('/api/cart', () =>
    HttpResponse.json({ items: [{ sku: 'ABC', qty: 2 }] }),
  ),
);

beforeAll(() => server.listen());
afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers());
afterAll(() => server.close());

it('retries automatically after a transient 503 and shows cart on success', async () => {
  // First request fails with 503; second request uses the baseline handler
  server.use(
    http.get('/api/cart', () =>
      new HttpResponse(null, { status: 503 }),
    { once: true }),
  );

  render(<CartPage />);
  await waitFor(() => screen.getByText('2 items in cart'), { timeout: 3000 });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `{ once: true }` handlers are consumed in registration order — if two `once` handlers are registered for the same route, the first matching one is consumed first. This is predictable but can be confusing when multiple `server.use()` calls accumulate inside a single test. Always call `server.resetHandlers()` in `afterEach` to prevent `once` handler state from leaking between tests, even though consumed handlers are already removed (a non-consumed `once` handler that didn't fire will persist into the next test).

---

### Pattern 261 — `faker.internet.jwt()` for bearer-token fixture generation in auth header tests [official]

`faker.internet.jwt({ header, payload })` generates a syntactically valid JWT string (three Base64url-encoded segments separated by dots) with controllable header algorithm and payload claims. Use it to test authentication middleware, token-parsing utilities, and protected-route components without setting up a real signing infrastructure.

```ts
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

function buildAuthHeaders(overrides: Record<string, unknown> = {}) {
  const now = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000);
  const token = faker.internet.jwt({
    header: { alg: 'HS256', typ: 'JWT' },
    payload: {
      sub: faker.string.uuid(),
      email: faker.internet.email(),
      roles: ['user'],
      iat: now,
      exp: now + 3600,
      ...overrides,
    },
  });
  return { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` };
}

// Test: expired token should be rejected by middleware
const expiredHeaders = buildAuthHeaders({ exp: Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) - 60 });

// Test: admin role should see admin panel
const adminHeaders = buildAuthHeaders({ roles: ['user', 'admin'] });

// Test: missing sub claim should return 401
const noSubHeaders = buildAuthHeaders({ sub: undefined });
```

**Tradeoff:** `faker.internet.jwt()` produces tokens with an empty or fake signature — they are not cryptographically valid and will fail real JWT verification middleware (`jsonwebtoken.verify()`, `jose`). This is intentional for unit and integration tests where the middleware is mocked; use real signing with `jsonwebtoken.sign()` for E2E tests that exercise actual verification logic. Do not commit fake JWT tokens to version control if they contain realistic-looking PII in the payload (even faker-generated data can trigger secret-scanner false positives).

---

### Pattern 262 — `fc.commands()` for stateful property testing of UI flows with a virtual state machine model [official]

`fc.commands()` generates sequences of command objects (each implementing `check()` and `run()`) that are applied to both a real system and a model. Fast-check shrinks failing command sequences to the minimal reproduction, making it ideal for testing shopping carts, form wizards, and undo/redo stacks.

```ts
import * as fc from 'fast-check';

interface CartModel { items: Map<string, number>; total: number }
interface CartReal  { add(sku: string, qty: number): void; remove(sku: string): void; getTotal(): number }

class AddItemCommand implements fc.Command<CartModel, CartReal> {
  constructor(private sku: string, private qty: number, private price: number) {}
  check(_model: Readonly<CartModel>) { return this.qty > 0; }
  run(model: CartModel, real: CartReal) {
    real.add(this.sku, this.qty);
    model.items.set(this.sku, (model.items.get(this.sku) ?? 0) + this.qty);
    model.total += this.qty * this.price;
    expect(real.getTotal()).toBeCloseTo(model.total, 2);
  }
  toString() { return `AddItem(${this.sku}, ${this.qty})`; }
}

class RemoveItemCommand implements fc.Command<CartModel, CartReal> {
  constructor(private sku: string) {}
  check(model: Readonly<CartModel>) { return model.items.has(this.sku); }
  run(model: CartModel, real: CartReal) {
    const qty = model.items.get(this.sku)!;
    real.remove(this.sku);
    model.items.delete(this.sku);
    model.total -= qty * 10; // simplified price
    expect(real.getTotal()).toBeCloseTo(model.total, 2);
  }
  toString() { return `RemoveItem(${this.sku})`; }
}

const skuArb = fc.constantFrom('SKU-A', 'SKU-B', 'SKU-C');
const addCmd = fc.tuple(skuArb, fc.integer({ min: 1, max: 5 }), fc.constant(10))
  .map(([sku, qty, price]) => new AddItemCommand(sku, qty, price));
const removeCmd = skuArb.map((sku) => new RemoveItemCommand(sku));

fc.assert(
  fc.property(fc.commands([addCmd, removeCmd], { maxCommands: 20 }), (cmds) => {
    const model: CartModel = { items: new Map(), total: 0 };
    const real = new RealCart();
    fc.modelRun(() => ({ model, real }), cmds);
  }),
);
```

**Tradeoff:** The `check()` method on each command must be a pure function of the model — it must not call `real` methods. Impure `check()` implementations will cause fast-check to enter infinite loops during shrinking because the model state diverges from what `check()` expects. Define a minimal model with only the state fields needed for `check()` guards — a bloated model that mirrors every real-system field increases memory allocation per generated sequence and slows down runs with `numRuns: 500` or higher.

---

### Pattern 263 — `faker.git.commitMessage()` and `faker.git.branch()` for VCS-domain fixture generation [official]

The `faker.git` module produces realistic commit messages, branch names, commit SHAs, and author info for testing git-hosting UIs, code-review dashboards, changelog generators, and CI/CD pipeline fixtures.

```ts
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

interface Commit {
  sha: string;
  shortSha: string;
  message: string;
  author: string;
  email: string;
  date: string;
  branch: string;
}

function buildCommit(overrides: Partial<Commit> = {}): Commit {
  const sha = faker.git.commitSha({ length: 40 });
  return {
    sha,
    shortSha: sha.slice(0, 7),
    message: faker.git.commitMessage(),
    author: faker.person.fullName(),
    email: faker.internet.email(),
    date: faker.date.recent({ days: 90 }).toISOString(),
    branch: faker.git.branch(),
    ...overrides,
  };
}

const commitHistory = Array.from({ length: 10 }, () => buildCommit());

// Build a PR fixture referencing the commits
const pullRequest = {
  id: faker.number.int({ min: 1, max: 9999 }),
  title: faker.git.commitMessage(),
  baseBranch: 'main',
  headBranch: faker.git.branch(),
  commits: commitHistory,
  status: faker.helpers.arrayElement(['open', 'merged', 'closed']),
};
```

**Tradeoff:** `faker.git.branch()` generates names like `"feature/fix-bug-123"` that look realistic but do not follow your team's actual branch naming convention. If your UI enforces branch name validation (e.g., Jira-prefix requirements), add a thin wrapper that prefixes the faker output: `` `JIRA-${faker.number.int(9999)}/` + faker.git.branch() ``. `faker.git.commitSha()` defaults to 7 characters (short SHA) — pass `{ length: 40 }` for full SHAs when testing systems that require the full hash for deduplication.

### Pattern 264 — `fc.bigInt()` and `fc.bigIntN()` for arbitrary-precision integer boundary testing [official]

JavaScript `BigInt` is used in financial systems, cryptographic key fixtures, and database ID generation. `fc.bigInt()` and `fc.bigIntN(n)` generate `BigInt` values across the full signed range (or an n-bit signed range), exposing overflow bugs in code that carelessly mixes `BigInt` and `Number`.

```ts
import * as fc from 'fast-check';

function splitPayment(totalCents: bigint, parts: number): bigint[] {
  const base = totalCents / BigInt(parts);
  const remainder = totalCents % BigInt(parts);
  return Array.from({ length: parts }, (_, i) =>
    i === 0 ? base + remainder : base,
  );
}

fc.assert(
  fc.property(
    fc.bigInt({ min: 1n, max: 1_000_000_000_000n }),
    fc.integer({ min: 1, max: 20 }),
    (total, parts) => {
      const splits = splitPayment(total, parts);
      const sum = splits.reduce((acc, v) => acc + v, 0n);
      expect(sum).toBe(total);               // Invariant: parts must sum to total
      expect(splits.length).toBe(parts);      // Invariant: correct number of parts
      expect(splits.every(v => v >= 0n)).toBe(true); // Invariant: no negative splits
    },
  ),
);

// Also test: mixing BigInt and Number throws TypeError
fc.assert(
  fc.property(fc.bigIntN(64), (n) => {
    expect(() => Number(n) === n).not.toThrow();
    // Note: Number(n) === n is false for large values — tests precision loss
  }),
);
```

**Tradeoff:** `fc.bigInt()` generates values across a very wide range by default (up to 2^252 − 1 in magnitude); constrain with `min`/`max` to match your domain. Shrinking `BigInt` arbitraries produces values approaching `0n` — if `0n` is not a valid input (e.g., divisor), add a `fc.pre()` guard or use `fc.bigInt({ min: 1n })`. Many JSON serialisation libraries (`JSON.stringify`) throw on `BigInt` values — test serialisation boundaries separately with `.toString()` coercion rather than assuming `JSON.stringify` handles them.

### Pattern 265 — MSW `HttpResponse.formData()` for multipart form fixture responses in file-upload flows [official]

MSW handlers can return `HttpResponse.formData()` to simulate backend endpoints that send back multipart data — useful for testing file-preview, image-resize confirmation, or chunked-upload status endpoints that respond with form-encoded metadata.

```ts
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw';
import { setupServer } from 'msw/node';

const server = setupServer(
  http.post('/api/upload', async ({ request }) => {
    const formData = await request.formData();
    const file = formData.get('file') as File;

    // Simulate server echoing back processed file metadata as FormData
    const responseForm = new FormData();
    responseForm.append('originalName', file.name);
    responseForm.append('storedKey', `uploads/${crypto.randomUUID()}/${file.name}`);
    responseForm.append('mimeType', file.type || 'application/octet-stream');
    responseForm.append('sizeBytes', String(file.size));
    responseForm.append('status', 'processed');

    return HttpResponse.formData(responseForm, { status: 200 });
  }),

  http.get('/api/upload/:key/status', ({ params }) => {
    const responseForm = new FormData();
    responseForm.append('key', params.key as string);
    responseForm.append('ready', 'true');
    responseForm.append('thumbnailUrl', `https://cdn.example.com/thumb/${params.key}.webp`);
    return HttpResponse.formData(responseForm);
  }),
);
```

**Tradeoff:** `HttpResponse.formData()` is available in MSW v2+ only — projects still on MSW v1 must construct the response manually using `new Response(formData)`. The `FormData` global used in Node.js test environments is the Node.js built-in (available since Node 18) — in older environments you must polyfill it with `form-data` or `node-fetch`'s `FormData`. Avoid using `HttpResponse.formData()` for JSON-native endpoints just because it is available; JSON responses are much easier to assert against in Vitest/Jest matchers and produce better failure messages.

### Pattern 266 — Fishery `factory.rewindSequence()` for deterministic sequential ID reset between test files [official]

Fishery's `sequence` counter increments globally across all `build()` calls in a process. `factory.rewindSequence()` resets the counter to 1, making sequential IDs in fixtures deterministic and reproducible when called in a `beforeEach()` block.

```ts
import { Factory } from 'fishery';
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

interface Product {
  id: number;
  sku: string;
  name: string;
  price: number;
}

const productFactory = Factory.define<Product>(({ sequence }) => ({
  id: sequence,
  sku: `SKU-${String(sequence).padStart(5, '0')}`,
  name: faker.commerce.productName(),
  price: faker.number.float({ min: 1, max: 999, multipleOf: 0.01 }),
}));

describe('ProductList', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    productFactory.rewindSequence();
    faker.seed(42);
  });

  it('renders first product with id 1 and sku SKU-00001', () => {
    const product = productFactory.build();
    expect(product.id).toBe(1);
    expect(product.sku).toBe('SKU-00001');
  });

  it('renders second product with id 2 after rewind', () => {
    productFactory.buildList(2);
    // After rewindSequence() in beforeEach, sequence is 1 again
    const second = productFactory.buildList(2)[1];
    expect(second.id).toBe(2);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `rewindSequence()` resets the counter on the specific factory instance only — if the same sequence is shared between a parent factory and its `extend()`-derived child factory, only the parent's counter resets, and the child's counter continues from wherever it was. In practice, each factory maintains its own sequence counter, so this is only a concern when using `factory.extend()` with explicit `({ sequence })` in the child's `define()` callback. Pair `rewindSequence()` with `faker.seed(n)` in `beforeEach()` to achieve full reproducibility of both sequential IDs and random field values.

### Pattern 267 — `faker.science.chemicalElement()` for domain-specific scientific UI fixture data [official]

`faker.science.chemicalElement()` returns an object with `name`, `symbol`, `atomicNumber`, and `atomicMass` for a randomly selected element from the periodic table. Use it for scientific data management apps, lab-management UIs, and any domain-specific system that references chemical entities.

```ts
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

interface SampleRecord {
  id: string;
  batchCode: string;
  element: { name: string; symbol: string; atomicNumber: number; atomicMass: number };
  concentration: number;
  unit: 'mol/L' | 'mg/L' | 'ppm';
  collectedAt: string;
  analyst: string;
}

function buildSampleRecord(overrides: Partial<SampleRecord> = {}): SampleRecord {
  const element = faker.science.chemicalElement();
  return {
    id: faker.string.uuid(),
    batchCode: `BATCH-${faker.string.alphanumeric(6).toUpperCase()}`,
    element,
    concentration: faker.number.float({ min: 0.001, max: 100, multipleOf: 0.001 }),
    unit: faker.helpers.arrayElement(['mol/L', 'mg/L', 'ppm']),
    collectedAt: faker.date.recent({ days: 7 }).toISOString(),
    analyst: faker.person.fullName(),
    ...overrides,
  };
}

const labReport = {
  reportId: faker.string.uuid(),
  samples: Array.from({ length: 5 }, () => buildSampleRecord()),
  approvedBy: faker.person.fullName(),
};
```

**Tradeoff:** The `faker.science` module has a small dataset (118 elements) — with large fixture arrays you will see frequent repetition of the same elements, which is appropriate for most UI tests but misleading for tests of uniqueness constraints. For uniqueness, combine with `faker.helpers.shuffle(allElements).slice(0, n)` using a pre-built array from `Array.from({ length: 118 }, (_, i) => faker.science.chemicalElement())` (which produces duplicates across calls — better to use `faker.helpers.arrayElements` on a known unique list). Also check that your UI can handle long element names (`"Nihonium"`, `"Oganesson"`, `"Moscovium"`) at the 40px column width you tested manually with `"Iron"`.

### Pattern 268 — `fc.sample()` for extracting fixed-size fixture arrays from arbitraries in non-property test contexts [official]

`fc.sample(arbitrary, n)` runs the arbitrary's generation once and returns an array of `n` values without running any assertions. It bridges property-based arbitraries into traditional unit test fixtures, letting you reuse complex arbitraries for snapshot tests, seed data scripts, and Storybook stories.

```ts
import * as fc from 'fast-check';
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

// Reuse a complex arbitrary outside of fc.assert()
const addressArbitrary = fc.record({
  street: fc.string({ minLength: 5, maxLength: 40 }),
  city: fc.constantFrom('London', 'Berlin', 'Paris', 'Madrid', 'Rome'),
  postcode: fc.stringMatching(/^[A-Z]{1,2}\d{1,2} \d[A-Z]{2}$/),
  country: fc.constantFrom('GB', 'DE', 'FR', 'ES', 'IT'),
});

// In a snapshot test — deterministic via seed
const addresses = fc.sample(addressArbitrary, { numSamples: 5, seed: 12345 });

// In a Storybook story
export const WithManyAddresses = {
  args: {
    addresses: fc.sample(addressArbitrary, { numSamples: 8, seed: 99 }),
  },
};

// In a DB seed script
const seedAddresses = fc.sample(addressArbitrary, 50);
console.log(JSON.stringify(seedAddresses, null, 2));
```

**Tradeoff:** `fc.sample()` does not perform shrinking — it is purely generative. Values are not necessarily minimal or edge-case-representative; they are drawn from the full distribution of the arbitrary. For snapshot tests, always pass `{ seed: n }` to make the output deterministic across runs — without a seed, `fc.sample()` uses a random seed and the snapshot will fail on the next run. Do not use `fc.sample()` inside `it()` blocks without a fixed seed; the non-determinism defeats the purpose of snapshot testing and creates flaky tests.

## Community Gotcha #170 — `faker.helpers.arrayElements()` with `{ min, max }` range options silently produces empty arrays when the source array has fewer elements than `min` in strict mode — no error is thrown [community]

**WHY: `faker.helpers.arrayElements(sourceArray, { min, max })` does not validate that `sourceArray.length >= min`. When `sourceArray.length < min`, the method silently returns a copy of the entire source array (all elements), which has fewer items than `min` requested. No exception, no warning, no `console.warn`. Tests that assert `result.length >= min` will fail with a confusing mismatch, but the call site shows no obvious error. This surfaces when building fixture factories for permission sets where the source array of available permissions is dynamically constructed and may be shorter than expected — for example, a test user seeded with only 2 permissions in a `beforeEach` hook calls `arrayElements(perms, { min: 3, max: 5 })` and receives only 2 items. The downstream assertion `expect(user.permissions.length).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(3)` fails with `"Expected 3, received 2"` — the stack trace points to the assertion, not to the `arrayElements` call.**

Fix: always validate `sourceArray.length >= min` before calling `arrayElements`. Add a guard in your factory helper: `if (source.length < min) throw new Error(\`arrayElements: source length \${source.length} < min \${min}\`)`. Alternatively, provide a source array that is always at least as long as your maximum requested count, using `faker.helpers.uniqueArray()` with a larger generator if needed.

## Community Gotcha #171 — `fc.string()` generates empty strings by default, and many validators that call `str.trim().length > 0` accept them, causing property tests to pass even when the production code has a hidden zero-length validation bug [community]

**WHY: `fc.string()` uses `{ minLength: 0 }` by default, which means the empty string `""` is always in the generated corpus and is typically the first value tried during shrinking. If your production validator does `if (!value.trim()) throw new Error('required')` but your unit test passes the validated value into a downstream function that does `if (!value) throw new Error('required')` (without trim), the empty-string case is a valid input to the validator but would have been caught by the downstream check — creating a subtle invariant gap. The property test passes with `fc.string()` because `""` is correctly rejected by the validator, but the trimmed-empty-string case (`"  "`) is not tested unless you explicitly include `fc.string({ minLength: 1 })` combined with whitespace-only strings. The real bug — passing a whitespace-only string through the validator and into a database `NOT NULL` column — goes untested.**

Fix: for fields that use `trim()` validation, always compose two arbitraries: `fc.oneof(fc.constant(''), fc.constant('   '), fc.string({ minLength: 1 }))`. This ensures the empty, whitespace-only, and non-empty cases are all represented. For required-field property tests specifically, use `fc.string({ minLength: 1 })` to exclude empty strings from the "valid input" arbitrary — then test the error case separately with `fc.constant('')` and `fc.stringMatching(/^\s+$/)`.

---

## Community Gotcha #172 — MSW `server.resetHandlers()` in `afterEach` does not reset `server.use()` handlers registered at the `describe` block level via a `beforeAll` — only handlers registered inside `it`/`test` bodies are removed [community]

**WHY: MSW's `resetHandlers()` removes handlers added dynamically via `server.use()` since the last `listen()` or `resetHandlers()` call. Handlers registered at module level (in `setupServer(...)`) are never removed by `resetHandlers()` — this is well-documented. However, the subtlety is that handlers added in `beforeAll()` are registered before any test runs, and since `resetHandlers()` only removes handlers added after the most recent `listen()` call (which runs in `beforeAll` before any dynamic registration), handlers from `beforeAll`-level `server.use()` are treated as baseline handlers and survive `resetHandlers()`. Developers who add a `beforeAll(() => server.use(errorHandler))` to simulate a global error condition for a `describe` block find that `afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers())` does not clean it up — the error handler persists into tests in sibling `describe` blocks that share the same server instance.**

Fix: for `describe`-scoped handler overrides, prefer `beforeEach(() => server.use(handler))` paired with `afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers())` — this ensures the handler is both registered and removed around each test. If you need a `beforeAll`-scoped handler, explicitly remove it in a matching `afterAll(() => server.resetHandlers())` at the same `describe` level. Alternatively, create a nested server instance scoped to the `describe` block: `const scopedServer = setupServer(handler); beforeAll(() => scopedServer.listen()); afterAll(() => scopedServer.close());`.

---

## Community Gotcha #173 — Fishery `factory.build()` with an `associations()` callback that calls `factory.create()` internally triggers async database operations during synchronous `build()` calls in unit tests — no error is thrown but the create promise is silently dropped [community]

**WHY: Fishery distinguishes between `build()` (synchronous, returns plain objects) and `create()` (asynchronous, calls the `onCreate` adapter). When an `associations()` callback in a factory's `define()` function calls `anotherFactory.create()` to build a related record, the async `create()` returns a `Promise` rather than the resolved object. Since `build()` is synchronous, it cannot `await` the promise — the factory receives the `Promise` object itself as the value of the association field, not the resolved entity. The object appears to have been built (`typeof result.user === 'object'`), but `result.user instanceof Promise` is `true`. TypeScript may not catch this because the Fishery types infer the association field as the entity type, not `Promise<EntityType>`. The test passes the malformed fixture to the component, which fails at runtime with `"Cannot read property 'name' of undefined"` (because the Promise's `name` property is `undefined`).**

Fix: never call `factory.create()` inside an `associations()` callback that will be used with `build()`. Use `otherFactory.build()` for synchronous association stubs. If you need real DB-persisted associations, use `factory.create()` at the top of the test and pass the created entity as an override: `const user = await userFactory.create(); const post = await postFactory.create({ authorId: user.id });`. Add an ESLint rule or a custom Fishery wrapper that throws a synchronous error if `create()` is called inside a `build()` context.

---

## Community Gotcha #174 — `faker.date.between({ from, to })` accepts `Date`, `string`, or `number` for bounds but silently swaps them if `from > to` in some Faker versions — producing dates outside the intended range without throwing [community]

**WHY: In Faker.js v8 and earlier, `faker.date.between({ from, to })` would silently swap `from` and `to` when `from > to`, returning a valid date from the reversed range instead of throwing a `RangeError`. This was changed to throw in v8.4+, but many projects pin to older patch versions. The silent swap is dangerous in fixtures that construct time-ordered event sequences: `const end = faker.date.recent(); const start = faker.date.between({ from: end, to: faker.date.past() })` — the developer intended `start` to precede `end`, but since `end` (a recent date) is greater than `faker.date.past()`, the bounds are swapped and `start` is actually generated after `end`. Tests that assert `start < end` fail intermittently (only when the seeded date values produce this ordering), creating a flaky test that passes on some CI runners and fails on others depending on execution time.**

Fix: always explicitly enforce `from < to` by sorting the two dates before passing them: `const [earlier, later] = [dateA, dateB].sort((a, b) => a.getTime() - b.getTime()); faker.date.between({ from: earlier, to: later })`. Pin your Faker version to v8.4+ in `package.json` to benefit from the throwing behaviour that surfaces the bug immediately rather than silently producing wrong data. Add an assertion in your factory helper: `if (from >= to) throw new RangeError(\`date.between: from (\${from}) must be before to (\${to})\`)`.

---

## Community Gotcha #175 — `fc.assert()` swallows `Error` subclasses thrown inside property functions and re-throws them as generic `fc.PreconditionFailure` when `fc.pre()` is used nearby — making the root cause invisible in CI output [community]

**WHY: `fc.pre(condition)` throws a special internal `PreconditionFailure` object when `condition` is `false` — fast-check catches this to filter invalid inputs and try a new sample. The problem is that if a user-defined `Error` subclass has `instanceof PreconditionFailure` return `true` due to prototype chain manipulation (e.g., a custom `QAError extends Error` that sets `this.name = 'PreconditionFailure'`), fast-check misidentifies real assertion failures as precondition failures and silently discards them. The property appears to pass (all samples are "filtered") but actually the test logic is never executing — fast-check discards every sample because it thinks the precondition is never met. CI shows a passing test with a warning: `"Too many pre-condition failures"`. This is discovered only when the warning threshold triggers an error after 10,000 filtered samples, at which point the failure message says "Could not satisfy pre-condition" rather than the actual application error.**

Fix: never name a custom `Error` subclass `PreconditionFailure` and never set `error.name = 'PreconditionFailure'` in a codebase that uses fast-check. If you see `"Too many pre-condition failures"` warnings in CI, enable `verbose: true` in `fc.assert()` options to log the raw generated values and check whether real errors are being swallowed. Prefer `fc.pre()` sparingly — use constrained arbitraries (`fc.integer({ min: 1 })` instead of `fc.integer()` + `fc.pre(n => n > 0)`) to avoid high filter rates that trigger the silent-swallowing edge case.

### Pattern 269 — `faker.airline.flightNumber()` for domain-specific transportation fixture data [official]

Generate realistic airline flight numbers, seat codes, aircraft types, and airport codes for travel-domain test suites. The `faker.airline` module (added in Faker v8.1) provides structured aviation data that is far more realistic than hand-written literals and immediately exercises parsers that validate IATA codes, seat row ranges, and flight identifier formats.

```typescript
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';
import { Factory } from 'fishery';

interface FlightBooking {
  flightNumber: string;
  departureAirport: string;
  arrivalAirport: string;
  seatNumber: string;
  aircraftType: string;
  recordLocator: string;
  passengerCount: number;
}

const flightBookingFactory = Factory.define<FlightBooking>(() => {
  // Ensure departure ≠ arrival by generating two distinct airports
  const [dep, arr] = faker.helpers.uniqueArray(
    () => faker.airline.airport().iataCode,
    2
  );
  return {
    flightNumber: faker.airline.flightNumber({ addLeadingZeros: true }),
    departureAirport: dep,
    arrivalAirport: arr,
    seatNumber: faker.airline.seat({ aircraftType: 'narrowbody' }),
    aircraftType: faker.airline.aircraftType(),
    recordLocator: faker.airline.recordLocator({ allowVisuallySimilarCharacters: false }),
    passengerCount: faker.number.int({ min: 1, max: 9 }),
  };
});

// Usage in a test
const booking = flightBookingFactory.build({ passengerCount: 1 });
expect(booking.departureAirport).not.toBe(booking.arrivalAirport);
expect(booking.seatNumber).toMatch(/^\d{1,2}[A-F]$/);
```

**Tradeoff:** `faker.airline.airport()` returns an object `{ name, iataCode }` — the `iataCode` is always 3 uppercase letters (IATA standard). However, the module does not cover ICAO codes (4-letter), military bases, or private airfields. For tests that require ICAO codes, fall back to `faker.string.alpha({ length: 4, casing: 'upper' })` with an explicit comment. The `allowVisuallySimilarCharacters: false` option on `recordLocator()` removes `0/O` and `1/I` confusion from PNR codes — essential when testing OCR or printed boarding pass parsing.

### Pattern 270 — `faker.food.dish()` and `faker.food.ingredient()` for hospitality and e-commerce menu fixture data [official]

The `faker.food` module (added in Faker v9.1) provides realistic restaurant menu data including dish names, ingredients, spice levels, descriptions, and ethnic cuisine categories. This is especially useful for testing restaurant-ordering apps, dietary restriction engines, and multi-language menu rendering.

```typescript
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

interface MenuItem {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  description: string;
  ingredients: string[];
  spiceLevel: string;
  ethnicCategory: string;
  priceInCents: number;
  isVegetarian: boolean;
  allergens: string[];
}

function buildMenuItem(overrides: Partial<MenuItem> = {}): MenuItem {
  const ingredients = Array.from(
    { length: faker.number.int({ min: 3, max: 8 }) },
    () => faker.food.ingredient()
  );
  return {
    id: faker.string.uuid(),
    name: faker.food.dish(),
    description: faker.food.description(),
    ingredients,
    spiceLevel: faker.food.spiceLevel(),
    ethnicCategory: faker.food.ethnicCategory(),
    priceInCents: faker.number.int({ min: 800, max: 4500 }),
    isVegetarian: faker.datatype.boolean({ probability: 0.35 }),
    allergens: faker.helpers.arrayElements(
      ['gluten', 'dairy', 'nuts', 'eggs', 'soy', 'shellfish'],
      { min: 0, max: 3 }
    ),
    ...overrides,
  };
}

// Build a full menu section
const appetizerSection = Array.from({ length: 6 }, () =>
  buildMenuItem({ priceInCents: faker.number.int({ min: 600, max: 1600 }) })
);
```

**Tradeoff:** The `faker.food` module does not provide allergen data directly — allergens must be constructed manually as shown above. Dish names are English-language only in the current Faker locale set; for multilingual restaurant apps, use a locale-specific Faker instance (`new Faker({ locale: [de, base] })`) and override `name` explicitly from your localisation fixtures rather than relying on `faker.food.dish()` for non-English names.

### Pattern 271 — `fc.uuid()` and `fc.uuidV()` for version-specific UUID property testing [official]

`fast-check` provides dedicated UUID arbitraries that generate structurally valid UUIDs. `fc.uuid()` generates UUID v4 (random); `fc.uuidV(version)` generates the specific version (1, 2, 3, 4, 5). Use these instead of `faker.string.uuid()` inside `fc.assert()` property blocks so that shrinking produces the minimal failing UUID rather than an unrelated random string.

```typescript
import * as fc from 'fast-check';

// Production code under test
function parseResourceId(id: string): { version: number; raw: string } {
  const versionChar = id.charAt(14);
  const version = parseInt(versionChar, 10);
  if (![1, 2, 3, 4, 5].includes(version)) {
    throw new RangeError(`Unsupported UUID version: ${version}`);
  }
  return { version, raw: id };
}

// Property: all v4 UUIDs round-trip through parseResourceId
fc.assert(
  fc.property(fc.uuid(), (id) => {
    const result = parseResourceId(id);
    expect(result.version).toBe(4);
    expect(result.raw).toBe(id);
  })
);

// Property: only versions 1-5 are accepted (no version 6/7/8)
fc.assert(
  fc.property(fc.uuidV(4), (id) => {
    expect(() => parseResourceId(id)).not.toThrow();
  })
);

// Negative: a non-UUID string should throw
fc.assert(
  fc.property(fc.string({ minLength: 1 }), (s) => {
    fc.pre(!s.match(/^[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[1-5][0-9a-f]{3}-[89ab][0-9a-f]{3}-[0-9a-f]{12}$/i));
    expect(() => parseResourceId(s)).toThrow();
  })
);
```

**Tradeoff:** `fc.uuidV(6)` does not exist in fast-check as of v3.x because UUID v6/v7/v8 are newer standards (RFC 9562, 2024) and fast-check's UUID implementation predates them. For testing UUID v7 time-ordered keys (used for database performance), fall back to a custom arbitrary: `fc.bigInt({ min: 0n, max: (1n << 122n) - 1n }).map(n => formatUUIDv7(n))`. Shrinking on `fc.uuid()` produces UUIDs with minimal variable portions — the first segment shrinks toward `00000000`, which aids in understanding which part of a UUID your parser fails on.

### Pattern 272 — `faker.hacker.phrase()` and `faker.hacker.abbreviation()` for tech-jargon placeholder content in UI tests [official]

When testing developer-facing UIs (dashboards, admin panels, log viewers), realistic-looking technical jargon is more useful than lorem ipsum. `faker.hacker` generates plausible-sounding tech terminology — buzz phrases, verbs, adjectives, nouns, and acronyms — that stress-tests text wrapping, truncation, and copy rendering without exposing the test as a dummy-data fixture.

```typescript
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

interface AlertRecord {
  id: string;
  title: string;
  description: string;
  severity: 'critical' | 'high' | 'medium' | 'low';
  component: string;
  abbreviation: string;
  timestamp: Date;
}

function buildAlertRecord(overrides: Partial<AlertRecord> = {}): AlertRecord {
  return {
    id: faker.string.nanoid(12),
    title: faker.hacker.phrase(),
    description: [
      faker.hacker.phrase(),
      faker.hacker.phrase(),
    ].join(' '),
    severity: faker.helpers.arrayElement(['critical', 'high', 'medium', 'low']),
    component: `${faker.hacker.adjective()}-${faker.hacker.noun()}`,
    abbreviation: faker.hacker.abbreviation(),
    timestamp: faker.date.recent({ days: 1 }),
    ...overrides,
  };
}

// Build a realistic alert dashboard dataset
const alerts = Array.from({ length: 20 }, buildAlertRecord);
const criticalAlerts = alerts.filter(a => a.severity === 'critical');
// Assert the UI can handle 0 critical alerts (edge case)
const emptyDashboard = alerts.map(a => ({ ...a, severity: 'low' as const }));
```

**Tradeoff:** `faker.hacker.phrase()` produces sentences like "Try to hack the TCP bandwidth, maybe it will index the multi-byte pixel!" These are clearly non-production content. For pixel-perfect snapshot tests where the exact text must be stable across runs, replace hacker phrases with `faker.lorem.sentence()` seeded with a fixed value, or hard-code the strings — hacker phrases are seeded but vary between Faker versions as the word lists change.

---

### Pattern 273 — `fc.emailAddress()` for property-based email validation and normalization testing [official]

`fast-check` provides `fc.emailAddress()` to generate RFC 5321-compliant email address strings. Using this in property tests catches edge cases in email normalisation (case folding, `+`-alias stripping, international domain names) that a fixed list of example emails would miss entirely.

```typescript
import * as fc from 'fast-check';

// Production normaliser under test
function normalizeEmail(email: string): string {
  const [local, domain] = email.toLowerCase().split('@');
  // Strip + aliases
  const cleanLocal = local.split('+')[0];
  return `${cleanLocal}@${domain}`;
}

// Property: normalised email is always lowercase
fc.assert(
  fc.property(fc.emailAddress(), (email) => {
    const normalised = normalizeEmail(email);
    expect(normalised).toBe(normalised.toLowerCase());
  })
);

// Property: normalised email still contains exactly one @
fc.assert(
  fc.property(fc.emailAddress(), (email) => {
    const normalised = normalizeEmail(email);
    expect(normalised.split('@')).toHaveLength(2);
  })
);

// Property: domain part is unchanged by normalisation
fc.assert(
  fc.property(fc.emailAddress(), (email) => {
    const originalDomain = email.toLowerCase().split('@')[1];
    const normalisedDomain = normalizeEmail(email).split('@')[1];
    expect(normalisedDomain).toBe(originalDomain);
  })
);

// Seeded run for deterministic CI
fc.assert(
  fc.property(fc.emailAddress(), (email) => {
    expect(normalizeEmail(email)).not.toContain('+');
  }),
  { seed: 42, numRuns: 200 }
);
```

**Tradeoff:** `fc.emailAddress()` generates syntactically valid RFC 5321 emails but does not guarantee DNS-resolvable domains — domains like `a.b` or `x.io` may not exist. For tests that call a real DNS lookup, combine with a mock or use `faker.internet.email()` (which draws from a curated domain list). `fc.emailAddress()` generates uppercase local parts in some samples; if your production code does not call `.toLowerCase()` before comparison, the property test will expose the case-sensitivity bug — which is exactly the intended behaviour.

---

### Pattern 274 — MSW `http.options()` handler for CORS preflight fixture simulation in cross-origin API tests [official]

When testing frontend code that makes cross-origin requests, the browser issues CORS preflight `OPTIONS` requests before the real method. MSW's `http.options()` handler intercepts these and lets you return the correct `Access-Control-*` headers from a factory, simulating different CORS server configurations without running a real backend.

```typescript
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw';
import { setupServer } from 'msw/node';

interface CorsConfig {
  allowedOrigins: string[];
  allowedMethods: string[];
  allowedHeaders: string[];
  maxAge: number;
}

function buildCorsHandler(config: CorsConfig) {
  return http.options('https://api.example.com/*', () => {
    return new HttpResponse(null, {
      status: 204,
      headers: {
        'Access-Control-Allow-Origin': config.allowedOrigins.join(', '),
        'Access-Control-Allow-Methods': config.allowedMethods.join(', '),
        'Access-Control-Allow-Headers': config.allowedHeaders.join(', '),
        'Access-Control-Max-Age': String(config.maxAge),
      },
    });
  });
}

// Permissive CORS config for development tests
const permissiveCors = buildCorsHandler({
  allowedOrigins: ['*'],
  allowedMethods: ['GET', 'POST', 'PUT', 'DELETE', 'PATCH'],
  allowedHeaders: ['Content-Type', 'Authorization'],
  maxAge: 86400,
});

// Restrictive CORS config for hardening tests
const restrictiveCors = buildCorsHandler({
  allowedOrigins: ['https://app.example.com'],
  allowedMethods: ['GET'],
  allowedHeaders: ['Content-Type'],
  maxAge: 0,
});

const server = setupServer(permissiveCors);
beforeAll(() => server.listen());
afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers());
afterAll(() => server.close());

it('rejects cross-origin POST from disallowed origin', () => {
  server.use(restrictiveCors);
  // ... test that the browser honours the restricted CORS response
});
```

**Tradeoff:** In Node.js (Vitest/Jest), the browser does not actually enforce CORS — the `OPTIONS` handler will be called if your production code explicitly fires a preflight, but `fetch()` in Node.js does not enforce same-origin policy. This pattern is most useful in Playwright browser tests where the real Chromium enforces CORS, or when testing that your SDK/client code correctly sends preflight-required headers. For Node.js unit tests, `http.options()` is more useful for testing that your API client correctly handles `204 No Content` preflight responses.

---

### Pattern 275 — Fishery `factory.params()` for reusable named build configurations without extending the factory [official]

`factory.params()` creates a named variant of a factory with pre-set overrides, avoiding the need to create a subclass or a new `Factory.define()` call for each variant. This is the Fishery equivalent of named Object Mother methods and produces cleaner, self-documenting test code.

```typescript
import { Factory } from 'fishery';
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

interface Order {
  id: string;
  status: 'pending' | 'processing' | 'shipped' | 'delivered' | 'cancelled';
  totalCents: number;
  itemCount: number;
  customerId: string;
  shippedAt: Date | null;
  cancelledAt: Date | null;
  cancelReason: string | null;
}

const orderFactory = Factory.define<Order>(() => ({
  id: faker.string.uuid(),
  status: 'pending',
  totalCents: faker.number.int({ min: 1000, max: 50000 }),
  itemCount: faker.number.int({ min: 1, max: 10 }),
  customerId: faker.string.uuid(),
  shippedAt: null,
  cancelledAt: null,
  cancelReason: null,
}));

// Named configurations — no subclassing required
const shippedOrder = orderFactory.params({
  status: 'shipped',
  shippedAt: faker.date.recent({ days: 3 }),
});

const cancelledOrder = orderFactory.params({
  status: 'cancelled',
  cancelledAt: faker.date.recent({ days: 1 }),
  cancelReason: faker.helpers.arrayElement([
    'customer_request',
    'out_of_stock',
    'payment_failed',
    'fraud_suspected',
  ]),
});

const largeOrder = orderFactory.params({
  itemCount: faker.number.int({ min: 20, max: 100 }),
  totalCents: faker.number.int({ min: 100000, max: 1000000 }),
});

// Usage: clean, intention-revealing test data
const order = shippedOrder.build();
const bulkOrder = largeOrder.build({ customerId: 'cust_vip_001' });
const refundCandidate = cancelledOrder.build({ totalCents: 25000 });
```

**Tradeoff:** `factory.params()` evaluates faker calls at factory-definition time, not at `build()` time, if you call `faker.*()` inline in the `params()` argument. To ensure randomness per build, wrap dynamic values in a thunk via `factory.define()` with `transientParams` or use `params()` only for static enum/status overrides and let the base factory handle all dynamic fields. If the `params()` object contains a `faker.*()` call, all builds from that variant will share the same value for that field.

---

### Pattern 276 — `fc.ipV4()` and `fc.ipV6()` for network-address property testing in firewall-rule and routing-table tests [official]

`fast-check` provides `fc.ipV4()`, `fc.ipV4Extended()` (includes CIDR notation), and `fc.ipV6()` for generating valid IP addresses. These arbitraries immediately expose bugs in IP-range validators, subnet calculators, and access-control list parsers that fixed test data would never reach.

```typescript
import * as fc from 'fast-check';

// Production code: simple IP allowlist checker
function isAllowedIp(ip: string, allowlist: string[]): boolean {
  // Naive implementation — exact match only (intentionally buggy for testing)
  return allowlist.includes(ip);
}

function isPrivateIpV4(ip: string): boolean {
  const parts = ip.split('.').map(Number);
  return (
    parts[0] === 10 ||
    (parts[0] === 172 && parts[1] >= 16 && parts[1] <= 31) ||
    (parts[0] === 192 && parts[1] === 168)
  );
}

// Property: private IPv4 addresses are correctly identified
fc.assert(
  fc.property(
    fc.ipV4().filter(ip => {
      const first = parseInt(ip.split('.')[0], 10);
      return first === 10 || first === 172 || first === 192;
    }),
    (ip) => {
      // This will fail for 172.x.x.x when second octet is outside 16-31
      // and for 192.x.x.x when second octet is not 168 — surfacing the bug
      const result = isPrivateIpV4(ip);
      expect(typeof result).toBe('boolean');
    }
  )
);

// Property: no public IPv4 looks like a private address to our checker
fc.assert(
  fc.property(fc.ipV6(), (ip) => {
    // IPv6 addresses should never match the IPv4 private range check
    expect(() => isPrivateIpV4(ip)).not.toThrow();
  })
);
```

**Tradeoff:** `fc.ipV4Extended()` generates CIDR notation like `192.168.1.0/24` — do not use it where plain dotted-decimal is expected, as the `/` will cause most plain parsers to fail. Shrinking on `fc.ipV4()` moves toward `0.0.0.0`, which is the minimal IP address representation; this is useful for debugging but may trigger special-casing for the all-zeros address in production code. For tests specifically targeting `127.0.0.1` (loopback), use `fc.constant('127.0.0.1')` — `fc.ipV4()` will only rarely generate loopback addresses.

---

### Pattern 277 — `faker.vehicle.vin()` and `faker.vehicle.vrm()` for automotive domain test data [official]

The `faker.vehicle` module provides Vehicle Identification Numbers (VINs), Vehicle Registration Marks (VRMs), manufacturer names, fuel types, and model names. VINs follow the ISO 3779 17-character format and are used in automotive insurance, fleet management, and parts-ordering systems where format validation is critical.

```typescript
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';
import { Factory } from 'fishery';

interface VehicleRecord {
  vin: string;
  vrm: string;
  manufacturer: string;
  model: string;
  type: string;
  fuel: string;
  color: string;
  mileage: number;
  year: number;
}

const vehicleFactory = Factory.define<VehicleRecord>(() => {
  const year = faker.number.int({ min: 2000, max: 2024 });
  return {
    vin: faker.vehicle.vin(),
    vrm: faker.vehicle.vrm(),
    manufacturer: faker.vehicle.manufacturer(),
    model: faker.vehicle.model(),
    type: faker.vehicle.type(),
    fuel: faker.vehicle.fuel(),
    color: faker.vehicle.color(),
    mileage: faker.number.int({ min: 0, max: 250000 }),
    year,
  };
});

// Build vehicles for a fleet management test
const fleet = vehicleFactory.buildList(10);

// High-mileage vehicles for maintenance-alert tests
const highMileageVehicles = vehicleFactory.buildList(5, {
  mileage: faker.number.int({ min: 180000, max: 350000 }),
});

// Assert VIN format: 17 chars, no I/O/Q
fleet.forEach(v => {
  expect(v.vin).toHaveLength(17);
  expect(v.vin).toMatch(/^[A-HJ-NPR-Z0-9]{17}$/);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `faker.vehicle.vin()` generates structurally valid VINs (correct length, excluded characters) but the check-digit (position 9) may not validate against the official VIN check-digit algorithm (modulo-11 formula). If your production code runs check-digit validation, `faker.vehicle.vin()` will fail validation roughly 90% of the time. For check-digit-valid VINs, either use a custom generator that computes the check digit, or use the `vins` library, or bypass VIN validation in the factory with `faker.string.alphanumeric(17).replace(/[ioq]/gi, 'X')` and override the check digit position explicitly.

---

### Pattern 278 — `fc.date()` with `min`/`max` for time-bounded property testing of date-arithmetic and scheduling logic [official]

`fast-check`'s `fc.date()` arbitrary generates JavaScript `Date` objects across a configurable range. Unlike `faker.date.*()`, `fc.date()` participates in shrinking — when a date causes a failure, fast-check reduces toward the epoch or range boundary to find the minimal failing date.

```typescript
import * as fc from 'fast-check';

// Production scheduling logic under test
function isWithinBusinessHours(date: Date): boolean {
  const hour = date.getUTCHours();
  const day = date.getUTCDay(); // 0=Sun, 6=Sat
  return day >= 1 && day <= 5 && hour >= 9 && hour < 17;
}

function nextBusinessDay(date: Date): Date {
  const next = new Date(date);
  next.setUTCDate(next.getUTCDate() + 1);
  while (next.getUTCDay() === 0 || next.getUTCDay() === 6) {
    next.setUTCDate(next.getUTCDate() + 1);
  }
  return next;
}

// Property: nextBusinessDay always returns a weekday
fc.assert(
  fc.property(
    fc.date({ min: new Date('2020-01-01'), max: new Date('2030-12-31') }),
    (date) => {
      const next = nextBusinessDay(date);
      const day = next.getUTCDay();
      expect(day).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(1);
      expect(day).toBeLessThanOrEqual(5);
    }
  ),
  { numRuns: 1000 }
);

// Property: nextBusinessDay is always after the input date
fc.assert(
  fc.property(
    fc.date({ min: new Date('2020-01-01'), max: new Date('2029-12-30') }),
    (date) => {
      expect(nextBusinessDay(date).getTime()).toBeGreaterThan(date.getTime());
    }
  )
);
```

**Tradeoff:** `fc.date()` shrinks toward `new Date(0)` (Unix epoch, 1 January 1970) when no `min` is provided — this is rarely useful for business-logic tests. Always provide `{ min, max }` to constrain shrinking to your domain's meaningful date range. `fc.date()` generates dates with millisecond precision; if your code truncates to seconds or days, many of the generated dates will produce identical effective values after truncation, which reduces the effective coverage. For date-only (no time) logic, map `fc.date()` through `d => new Date(d.toISOString().split('T')[0])` to strip the time component.

---

### Pattern 279 — MSW `bypass()` utility for selectively passing requests through to the real network in integration tests [official]

MSW's `bypass()` function allows a handler to explicitly forward a request to the real network, bypassing interception. This is essential in hybrid integration test setups where most API calls should be mocked but specific requests (e.g., to a shared test database, a local service, or a third-party sandbox) should reach the real endpoint.

```typescript
import { http, bypass, HttpResponse } from 'msw';
import { setupServer } from 'msw/node';

// Factory for building auth token fixtures
function buildAuthHeader(userId: string): string {
  return `Bearer test-token-${userId}`;
}

const server = setupServer(
  // Mock all product API calls with factory data
  http.get('https://api.example.com/products/:id', ({ params }) => {
    return HttpResponse.json({
      id: params.id,
      name: 'Mocked Product',
      price: 1999,
      inStock: true,
    });
  }),

  // Pass auth calls through to the real local auth service
  http.post('https://auth.local:3001/token', async ({ request }) => {
    // Forward to the real auth server — useful when testing against
    // a real local service while mocking all external dependencies
    const realResponse = await fetch(bypass(request));
    return realResponse;
  }),

  // Mock the analytics endpoint as a no-op to prevent test noise
  http.post('https://analytics.example.com/events', () => {
    return new HttpResponse(null, { status: 204 });
  })
);

beforeAll(() => server.listen({ onUnhandledRequest: 'error' }));
afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers());
afterAll(() => server.close());

it('loads product with mocked data while auth token is real', async () => {
  const header = buildAuthHeader('user-123');
  // The auth call goes to the real local service;
  // the product call returns the mocked factory response
  const response = await fetch('https://api.example.com/products/42', {
    headers: { Authorization: header },
  });
  expect(response.status).toBe(200);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `bypass()` defeats the isolation guarantee of MSW — any test that uses `bypass()` depends on real network availability and introduces flakiness in offline environments or CI runners without network access. Restrict `bypass()` usage to a dedicated integration test layer (e.g., `*.integration.test.ts` files) and never use it in unit tests. Use `onUnhandledRequest: 'error'` in `server.listen()` to catch unintentional passthroughs that should have been mocked — `bypass()` calls are intentional and do not trigger this error handler.

---

### Pattern 280 — `faker.string.nanoid()` for URL-safe, collision-resistant short ID fixture generation [official]

`faker.string.nanoid()` (available since Faker v8) generates Nano IDs — URL-safe, alphanumeric IDs shorter than UUIDs. These are the format used by many modern databases (PlanetScale, Supabase row IDs, URL shorteners, Prisma cuid2 alternatives) and are preferable to UUIDs in fixture data for tests that assert URL path structure or ID length constraints.

```typescript
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

interface Resource {
  id: string;            // nanoid (21 chars, URL-safe)
  slug: string;          // custom length nanoid for slugs
  shortCode: string;     // 8-char nanoid for share links
  createdAt: Date;
  updatedAt: Date;
}

function buildResource(overrides: Partial<Resource> = {}): Resource {
  const now = new Date();
  return {
    id: faker.string.nanoid(),             // default 21 chars
    slug: faker.string.nanoid(32),         // longer for slugs
    shortCode: faker.string.nanoid(8),     // short for share links
    createdAt: faker.date.past({ years: 1 }),
    updatedAt: now,
    ...overrides,
  };
}

// Test: URL-safe IDs do not break URL path parsing
const resource = buildResource();
const url = new URL(`https://app.example.com/r/${resource.shortCode}`);
expect(url.pathname).toBe(`/r/${resource.shortCode}`);
expect(resource.id).toMatch(/^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{21}$/);
expect(resource.shortCode).toHaveLength(8);

// Build a list for pagination tests
const resources = Array.from({ length: 50 }, buildResource);
const ids = resources.map(r => r.id);
// All IDs should be unique
expect(new Set(ids).size).toBe(ids.length);
```

**Tradeoff:** `faker.string.nanoid()` uses the alphabet `A-Za-z0-9_-` (URL-safe) by default. If your database or ID column uses a different character set (e.g., Cuid2 uses lowercase + digits only), the generated IDs will not match the production format and may cause false-positive format validations. For Cuid2-compatible IDs, use `faker.string.fromCharacters('abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789', 25)`. Nano IDs are not time-ordered — for tests asserting chronological sort by ID, use UUID v7 or ULID patterns instead.

---

### Pattern 281 — `fc.mapToConstant()` for enumerating a finite set of discriminated-union values in property tests [official]

`fc.mapToConstant()` maps integer samples to constant values in a weighted fashion, making it the idiomatic fast-check way to generate members of a TypeScript discriminated union or enum in property tests. Unlike `fc.constantFrom()`, it allows non-uniform weighting so that rare variants are generated proportionally less often but still covered.

```typescript
import * as fc from 'fast-check';

type PaymentMethod =
  | { type: 'card'; last4: string; brand: 'visa' | 'mastercard' | 'amex' }
  | { type: 'bank_transfer'; iban: string }
  | { type: 'wallet'; provider: 'paypal' | 'apple_pay' | 'google_pay' };

const paymentMethodArbitrary: fc.Arbitrary<PaymentMethod> = fc.mapToConstant(
  {
    num: 6, // 6 weight units for card (most common)
    build: (n) => ({
      type: 'card' as const,
      last4: String(1000 + (n % 9000)).padStart(4, '0'),
      brand: (['visa', 'mastercard', 'amex'] as const)[n % 3],
    }),
  },
  {
    num: 2, // 2 weight units for bank transfer
    build: (n) => ({
      type: 'bank_transfer' as const,
      iban: `GB${String(n).padStart(22, '0')}`,
    }),
  },
  {
    num: 2, // 2 weight units for wallet
    build: (n) => ({
      type: 'wallet' as const,
      provider: (['paypal', 'apple_pay', 'google_pay'] as const)[n % 3],
    }),
  }
);

// Property: all payment methods produce a non-empty display string
fc.assert(
  fc.property(paymentMethodArbitrary, (method) => {
    const display = (() => {
      switch (method.type) {
        case 'card': return `${method.brand} ****${method.last4}`;
        case 'bank_transfer': return `Bank: ${method.iban.slice(0, 8)}...`;
        case 'wallet': return `${method.provider}`;
      }
    })();
    expect(display.length).toBeGreaterThan(0);
  }),
  { numRuns: 500 }
);
```

**Tradeoff:** `fc.mapToConstant()` requires each `build` function to be deterministic given `n` — the integer argument is drawn from `[0, num)`. If your `build` function calls `faker.*()` or `Math.random()`, the output will be non-deterministic and shrinking will be unreliable (the shrunken input `n` maps to a different value on re-execution). Keep `build` functions as pure mappings from integer to constant value. For generating full entity objects with faker randomness, compose `fc.mapToConstant()` for the discriminant only and use `fc.record()` for the payload fields.

---

### Pattern 282 — `faker.string.hexadecimal()` for generating hex fixture values in colour, crypto-hash, and binary-encoding tests [official]

`faker.string.hexadecimal()` generates hexadecimal strings of a given length, useful for color codes, hash digests, API keys, and binary-encoding tests. The `{ length, casing, prefix }` options provide full control over the output format, making it suitable for consistent snapshot comparisons and format-validation tests.

```typescript
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

interface CryptographicFixture {
  sha256Hash: string;
  md5Hash: string;
  apiKey: string;
  webhookSecret: string;
  colorHex: string;
  sessionToken: string;
}

function buildCryptographicFixture(
  overrides: Partial<CryptographicFixture> = {}
): CryptographicFixture {
  return {
    sha256Hash: faker.string.hexadecimal({ length: 64, casing: 'lower', prefix: '' }),
    md5Hash: faker.string.hexadecimal({ length: 32, casing: 'lower', prefix: '' }),
    apiKey: `sk_test_${faker.string.hexadecimal({ length: 32, casing: 'lower', prefix: '' })}`,
    webhookSecret: `whsec_${faker.string.base64({ length: 32 })}`,
    colorHex: `#${faker.string.hexadecimal({ length: 6, casing: 'lower', prefix: '' })}`,
    sessionToken: faker.string.hexadecimal({ length: 128, casing: 'lower', prefix: '' }),
    ...overrides,
  };
}

// Test: all hex values are the correct length and character set
const fixture = buildCryptographicFixture();
expect(fixture.sha256Hash).toHaveLength(64);
expect(fixture.sha256Hash).toMatch(/^[0-9a-f]{64}$/);
expect(fixture.colorHex).toMatch(/^#[0-9a-f]{6}$/);
expect(fixture.apiKey).toMatch(/^sk_test_[0-9a-f]{32}$/);

// Build a set of API keys for a key-rotation test
const rotatedKeys = Array.from({ length: 5 }, () =>
  buildCryptographicFixture().apiKey
);
expect(new Set(rotatedKeys).size).toBe(5); // all unique
```

**Tradeoff:** `faker.string.hexadecimal()` with `{ prefix: '' }` is the correct way to get a bare hex string (no `0x` prefix). The `casing` option (`'lower'` | `'upper'` | `'mixed'`) defaults to `'mixed'` — always specify `'lower'` explicitly for snapshot tests to prevent case-mismatch failures. For cryptographically secure fixture values (e.g., testing a secrets manager), use `node:crypto`'s `randomBytes(n).toString('hex')` instead of Faker — Faker is not cryptographically random and should not be used where actual entropy is required.

### Pattern 283 — Fishery `afterBuild` hook for synchronous post-construction transforms and computed field population [official]

Fishery's `afterBuild` lifecycle hook runs after a factory builds an object and before it is returned. It is the correct place for computed fields (e.g., derived slugs, checksums, denormalised counts) that depend on other randomly generated fields, keeping the factory DRY and ensuring consistency without requiring callers to pass derived values manually.

```typescript
import { Factory } from 'fishery';
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

interface BlogPost {
  id: string;
  title: string;
  slug: string;           // computed from title
  body: string;
  excerpt: string;        // first 160 chars of body
  wordCount: number;      // computed from body
  authorId: string;
  publishedAt: Date | null;
  isPublished: boolean;   // derived from publishedAt
  tags: string[];
  tagCount: number;       // computed from tags.length
}

const blogPostFactory = Factory.define<BlogPost>(({ afterBuild }) => {
  const body = faker.lorem.paragraphs(faker.number.int({ min: 2, max: 5 }));
  const tags = faker.helpers.uniqueArray(
    () => faker.word.noun(),
    faker.number.int({ min: 1, max: 5 })
  );
  const publishedAt = faker.helpers.maybe(() => faker.date.past({ years: 1 }), {
    probability: 0.7,
  }) ?? null;

  afterBuild((post) => {
    // Derive slug from whatever title was set (including overrides)
    post.slug = post.title
      .toLowerCase()
      .replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, '-')
      .replace(/^-|-$/g, '');
    // Derive excerpt from whatever body was set
    post.excerpt = post.body.slice(0, 160).trimEnd();
    // Derive wordCount from body
    post.wordCount = post.body.split(/\s+/).length;
    // Derive isPublished from publishedAt
    post.isPublished = post.publishedAt !== null &&
      post.publishedAt.getTime() <= Date.now();
    // Derive tagCount from tags array
    post.tagCount = post.tags.length;
  });

  return {
    id: faker.string.uuid(),
    title: faker.lorem.sentence({ min: 3, max: 8 }),
    slug: '',          // populated by afterBuild
    body,
    excerpt: '',       // populated by afterBuild
    wordCount: 0,      // populated by afterBuild
    authorId: faker.string.uuid(),
    publishedAt,
    isPublished: false, // populated by afterBuild
    tags,
    tagCount: 0,       // populated by afterBuild
  };
});

// Override the title — slug will still be correctly derived
const post = blogPostFactory.build({ title: 'Hello World Test Post' });
expect(post.slug).toBe('hello-world-test-post');
expect(post.tagCount).toBe(post.tags.length);
expect(post.wordCount).toBeGreaterThan(0);
```

**Tradeoff:** `afterBuild` runs after overrides are applied, so computed fields always reflect the final values of their source fields — including any caller-supplied overrides. However, if a caller overrides a computed field directly (e.g., `blogPostFactory.build({ slug: 'custom-slug' })`), `afterBuild` will overwrite that override because it runs after `build()` merges the overrides. To allow callers to override computed fields, add an early-return guard: `if (post.slug !== '') return;` inside `afterBuild`. This is a deliberate design choice: decide per-factory whether computed fields should be overridable.

## Community Gotcha #176 — `faker.helpers.uniqueArray()` with a generator function uses `JSON.stringify` for uniqueness tracking — objects with identical JSON but different property order are treated as non-identical, producing spurious duplicates [community]

**WHY: `faker.helpers.uniqueArray(generator, count)` tracks uniqueness by calling `JSON.stringify()` on each generated value and storing the result in a `Set`. When `generator` returns objects — for example `() => faker.airline.airport()` — two airports with the same `{ name, iataCode }` values are considered duplicates (correctly). However, objects that differ only in property ordering produce different JSON strings in some JavaScript environments (`{ a: 1, b: 2 }` vs `{ b: 2, a: 1 }`) and are treated as distinct by `uniqueArray`, even though they represent the same logical value. This causes `uniqueArray()` to produce arrays with more elements than expected when the objects are logically equivalent but structurally different in property order — the count is satisfied but the "uniqueness" guarantee has false positives. More dangerously, objects that are logically distinct but have identical JSON (e.g., due to non-enumerable or Symbol-keyed properties being omitted by `JSON.stringify`) are incorrectly treated as duplicates and retried indefinitely, eventually exhausting the `maxTime` budget and throwing a `"Unable to generate enough unique values"` error.**

Fix: for object generators, always return objects with a consistent property order, or provide a custom comparator. Alternatively, extract the scalar key field and use `faker.helpers.uniqueArray(() => faker.airline.airport().iataCode, count)` to compare by string IATA code, then map to full objects. If true uniqueness on a specific field matters, validate after generation: `expect(new Set(results.map(r => r.key)).size).toBe(results.length)`.

## Community Gotcha #177 — `fc.date({ min, max })` generates UTC timestamps but `.toLocaleDateString()` returns host-timezone-dependent values — the same fast-check seed produces different date strings in CI (UTC) vs developer machines (UTC+N) [community]

**WHY: `fc.date()` generates `Date` objects using `new Date(n)` where `n` is a Unix timestamp in milliseconds. The `Date` object stores UTC internally but `.toLocaleDateString()`, `.getMonth()`, `.getDate()`, and `.getHours()` return values in the local time zone of the host OS. A CI runner running in UTC sees `new Date('2024-03-31T23:30:00Z')` as "31 March 2024", but a developer machine set to UTC+1 sees it as "1 April 2024". Property tests that call `.toLocaleDateString()` or compare `.getDate()` directly will pass on the developer machine and fail in CI (or vice versa) for the same fast-check seed. This creates a class of seed-reproducible-but-environment-sensitive failures that are extremely confusing to debug — the seed is known from CI output, but running the same seed locally produces a different date comparison result because the local-time methods read from the OS clock timezone.**

Fix: always use UTC methods (`date.getUTCDate()`, `date.getUTCMonth()`, `date.toISOString().split('T')[0]`) instead of local methods in property-tested date logic. Set `TZ=UTC` in your CI environment and in your local `.env.test` to ensure consistent behaviour across all environments. Add an ESLint rule flagging `.getDate()`, `.getMonth()`, and `.toLocaleDateString()` calls in test files as errors.
