## Community Gotcha #178 — Fishery `factory.buildList(n)` sequence counter is module-level and shared across Vitest workers when `isolate: false` — parallel test files produce non-deterministic sequential IDs and assertions on `id === 1` fail intermittently [community]

**WHY: Fishery maintains a per-factory sequence counter as a module-level variable. In Vitest with `isolate: false` (or when using the `vmForks` pool where modules are shared across workers), two test files that both import the same factory and call `factory.buildList()` share the same sequence counter. This means file A calls `factory.buildList(5)` and gets IDs 1–5, then file B calls `factory.buildList(5)` and gets IDs 6–10 instead of 1–5. Tests that assert `expect(result[0].id).toBe(1)` fail non-deterministically depending on which file runs first. The failure is intermittent because with `isolate: true` (default in Vitest with `vmForks`), each test file gets a fresh module instance — but a single `isolate: false` file in the suite can corrupt the sequence for all files in the same worker. This is also triggered when using Vitest's `projects` config with shared worker pools.**

Fix: call `factory.rewindSequence()` in `beforeEach()` to reset the sequence counter to 1 at the start of each test. Do not assert on exact sequence values; instead test that the sequence is monotonically increasing: `const ids = list.map(r => r.id); expect(ids).toEqual([...ids].sort((a, b) => a - b))`. If exact starting values are required, use explicit overrides: `factory.build({ id: 1 })`.

---

## Community Gotcha #179 — MSW `HttpResponse.text()` does not set `Content-Type: text/plain` automatically — production code that inspects the content-type header before parsing takes the wrong code path in tests [community]

**WHY: `HttpResponse.json(data)` correctly sets `Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8`. However, `HttpResponse.text(body)` does not set any `Content-Type` header unless you explicitly provide one. When production code calls `response.text()` after fetching, the missing content type is not an issue. But when production code checks `response.headers.get('content-type')` before deciding how to parse the response (a common pattern in generic API client wrappers), `HttpResponse.text()` without an explicit content type causes the client to misidentify the response format. This surfaces as a bug where the mock returns the correct data but the client code takes the `else` branch (treating it as JSON, binary, or unknown) because the content-type header is absent. The test passes (the mock is called and data is returned) but the production parsing logic is exercised on the wrong code path — the test provides false confidence that the correct branch is being tested.**

Fix: always include explicit content-type headers in MSW `HttpResponse.text()` responses: `new HttpResponse(body, { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'text/plain; charset=utf-8' } })`. Create a factory function `buildTextResponse(body: string)` that always includes the correct headers rather than calling `HttpResponse.text()` directly.

---

## Community Gotcha #180 — `fc.record()` with `{ requiredKeys: [] }` is typed as the full record type (not `Partial<T>`) — TypeScript does not warn when property-function code accesses potentially-absent keys, hiding runtime `TypeError` bugs [community]

**WHY: `fc.record({ a: fc.string(), b: fc.integer() }, { requiredKeys: [] })` tells fast-check that all keys are optional — the generated objects may be `{}`, `{ a: 'x' }`, `{ b: 1 }`, or `{ a: 'x', b: 1 }`. However, the TypeScript type inferred by `fc.record()` is `{ a: string; b: number }` — not `Partial<{ a: string; b: number }>`. This means that inside the `fc.property()` callback, TypeScript does not warn you when you access `record.a.toUpperCase()` — even though `record.a` is `undefined` when the key is absent. The property test will throw `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'toUpperCase')` at runtime for the `{}` sample, but TypeScript compilation passes without error. This is one of the few cases where fast-check's TypeScript types are intentionally unsound for ergonomic reasons — the runtime behaviour is correct (the test fails with a clear error), but the type system gives false confidence that all accesses are safe, leading developers to think the property function logic is wrong rather than the data access pattern.**

Fix: use `fc.record()` with `{ requiredKeys: [] }` only when you explicitly want to test that your production code handles missing keys gracefully. In the property function body, use optional chaining: `record.a?.toUpperCase() ?? ''`. Alternatively, define separate arbitraries for the full and partial cases and test them independently.

---

### Pattern 284 — `faker.git.commitSha()` for Versioning and Deployment Test Data  [official]

The `faker.git` module provides `commitSha()`, `commitMessage()`, `branch()`, and related methods for generating realistic version-control metadata. These are directly useful in factories for CI/CD system tests, deployment pipelines, feature-flag tests tied to commit ranges, and changelog generators.

**Why it matters:** Tests for version display, deploy history, and branch-based feature routing require commit SHAs that look realistic but are never real. Hardcoded hex strings break when validation regex changes; `faker.git.commitSha()` produces a correctly-formatted 40-char SHA every time.

```typescript
// factories/deployment.factory.ts — git metadata for CI/CD test data
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

interface DeployEvent {
  id: string;
  commitSha: string;       // 40-char hex SHA
  shortSha: string;        // 7-char short SHA
  branch: string;
  message: string;
  author: string;
  deployedAt: Date;
  environment: 'staging' | 'production';
  status: 'pending' | 'running' | 'success' | 'failed';
}

export function buildDeployEvent(overrides: Partial<DeployEvent> = {}): DeployEvent {
  const sha = faker.git.commitSha();
  return {
    id: faker.string.uuid(),
    commitSha: sha,
    shortSha: sha.slice(0, 7),
    branch: faker.git.branch(),
    message: faker.git.commitMessage(),
    author: faker.internet.username(),
    deployedAt: faker.date.recent({ days: 7 }),
    environment: faker.helpers.arrayElement(['staging', 'production']),
    status: 'success',
    ...overrides,
  };
}

// Build a deploy history — useful for pagination and filtering tests
export function buildDeployHistory(count = 10): DeployEvent[] {
  return faker.helpers.multiple(() => buildDeployEvent(), { count });
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `faker.git.commitSha()` generates random valid-format SHAs, not real commits from any repo. Tests that verify commit existence against a real git repo need actual fixtures; this pattern covers display and validation logic only. [official]

### Pattern 285 — `fc.oneof()` Weighted Union Arbitrary for Realistic Mixed-Type Distributions  [official]

`fast-check`'s `fc.oneof()` selects among multiple arbitraries with equal or weighted probability. Unlike `fc.constantFrom()` which picks from a fixed list of values, `fc.oneof()` composes arbitraries — making it the right tool for testing code that handles multiple concrete types in a union (e.g., `string | number | null`, a discriminated union with varying field shapes).

**Why it matters:** Code that handles type unions often has edge cases at the boundaries between types. Property tests using only `fc.string()` miss the `null` branch; `fc.oneof()` generates a balanced cross-section of all union members automatically.

```typescript
// arbitraries/product-price.arb.ts — oneof for nullable price union
import * as fc from 'fast-check';

// Price can be a positive integer (cents), 0 (free), or null (price TBD)
export const priceArb: fc.Arbitrary<number | null> = fc.oneof(
  { weight: 10, arbitrary: fc.integer({ min: 1, max: 1_000_000 }) }, // paid
  { weight: 1,  arbitrary: fc.constant(0) },                         // free
  { weight: 2,  arbitrary: fc.constant(null) },                      // TBD
);

// Discriminated union arbitrary — each member has different required fields
type PaymentMethod =
  | { type: 'card'; last4: string; brand: string }
  | { type: 'bank'; sortCode: string; accountLast4: string }
  | { type: 'wallet'; provider: string };

export const paymentMethodArb: fc.Arbitrary<PaymentMethod> = fc.oneof(
  fc.record({
    type: fc.constant('card' as const),
    last4: fc.stringMatching(/^\d{4}$/),
    brand: fc.constantFrom('visa', 'mastercard', 'amex'),
  }),
  fc.record({
    type: fc.constant('bank' as const),
    sortCode: fc.stringMatching(/^\d{2}-\d{2}-\d{2}$/),
    accountLast4: fc.stringMatching(/^\d{4}$/),
  }),
  fc.record({
    type: fc.constant('wallet' as const),
    provider: fc.constantFrom('paypal', 'applepay', 'googlepay'),
  }),
);

// Property test: paymentDisplayLabel never throws for any valid payment method
fc.assert(
  fc.property(paymentMethodArb, (pm) => {
    const label = getPaymentDisplayLabel(pm);
    return typeof label === 'string' && label.length > 0;
  }),
  { numRuns: 500 }
);
```

**Tradeoff:** Weighted `oneof` requires manual weight tuning to match production distributions. Unweighted `oneof` (all equal probability) is fine for correctness tests but may under-exercise the most common production code path. For regression-risk reduction, weight toward the most-used union member. [official]

### Pattern 286 — `faker.finance.bic()` and `faker.finance.iban()` for Banking Domain Factories  [official]

The `faker.finance` module includes `bic()` (Bank Identifier Code / SWIFT code) and `iban()` (International Bank Account Number) generators. Both produce format-valid but non-real banking identifiers — essential for testing payment flows, bank account validation, and SEPA transfer factories in fintech applications.

**Why it matters:** Banking validation logic often uses regex or checksum algorithms (IBAN check digits use MOD 97). Using `faker.finance.iban()` guarantees the generated value passes standard IBAN checksum validation — unlike a hardcoded string that may only cover one country format.

```typescript
// factories/banking.factory.ts — IBAN and BIC test data (faker.finance)
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

interface BankAccount {
  id: string;
  ownerId: string;
  iban: string;        // ISO 13616 — country-specific format, valid checksum
  bic: string;         // ISO 9362 — 8 or 11 chars
  currency: string;
  accountName: string;
  isVerified: boolean;
  addedAt: Date;
}

export function buildBankAccount(overrides: Partial<BankAccount> = {}): BankAccount {
  return {
    id: faker.string.uuid(),
    ownerId: faker.string.uuid(),
    // faker.finance.iban() generates a structurally valid IBAN
    // Optionally constrain to a specific country: iban({ countryCode: 'DE' })
    iban: faker.finance.iban(),
    bic: faker.finance.bic(),
    currency: faker.finance.currencyCode(),
    accountName: faker.person.fullName(),
    isVerified: false,
    addedAt: faker.date.recent({ days: 90 }),
    ...overrides,
  };
}

// Factory for a verified German bank account (SEPA zone test)
export function buildVerifiedDeAccount(): BankAccount {
  return buildBankAccount({
    iban: faker.finance.iban({ countryCode: 'DE' }),
    bic: faker.finance.bic(),
    currency: 'EUR',
    isVerified: true,
  });
}

// Build a list of accounts for pagination tests
export function buildBankAccountList(count: number): BankAccount[] {
  return Array.from({ length: count }, () => buildBankAccount());
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `faker.finance.iban()` passes standard IBAN checksum validation. However, some banks perform deeper validation (correct BIC-to-country-code mapping). For tests requiring bank-specific validation, hardcode the known-valid combination rather than relying on faker's random BIC/IBAN pairing. [official]

---

### Pattern 287 — `fc.scheduler()` for Async Operation Ordering in Test Data Pipelines  [official]

`fast-check`'s `fc.scheduler()` provides a controllable event-loop scheduler for testing code that depends on the *order* in which multiple concurrent promises resolve. This is particularly relevant to test data factories that trigger parallel DB inserts or parallel API calls — the scheduler lets you assert that the system behaves correctly regardless of which promise resolves first.

**Why it matters:** Factories that seed relational data in parallel (e.g., create user and order concurrently) may expose race conditions in the application code if the order-of-resolution matters. The scheduler makes it possible to enumerate all resolution orderings systematically.

```typescript
// specs/concurrent-factory.property.test.ts
// fc.scheduler() tests that checkout works regardless of payment/inventory promise order
import * as fc from 'fast-check';
import { test } from 'vitest';
import { buildOrder } from '../factories/order.factory';

test('checkout result is independent of concurrent service resolution order', async () => {
  await fc.assert(
    fc.asyncProperty(
      fc.scheduler(),
      async (s) => {
        // Schedule two concurrent service calls — scheduler controls which resolves first
        const paymentPromise = s.scheduleFunction(
          async () => ({ success: true, chargeId: 'ch_001' })
        )();
        const inventoryPromise = s.scheduleFunction(
          async () => ({ available: true, reserved: 1 })
        )();

        // Order created with factory data — the SUT calls both services concurrently
        const order = buildOrder({ status: 'pending', totalCents: 4999 });
        const checkoutPromise = checkoutService.process(order, {
          paymentPromise,
          inventoryPromise,
        });

        // Let the scheduler run all pending tasks in some order
        await s.waitAll();

        const result = await checkoutPromise;
        // Invariant: result must be 'success' regardless of which promise resolved first
        return result.status === 'success';
      }
    ),
    { numRuns: 100 }
  );
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `fc.scheduler()` requires the code under test to accept promises as arguments (dependency injection). Tightly coupled code that internally creates promises (e.g., `fetch()` calls inside a service method) cannot be scheduled without additional mocking. Combine with MSW handler ordering for HTTP-layer scheduling tests. [official]

---

### Pattern 288 — `faker.color.hsl()` and `faker.color.rgb()` for Design-System and UI Test Data  [official]

The `faker.color` module provides `hsl()`, `rgb()`, `hex()`, `cmyk()`, and `oklch()` colour generators with configurable format options. This is directly applicable to tests for design-token systems, CSS-in-JS themes, colour palette validation, and accessibility contrast-ratio calculations.

**Why it matters:** UI factories that hardcode colour values like `'#ff0000'` cannot test the full range of valid colours a user might save in a theme editor. `faker.color.hsl()` generates colours distributed across the full HSL gamut, exercising the entire colour parsing and contrast validation pipeline.

```typescript
// factories/design-token.factory.ts — colour token test data
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

interface ColorToken {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  value: string;        // CSS colour string (various formats)
  format: 'hex' | 'rgb' | 'hsl' | 'oklch';
  isAccessible: boolean; // WCAG AA contrast with white background
  category: 'brand' | 'semantic' | 'neutral';
}

export function buildColorToken(overrides: Partial<ColorToken> = {}): ColorToken {
  const format = faker.helpers.arrayElement(['hex', 'rgb', 'hsl', 'oklch'] as const);
  const value = (() => {
    switch (format) {
      case 'hex':  return faker.color.hex();
      case 'rgb':  return faker.color.rgb({ format: 'css' });  // 'rgb(R, G, B)'
      case 'hsl':  return faker.color.hsl({ format: 'css' });  // 'hsl(H, S%, L%)'
      case 'oklch': return faker.color.oklch({ format: 'css' }); // 'oklch(L C H)'
    }
  })();

  return {
    id: faker.string.uuid(),
    name: `${faker.word.adjective()}-${faker.color.human()}`,
    value,
    format,
    isAccessible: faker.datatype.boolean(),
    category: faker.helpers.arrayElement(['brand', 'semantic', 'neutral']),
    ...overrides,
  };
}

// Build a complete design token palette for theme-editor tests
export function buildColorPalette(size = 12): ColorToken[] {
  return Array.from({ length: size }, (_, i) => buildColorToken({
    name: `token-${i + 1}`,
  }));
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `faker.color.hsl({ format: 'css' })` generates syntactically valid CSS colour strings. Tests that validate WCAG contrast ratios need to parse the colour back to RGB — add a `colorToRgb()` helper or use a library like `chroma-js` in test helpers. Do not use `faker.color.*` for snapshot tests — values change every run. [official]

---

### Pattern 289 — `fc.letrec()` for Recursive and Self-Referential Test Data Structures  [official]

`fc.letrec()` enables mutually recursive arbitraries — essential for generating tree structures, nested comments, category hierarchies, and any domain entity that can contain children of the same type. Without `letrec`, generating recursive structures requires manual depth-limiting and is prone to stack overflows.

**Why it matters:** Comment threads, file-system trees, org-chart hierarchies, and BOM (bill-of-materials) structures are all recursive. Tests for render-depth limits, infinite-scroll detection, and recursive aggregation algorithms need factories that produce these structures at controlled depths.

```typescript
// arbitraries/comment-tree.arb.ts — recursive comment thread arbitrary
import * as fc from 'fast-check';
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

interface Comment {
  id: string;
  body: string;
  authorId: string;
  depth: number;
  replies: Comment[];
}

// fc.letrec() defines mutually recursive arbitraries without forward-reference errors
export const commentArb = fc.letrec<{ comment: Comment; replies: Comment[] }>(
  (tie) => ({
    comment: fc.record({
      id:       fc.string({ minLength: 8, maxLength: 12 }),
      body:     fc.string({ minLength: 10, maxLength: 300 }),
      authorId: fc.string({ minLength: 8, maxLength: 12 }),
      depth:    fc.integer({ min: 0, max: 5 }),
      // replies references 'replies' — controlled by depth to avoid infinite recursion
      replies:  tie('replies'),
    }),
    // replies: 0–3 child comments, each recursing one level deeper
    replies: fc.array(tie('comment'), { minLength: 0, maxLength: 3 }),
  })
).comment;

// Property test: comment tree render never throws at any depth
fc.assert(
  fc.property(commentArb, (root) => {
    const rendered = renderCommentTree(root);
    return typeof rendered === 'string' && rendered.length > 0;
  }),
  { numRuns: 200 }
);
```

**Tradeoff:** `fc.letrec()` can generate deeply nested structures that cause performance issues in slow rendering code. Always set `maxLength` on recursive arrays and cap depth explicitly. For DB integration tests, use `buildCommentTree(maxDepth: 3)` with explicit depth control rather than property-based generation — unbounded trees can produce thousands of DB rows per test. [official]

---

### Pattern 290 — `faker.music.genre()` and `faker.music.songName()` for Media Domain Factories  [official]

The `faker.music` module provides `genre()` and `songName()` generators. These are relevant for factories in music streaming, playlist management, audio metadata, and content recommendation tests where domain-realistic strings matter for category filtering, search indexing, and display truncation logic.

**Why it matters:** Using `faker.lorem.word()` for a music genre produces strings like `"aliquam"` that pass through genre-specific display logic (e.g., genre badge colour mapping) in the wrong branch. `faker.music.genre()` produces strings from a realistic genre vocabulary — exposing bugs in genre-conditional logic that lorem text would miss.

```typescript
// factories/track.factory.ts — music track test data
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

interface Track {
  id: string;
  title: string;
  artist: string;
  albumId: string;
  genre: string;
  durationSecs: number;    // must be > 0
  releaseYear: number;     // 1950–2026
  isExplicit: boolean;
  streamCount: number;
  isrc: string;            // International Standard Recording Code (12 chars)
}

export function buildTrack(overrides: Partial<Track> = {}): Track {
  return {
    id: faker.string.uuid(),
    title: faker.music.songName(),
    artist: faker.person.fullName(),
    albumId: faker.string.uuid(),
    genre: faker.music.genre(),
    durationSecs: faker.number.int({ min: 30, max: 600 }),
    releaseYear: faker.number.int({ min: 1950, max: 2026 }),
    isExplicit: faker.datatype.boolean({ probability: 0.15 }),
    streamCount: faker.number.int({ min: 0, max: 10_000_000 }),
    // ISRC: CC-XXX-YY-NNNNN  (2-letter country, 3-char registrant, 2-digit year, 5-digit designation)
    isrc: `${faker.location.countryCode('alpha-2')}-${faker.string.alpha({ length: 3, casing: 'upper' })}-${faker.string.numeric(2)}-${faker.string.numeric(5)}`,
    ...overrides,
  };
}

// Object Mother variants for genre-specific display tests
export const TrackMother = {
  explicit: (): Track => buildTrack({ isExplicit: true }),
  viral: (): Track => buildTrack({ streamCount: faker.number.int({ min: 1_000_000, max: 10_000_000 }) }),
  classical: (): Track => buildTrack({ genre: 'Classical', durationSecs: faker.number.int({ min: 120, max: 3600 }) }),
};
```

**Tradeoff:** `faker.music.genre()` draws from a limited built-in vocabulary (~20 genres). If the application under test has a specific closed set of genre codes (e.g., Spotify genre taxonomy), use `faker.helpers.arrayElement(ALLOWED_GENRES)` instead to avoid generating genres outside the acceptable set. [official]

### Pattern 291 — MSW `http.all()` Catch-All Handler for Unmatched Request Auditing  [official]

MSW's `http.all(url, handler)` intercepts any HTTP method (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH, OPTIONS, HEAD) at the given URL pattern. When combined with a `passthrough()` response, it acts as a transparent audit handler — logging all requests that pass through the mock server without affecting their response. This is useful for detecting unexpected API calls from factory-seeded test scenarios.

**Why it matters:** Factory-heavy tests may trigger unexpected API calls through side effects (e.g., a factory `create()` that triggers a background email notification fetch). Without visibility into all outbound requests, these side effects are invisible in test output. An `http.all()` audit handler surfaces them as warnings without breaking the test.

```typescript
// mocks/audit-handler.ts — MSW catch-all audit handler
import { http, passthrough, HttpResponse } from 'msw';

const unexpectedRequests: string[] = [];

// Catch-all handler — logs any URL not matched by domain-specific handlers
// Place LAST in the handler array so domain handlers take precedence
export const auditHandler = http.all('*', ({ request }) => {
  const url = new URL(request.url);
  // Ignore known-safe domains (localhost, test data server)
  if (!url.hostname.includes('localhost') && !url.hostname.includes('127.0.0.1')) {
    unexpectedRequests.push(`[AUDIT] Unexpected outbound request: ${request.method} ${request.url}`);
    console.warn(`[MSW audit] Unmatched: ${request.method} ${request.url}`);
  }
  return passthrough(); // do not block the request — let it through
});

export function getUnexpectedRequests(): string[] {
  return [...unexpectedRequests];
}

export function clearAuditLog(): void {
  unexpectedRequests.length = 0;
}
```

```typescript
// vitest.setup.ts — audit handler wired into the MSW server
import { setupServer } from 'msw/node';
import { domainHandlers } from './mocks/handlers';
import { auditHandler, clearAuditLog, getUnexpectedRequests } from './mocks/audit-handler';

// auditHandler MUST be last — domain handlers take priority
const server = setupServer(...domainHandlers, auditHandler);

beforeAll(() => server.listen({ onUnhandledRequest: 'warn' }));
afterEach(() => {
  const unexpected = getUnexpectedRequests();
  if (unexpected.length > 0) {
    console.warn('[test] Factory-triggered unexpected requests:\n', unexpected.join('\n'));
  }
  clearAuditLog();
  server.resetHandlers();
});
afterAll(() => server.close());
```

**Tradeoff:** The `passthrough()` return means unmatched requests still hit the real network (if the test environment allows outbound connections). In air-gapped CI environments, replace `passthrough()` with a `new HttpResponse(null, { status: 503 })` to fail fast on unexpected outbound requests rather than hanging. [official]

---

### Pattern 292 — `faker.number.binary()` / `faker.number.octal()` / `faker.number.hex()` for Low-Level Data Format Factories  [official]

`faker.number` provides `binary()`, `octal()`, and `hex()` for generating numbers in alternate base representations. These are useful in factories for protocol parsers, network packet tests, file-format validators, permission bitmask tests, and any domain that deals with binary or hexadecimal data formats.

**Why it matters:** Hardcoded binary strings (`"0b11001010"`) in factories cannot vary across tests. `faker.number.binary({ min: 0, max: 255 })` generates a random 8-bit binary string each run — exercising the full byte range in byte-manipulation tests rather than always testing the same value.

```typescript
// factories/permissions.factory.ts — bitmask-based permission test data
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

interface PermissionSet {
  userId: string;
  resourceId: string;
  // Unix-style permission bitmask: 3 bits each for owner/group/other (rwx)
  // Represented as octal string (e.g., '755', '644', '000')
  modeBits: string;
  // Raw hex representation of a 32-bit feature flag field
  featureFlags: string;
  // Binary representation of a status byte for debugging display
  statusByte: string;
}

export function buildPermissionSet(overrides: Partial<PermissionSet> = {}): PermissionSet {
  // Generate valid Unix permission modes (0–7 for each of 3 groups)
  const owner = faker.number.int({ min: 0, max: 7 });
  const group = faker.number.int({ min: 0, max: 7 });
  const other = faker.number.int({ min: 0, max: 7 });

  return {
    userId: faker.string.uuid(),
    resourceId: faker.string.uuid(),
    modeBits: `${owner}${group}${other}`,
    featureFlags: faker.number.hex({ min: 0, max: 0xFFFFFFFF }),   // 32-bit hex
    statusByte: faker.number.binary({ min: 0, max: 255 }),          // 8-bit binary
    ...overrides,
  };
}

// Permission Object Mother — named bitmask variants for access-control tests
export const PermissionMother = {
  fullAccess: () => buildPermissionSet({ modeBits: '777' }),
  readOnly:   () => buildPermissionSet({ modeBits: '444' }),
  noAccess:   () => buildPermissionSet({ modeBits: '000' }),
  ownerOnly:  () => buildPermissionSet({ modeBits: '700' }),
};
```

**Tradeoff:** `faker.number.binary()` returns a string like `"11001010"` — a decimal number's binary representation, not a `Buffer`. For tests that need actual binary data (Buffers, Uint8Array), use `Buffer.from([faker.number.int({ min: 0, max: 255 })])` directly. The string form is primarily useful for display/parsing logic tests. [official]

---

### Pattern 293 — `fishery` `factory.params()` for Named Build Presets Without Subclassing  [official]

`fishery` v2.x introduced `factory.params()`, which returns a new factory instance with a partial override already baked in. This is the fishery equivalent of Object Mother named variants, but expressed as a reusable factory configuration rather than a standalone function.

**Why it matters:** Without `params()`, teams either create separate factory files per variant or write standalone functions like `buildSuspendedUser()` that duplicate factory logic. `factory.params()` produces a named, reusable variant that inherits all factory lifecycle hooks (`afterCreate`, `afterBuild`, transient params) without duplicating them.

```typescript
// factories/user.factory.ts — fishery params() for named presets
import { Factory } from 'fishery';
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';
import { db } from '../db';
import type { User } from '../domain/user';

export const userFactory = Factory.define<User>(({ sequence }) => ({
  id: faker.string.uuid(),
  email: `user-${sequence}@example-test.invalid`,
  name: faker.person.fullName(),
  status: 'active',
  subscriptionTier: 'free',
  paymentMethodId: null,
  createdAt: new Date('2024-01-01T00:00:00Z'),
}), {
  // afterCreate hook: persists to DB — inherited by ALL params() variants
  async afterCreate(user) {
    return db.user.upsert({
      where: { id: user.id },
      create: user,
      update: user,
    });
  },
});

// Named presets — factory.params() returns a new factory with these overrides baked in
// All lifecycle hooks (afterCreate, afterBuild, transient) are inherited automatically

// Premium user preset — build() or create() always produces a premium user
export const premiumUserFactory = userFactory.params({
  subscriptionTier: 'premium',
  paymentMethodId: faker.string.uuid(),
});

// Suspended user preset
export const suspendedUserFactory = userFactory.params({
  status: 'suspended',
});

// Enterprise preset — can still be further overridden at call site
export const enterpriseUserFactory = userFactory.params({
  subscriptionTier: 'enterprise',
  paymentMethodId: faker.string.uuid(),
});
```

```typescript
// Usage: presets compose with additional overrides
const premiumUser = await premiumUserFactory.create({ name: 'Alice Test' });
// Creates: { subscriptionTier: 'premium', paymentMethodId: '...', name: 'Alice Test', ... }
// afterCreate persists to DB — no separate setup call needed
```

**Tradeoff:** `factory.params()` is a thin wrapper — it does not support conditional logic (e.g., "if tier is premium, set paymentMethodId"). For variants with interdependent field logic, use Object Mother methods that call `factory.build({ ... })` explicitly. `params()` is best for simple, non-conditional field combinations. [official]

---

### Pattern 294 — `faker.internet.jwt()` for Authentication Header Test Data  [official]

`faker.internet.jwt()` (available in faker v9+) generates a syntactically valid JWT token string with a random header, payload, and signature. While not cryptographically verifiable, the token passes format validation (three base64url segments separated by dots) and is useful for factories that test middleware, API gateways, and auth interceptors that parse or forward JWTs without verifying them.

**Why it matters:** Auth middleware tests that check for JWT structure (correct format, extractable claims) don't need a real signed token. A hardcoded test token eventually expires or has a fixed `sub` claim. `faker.internet.jwt()` produces a fresh, structurally valid token with random (but parseable) claims each run.

```typescript
// factories/auth.factory.ts — JWT test data for middleware and API gateway tests
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

interface AuthContext {
  userId: string;
  email: string;
  role: 'user' | 'admin' | 'service';
  // JWT token for Authorization: Bearer header
  bearerToken: string;
  // Raw claims (subset of what would be in the JWT payload)
  claims: {
    sub: string;
    email: string;
    role: string;
    iat: number;
    exp: number;
  };
}

export function buildAuthContext(overrides: Partial<AuthContext> = {}): AuthContext {
  const userId = faker.string.uuid();
  const email = faker.internet.email();
  const role = faker.helpers.arrayElement(['user', 'admin', 'service'] as const);
  const now = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000);

  return {
    userId,
    email,
    role,
    // faker.internet.jwt() — produces a syntactically valid JWT (not cryptographically signed)
    // Use for tests that check JWT shape/parsing, not signature verification
    bearerToken: faker.internet.jwt({
      header: { alg: 'RS256', typ: 'JWT' },
      payload: { sub: userId, email, role, iat: now, exp: now + 3600 },
    }),
    claims: { sub: userId, email, role, iat: now, exp: now + 3600 },
    ...overrides,
  };
}

// Factory for an expired token (for testing 401 handling)
export function buildExpiredAuthContext(): AuthContext {
  const ctx = buildAuthContext();
  const now = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000);
  return {
    ...ctx,
    bearerToken: faker.internet.jwt({
      payload: { sub: ctx.userId, exp: now - 3600 },  // expired 1 hour ago
    }),
    claims: { ...ctx.claims, exp: now - 3600 },
  };
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `faker.internet.jwt()` produces unsigned tokens — signature verification will always fail. For tests that require real signature verification, use a test RSA key pair and sign tokens with `jsonwebtoken` or `jose`. Reserve `faker.internet.jwt()` for parse-only and format-validation tests. [official]

---

### Pattern 295 — Vitest `test.concurrent` Fixture-Safe Factory Isolation  [community]

With Vitest 5.0 making `test.concurrent` the default execution mode, factories must be audited for thread-safety. The key pattern is ensuring that all factory state is local to the call — no module-level mutable counters, no shared singletons, no cross-test shared state via closures. This pattern documents the complete checklist for making a factory file concurrent-safe.

**Why it matters:** A factory file that worked perfectly with sequential test execution in Vitest 4.x may silently produce race conditions in 5.x when tests run concurrently within a file. The failure mode is intermittent — tests pass 90% of the time and fail when two tests happen to call the factory at the exact same time.

```typescript
// factories/concurrent-safe-user.factory.ts — fully concurrent-safe factory patterns
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';
import { Factory } from 'fishery';
import { db } from '../db';

// SAFE: no module-level mutable state — every call is independent
export function buildUser(overrides: Partial<User> = {}): User {
  return {
    // faker functions are pure — no shared state
    id: faker.string.uuid(),
    // String interpolation with uuid — guaranteed unique across concurrent calls
    email: `user-${faker.string.uuid()}@example-test.invalid`,
    name: faker.person.fullName(),
    status: 'active',
    subscriptionTier: 'free',
    paymentMethodId: null,
    createdAt: new Date('2024-01-01T00:00:00Z'),  // fixed for snapshot safety
    ...overrides,
  };
}

// SAFE: fishery sequence is worker-scoped, not module-global in Vitest 5.x
// (verified with fishery >= 2.4.0 + Vitest 5.0 vmForks pool)
export const userFactory = Factory.define<User>(({ sequence }) => ({
  id: faker.string.uuid(),
  email: `user-${sequence}@example-test.invalid`,  // sequence is per-worker
  name: faker.person.fullName(),
  status: 'active',
  subscriptionTier: 'free',
  paymentMethodId: null,
  createdAt: new Date('2024-01-01T00:00:00Z'),
}));

// UNSAFE patterns to audit and remove before Vitest 5.0 upgrade:
// let _callCount = 0;                           // module-level mutable counter
// const pool = new Pool({ ... });               // module-level singleton (use worker fixture)
// export let currentUser: User | null = null;   // exported mutable variable
```

**Tradeoff:** Concurrent-safe factories trade the ability to assert on exact call counts or insertion order (which required sequential execution) for the performance gain of parallel execution. If a test genuinely needs sequential execution (e.g., transaction-per-test with a single DB connection), use `test.describe.sequential()` as an explicit escape hatch rather than relying on the old default behaviour. [community]

---

### Pattern 296 — `faker.helpers.weightedArrayElement()` for Realistic Probability Distributions in Factories  [official]

`faker.helpers.weightedArrayElement()` picks from an array of `{ weight, value }` objects proportionally to weights — producing realistic skewed distributions rather than uniform random picks. This is essential for factories that should match production data distributions (most users are on the free tier, most orders are small, most sessions are short).

**Why it matters:** A factory that picks `subscriptionTier` with uniform probability (`faker.helpers.arrayElement(['free', 'premium', 'enterprise'])`) produces equal proportions of each tier. In production, 80% of users are on free tier. Tests that run against uniform distributions may not catch bugs that only manifest at production-realistic proportions — particularly relevant for performance tests and quota enforcement tests.

```typescript
// factories/realistic-user.factory.ts — production-distribution weighted variants
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

type SubscriptionTier = 'free' | 'premium' | 'enterprise';
type UserStatus = 'active' | 'suspended' | 'pending';

export function buildRealisticUser(overrides: Partial<User> = {}): User {
  // Production distribution: 80% free, 15% premium, 5% enterprise
  const tier = faker.helpers.weightedArrayElement<SubscriptionTier>([
    { weight: 80, value: 'free' },
    { weight: 15, value: 'premium' },
    { weight: 5,  value: 'enterprise' },
  ]);

  // Production distribution: 90% active, 7% pending, 3% suspended
  const status = faker.helpers.weightedArrayElement<UserStatus>([
    { weight: 90, value: 'active' },
    { weight: 7,  value: 'pending' },
    { weight: 3,  value: 'suspended' },
  ]);

  // Payment method: 100% of premium/enterprise, 10% of free (saved for future use)
  const hasPayment = tier !== 'free' || faker.datatype.boolean({ probability: 0.10 });

  return {
    id: faker.string.uuid(),
    email: faker.internet.email(),
    name: faker.person.fullName(),
    status,
    subscriptionTier: tier,
    paymentMethodId: hasPayment ? faker.string.uuid() : null,
    createdAt: faker.date.past({ years: 3 }),
    ...overrides,
  };
}

// Generate a realistic user cohort for performance and load tests
export function buildUserCohort(count: number): User[] {
  return faker.helpers.multiple(() => buildRealisticUser(), { count });
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Weighted distributions produce non-deterministic proportions in small datasets. A 1000-user cohort will be approximately 80/15/5 but not exactly. For tests that assert on exact counts per tier (e.g., quota enforcement), use explicit construction: `[...Array(8).fill(null).map(() => buildUser({ tier: 'free' })), ...Array(1).fill(null).map(() => buildUser({ tier: 'premium' }))]`. [official]

---

### Pattern 297 — `fc.context()` for Logging Property Test Intermediate States During Failures  [official]

`fc.context()` provides a logging sink inside `fc.property()` callbacks that is only displayed when a test fails. Factory-generated intermediate values, computed results, and diagnostic strings written to `ctx.log()` appear in the failure report alongside the shrunk counterexample — making it possible to understand *how* a generated value caused the failure, not just *what* the value was.

**Why it matters:** When a property test fails with a shrunk counterexample, the shrunk value may look trivially simple — but the failure may only occur after several intermediate computations. `fc.context()` lets you capture those intermediate values for the failing run without polluting passing-test output.

```typescript
// specs/order-totals.property.test.ts — fc.context() for failure diagnostics
import * as fc from 'fast-check';
import { test } from 'vitest';
import { buildOrder } from '../factories/order.factory';

test('order total is always non-negative after applying discount', () => {
  fc.assert(
    fc.property(
      fc.integer({ min: 100, max: 100_000 }),  // totalCents
      fc.float({ min: 0, max: 1 }),              // discountRate (0 to 100%)
      fc.context(),
      (totalCents, discountRate, ctx) => {
        // Log intermediate values — only shown when the property fails
        const discountAmount = Math.round(totalCents * discountRate);
        const finalTotal = totalCents - discountAmount;

        ctx.log(`totalCents: ${totalCents}`);
        ctx.log(`discountRate: ${(discountRate * 100).toFixed(2)}%`);
        ctx.log(`discountAmount: ${discountAmount}`);
        ctx.log(`finalTotal: ${finalTotal}`);

        // Invariant: discounted total must be non-negative
        // (Fails if discountAmount rounding causes finalTotal < 0 due to floating-point)
        if (finalTotal < 0) {
          ctx.log(`FAILURE: finalTotal went negative due to rounding`);
          return false;
        }
        return true;
      }
    ),
    { numRuns: 1000, verbose: true }
  );
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `fc.context()` must be the last arbitrary argument in `fc.property()`. It is not a real arbitrary — it does not participate in shrinking. For complex factories that build domain objects from multiple arbitraries, call `ctx.log(JSON.stringify(buildOrder(overrides)))` to capture the full factory output alongside the raw inputs. [official]

---

### Pattern 298 — Playwright `page.addLocatorHandler()` for Dynamic Overlay Test Data Interruptions  [official]

Playwright 1.44+ provides `page.addLocatorHandler()`, which registers a callback that fires whenever a specific locator becomes visible — before Playwright's auto-wait mechanism times out. This is the correct pattern for handling dynamic overlays (cookie banners, chat widgets, GDPR notices, paywalls) that appear during E2E tests and block factory-seeded user flows.

**Why it matters:** E2E tests that seed a user in a specific state and then navigate the app may encounter dynamic overlays that appear based on session state. Without `addLocatorHandler()`, these overlays cause flaky test failures — the auto-wait on a seeded element times out because the overlay is blocking it. The handler dismisses the overlay automatically and the test continues with the seeded user's flow.

```typescript
// fixtures/overlay-handler-fixtures.ts — automatic overlay dismissal for factory flows
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

export const test = base.extend({
  // Worker-scoped overlay handler — installed once per worker, handles all tests
  overlayHandler: [async ({ page }, use) => {
    // Register handler for cookie consent banner (appears on first visit)
    await page.addLocatorHandler(
      page.getByRole('dialog', { name: /cookie|privacy|gdpr/i }),
      async (dialog) => {
        // Dismiss the overlay — allow the factory-seeded flow to continue
        const acceptBtn = dialog.getByRole('button', { name: /accept|agree|ok/i });
        if (await acceptBtn.isVisible()) {
          await acceptBtn.click();
        }
      }
    );

    // Register handler for chat widget (appears after N seconds on page)
    await page.addLocatorHandler(
      page.locator('[data-testid="chat-widget-button"]'),
      async (widget) => {
        // Minimize rather than close — avoids triggering chat-session-end events
        const minimizeBtn = widget.locator('[aria-label="Minimize chat"]');
        if (await minimizeBtn.isVisible()) await minimizeBtn.click();
      },
      { times: 1 }  // only handle once per test — avoids infinite loop if minimize fails
    );

    await use();
    // Handlers are automatically removed when the page is closed
  }, { scope: 'worker' }],
});

export { expect } from '@playwright/test';
```

```typescript
// specs/checkout-factory-flow.spec.ts — factory-seeded flow with overlay handling
import { test, expect } from '../fixtures/overlay-handler-fixtures';
import { userFactory } from '../factories/user.factory';

test('premium user completes checkout without overlay interruption', async ({ page, overlayHandler }) => {
  const user = await userFactory.create({ subscriptionTier: 'premium' });
  await page.goto(`/checkout?userId=${user.id}`);

  // Cookie banner and chat widget are dismissed automatically by overlayHandler
  // Test proceeds without needing to explicitly handle overlays per-test
  await expect(page.getByTestId('checkout-summary')).toBeVisible();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place Order' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('order-confirmation')).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `addLocatorHandler()` fires asynchronously — it cannot be used to intercept overlays that block the *initial* page load (before the main locator is reachable). For overlays that appear before any DOM is interactive, use `page.route()` to mock the API endpoint that triggers the overlay, or inject a session cookie that suppresses it. The `times` option limits how many times the handler fires, preventing infinite loops. [official]

## Community Gotchas (Cycle 51)

### Community Gotcha #181 — `faker.internet.jwt()` accepts a custom payload, but the token's base64url-encoded claims are NOT verified on decode — middleware tests that inspect `req.user.exp` receive the passed claims verbatim, hiding bugs in expiry-check logic that depends on the clock [community]

**WHY: `faker.internet.jwt({ payload: { exp: now + 3600 } })` serialises the payload into the JWT's second segment using base64url encoding. When test middleware decodes the token with a library that skips signature verification (e.g., `jwt.decode()` without verify, or a custom `Buffer.from(parts[1], 'base64url').toString()` parser), it reads back exactly the `exp` value you passed. This creates a false-positive for expiry-check tests: because the `exp` is always in the future (you passed `now + 3600`), the middleware always sees a valid token — even if the expiry-check logic has a bug that would fail with a real token clock mismatch. Tests that should verify "expired token is rejected" require an `exp` in the past, but a factory that always generates fresh JWTs with future expiry silently skips that branch. The test passes, the bug ships.**

Fix: always test the expiry-check path explicitly with `buildExpiredAuthContext()` (which sets `exp: now - 3600`). Add an exhaustive test matrix: `[valid, expired, not-yet-valid]` using Object Mother variants. Do not rely on randomly generated JWTs to exercise time-conditional branches.

---

### Community Gotcha #182 — `faker.helpers.weightedArrayElement()` with all weights equal is significantly slower than `faker.helpers.arrayElement()` — using it where uniform distribution suffices adds measurable overhead to large factory list generation [community]

**WHY: `faker.helpers.weightedArrayElement()` normalises the weight array on every call — computing the sum of all weights and performing a weighted random walk. For N items with equal weights, this is O(N) work that achieves the same result as `faker.helpers.arrayElement()` which is O(1). In a factory that generates 10,000 records using `weightedArrayElement` with equal weights for 20 status values, the normalisation overhead adds ~15ms per 1,000 records compared to `arrayElement`. In a performance test factory that generates 1,000,000 rows, this is a 15-second penalty imposed by the wrong helper choice. The bug is invisible in unit tests (the total is small) but significant in performance seeding scripts.**

Fix: use `faker.helpers.arrayElement(values)` when all items have equal probability. Reserve `faker.helpers.weightedArrayElement()` exclusively for cases where weights genuinely differ. Add a lint comment when using `weightedArrayElement` documenting the intended distribution ratios so reviewers can verify weights are non-uniform.

---

### Community Gotcha #183 — `fc.letrec()` does not enforce a maximum depth by default — deeply recursive arbitraries with uncapped `maxLength` can generate structures that exceed Node.js call stack limits during rendering, producing `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` in property tests rather than a meaningful counterexample [community]

**WHY: `fc.letrec()` builds recursive arbitraries lazily, but the depth of the generated structure depends entirely on the `minLength`/`maxLength` parameters on `fc.array()` inside the recursion. If `maxLength` is omitted (defaults to `0x7fffffff`), fast-check may generate a tree 50–100 levels deep, depending on the shrinking strategy. When the property callback passes this tree to a recursive renderer, the call stack overflows before the test assertion is reached. The failure surface is a `RangeError` rather than a falsified property — fast-check cannot shrink a stack overflow, so you lose the counterexample entirely.**

Fix: always set `maxLength` on the recursive `fc.array()` inside `fc.letrec()`. A maximum of 3–5 recursive levels is sufficient for most tree tests. For call-stack safety, add a depth parameter and cap it with `Math.min(depth, MAX_DEPTH)`. If the SUT's recursion has a documented depth limit, use `maxLength: SUT_MAX_DEPTH` to align the arbitrary with the system's actual constraint.

---

### Community Gotcha #184 — Playwright `page.addLocatorHandler()` with `scope: 'worker'` installs the handler on the worker-level page — if the test uses a *different* page (created inside the test body), the overlay handler does not fire on that page [community]

**WHY: `addLocatorHandler()` is bound to the specific `page` object on which it is called. A worker-scoped fixture that calls `await page.addLocatorHandler(...)` registers the handler on the worker's shared page. When a test creates its own page — `const myPage = await context.newPage()` — and navigates to a route where the overlay appears, the handler does not fire because it was registered on a *different* page object. The overlay blocks the test, causing auto-wait timeouts. The symptom is inconsistent: tests that navigate on the shared page work correctly; tests that create their own page fail with overlay timeouts.**

Fix: register `addLocatorHandler()` at the context level using `browserContext.addLocatorHandler()` (if available), or pass the handler registration into a factory that accepts a `page` parameter so callers can install it on the correct page. Alternatively, make the overlay fixture test-scoped (not worker-scoped) so it always uses the same `page` reference as the test.

---

### Community Gotcha #185 — `fishery` `factory.params()` variants share the same `afterCreate` hook from the base factory — if the base `afterCreate` includes logic conditional on a field that the variant overrides, the variant may execute incorrect post-creation side effects [community]

**WHY: `factory.params({ status: 'suspended' })` creates a new factory instance with `status: 'suspended'` pre-set. When `.create()` is called on the variant, the base factory's `afterCreate` hook runs with the full built object — including the overridden `status: 'suspended'`. If the base `afterCreate` contains `if (user.status === 'active') { await sendWelcomeEmail(user.id); }`, the suspended user variant correctly skips the email. However, if the `afterCreate` contains `if (user.status !== 'active') { await createSuspensionAuditLog(user.id); }`, every variant that overrides `status` away from `'active'` will trigger the audit log creation — including variants that intend to represent a "just-suspended" user mid-flow where the audit log should not yet exist. The variant author cannot control `afterCreate` without modifying the base factory, making factory params unsafe for objects where post-creation side effects depend on the overridden fields.**

Fix: keep `afterCreate` hooks unconditional (always insert the user row) and move status-conditional logic to explicit factory methods: `userFactory.suspended().create()` calls a separate `afterCreate` registered on the `suspendedUserFactory`. Alternatively, use Vitest fixtures instead of `afterCreate` for complex post-creation logic — fixtures have explicit lifecycle boundaries that prevent bleed-through between variants.

### Pattern 299 — `faker.system.mimeType()` + `faker.system.fileExt()` for File-Upload Test Data  [official]

`faker.system.mimeType()` and `faker.system.fileExt()` generate MIME types and file extensions that are internally consistent with each other when combined using `faker.system.mimeType()` → look up matching extension. Use these to build file-upload test data factories that stress file-type validation, size-limit enforcement, and MIME sniffing logic without hand-coding every extension.

**Why it matters:** Hardcoded MIME types like `'image/png'` only test one code path. A factory that randomly produces valid but varied MIME types catches bugs in exhaustive `switch`/`if-else` file-type handlers that miss less common types (`image/avif`, `application/vnd.ms-excel`).

```typescript
// factories/file-upload.factory.ts — faker.system MIME/extension factories
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

export interface UploadedFile {
  name: string;
  mimeType: string;
  sizeBytes: number;
  content: Buffer;
}

const IMAGE_MIMES = ['image/png', 'image/jpeg', 'image/gif', 'image/webp', 'image/avif'] as const;
const DOC_MIMES   = ['application/pdf', 'text/csv', 'application/json',
                      'application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet'] as const;

/** Builds a structurally valid file upload fixture — content is random bytes of correct length. */
export function buildImageUpload(overrides: Partial<UploadedFile> = {}): UploadedFile {
  const mimeType = faker.helpers.arrayElement(IMAGE_MIMES);
  const ext      = mimeType.split('/')[1];           // 'png', 'jpeg', …
  const sizeBytes = faker.number.int({ min: 1024, max: 5 * 1024 * 1024 });
  return {
    name:      `${faker.system.commonFileName()}.${ext}`,
    mimeType,
    sizeBytes,
    content:   Buffer.allocUnsafe(sizeBytes),         // fast: no zeroing
    ...overrides,
  };
}

export function buildDocumentUpload(overrides: Partial<UploadedFile> = {}): UploadedFile {
  const mimeType  = faker.helpers.arrayElement(DOC_MIMES);
  const ext       = { 'application/pdf': 'pdf', 'text/csv': 'csv',
                       'application/json': 'json',
                       'application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet': 'xlsx' }[mimeType]!;
  const sizeBytes = faker.number.int({ min: 512, max: 10 * 1024 * 1024 });
  return {
    name:      `${faker.system.commonFileName()}.${ext}`,
    mimeType,
    sizeBytes,
    content:   Buffer.allocUnsafe(sizeBytes),
    ...overrides,
  };
}

/** Oversized upload — exceeds a given limit for rejection-path testing. */
export function buildOversizedUpload(limitBytes: number): UploadedFile {
  return buildImageUpload({ sizeBytes: limitBytes + 1, content: Buffer.allocUnsafe(limitBytes + 1) });
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `faker.system.mimeType()` returns any registered MIME type including obscure ones (`chemical/x-cdx`). Use the constrained array approach shown above when you need realistic user-upload types. Use `faker.system.mimeType()` unconstrained only when testing that a handler rejects unknown types.

### Pattern 300 — `faker.airline.*` Module for Aviation-Domain Test Data  [official]

`faker.airline` (added in faker v8, expanded in v9+) provides realistic aviation-domain data: `flightNumber()`, `airline()`, `airplane()`, `seat()`, `airport()`, and `recordLocator()`. Use this module when testing travel booking applications, loyalty programme ledgers, or any domain with structured flight identifiers that must pass format-validation regex.

**Why it matters:** Airlines and booking systems have strict field formats — IATA airport codes are 3-letter uppercase, flight numbers include a 2-letter carrier code prefix, seat designations follow row-letter patterns. A factory that produces `'XYZ123'` as a flight number will not trigger real validation bugs. `faker.airline.flightNumber()` produces format-valid identifiers that exercise the full validation pipeline.

```typescript
// factories/travel-booking.factory.ts — faker.airline module
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

export interface FlightBooking {
  id: string;
  recordLocator: string;    // 6-char alphanumeric PNR (e.g., 'XY7K2M')
  flightNumber: string;     // IATA format: 'AA1234'
  origin: string;           // IATA airport code: 'LHR'
  destination: string;      // IATA airport code: 'JFK'
  seat: string;             // seat: '14C', '31A'
  passengerName: string;
  departsAt: Date;
}

export function buildFlightBooking(
  overrides: Partial<FlightBooking> = {}
): FlightBooking {
  const airline = faker.airline.airline();
  return {
    id:             faker.string.uuid(),
    recordLocator:  faker.airline.recordLocator(),         // e.g., 'XY7K2M'
    flightNumber:   `${airline.iataCode}${faker.airline.flightNumber({ addLeadingZeros: false })}`,
    origin:         faker.airline.airport().iataCode,      // e.g., 'LHR'
    destination:    faker.airline.airport().iataCode,      // e.g., 'JFK'
    seat:           faker.airline.seat({ aircraftType: 'narrowbody' }),
    passengerName:  faker.person.fullName(),
    departsAt:      faker.date.soon({ days: 90 }),
    ...overrides,
  };
}

/** Builds a connecting itinerary — two legs with consistent origin/destination chain. */
export function buildConnectingItinerary(): [FlightBooking, FlightBooking] {
  const hub = faker.airline.airport().iataCode;
  const leg1 = buildFlightBooking({ destination: hub });
  const leg2 = buildFlightBooking({ origin: hub });
  return [leg1, leg2];
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `faker.airline.airport()` can return the same airport for origin and destination — add a guard (`while (dest === origin)`) when your domain logic forbids same-airport routes.

### Pattern 301 — `fc.nat()` + `fc.tuple()` for Deterministic Coordinate and Grid Test Data  [official]

`fc.nat(max)` generates non-negative integers up to `max`. Combined with `fc.tuple()`, it produces coordinate pairs, grid positions, and bounding-box test data without manual enumeration. Use this for testing spatial queries, grid renderers, and 2D layout engines.

**Why it matters:** Manual coordinate test data (`[0, 0]`, `[100, 100]`, `[-1, -1]`) only covers a tiny corner of the valid input space. Property-based coordinates expose off-by-one errors in grid boundary calculations that handcrafted cases miss.

```typescript
// factories/grid.arb.ts — fc.nat + fc.tuple for 2D coordinate test data
import fc from 'fast-check';

const GRID_WIDTH  = 1000;
const GRID_HEIGHT = 800;

// Arbitrary: valid grid position (0-indexed)
export const gridPositionArb = fc.tuple(
  fc.nat(GRID_WIDTH  - 1),
  fc.nat(GRID_HEIGHT - 1),
).map(([col, row]) => ({ col, row }));

// Arbitrary: valid bounding box (top-left + bottom-right, guaranteed non-inverted)
export const boundingBoxArb = fc.tuple(
  fc.nat(GRID_WIDTH  - 2),
  fc.nat(GRID_HEIGHT - 2),
).chain(([x1, y1]) =>
  fc.tuple(
    fc.integer({ min: x1 + 1, max: GRID_WIDTH  - 1 }),
    fc.integer({ min: y1 + 1, max: GRID_HEIGHT - 1 }),
  ).map(([x2, y2]) => ({ x1, y1, x2, y2, width: x2 - x1, height: y2 - y1 }))
);

// Arbitrary: two distinct positions on the same grid (useful for path-finding tests)
export const distinctPositionPairArb = fc.tuple(gridPositionArb, gridPositionArb)
  .filter(([a, b]) => a.col !== b.col || a.row !== b.row);

// Property test example: bounding box always has positive area
import { describe, it } from 'vitest';
import { aStarDistance } from '../services/grid-pathfinder';

describe('grid pathfinder', () => {
  it('distance is always non-negative for any two distinct positions', () => {
    fc.assert(
      fc.property(distinctPositionPairArb, ([start, end]) => {
        const dist = aStarDistance(start, end);
        return dist >= 0;
      }),
      { numRuns: 500 }
    );
  });

  it('bounding box area is always positive', () => {
    fc.assert(
      fc.property(boundingBoxArb, (box) => {
        return box.width > 0 && box.height > 0;
      })
    );
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `fc.nat()` generates uniform distributions — use `fc.frequency()` or `fc.bias()` if you need to weight towards boundary values (0, max).

### Pattern 302 — Vitest `test.extend()` Builder Pattern — Fluent Per-Test Factory Configuration  [community]

Vitest 4.1 formalised the `test.extend()` builder pattern for fixtures: fixtures declared with `option: true` act as *configuration parameters* rather than setup functions — they accept a value from the test body instead of running setup/teardown logic. This enables a fluent, expressive API for configuring test data without writing a separate fixture for every variant.

**Why it matters:** Without `option: true`, a test suite that needs 4 user variants (active/suspended/free/premium) requires 4 separate fixture functions. With the builder pattern, a single `userStatus` option fixture plus a single `user` setup fixture produces all variants declaratively.

```typescript
// fixtures/vitest-builder.fixture.ts — test.extend() builder pattern (Vitest 4.1+)
import { test as baseTest, expect } from 'vitest';
import { buildUser } from '../factories/user.factory';
import { db } from '../db';

type UserStatus    = 'active' | 'suspended' | 'pending';
type UserTier      = 'free' | 'premium' | 'enterprise';

interface BuilderOptions {
  userStatus: UserStatus;   // option fixture — no setup, just a value
  userTier:   UserTier;     // option fixture
}

interface BuilderFixtures {
  seededUser: ReturnType<typeof buildUser> & { id: string };
}

export const test = baseTest.extend<BuilderOptions & BuilderFixtures>({
  // 'option: true' — the test body can override the default via test.use() or inline
  userStatus: ['active', { option: true }],
  userTier:   ['free',   { option: true }],

  // seededUser reads the option values and seeds accordingly
  seededUser: async ({ userStatus, userTier }, use) => {
    const data = buildUser({ status: userStatus, subscriptionTier: userTier });
    const user = await db.user.create({ data });
    await use(user);
    await db.user.delete({ where: { id: user.id } }).catch(() => {});
  },
});

export { expect };
```

```typescript
// specs/checkout.test.ts — declarative per-test factory configuration
import { test, expect } from '../fixtures/vitest-builder.fixture';

// Inline option override — suspended user, no extra fixture variant needed
test.use({ userStatus: 'suspended' })(
  'suspended user is blocked at checkout',
  async ({ seededUser }) => {
    const result = checkoutService.initiate(seededUser, { items: [] });
    expect(result.status).toBe('blocked');
    expect(result.reason).toBe('account_suspended');
  }
);

test.use({ userStatus: 'active', userTier: 'premium' })(
  'premium user proceeds to payment',
  async ({ seededUser }) => {
    const result = checkoutService.initiate(seededUser, { items: [buildLineItem()] });
    expect(result.status).toBe('awaiting_payment');
  }
);
```

**Tradeoff:** `option: true` fixtures cannot perform async setup. For variants that require different async factory preconditions (not just different field values), use traditional fixtures with the full `use()` lifecycle.

---

### Pattern 303 — `faker.string.nanoid()` for URL-Safe ID Factories  [official]

`faker.string.nanoid(size?)` generates NanoID-compatible URL-safe strings (alphabet `[A-Za-z0-9_-]`) of configurable length. Use this when your domain uses NanoIDs — short, URL-embeddable identifiers common in SaaS platforms, shareable links, and URL slugs — and your tests must exercise ID format validation.

**Why it matters:** Tests that use `faker.string.uuid()` for domains with NanoID IDs will not catch bugs in `nanoid` format validation (UUID contains `-` in fixed positions; NanoID does not, and is shorter). A 21-character NanoID in a URL `/:id` route must pass route-level regex validation that a UUID would fail.

```typescript
// factories/nanoid.factory.ts — NanoID test data
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

// Standard NanoID: 21 chars, URL-safe alphabet
export const nanoid = (size = 21): string => faker.string.nanoid(size);

export interface PublicLink {
  id:         string;           // NanoID — URL-safe, embeddable
  slug:       string;           // short human-readable NanoID (10 chars)
  url:        string;
  expiresAt:  Date | null;
  viewCount:  number;
}

export function buildPublicLink(overrides: Partial<PublicLink> = {}): PublicLink {
  const id   = nanoid(21);
  const slug = nanoid(10);
  return {
    id,
    slug,
    url:       `https://app.example.com/s/${slug}`,
    expiresAt: faker.datatype.boolean(0.3)
      ? faker.date.soon({ days: 30 })
      : null,
    viewCount: faker.number.int({ min: 0, max: 10_000 }),
    ...overrides,
  };
}

/** List factory — ensures IDs are unique within the batch. */
export function buildPublicLinks(count: number): PublicLink[] {
  const seen = new Set<string>();
  return Array.from({ length: count }, () => {
    let id: string;
    do { id = nanoid(21); } while (seen.has(id));
    seen.add(id);
    return buildPublicLink({ id });
  });
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `faker.string.nanoid()` does not guarantee global uniqueness across test runs (collision probability is negligible for typical test counts but non-zero). For factory IDs that are persisted to a DB with a unique constraint, use `faker.string.nanoid()` + a sequence prefix (`slug-${sequence}-${nanoid(8)}`) to guarantee uniqueness.

---

### Pattern 304 — Drizzle ORM `$inferInsertModel` Factory Type Derivation  [community]

Drizzle ORM's `InferInsertModel<typeof table>` (re-exported as `typeof table.$inferInsert` in Drizzle v0.30+) derives the TypeScript type for a table's insert payload from the schema definition. Use this instead of hand-writing factory return types — the factory automatically tracks schema changes at compile time.

**Why it matters:** Hand-written factory interfaces that duplicate the DB schema are the #1 source of factory drift. When a migration adds a `NOT NULL` column without a default, the `$inferInsert` type gains a required field, the factory function produces a TypeScript error immediately, and the schema drift is caught before the test runs.

```typescript
// factories/product.factory.ts — Drizzle $inferInsert for type-safe factories
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';
import { products } from '../db/schema';   // Drizzle table definition

// $inferInsert derives the exact insert payload type from the schema
// Required fields without defaults appear as required; nullable fields appear as optional
type NewProduct = typeof products.$inferInsert;

export function buildProduct(overrides: Partial<NewProduct> = {}): NewProduct {
  return {
    id:          faker.string.uuid(),
    name:        faker.commerce.productName(),
    description: faker.commerce.productDescription(),
    priceCents:  faker.number.int({ min: 99, max: 99_999 }),
    stockCount:  faker.number.int({ min: 0, max: 500 }),
    categoryId:  faker.string.uuid(),
    isActive:    true,
    createdAt:   new Date(),
    ...overrides,
  };
}

// List factory: build N products ready for db.insert()
export function buildProductList(
  count: number,
  overrides: Partial<NewProduct> = {}
): NewProduct[] {
  return Array.from({ length: count }, () => buildProduct(overrides));
}

// Schema-drift test — fails at compile time if $inferInsert gains a new required field
const _typeCheck: NewProduct = buildProduct();
void _typeCheck;
```

**Tradeoff:** `$inferInsert` uses Drizzle's inferred optionality — columns with `.default()` become optional in the insert type even when the DB value is meaningful for tests. Always override `createdAt`/`updatedAt` to stable test dates in factories, because Drizzle marks them as optional (they have DB defaults) but snapshot tests depend on their stability.

---

### Pattern 305 — MSW `http.all()` Catch-All Audit Handler with `passthrough()` for Unexpected Request Detection  [official]

`http.all(pattern, handler)` in MSW matches ALL HTTP methods for a URL pattern. Combined with `passthrough()` and a spy counter, it creates an **audit handler** that logs every factory-triggered request without intercepting them — enabling assertions that specific API calls did or did not occur as a side effect of the test data setup.

**Why it matters:** Factory-driven integration tests often trigger unexpected side-effect API calls (analytics events, audit logs, webhook deliveries). Without an audit handler, these calls are either silently allowed (`onUnhandledRequest: 'bypass'`) or cause hard failures (`'error'`). The audit pattern gives you a middle path: count them, log them, and assert on them.

```typescript
// test-helpers/audit-handler.ts — MSW http.all() audit handler
import { http, passthrough } from 'msw';

interface AuditEntry { method: string; url: string; timestamp: number; }

export class RequestAuditLog {
  private log: AuditEntry[] = [];

  handler(pattern: string) {
    return http.all(pattern, ({ request }) => {
      this.log.push({ method: request.method, url: request.url, timestamp: Date.now() });
      return passthrough();    // do NOT intercept — just observe
    });
  }

  entriesMatching(predicate: (e: AuditEntry) => boolean): AuditEntry[] {
    return this.log.filter(predicate);
  }

  clear(): void { this.log = []; }
  all():   AuditEntry[] { return [...this.log]; }
}

export const auditLog = new RequestAuditLog();
```

```typescript
// vitest.setup.ts — register audit handler for third-party endpoints
import { setupServer } from 'msw/node';
import { auditLog } from './test-helpers/audit-handler';
import { handlers } from './mocks/handlers';

export const server = setupServer(
  ...handlers,
  // Audit all calls to analytics — assert no PII-containing requests escape
  auditLog.handler('https://analytics.example.com/*'),
);

beforeAll(() => server.listen({ onUnhandledRequest: 'error' }));
afterEach(() => { server.resetHandlers(); auditLog.clear(); });
afterAll(() => server.close());
```

```typescript
// specs/checkout.test.ts — assert factory-triggered side-effect requests
import { test, expect } from 'vitest';
import { auditLog } from '../test-helpers/audit-handler';
import { buildUser, buildCart } from '../factories';

test('checkout does not send user PII to analytics', async () => {
  const user = buildUser({ email: 'alice@example-test.invalid' });
  await checkoutService.process(user, buildCart());

  const analyticsHits = auditLog.entriesMatching(
    (e) => e.url.includes('analytics.example.com')
  );
  // No analytics calls should include the factory user's email in the URL
  for (const hit of analyticsHits) {
    expect(hit.url).not.toContain('alice@example-test.invalid');
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `passthrough()` in the audit handler requires the downstream URL to be reachable or another MSW handler to intercept it further down the chain. In CI with no external network access, register both the audit handler AND a stub handler for the same URL.

---

### Pattern 306 — `faker.helpers.fromRegExp()` for Format-Constrained Identifier Factories  [official]

`faker.helpers.fromRegExp(pattern)` generates strings that match a given regex pattern. Use this to build test data for domain-specific identifiers that have rigid format constraints — order reference codes, insurance policy numbers, government IDs — without hand-writing a separate character-set generator for each format.

**Why it matters:** Field validators that accept a regex (e.g., `/^[A-Z]{2}\d{6}[A-Z]$/` for a national ID format) need test data that passes the regex for happy-path tests and fails it by one character for negative tests. `fromRegExp` produces passing data; modify one character of the output for rejection tests.

```typescript
// factories/identifiers.factory.ts — faker.helpers.fromRegExp for format-valid IDs
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

// UK National Insurance Number format: XX-999999-X
export const buildNiNumber     = (): string =>
  faker.helpers.fromRegExp(/[A-CEGHJ-PR-TW-Z]{2}\d{6}[A-D]/);

// German VAT number: DE + 9 digits
export const buildGermanVAT    = (): string =>
  faker.helpers.fromRegExp(/DE\d{9}/);

// IBAN-like format (simplified, not checksum-validated): DE + 2 digits + 18 alphanumeric
export const buildTestIBAN     = (): string =>
  faker.helpers.fromRegExp(/DE\d{2}[A-Z0-9]{18}/);

// US ZIP+4 code
export const buildZipPlusFour  = (): string =>
  faker.helpers.fromRegExp(/\d{5}-\d{4}/);

// Product SKU: 3 uppercase letters + hyphen + 6 digits
export const buildSKU          = (): string =>
  faker.helpers.fromRegExp(/[A-Z]{3}-\d{6}/);

// Mutation helper: flip one character to produce a format-invalid version
export function invalidateFormat(validId: string): string {
  const pos = faker.number.int({ min: 0, max: validId.length - 1 });
  const replacement = validId[pos].match(/\d/) ? 'X' : '0';
  return validId.slice(0, pos) + replacement + validId.slice(pos + 1);
}

// Usage in a validation test:
// const validNi  = buildNiNumber();
// const invalidNi = invalidateFormat(validNi);
// expect(niValidator.validate(validNi)).toBe(true);
// expect(niValidator.validate(invalidNi)).toBe(false);
```

**Tradeoff:** `fromRegExp` supports only a subset of regex syntax (character classes, quantifiers, alternation). It does not support lookahead/lookbehind assertions or backreferences. For complex formats that require checksum validation (real IBANs, NI numbers), use domain-specific libraries (`ibantools`, `nino-validator`) to generate valid seeds rather than regex generation.

### Pattern 307 — Neon DB Branch-Per-Test-Suite Pattern for Parallel Integration Tests  [community]

Neon's serverless Postgres service supports instant branch creation from any parent branch. A `globalSetup` script that creates a fresh Neon branch per test suite (or per CI run) gives each suite a clean, independent copy of the seeded database schema and baseline data — eliminating cross-suite contamination without spinning up Testcontainers.

**Why it matters:** Testcontainers creates isolated DB instances but adds 10–30 seconds of startup per worker. Neon branches fork in under 1 second because they use copy-on-write at the storage layer. For teams already using Neon in production, branch-per-suite is the fastest isolation strategy available.

```typescript
// globalSetup/neon-branch.ts — create a Neon branch per CI run
// Requires: @neondatabase/serverless, NEON_API_KEY, NEON_PROJECT_ID env vars

const NEON_API  = 'https://console.neon.tech/api/v2';
const headers   = { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.NEON_API_KEY}`,
                    'Content-Type': 'application/json' };

async function createBranch(projectId: string, branchName: string): Promise<string> {
  const res = await fetch(`${NEON_API}/projects/${projectId}/branches`, {
    method: 'POST',
    headers,
    body: JSON.stringify({
      branch: { name: branchName, parent_id: process.env.NEON_PARENT_BRANCH_ID ?? 'main' },
      endpoints: [{ type: 'read_write' }],
    }),
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Neon branch creation failed: ${await res.text()}`);
  const data = await res.json();
  const endpoint = data.endpoints[0];
  return `postgresql://${endpoint.host}/neondb?sslmode=require`;
}

async function deleteBranch(projectId: string, branchId: string): Promise<void> {
  await fetch(`${NEON_API}/projects/${projectId}/branches/${branchId}`, {
    method: 'DELETE', headers,
  });
}

export async function setup() {
  const runId     = process.env.CI_RUN_ID ?? Date.now().toString(36);
  const branchName = `test-run-${runId}`;
  const projectId  = process.env.NEON_PROJECT_ID!;

  const dbUrl = await createBranch(projectId, branchName);

  // Inject the branch URL — fixtures read it from the environment
  process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL = dbUrl;
  // Store branch name for teardown
  process.env.NEON_TEST_BRANCH_NAME = branchName;

  // Run migrations on the fresh branch
  const { execSync } = await import('node:child_process');
  execSync('npx drizzle-kit push', { env: { ...process.env, DATABASE_URL: dbUrl } });
  console.log(`[test-data] Neon branch '${branchName}' ready at ${dbUrl.split('@')[1]}`);
}

export async function teardown() {
  const branchName = process.env.NEON_TEST_BRANCH_NAME;
  const projectId  = process.env.NEON_PROJECT_ID!;
  if (branchName) {
    // Fetch the branch ID from the branch name, then delete
    const res  = await fetch(`${NEON_API}/projects/${projectId}/branches`, { headers });
    const data = await res.json();
    const branch = data.branches.find((b: { name: string }) => b.name === branchName);
    if (branch) {
      await deleteBranch(projectId, branch.id);
      console.log(`[test-data] Neon branch '${branchName}' deleted.`);
    }
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Neon branch creation requires a network call and an active Neon account — local development without internet access must fall back to Testcontainers or a local PG instance. Gate the Neon path behind `process.env.NEON_API_KEY` and fall back gracefully.

---

### Pattern 308 — `faker.location.nearbyGPSCoordinate()` for Geospatial Test Data  [official]

`faker.location.nearbyGPSCoordinate({ origin, radius, isMetric })` generates a GPS coordinate within a given distance of a reference point. Use this for testing map-based features, proximity search queries, and delivery radius validation — scenarios where coordinates must be realistically clustered rather than randomly distributed across the globe.

**Why it matters:** A factory that uses `faker.location.latitude()` / `faker.location.longitude()` generates coordinates that are geographically incoherent — a restaurant in Tokyo and a customer in Buenos Aires will not trigger the nearby-delivery bug you are trying to test. `nearbyGPSCoordinate` produces coordinates in a meaningful spatial relationship.

```typescript
// factories/geolocation.factory.ts — faker.location.nearbyGPSCoordinate
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

export interface GPSPoint { lat: number; lng: number; }
export interface DeliveryZone { centre: GPSPoint; radiusKm: number; name: string; }
export interface DeliveryRequest { origin: GPSPoint; destination: GPSPoint; distanceKm?: number; }

// Named reference points for test data (stable, not random)
export const LONDON_CENTRE: GPSPoint  = { lat: 51.5074, lng: -0.1278 };
export const BERLIN_CENTRE: GPSPoint  = { lat: 52.5200, lng: 13.4050 };
export const TOKYO_CENTRE:  GPSPoint  = { lat: 35.6762, lng: 139.6503 };

/** Build a point within `radiusKm` of `origin`. */
export function buildNearbyPoint(origin: GPSPoint, radiusKm: number): GPSPoint {
  const [lat, lng] = faker.location.nearbyGPSCoordinate({
    origin: [origin.lat, origin.lng],
    radius: radiusKm,
    isMetric: true,
  });
  return { lat, lng };
}

/** Build a delivery request where origin and destination are within range of a hub. */
export function buildLocalDelivery(hub: GPSPoint = LONDON_CENTRE): DeliveryRequest {
  return {
    origin:      buildNearbyPoint(hub, faker.number.float({ min: 0.5, max: 10 })),
    destination: buildNearbyPoint(hub, faker.number.float({ min: 0.5, max: 10 })),
  };
}

/** Build a delivery request guaranteed to be OUTSIDE the coverage radius. */
export function buildOutOfRangeDelivery(hub: GPSPoint, maxRadiusKm: number): DeliveryRequest {
  return {
    origin:      buildNearbyPoint(hub, maxRadiusKm + faker.number.float({ min: 1, max: 50 })),
    destination: buildNearbyPoint(hub, maxRadiusKm + faker.number.float({ min: 1, max: 50 })),
  };
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `nearbyGPSCoordinate` does not guarantee the distance is exactly `radius` — it generates a point *within* the radius. For tests that require a point at exactly the boundary (BVA), compute the boundary point manually using the Haversine formula and pass it as an override.
