### Pattern 309 — Vitest `vi.setSystemTime()` + Factory Clock Injection for Time-Sensitive Domain Logic  [official]

`vi.setSystemTime(date)` (Vitest, using `@vitest/fake-timers`) freezes `Date.now()`, `new Date()`, and `setTimeout` to a stable anchor. Combined with factories that reference `new Date()` for `createdAt`, `expiresAt`, and `scheduledAt` fields, this produces deterministic time-sensitive test data without hardcoded timestamp strings.

**Why it matters:** A factory that writes `createdAt: new Date()` produces a different timestamp on every run — breaking snapshot tests and making relative-time assertions (`'expires in 7 days'`) flaky. Freezing the system time before factory calls gives you stable, deterministic timestamps anchored to a meaningful point (e.g., "2026-01-15T09:00:00Z — start of a test billing cycle").

```typescript
// factories/time-sensitive.factory.ts — factories designed for vi.setSystemTime
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

export interface TrialSubscription {
  id:          string;
  userId:      string;
  trialStart:  Date;          // set to Date.now() at creation
  trialEnd:    Date;          // trialStart + 14 days
  isExpired:   boolean;       // computed: trialEnd < Date.now()
}

// Factory reads new Date() — call vi.setSystemTime() before invoking for stable output
export function buildTrialSubscription(
  overrides: Partial<TrialSubscription> = {}
): TrialSubscription {
  const trialStart = new Date();   // reads the (possibly frozen) system clock
  const trialEnd   = new Date(trialStart.getTime() + 14 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000);
  return {
    id:         faker.string.uuid(),
    userId:     faker.string.uuid(),
    trialStart,
    trialEnd,
    isExpired:  trialEnd < new Date(),
    ...overrides,
  };
}
```

```typescript
// specs/trial-expiry.test.ts — vi.setSystemTime + factory clock injection
import { it, expect, vi, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { buildTrialSubscription } from '../factories/time-sensitive.factory';
import { trialService } from '../services/trial.service';

afterEach(() => vi.useRealTimers());

it('active trial is not expired when created today', () => {
  vi.useFakeTimers();
  vi.setSystemTime(new Date('2026-01-15T09:00:00Z'));

  const sub = buildTrialSubscription();   // trialEnd = 2026-01-29T09:00:00Z
  expect(sub.isExpired).toBe(false);
  expect(trialService.daysRemaining(sub)).toBe(14);
});

it('trial is expired when system clock is past trialEnd', () => {
  vi.useFakeTimers();
  vi.setSystemTime(new Date('2026-01-30T00:00:00Z'));  // 1 day after trial ends

  const sub = buildTrialSubscription();   // trialEnd = 2026-02-13T00:00:00Z... wait
  // Better: build with overridden trialEnd to simulate past expiry
  const expiredSub = buildTrialSubscription({
    trialEnd: new Date('2026-01-29T23:59:59Z'),  // 1 second before current frozen time
  });
  expect(expiredSub.isExpired).toBe(true);
  expect(trialService.daysRemaining(expiredSub)).toBe(0);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `vi.useFakeTimers()` affects `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, and `Date.now()` globally within the test — including any library code that uses timers. Always call `vi.useRealTimers()` in `afterEach`. Use `vi.setSystemTime()` (not `vi.advanceTimersByTime()`) for factory timestamp anchoring — advancing timers also fires pending callbacks, which may be unwanted.

---

### Pattern 310 — `fast-check` `fc.emailAddress()` + `fc.domain()` for Email Validation Property Tests  [official]

`fc.emailAddress()` generates RFC 5322-compliant email addresses; `fc.domain()` generates valid hostnames. Use these arbitraries for property tests on email parsers, normalization functions, and validators — covering edge cases like addresses with subaddressing (`user+tag@domain.com`), international domains, and quoted local parts.

**Why it matters:** Email validators are notoriously buggy at the edges. `fc.emailAddress()` generates addresses that are structurally valid but include unusual forms (`"quoted"@example.com`, `x@subdomain.example.co.uk`) that regex-based validators commonly reject incorrectly.

```typescript
// specs/email-validator.property.test.ts — fc.emailAddress for email validation properties
import { describe, it } from 'vitest';
import fc from 'fast-check';
import { emailValidator }   from '../services/email-validator';
import { normalizeEmail }   from '../utils/email-normalizer';

describe('email validator properties', () => {
  it('accepts all RFC 5322-compliant email addresses generated by fc.emailAddress()', () => {
    fc.assert(
      fc.property(fc.emailAddress(), (email) => {
        const result = emailValidator.validate(email);
        // MUST accept all structurally valid emails — if this fails, validator is too strict
        return result.valid === true;
      }),
      { numRuns: 1000 }
    );
  });

  it('normalized email is always a valid email', () => {
    fc.assert(
      fc.property(fc.emailAddress(), (email) => {
        const normalized = normalizeEmail(email);
        // Invariant: normalizing a valid email must produce another valid email
        return emailValidator.validate(normalized).valid === true;
      }),
      { numRuns: 500 }
    );
  });

  it('email normalization is idempotent', () => {
    fc.assert(
      fc.property(fc.emailAddress(), (email) => {
        // normalize(normalize(x)) === normalize(x)
        return normalizeEmail(normalizeEmail(email)) === normalizeEmail(email);
      }),
      { numRuns: 500 }
    );
  });

  it('domain extractor returns the part after @', () => {
    fc.assert(
      fc.property(
        // Compose: fc.emailAddress() + fc.domain() to test multi-domain scenarios
        fc.record({ email: fc.emailAddress(), domain: fc.domain() }),
        ({ email }) => {
          const extractedDomain = email.split('@')[1];
          return typeof extractedDomain === 'string' && extractedDomain.includes('.');
        }
      )
    );
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `fc.emailAddress()` may generate addresses with quoted local parts (`"foo bar"@example.com`) that some production systems refuse even though they are technically RFC-valid. Constrain with `fc.emailAddress({ local: fc.stringMatching(/^[a-zA-Z0-9._%+-]+$/) })` if your domain only accepts simple local parts.

---

### Pattern 311 — Playwright `page.addLocatorHandler()` for Factory-Seeded Overlay Dismissal  [official]

`page.addLocatorHandler(locator, handler)` (Playwright 1.44+) registers a callback that fires whenever a specified element becomes visible during test execution. Use this to automatically dismiss cookie banners, chat widgets, subscription modals, and other overlays that factory-seeded application state may trigger — preventing them from blocking subsequent assertions.

**Why it matters for test data:** Some overlays only appear when specific factory conditions are met — a cookie consent banner that only shows for new (unseeded) sessions, or a "upgrade your plan" modal that factory data with `subscriptionTier: 'free'` triggers. Without `addLocatorHandler`, these overlays intercept locator interactions mid-test, causing `ElementInterceptedError`.

```typescript
// fixtures/overlay-handler.fixture.ts — addLocatorHandler for factory-triggered overlays
import { test as base, expect } from '@playwright/test';

/** Fixture: automatically dismiss known overlay patterns triggered by factory data. */
export const test = base.extend<{ noOverlays: void }>({
  noOverlays: async ({ page }, use) => {
    // Cookie consent banner — appears for unseeded/anonymous sessions
    await page.addLocatorHandler(
      page.getByRole('dialog', { name: /cookie/i }),
      async (dialog) => {
        await dialog.getByRole('button', { name: /accept|allow all/i }).click();
      }
    );

    // Free-tier upgrade modal — triggered by factory users with subscriptionTier: 'free'
    await page.addLocatorHandler(
      page.getByTestId('upgrade-modal'),
      async (modal) => {
        await modal.getByRole('button', { name: /maybe later|dismiss/i }).click();
      }
    );

    // Onboarding checklist — appears for newly-created factory users (status: 'pending')
    await page.addLocatorHandler(
      page.getByTestId('onboarding-checklist'),
      async (checklist) => {
        await checklist.getByRole('button', { name: /skip|close/i }).click();
      }
    );

    await use();

    // Remove all handlers after the test — prevents handler accumulation on shared pages
    await page.removeAllLocatorHandlers();
  },
});

export { expect };
```

```typescript
// Usage: noOverlays fixture ensures factory-triggered dialogs don't block assertions
import { test, expect } from '../fixtures/overlay-handler.fixture';
import { userFactory } from '../factories/user.factory';

test('free tier user sees dashboard after overlay dismissal', async ({ page, noOverlays }) => {
  const user = await userFactory.create({ subscriptionTier: 'free' });
  await page.goto(`/dashboard?userId=${user.id}`);

  // upgrade-modal is triggered by free-tier factory data — noOverlays dismisses it automatically
  await expect(page.getByTestId('main-dashboard')).toBeVisible();
  await userFactory.cleanup(user.id);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `addLocatorHandler` is page-scoped — it does not fire for overlays on pages opened in new tabs or popup contexts. For suites with popup workflows, register the handler at the `browserContext` level instead (`context.addLocatorHandler()` is available in Playwright 1.52+).

---

### Pattern 312 — `faker.internet.jwt()` for Auth-Token Test Data in Middleware Tests  [official]

`faker.internet.jwt({ header?, payload?, refDate? })` (added in faker v9.2) generates base64url-encoded JWT tokens with a structurally valid header, payload, and signature. The `payload` parameter accepts any object — use it to inject specific claims (`sub`, `role`, `exp`, `iss`) that your middleware extracts and validates.

**Why it matters:** Tests for JWT-parsing middleware need tokens with specific claims. Before `faker.internet.jwt()`, teams either used a real JWT library (`jsonwebtoken.sign()`) or hardcoded base64 strings. The faker approach is lighter (no key management, no library import in tests) and produces claim-specific tokens in one line.

```typescript
// factories/auth.factory.ts — faker.internet.jwt() for middleware test data
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

export interface AuthContext {
  token:   string;
  userId:  string;
  role:    'admin' | 'user' | 'service';
  scopes:  string[];
  exp:     number;    // Unix timestamp
}

const ROLES = ['admin', 'user', 'service'] as const;

export function buildAuthContext(
  overrides: Partial<AuthContext> = {}
): AuthContext {
  const userId = overrides.userId ?? faker.string.uuid();
  const role   = overrides.role   ?? faker.helpers.arrayElement(ROLES);
  const exp    = overrides.exp    ?? Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) + 3600;  // 1h from now
  const scopes = overrides.scopes ?? (role === 'admin' ? ['read', 'write', 'delete'] : ['read']);

  const token = faker.internet.jwt({
    payload: { sub: userId, role, scopes, exp, iss: 'test-issuer' },
  });

  return { token, userId, role, scopes, exp, ...overrides };
}

/** Auth context with an already-expired token — for expiry-rejection tests. */
export function buildExpiredAuthContext(): AuthContext {
  const userId = faker.string.uuid();
  const exp    = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) - 3600;  // 1 hour in the past
  const token  = faker.internet.jwt({
    payload: { sub: userId, role: 'user', exp, iss: 'test-issuer' },
  });
  return { token, userId, role: 'user', scopes: ['read'], exp };
}

/** Auth context with a service-account token — for inter-service auth tests. */
export function buildServiceAuthContext(): AuthContext {
  return buildAuthContext({ role: 'service', scopes: ['internal:read', 'internal:write'] });
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `faker.internet.jwt()` tokens have a dummy signature — they are NOT cryptographically valid. Middleware that calls `jwt.verify()` with a real secret will reject them. This factory is only suitable for tests where the middleware uses `jwt.decode()` (no signature check) or where the JWT verification is mocked. Use `jsonwebtoken.sign()` with a test secret when real verification is required.

---

### Pattern 313 — `fishery` `factory.rewindSequence()` for Deterministic Sequential IDs in Parallel Vitest Workers  [community]

`fishery` factories maintain a module-level sequence counter that increments with each `.build()` or `.create()` call. When Vitest runs test files in parallel workers with `isolate: false` (shared module registry), the counter is shared across files — producing non-deterministic IDs. `factory.rewindSequence()` (fishery v2.3+) resets the counter to 1 in `beforeEach`, restoring per-test determinism.

**Why it matters:** Factories that produce IDs like `user-1`, `user-2` are common for readable test data and snapshot assertions. When the counter bleeds across workers, a snapshot that expects `user-1` receives `user-4` and fails — but only when tests run in a specific parallel order, making the failure impossible to reproduce locally with a single worker.

```typescript
// factories/user.factory.ts — fishery with sequence-based IDs
import { Factory } from 'fishery';
import type { User } from '../domain/user';

export const userFactory = Factory.define<User>(({ sequence }) => ({
  id:               `user-${sequence}`,
  email:            `user-${sequence}@example-test.invalid`,
  name:             `Test User ${sequence}`,
  status:           'active' as const,
  subscriptionTier: 'free'   as const,
  createdAt:        new Date('2024-01-01T00:00:00Z'),
  paymentMethodId:  null,
}));
```

```typescript
// test/setup.ts — rewind sequence before each test to prevent cross-test/cross-worker drift
import { userFactory }    from '../factories/user.factory';
import { orderFactory }   from '../factories/order.factory';
import { productFactory } from '../factories/product.factory';

beforeEach(() => {
  // Reset all sequence counters — ensures test 1 always gets id=1 regardless of worker
  userFactory.rewindSequence();
  orderFactory.rewindSequence();
  productFactory.rewindSequence();
});
```

```typescript
// specs/user-list.test.ts — snapshot test that depends on stable sequence IDs
import { test, expect } from 'vitest';
import { userFactory }  from '../factories/user.factory';

test('user list renders with correct IDs', () => {
  // Without rewindSequence: id varies by worker order — snapshot fails in CI
  // With rewindSequence in beforeEach: always user-1, user-2, user-3
  const users = userFactory.buildList(3);

  expect(users.map(u => u.id)).toStrictEqual(['user-1', 'user-2', 'user-3']);
  expect(users[0]).toMatchInlineSnapshot(`
    {
      "createdAt": 2024-01-01T00:00:00.000Z,
      "email": "user-1@example-test.invalid",
      "id": "user-1",
      "name": "Test User 1",
      "paymentMethodId": null,
      "status": "active",
      "subscriptionTier": "free",
    }
  `);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `rewindSequence()` is a global reset — if a test relies on the sequence continuing from where a previous test left off (intentional cumulative sequencing), the rewind breaks that assumption. Only use `rewindSequence()` in projects where each test is expected to be fully independent of the sequence position. For tests that need a specific starting sequence number, call `factory.rewindSequence(startingAt)` (fishery v2.4+).

## Community Gotcha #186 — `faker.helpers.fromRegExp()` does not support named capture groups — patterns with `(?<name>...)` throw a runtime `SyntaxError` in some V8 versions  [community]

**[community]** `faker.helpers.fromRegExp()` parses regex patterns internally to extract character sets and quantifiers. Named capture group syntax (`(?<name>...)`) is not handled by faker's internal regex parser — on Node.js runtimes backed by V8 versions below 11.4, the parser throws a `SyntaxError: Invalid regular expression`. On newer V8 versions it may silently produce an incorrect string that does not match the original pattern. **WHY: The faker regex parser was written against a simpler subset of regex syntax and the named capture group feature was never added. The runtime JavaScript engine's native `RegExp` object accepts named groups correctly, but faker never delegates to the native engine for generation.** Fix: replace named groups with non-capturing groups `(?:...)` or plain groups `(...)` before passing the pattern to `fromRegExp`. If you need named-group syntax in your domain format documentation, document the pattern separately from the factory.

```typescript
// BROKEN: named capture group causes SyntaxError in faker's regex parser
const id = faker.helpers.fromRegExp(/(?<prefix>[A-Z]{2})(?<digits>\d{6})/);

// CORRECT: replace named groups with non-capturing groups
const id = faker.helpers.fromRegExp(/(?:[A-Z]{2})(?:\d{6})/);
// Or with plain groups (faker ignores capture semantics anyway):
const id = faker.helpers.fromRegExp(/([A-Z]{2})(\d{6})/);
```

---

## Community Gotcha #187 — Vitest `vi.setSystemTime()` does not affect `performance.now()` — factories that compute durations using `performance.now()` produce non-deterministic values even with fake timers active  [community]

**[community]** `vi.useFakeTimers()` and `vi.setSystemTime()` override `Date`, `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, and `Date.now()` — but they do NOT override `performance.now()`. The Web Performance API's high-resolution timer continues to read the real system clock. Factories or services that measure elapsed time using `performance.now() - startTime` (common in analytics, performance budgets, and rate-limiter factories) produce non-deterministic duration values even inside a frozen clock test. **WHY: Vitest's fake timer implementation (based on `@sinonjs/fake-timers`) intentionally does not mock `performance.now()` by default because it requires separate configuration. The oversight is easy to miss because `Date.now()` is frozen and `performance.now()` looks similar.** Fix: pass `{ toFake: ['Date', 'performance'] }` to `vi.useFakeTimers()` to also mock `performance`.

```typescript
// BROKEN: performance.now() is still real even with vi.setSystemTime()
vi.useFakeTimers();
vi.setSystemTime(new Date('2026-01-15T09:00:00Z'));
const start = performance.now();
// ... factory work ...
const elapsed = performance.now() - start;  // real elapsed time, not frozen!

// CORRECT: explicitly include 'performance' in the faked APIs
vi.useFakeTimers({ toFake: ['Date', 'performance', 'setTimeout', 'setInterval'] });
vi.setSystemTime(new Date('2026-01-15T09:00:00Z'));
const start = performance.now();   // now returns 0 (frozen at system time anchor)
```

---

## Community Gotcha #188 — `faker.location.nearbyGPSCoordinate()` can return the exact same coordinates as the origin point when `radius` is very small — proximity assertions that require `distance > 0` fail  [community]

**[community]** `faker.location.nearbyGPSCoordinate()` generates a point within the given radius using floating-point arithmetic. When `radius` is set to a very small value (< 0.01 km), floating-point precision limits cause the generated coordinate to round back to the origin's latitude/longitude — producing a point at distance 0. **WHY: The internal calculation uses `Math.random() * radius * cosine(angle)` which, when `radius * cosine < Number.EPSILON`, rounds to the origin value.** This breaks test assertions like `expect(distance(origin, nearby)).toBeGreaterThan(0)`. Fix: use a minimum radius of at least 0.1 km, or add a post-generation guard that re-generates if the distance is exactly 0.

```typescript
// FRAGILE: tiny radius may produce identical coordinates
const nearby = buildNearbyPoint(LONDON_CENTRE, 0.001);  // may equal LONDON_CENTRE exactly
expect(distance(LONDON_CENTRE, nearby)).toBeGreaterThan(0);  // may fail!

// ROBUST: enforce minimum separation with a retry guard
export function buildNearbyPointNonZero(
  origin: GPSPoint,
  radiusKm: number,
  minKm = 0.1
): GPSPoint {
  let point: GPSPoint;
  let attempts = 0;
  do {
    point = buildNearbyPoint(origin, Math.max(radiusKm, minKm));
    attempts++;
  } while (
    point.lat === origin.lat && point.lng === origin.lng && attempts < 10
  );
  return point;
}
```

## Community Gotcha #189 — `fc.emailAddress()` generates quoted local parts (`"foo bar"@domain`) that are valid per RFC 5322 but rejected by most databases' `TEXT CHECK` constraints and front-end validators  [community]

**[community]** `fc.emailAddress()` follows the RFC 5322 specification which permits quoted local parts: `"john doe"@example.com`, `"a@b"@example.com`. Many applications reject these with validators that only allow unquoted local parts (`/^[a-zA-Z0-9._%+-]+@/`). A property test that uses `fc.emailAddress()` to prove "the validator accepts all valid emails" will fail on quoted-local-part addresses — not because the validator is wrong, but because the validator intentionally restricts to a common subset. **WHY: RFC 5322 and RFC 5321 (SMTP) define a superset of what most production email systems actually accept. A validator that rejects quoted local parts is making a domain-appropriate tradeoff, not a standards violation.** Fix: constrain `fc.emailAddress()` with `{ constraints: { localPart: fc.stringMatching(/^[a-zA-Z0-9._%+-]{1,64}$/) } }` when testing a validator that intentionally excludes quoted forms.

```typescript
// WILL FAIL for quoted-local validators — generates "foo bar"@example.com etc.
fc.assert(fc.property(fc.emailAddress(), (email) => myValidator.isValid(email)));

// CORRECT: constrain to the common unquoted subset your validator actually accepts
const simpleEmailArb = fc.emailAddress({
  localPartArb: fc.stringMatching(/^[a-zA-Z0-9._%+\-]{1,64}$/),
});
fc.assert(fc.property(simpleEmailArb, (email) => myValidator.isValid(email)));
```

## Community Gotcha #190 — `fishery` `factory.buildList(n)` does not call `afterCreate` hooks — factories with DB-side default population (e.g., `RETURNING` triggers) produce different objects from `buildList` vs `createMany`  [community]

**[community]** `fishery`'s `factory.buildList(n)` calls the factory's build function N times and returns the array — it does NOT call `afterCreate` hooks and does NOT persist to a database. When a production schema uses DB triggers or `RETURNING`-clause defaults to populate computed fields (`full_text_search_vector`, `slug`, `display_name`), the built objects lack those fields. **WHY: `buildList` is intentionally a pure in-memory operation. The distinction between build (in-memory) and create (persisted) is fundamental to fishery's design — `afterCreate` only fires on `.create()` / `.createList()`.** Tests that call `buildList` and then assert on computed fields that the DB trigger would fill will fail against a real DB or produce false positives against a stub. Fix: use `createList` for DB-persisted tests; use `buildList` only for pure in-memory/service-layer tests where computed fields are not needed.

```typescript
// WRONG: using buildList for a test that asserts on a DB-computed field
const products = productFactory.buildList(5);
// product.slug is null — the afterCreate hook that calls db.product.create() never ran
expect(products[0].slug).toMatch(/^[a-z-]+$/);  // fails — slug is null

// CORRECT: use createList for DB-persisted tests that need computed fields
const products = await productFactory.createList(5);
// afterCreate ran → slug is populated by the RETURNING clause
expect(products[0].slug).toMatch(/^[a-z-]+$/);  // passes

// CORRECT: use buildList for service-layer unit tests — stub the slug if needed
const products = productFactory.buildList(5, { slug: 'test-product' });
expect(checkoutService.formatTitle(products[0])).toContain('test-product');
```

### Pattern 314 — `faker.commerce.*` Domain Factories for E-Commerce Price, SKU, and Category Test Data  [official]

`faker.commerce` provides `price({ min, max, dec, symbol })`, `productName()`, `productAdjective()`, `productMaterial()`, `department()`, and `isbn()` for building realistic e-commerce domain objects. These generate semantically coherent tuples like `{ name: "Ergonomic Rubber Hat", price: "42.99", department: "Sports" }` that trigger business-rule paths a plain `{ name: "test" }` object never reaches — including currency-format guards, price-range validators, and category-specific shipping logic.

```typescript
// factories/product.factory.ts
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';
import { Factory } from 'fishery';

interface Product {
  id: string;
  sku: string;
  name: string;
  price: number;
  department: string;
  isbn?: string;
}

export const productFactory = Factory.define<Product>(({ sequence }) => ({
  id: faker.string.uuid(),
  sku: `SKU-${faker.string.alphanumeric({ length: 8, casing: 'upper' })}`,
  name: `${faker.commerce.productAdjective()} ${faker.commerce.productMaterial()} ${faker.commerce.product()}`,
  price: parseFloat(faker.commerce.price({ min: 0.99, max: 9999.99, dec: 2 })),
  department: faker.commerce.department(),
  isbn: undefined,
}));

// Trait: book-department products include an ISBN
export const bookProductFactory = productFactory.params({
  department: 'Books',
  isbn: faker.commerce.isbn(),
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `faker.commerce.price()` returns a string — always `parseFloat()` before asserting against numeric comparators. `productName()` concatenates adjective + material + product internally, so combining those manually (as above) gives finer per-field override control at the cost of minor redundancy.

### Pattern 315 — `fc.date()` Arbitrary with `{ min, max }` Bounds for Time-Window Property Tests  [official]

`fc.date({ min: new Date(...), max: new Date(...) })` generates `Date` objects within a constrained range. Combined with `fc.tuple()` and a sort step, this produces ordered date pairs for testing interval logic: booking windows, subscription periods, trial expiry, and SLA deadline calculations. Without bounds, `fc.date()` generates dates across the full JavaScript timestamp range (±8640 billion ms), causing integer overflow in date-arithmetic code that would never see those values in production.

```typescript
// property-tests/booking-window.property.test.ts
import fc from 'fast-check';
import { describe, it } from 'vitest';
import { calculateNights } from '../src/booking';

const nowMs = Date.now();
const thirtyDaysMs = 30 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000;

// Ordered date pair: checkIn always before checkOut, both within next 30 days
const bookingWindowArb = fc
  .tuple(
    fc.date({ min: new Date(nowMs), max: new Date(nowMs + thirtyDaysMs) }),
    fc.date({ min: new Date(nowMs), max: new Date(nowMs + thirtyDaysMs) })
  )
  .map(([a, b]) => (a <= b ? [a, b] : [b, a]) as [Date, Date]);

describe('calculateNights', () => {
  it('always returns a non-negative integer for valid booking windows', () => {
    fc.assert(
      fc.property(bookingWindowArb, ([checkIn, checkOut]) => {
        const nights = calculateNights(checkIn, checkOut);
        return Number.isInteger(nights) && nights >= 0;
      })
    );
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Using `.map()` to sort the tuple discards one degree of freedom — `fc.tuple()` does not natively support `min < max` ordering constraints between elements. Alternatively, use `fc.integer({ min: 0, max: 29 })` twice and construct dates from offsets; this is more explicit but less readable.

### Pattern 316 — MSW `http.post()` + `HttpResponse.json()` with Request Body Inspection for Factory-Seeded Side-Effect Assertions  [official]

MSW handlers can inspect the request body to return context-aware responses and capture the payload for later assertion. This replaces a spy on `fetch` or `axios` — the handler acts as both a mock response source and a call recorder. Factories seed the request payload; the handler captures what was actually sent, enabling "did the factory-built object round-trip correctly through the serialiser?" assertions without a real server.

```typescript
// mocks/handlers/order.handlers.ts
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw';

interface OrderRequest { items: Array<{ sku: string; qty: number }>; total: number }
interface CapturedOrder { body: OrderRequest; capturedAt: Date }

const capturedOrders: CapturedOrder[] = [];
export const getCapturedOrders = () => [...capturedOrders];
export const clearCapturedOrders = () => { capturedOrders.length = 0; };

export const orderHandlers = [
  http.post<never, OrderRequest>('/api/orders', async ({ request }) => {
    const body = await request.json();
    capturedOrders.push({ body, capturedAt: new Date() });

    return HttpResponse.json(
      { id: `ORD-${Date.now()}`, status: 'pending', items: body.items },
      { status: 201 }
    );
  }),
];

// order.test.ts
import { orderFactory } from '../factories/order.factory';
import { getCapturedOrders, clearCapturedOrders } from '../mocks/handlers/order.handlers';

beforeEach(() => clearCapturedOrders());

it('serialises all line-items to the order API', async () => {
  const order = orderFactory.build({ items: [{ sku: 'SKU-ABC123', qty: 3 }] });
  await submitOrder(order);
  const [captured] = getCapturedOrders();
  expect(captured.body.items).toEqual(order.items);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** The capture array is module-level state — `clearCapturedOrders()` must be called in `beforeEach` to prevent cross-test bleed. For parallel Vitest workers, prefer per-worker server instances (`setupFilesAfterEach`) or switch to a Map keyed by a test ID injected as a custom header.

---

### Pattern 317 — Zod `.default()` Chaining in Factory Schemas for Optional-Field Test Data Without `undefined` Noise  [official]

When a Zod schema uses `.default()`, calling `schema.parse({})` returns an object with all defaults applied. Factory builders that construct objects from `schema.parse(overrides)` automatically inherit schema defaults, eliminating the need to manually specify every optional field in every factory variant. This keeps factories and schemas in sync: change the schema default once, all factories update automatically.

```typescript
// schemas/user.schema.ts
import { z } from 'zod';

export const UserSchema = z.object({
  id: z.string().uuid(),
  email: z.string().email(),
  role: z.enum(['admin', 'member', 'viewer']).default('member'),
  preferences: z.object({
    theme: z.enum(['light', 'dark']).default('light'),
    notifications: z.boolean().default(true),
  }).default({}),
  createdAt: z.date().default(() => new Date()),
});

export type User = z.infer<typeof UserSchema>;

// factories/user.factory.ts
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';
import { UserSchema, type User } from '../schemas/user.schema';

export function buildUser(overrides: Partial<User> = {}): User {
  return UserSchema.parse({
    id: faker.string.uuid(),
    email: faker.internet.email(),
    ...overrides,   // caller only needs to provide fields they care about
  });
  // role, preferences, createdAt are filled by Zod defaults
}

// Usage — clean, no undefined noise
const adminUser = buildUser({ role: 'admin' });
const darkThemeUser = buildUser({ preferences: { theme: 'dark', notifications: false } });
```

**Tradeoff:** `schema.parse()` throws `ZodError` on invalid overrides, giving excellent factory misuse feedback. However, `.default()` on nested objects (`.default({})`) evaluates the default once at schema definition time in Zod v3 — if the default object is mutated, all subsequent parses share the mutation. Zod v4 fixes this via `z.defaultLazy(() => ({}))`. Upgrade or use `z.object({}).default(() => ({}))` in Zod v3.

---

### Pattern 318 — `faker.helpers.weightedArrayElement()` for Realistic Distribution of Enum Test Data  [official]

`faker.helpers.weightedArrayElement(weights)` draws from a weighted array, enabling factories to mirror production data distributions. Rather than uniform random selection (which generates equal numbers of `active`, `suspended`, `pending_verification`, and `deactivated` users), factories can reflect a production-like 80% `active` / 15% `pending_verification` / 4% `suspended` / 1% `deactivated` split. This distribution-aware generation catches bugs in dashboards and aggregation queries that only surface when counts are heavily skewed.

```typescript
// factories/account.factory.ts
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';
import { Factory } from 'fishery';

type AccountStatus = 'active' | 'pending_verification' | 'suspended' | 'deactivated';

interface Account {
  id: string;
  email: string;
  status: AccountStatus;
  plan: 'free' | 'pro' | 'enterprise';
}

const statusWeights: Array<{ weight: number; value: AccountStatus }> = [
  { weight: 80, value: 'active' },
  { weight: 15, value: 'pending_verification' },
  { weight: 4,  value: 'suspended' },
  { weight: 1,  value: 'deactivated' },
];

const planWeights = [
  { weight: 60, value: 'free' as const },
  { weight: 30, value: 'pro' as const },
  { weight: 10, value: 'enterprise' as const },
];

export const accountFactory = Factory.define<Account>(() => ({
  id: faker.string.uuid(),
  email: faker.internet.email(),
  status: faker.helpers.weightedArrayElement(statusWeights),
  plan: faker.helpers.weightedArrayElement(planWeights),
}));
```

**Tradeoff:** Weighted distribution makes individual test assertions harder to write — you cannot predict which status a given build call returns. For tests that need a specific status, always pass an explicit override: `accountFactory.build({ status: 'suspended' })`. Reserve `weightedArrayElement` for bulk/list builds that seed dashboards or aggregation tests.

---

### Pattern 319 — Playwright `page.routeFromHAR()` with `update: 'minimal'` for HAR Pruning in CI  [official]

`page.routeFromHAR(harPath, { update: 'minimal' })` in Playwright 1.60+ records only the minimal subset of the HAR needed to replay the test — omitting large response bodies, binary assets, and irrelevant headers. Combined with `update: false` in CI, this produces deterministic replays of complex API sequences without a running backend, while keeping HAR files small enough for version control. The pattern is ideal for test data that is expensive to generate (multi-step OAuth flows, large paginated API responses, third-party enrichment APIs).

```typescript
// e2e/fixtures/har-fixture.ts
import { test as baseTest, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';

const harDir = path.join(__dirname, '../hars');

export const test = baseTest.extend<{ withHar: (name: string) => Promise<void> }>({
  withHar: async ({ page }, use) => {
    await use(async (name: string) => {
      const harPath = path.join(harDir, `${name}.har`);
      const isCI = !!process.env.CI;

      await page.routeFromHAR(harPath, {
        // In CI: replay from HAR (no network); locally: update minimal subset
        update: isCI ? false : 'minimal',
        url: '**/api/**',
        // Fallback to network when HAR has no matching entry (local dev only)
        notFound: isCI ? 'abort' : 'fallthrough',
      });
    });
  },
});

// e2e/checkout.spec.ts
test('completes checkout with mocked payment API', async ({ page, withHar }) => {
  await withHar('checkout-flow');
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.fill('[data-testid="card-number"]', '4242424242424242');
  await page.click('[data-testid="pay-now"]');
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="success-banner"]')).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `update: 'minimal'` only re-records entries whose URL was actually requested during the run — entries for paths not visited in the latest run are preserved. This means stale HAR entries accumulate over time. Periodically run with `update: true` (full re-record) to flush stale entries, then commit the pruned result.

---

### Pattern 320 — `fishery` `afterBuild` Hook for Synchronous Post-Processing Without a Database  [official]

`fishery` v2's `afterBuild` hook (distinct from `afterCreate`) runs after in-memory object construction, before the caller receives the value. This is the right place for computed fields that derive from other factory-built fields — slugs from titles, display names from first/last name, checksums, content hashes — without coupling the factory to a database or async I/O.

```typescript
// factories/article.factory.ts
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';
import { Factory } from 'fishery';

interface Article {
  id: string;
  title: string;
  slug: string;
  authorName: string;
  wordCount: number;
  readingTimeMinutes: number;
}

export const articleFactory = Factory.define<Article>(({ afterBuild }) => {
  afterBuild((article) => {
    // Derived fields computed from other factory fields after build
    article.slug = article.title
      .toLowerCase()
      .replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, '-')
      .replace(/^-|-$/g, '');
    article.readingTimeMinutes = Math.ceil(article.wordCount / 200);
  });

  return {
    id: faker.string.uuid(),
    title: faker.lorem.sentence({ min: 4, max: 8 }),
    slug: '', // populated by afterBuild
    authorName: faker.person.fullName(),
    wordCount: faker.number.int({ min: 300, max: 3000 }),
    readingTimeMinutes: 0, // populated by afterBuild
  };
});

// Override-friendly: providing title explicitly still re-derives slug correctly
const article = articleFactory.build({ title: 'Hello World' });
// article.slug === 'hello-world'
```

**Tradeoff:** `afterBuild` runs synchronously — it cannot await async operations like DB sequence lookups. For async post-processing, use `afterCreate` paired with an async factory function. Also note that if the caller overrides `slug` explicitly, `afterBuild` overwrites it — add an `if (!article.slug)` guard to respect explicit overrides.

---

### Pattern 321 — `fc.record()` with `{ requiredKeys }` for Optional-Field Boundary Testing  [official]

`fc.record(model, { requiredKeys: [...] })` generates objects where only the listed keys are guaranteed present; all other keys from `model` are randomly included or omitted. This makes property tests automatically explore the full space of optional-field combinations — exactly the data shapes that exercise `?.` optional chaining, `?? fallback` null coalescing, and `if (field)` guard branches. A single `fc.record()` call replaces dozens of manually written `buildUser({ middleName: undefined })` variants.

```typescript
// property-tests/user-display.property.test.ts
import fc from 'fast-check';
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { formatUserDisplayName } from '../src/formatters';

const userArb = fc.record(
  {
    firstName: fc.string({ minLength: 1, maxLength: 50 }),
    lastName: fc.string({ minLength: 1, maxLength: 50 }),
    middleName: fc.string({ minLength: 1, maxLength: 50 }),
    preferredName: fc.string({ minLength: 1, maxLength: 50 }),
    title: fc.constantFrom('Mr', 'Mrs', 'Ms', 'Dr', 'Prof'),
  },
  // Only firstName and lastName are required; the rest may be absent
  { requiredKeys: ['firstName', 'lastName'] }
);

describe('formatUserDisplayName', () => {
  it('never throws for any combination of optional name fields', () => {
    fc.assert(
      fc.property(userArb, (user) => {
        expect(() => formatUserDisplayName(user)).not.toThrow();
      })
    );
  });

  it('always includes at least the first name in the output', () => {
    fc.assert(
      fc.property(userArb, (user) => {
        const display = formatUserDisplayName(user);
        expect(display).toContain(user.firstName);
      })
    );
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `fc.record()` with `requiredKeys` generates a combinatorial explosion of shapes — `2^(n_optional)` possible key sets. For objects with many optional fields this produces excellent coverage but can make shrinking slow. Limit optional keys to those your code actually branches on.

---

### Pattern 322 — Vitest `test.each()` with Factory-Built Table Rows for Parameterised Domain Coverage  [official]

`test.each(cases)` paired with factory-built rows decouples parameterised test authorship from data construction. Instead of inlining raw object literals in the table (which diverge from the schema as the model evolves), the table rows are factory-built objects that stay in sync with the domain model. The factory provides valid defaults; the table provides the intent — the field(s) being varied across cases.

```typescript
// src/pricing/pricing.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, test } from 'vitest';
import { subscriptionFactory } from '../factories/subscription.factory';
import { calculateMonthlyInvoice } from './pricing';

// Each row is a factory build — only the fields that drive the pricing variation are overridden
const pricingCases = [
  subscriptionFactory.build({ plan: 'free',       seats: 1,  addOns: [] }),
  subscriptionFactory.build({ plan: 'pro',        seats: 5,  addOns: ['analytics'] }),
  subscriptionFactory.build({ plan: 'pro',        seats: 10, addOns: ['analytics', 'sso'] }),
  subscriptionFactory.build({ plan: 'enterprise', seats: 50, addOns: ['analytics', 'sso', 'audit-log'] }),
] as const;

describe('calculateMonthlyInvoice', () => {
  test.each(pricingCases)(
    'plan=$plan seats=$seats produces a non-negative invoice',
    (subscription) => {
      const invoice = calculateMonthlyInvoice(subscription);
      expect(invoice.totalCents).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(0);
      expect(invoice.lineItems).toHaveLength(1 + subscription.addOns.length);
    }
  );
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `test.each()` with factory objects produces less readable test names than inline literals. Use template literal syntax (`plan=$plan seats=$seats`) to inject relevant discriminating fields into the name. Factory-built rows must be constructed at module scope (not inside `describe`) so they are available during test collection.

---

### Pattern 323 — `faker.helpers.multiple()` with a Factory Callback for Bulk In-Memory List Generation  [official]

`faker.helpers.multiple(fn, { count })` calls a factory callback `count` times and returns the array. This is the idiomatic Faker alternative to `Array.from({ length: n }, fn)` for generating lists without a full `fishery` Factory class. The callback receives the zero-based index, enabling sequential IDs and rank fields without a stateful sequence counter.

```typescript
// factories/leaderboard.factory.ts
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

interface LeaderboardEntry {
  rank: number;
  userId: string;
  username: string;
  score: number;
  country: string;
}

export function buildLeaderboard(count = 10): LeaderboardEntry[] {
  return faker.helpers.multiple(
    (_, index) => ({
      rank: index + 1,
      userId: faker.string.uuid(),
      username: faker.internet.username(),
      score: faker.number.int({ min: 1000, max: 100_000 }),
      country: faker.location.countryCode('alpha-2'),
    }),
    { count }
  );
}

// Usage
const top100 = buildLeaderboard(100);
// Entries are rank-1 to rank-100, each with unique userId, realistic username/score/country
```

**Tradeoff:** `faker.helpers.multiple()` does not guarantee uniqueness across calls — two entries may share a `username` or `score`. For uniqueness, use `faker.helpers.uniqueArray()` or post-process with `new Set()`. The index parameter is only available in Faker v9+ (TypeScript: `(fn: (value: unknown, index: number) => T)`).

---

### Pattern 324 — Drizzle ORM `db.transaction()` Rollback Fixture for Zero-Cleanup Integration Tests  [community]

Wrapping each integration test in a `db.transaction()` that rolls back in teardown gives true data isolation without truncation or re-seeding. The test sees a real Postgres transaction (constraints, triggers, `RETURNING` clauses all fire) while the database is unchanged after every test. This pattern eliminates the "truncate tables in afterEach" antipattern that causes cascade-delete failures and FK-constraint ordering headaches.

```typescript
// fixtures/db-transaction-fixture.ts
import { test as baseTest } from 'vitest';
import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/node-postgres';
import { Pool } from 'pg';
import * as schema from '../db/schema';

type TransactionClient = Parameters<Parameters<ReturnType<typeof drizzle>['transaction']>[0]>[0];

const pool = new Pool({ connectionString: process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL });

export const test = baseTest.extend<{ tx: TransactionClient }>({
  tx: async ({}, use) => {
    const db = drizzle(pool, { schema });
    let rollbackFn!: () => Promise<void>;

    // Open a transaction and yield the tx client to the test
    await db.transaction(async (tx) => {
      rollbackFn = async () => { throw new Error('rollback'); }; // force rollback
      await use(tx);
      // After use() returns the test has completed — throw to roll back
      throw new Error('rollback');
    }).catch((err) => {
      if (err.message !== 'rollback') throw err;
    });
  },
});

// order.integration.test.ts
test('creates an order with correct line items', async ({ tx }) => {
  const user = await tx.insert(schema.users).values({
    id: faker.string.uuid(),
    email: faker.internet.email(),
  }).returning();
  // ... full test using tx ...
  // Rolls back automatically — no cleanup needed
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Savepoint-based rollback works only for tests that do not commit explicitly or spawn external processes that bypass the transaction. It does not work for tests that interact with an external queue, cache, or service that reads/writes outside the transaction boundary. Also, Drizzle's `transaction()` method signature differs from raw `pg` client syntax — check the version-specific API before adopting.

---

### Pattern 325 — `faker.git.*` for Version-Control and Diff Test Data in CI/CD Pipeline Tests  [official]

`faker.git` provides `branch()`, `commitEntry()`, `commitMessage()`, `commitDate()`, `shortSha()`, and `commitSha()` for factories that model version-control events. CI/CD pipeline tests, webhook handler tests, and Git integration tests need realistic commit SHAs, branch names, and commit messages — not `"abc123"` or `"test branch"`. Realistic branch names (`"feature/JIRA-1234-add-oauth"`) trigger regex-based routing rules; realistic commit messages exercise Conventional Commits parsers.

```typescript
// factories/github-webhook.factory.ts
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

interface PushEvent {
  ref: string;
  before: string;
  after: string;
  commits: Array<{ id: string; message: string; author: { name: string; email: string } }>;
  repository: { full_name: string };
}

export function buildGitHubPushEvent(overrides: Partial<PushEvent> = {}): PushEvent {
  const branch = faker.git.branch();
  const commitCount = faker.number.int({ min: 1, max: 5 });

  return {
    ref: `refs/heads/${branch}`,
    before: faker.git.commitSha(),
    after: faker.git.commitSha(),
    commits: faker.helpers.multiple(
      () => ({
        id: faker.git.commitSha(),
        message: faker.git.commitMessage(),
        author: { name: faker.person.fullName(), email: faker.internet.email() },
      }),
      { count: commitCount }
    ),
    repository: { full_name: `${faker.internet.username()}/${faker.lorem.slug(2)}` },
    ...overrides,
  };
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `faker.git.commitMessage()` returns generic messages like `"feat: add new feature"` without Jira ticket numbers or scope suffixes. For Conventional Commits parser tests, augment with `faker.helpers.fromRegExp(/^(feat|fix|chore|docs)\([\w-]{3,12}\): .{10,60}$/)` to generate scope-qualified messages.

### Pattern 326 — `fc.scheduler()` for Concurrency and Race-Condition Property Tests  [official]

`fc.scheduler()` from fast-check generates all possible interleavings of concurrent async operations, exposing race conditions that normal `Promise.all()` tests cannot detect. Each scheduled task is a named async callback; fast-check's scheduler controls execution order across shrinkable interleavings. This is uniquely powerful for testing optimistic UI updates, cache invalidation, and concurrent write de-duplication — scenarios where the ordering of side effects determines correctness.

```typescript
// property-tests/cart.concurrency.property.test.ts
import fc from 'fast-check';
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { buildCart } from '../factories/cart.factory';
import { CartService } from '../src/cart/cart.service';

describe('CartService concurrent item addition', () => {
  it('never double-counts an item regardless of add/remove interleaving', async () => {
    await fc.assert(
      fc.asyncProperty(fc.scheduler(), async (s) => {
        const cart = buildCart();
        const service = new CartService(cart);

        // Schedule concurrent add and remove of the same item
        const addTask = s.scheduleSequence([
          { label: 'add item A', builder: () => service.addItem('ITEM-A', 1) },
          { label: 'add item A again', builder: () => service.addItem('ITEM-A', 1) },
        ]);
        const removeTask = s.schedule(
          Promise.resolve().then(() => service.removeItem('ITEM-A')),
          'remove item A'
        );

        // Let the scheduler run all tasks in an arbitrary order
        await s.waitAll();

        const itemCount = cart.items.filter((i) => i.sku === 'ITEM-A').length;
        expect(itemCount).toBeLessThanOrEqual(1);
      })
    );
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `fc.scheduler()` only controls code that explicitly uses `s.schedule()` or `s.scheduleSequence()`. Async operations inside the SUT that use `setTimeout`, `setImmediate`, or `process.nextTick` internally are not intercepted. Use fake timers (`vi.useFakeTimers()`) alongside the scheduler to bring timer-based async under control.

---

### Pattern 327 — `faker.number.bigInt({ min, max })` for Large-Integer Boundary Test Data  [official]

`faker.number.bigInt({ min, max })` generates `BigInt` values within a specified range, added in Faker v10. This fills a gap in numeric factory coverage: database row IDs using `BIGSERIAL` (values up to ~9.2 × 10^18), financial systems using 64-bit integer amounts in minor currency units, and cryptographic nonce values. Testing with `BigInt` factory data surfaces bugs in JSON serialisation (JSON does not support `BigInt`), ORM type coercion, and arithmetic overflow in payment amount calculations.

```typescript
// factories/transaction.factory.ts
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';
import { Factory } from 'fishery';

interface FinancialTransaction {
  id: bigint;
  amountMinorUnits: bigint;   // e.g., cents: 100 = $1.00
  currencyCode: string;
  createdAt: Date;
}

export const transactionFactory = Factory.define<FinancialTransaction>(() => ({
  id: faker.number.bigInt({ min: 1n, max: 9_223_372_036_854_775_807n }), // max BIGSERIAL
  amountMinorUnits: faker.number.bigInt({ min: 1n, max: 9_999_999_99n }), // max $99,999,999.99
  currencyCode: faker.finance.currencyCode(),
  createdAt: faker.date.recent(),
}));

// Test: JSON serialisation must handle BigInt explicitly
it('serialises transaction without throwing on BigInt', () => {
  const tx = transactionFactory.build();
  // BigInt is not JSON-serialisable by default — must use a replacer
  const serialise = () => JSON.stringify(tx, (_, v) =>
    typeof v === 'bigint' ? v.toString() : v
  );
  expect(serialise).not.toThrow();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `BigInt` literals (`1n`) require TypeScript `"target": "ES2020"` or higher. Passing `BigInt` values to Drizzle or Prisma ORM methods that expect `number` causes silent truncation for values above `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`. Always verify that your ORM layer has explicit `bigint` column mappings before using `BigInt` factory data in integration tests.

### Pattern 328 — MSW `server.boundary()` for Scoped Per-Test Handler Overrides Without Global State  [official]

MSW v2.x `server.boundary(fn)` creates a scoped MSW boundary within which handler overrides are isolated to that scope without affecting the global server state. This replaces the `server.use()` + `server.resetHandlers()` pattern for test-local overrides, eliminating the risk of forgetting a `resetHandlers()` call that bleeds overrides into subsequent tests. Each boundary is a clean override scope.

```typescript
// mocks/server.ts
import { setupServer } from 'msw/node';
import { baseHandlers } from './handlers';
export const server = setupServer(...baseHandlers);

// user-profile.test.ts
import { server } from '../mocks/server';
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw';
import { userFactory } from '../factories/user.factory';

it('renders the error banner when profile fetch fails', async () => {
  // server.boundary() — override only visible within this callback
  await server.boundary(async () => {
    server.use(
      http.get('/api/profile', () =>
        HttpResponse.json({ message: 'Not Found' }, { status: 404 })
      )
    );
    render(<UserProfilePage />);
    expect(await screen.findByRole('alert')).toBeInTheDocument();
  })();
  // Outside the boundary — original handler is restored automatically
});

it('renders the user name on successful fetch', async () => {
  const user = userFactory.build({ name: 'Alice Liddell' });
  // server.boundary() — different override, doesn't see the 404 handler above
  await server.boundary(async () => {
    server.use(http.get('/api/profile', () => HttpResponse.json(user)));
    render(<UserProfilePage />);
    expect(await screen.findByText('Alice Liddell')).toBeInTheDocument();
  })();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `server.boundary()` is available in MSW v2.3+ (`msw@2.3.0`). It does not replace `beforeAll(server.listen)` / `afterAll(server.close)` — those still manage the server lifecycle. Boundaries only scope `server.use()` overrides within their callback. Using boundaries alongside `server.resetHandlers()` in `afterEach` is redundant and can cause double-reset warnings.

## Community Gotcha #191 — `faker.helpers.multiple()` index parameter is `undefined` when using the `(value, index)` signature in Faker v8 and earlier  [community]

**[community]** `faker.helpers.multiple(fn, { count })` added the `(value: unknown, index: number)` callback signature in Faker v9.0. In Faker v8.x and earlier, the callback receives no arguments — `index` is `undefined`. Code that uses the index to build rank-ordered lists or sequential IDs silently produces `NaN` ranks or `undefined`-keyed objects in Faker v8. **WHY: The callback signature was unspecified in the v8 API — `multiple` was designed as a "call this N times" helper with no index intent; the index was added as a convenience feature in v9 after community demand.** Migration: upgrade to Faker v9+ or fall back to `Array.from({ length: count }, (_, i) => fn(i))`.

```typescript
// SILENT BUG in Faker v8: index is undefined → rank becomes NaN
const entries = faker.helpers.multiple((_, index) => ({ rank: index + 1 }), { count: 5 });
// entries[0].rank === NaN (Faker v8)
// entries[0].rank === 1   (Faker v9+)

// Safe across all versions:
const entriesSafe = Array.from({ length: 5 }, (_, i) => ({ rank: i + 1 }));
```

---

## Community Gotcha #192 — Drizzle `db.transaction()` rollback-via-throw pattern causes misleading `"rollback"` errors in test runner output  [community]

**[community]** The Drizzle rollback fixture pattern (Pattern 324) deliberately throws `new Error('rollback')` to force the transaction to abort. If not caught properly in the fixture teardown, this error surfaces in the Vitest output as a test error, not a test pass — even though the test itself succeeded. **WHY: Drizzle's `transaction()` method re-throws any error thrown inside the callback; it does not have a `tx.rollback()` imperative API. The throw-to-rollback idiom is the intended pattern, but requires a `.catch((err) => { if (err.message !== 'rollback') throw err; })` wrapper that is easy to omit.** Always wrap the outer `db.transaction()` call with the error filter or use a helper that encapsulates the pattern.

```typescript
// WRONG: rollback error bubbles up as test failure
await db.transaction(async (tx) => {
  await use(tx);
  throw new Error('rollback');
}); // ← Error: rollback — appears as test failure in Vitest

// CORRECT: filter the sentinel error
await db.transaction(async (tx) => {
  await use(tx);
  throw new Error('rollback');
}).catch((err) => {
  if ((err as Error).message !== 'rollback') throw err;
});
```

---

## Community Gotcha #193 — `fc.scheduler()` does not intercept `setTimeout`/`setInterval` — race conditions in timer-based code are invisible to the scheduler  [community]

**[community]** `fc.scheduler()` controls interleaving of explicitly scheduled Promises using `s.schedule()` / `s.scheduleSequence()`. It has no awareness of `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, or `process.nextTick` — those timers run at their own cadence outside the scheduler's control. Code paths that use `setTimeout(fn, 0)` as a microtask-escape or debounce implementation appear sequential to the scheduler and do not produce interleaving variants. **WHY: The scheduler operates at the Promise resolution layer, not at the event loop timer layer. TC39's Temporal and Node's `timers/promises` equivalents are also out of scope.** Fix: combine `fc.scheduler()` with `vi.useFakeTimers()` and advance timers inside scheduler callbacks to bring timer-based async under scheduler control.

```typescript
// Timer-based debounce is invisible to the scheduler:
// This test will NOT find debounce race conditions
await fc.assert(fc.asyncProperty(fc.scheduler(), async (s) => {
  // debounce internally uses setTimeout — scheduler cannot interleave it
  const result = s.schedule(Promise.resolve(debounce(() => {}, 200)));
  await s.waitAll();
}));

// CORRECT: use fake timers alongside the scheduler
vi.useFakeTimers();
await fc.assert(fc.asyncProperty(fc.scheduler(), async (s) => {
  const task = s.schedule(Promise.resolve().then(() => {
    vi.advanceTimersByTime(300); // flush debounce
    return debounceTarget();
  }));
  await s.waitAll();
}));
vi.useRealTimers();
```

---

## Community Gotcha #194 — `fishery` `afterBuild` silently skips if the factory is called via `.params()` chaining with a full override of the affected field  [community]

**[community]** `fishery`'s `afterBuild` hook runs after the base factory build, before returning to the caller. However, when a `.params()` variant explicitly sets the same field that `afterBuild` computes (e.g., `slug`), `afterBuild` still runs and overwrites the `.params()` value — the caller's intent is silently discarded. **WHY: `afterBuild` runs unconditionally on every build invocation, including those from `.params()` variants. There is no built-in "skip afterBuild if field is already set" mechanism.** Fix: add an explicit guard at the top of the `afterBuild` callback: `if (article.slug) return;` to preserve explicit overrides.

```typescript
// WRONG: afterBuild always overwrites slug, even when caller provided one via .params()
afterBuild((article) => {
  article.slug = article.title.toLowerCase().replace(/\s+/g, '-');
});
const customSlugFactory = articleFactory.params({ slug: 'my-custom-slug' });
const a = customSlugFactory.build();
// a.slug === 'the-title-in-lowercase' — NOT 'my-custom-slug' (silently overwritten)

// CORRECT: guard before computing derived field
afterBuild((article) => {
  if (article.slug) return; // respect explicit overrides
  article.slug = article.title.toLowerCase().replace(/\s+/g, '-');
});
```

---

## Community Gotcha #195 — `faker.number.bigInt()` argument must use `BigInt` literals (`1n`) not `number` literals — passing plain `number` throws a `TypeError` at runtime  [community]

**[community]** `faker.number.bigInt({ min: 1, max: 9999 })` — with plain `number` literals — throws `TypeError: Cannot mix BigInt and other types` at runtime in Faker v10. The `min` and `max` options must be `BigInt` literals (`1n`, `9999n`) or values produced by the `BigInt()` constructor. TypeScript types this correctly (`min?: bigint | number`) but the runtime enforces pure BigInt boundaries. **WHY: JavaScript's BigInt arithmetic operators (`+`, `-`, `*`) do not accept mixed operand types — combining `Number` and `BigInt` in a range calculation inside `faker.number.bigInt()` throws immediately.** Fix: always suffix numeric bounds with `n` when using `faker.number.bigInt()`, or wrap dynamic numeric bounds with `BigInt(myNumber)`.

```typescript
// THROWS at runtime: TypeError: Cannot mix BigInt and other types
const id = faker.number.bigInt({ min: 1, max: 9_223_372_036_854_775_807 });

// CORRECT: use BigInt literals
const id = faker.number.bigInt({ min: 1n, max: 9_223_372_036_854_775_807n });

// CORRECT: wrap dynamic number bounds
const maxId = getMaxIdFromConfig(); // returns a number
const id2 = faker.number.bigInt({ min: 1n, max: BigInt(maxId) });
```
